questions.stem: A surgeon administers lidocaine for local anesthesia during a minor surgical procedure. Shortly afterward, the patient begins exhibiting symptoms suggestive of lidocaine toxicity. The surgeon suspects a possible overdose. Which of the following is an early sign of lidocaine toxicity?

why.B: Convulsions are a later CNS feature, appearing once levels rise further; they mark moderate to severe toxicity, not an early warning.
why.C: Bradycardia, conduction block and arrhythmia are late cardiovascular effects, usually after the CNS signs (bupivacaine can hit the heart earlier).
why.D: Mydriasis is not a recognised feature of lidocaine toxicity; it suggests anticholinergic or sympathomimetic poisoning instead.

questions.right: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity unfolds from CNS excitation to seizures to cardiovascular collapse. The early features are subjective neurological symptoms: circumoral or tongue numbness, metallic taste, lightheadedness and tinnitus . The lead-in asks for an early sign, so tinnitus is the answer.
questions.kc: Lidocaine (LAST) progresses from early sensory symptoms to seizures and then cardiac collapse. Early: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness Then: confusion, muscle twitching, seizures, coma Late: bradycardia, arrhythmia, hypotension, arrest Treatment: stop injection, airway and oxygen, benzodiazepine for seizures, IV lipid emulsion
questions.ep: "Early" means subjective CNS symptoms (tinnitus, perioral numbness); seizures and bradycardia come later.

questions.stem: A surgeon is performing a back lipoma excision under local anesthesia using lidocaine. During the procedure, he suspects that an excessive dose of lidocaine may have been administered. What is the earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity?

why.A: Skin rash points to an allergic reaction, which is rare with amide anesthetics like lidocaine and is not a sign of dose toxicity.
why.B: Bradycardia, hypotension and arrhythmias are late cardiovascular signs that appear after the CNS signs at higher plasma levels.
why.C: Seizures are a later, more severe CNS stage that follows the early sensory symptoms such as tinnitus and perioral numbness.

questions.right: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity starts in the CNS before the heart. The earliest features are subjective: circumoral and tongue numbness, metallic taste, lightheadedness and tinnitus . These come before muscle twitching, then seizures, then CNS depression and finally cardiovascular collapse, so tinnitus is the earliest listed sign.
questions.kc: Lidocaine toxicity progresses in a predictable order. Early: perioral or tongue numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness Then: visual disturbance, slurred speech, muscle twitching Then: seizures Then: coma and respiratory arrest Last: cardiovascular collapse (bradycardia, arrhythmia, arrest) Treatment: stop injecting, airway, benzodiazepine for seizures, IV lipid emulsion
questions.ep: If perioral numbness is an option it competes with tinnitus as the earliest sign; seizures and bradycardia are never the earliest.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of heart disease presents with a small lesion on the ear pinna for 2 months. What is the safest and most appropriate type of anesthesia for excision?

opts.D: Local anesthesia with ropivacaine and adrenaline

why.B: A regional block with levobupivacaine is unnecessary for a small pinna lesion; long acting amides carry more cardiotoxicity than lidocaine if absorbed or injected intravascularly.
why.C: Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic, which matters most in a patient with heart disease, and a regional block is excessive for a small lesion.
why.D: Adrenaline containing solutions are avoided here because of the cardiac history and the pinna's end artery reputation; ropivacaine is a long acting agent better suited to nerve blocks.

questions.right: A small lesion on the ear pinna needs only local infiltration , and plain 1% lidocaine is the safest choice in a patient with heart disease : it has a fast onset, a wide safety margin and is the standard agent for minor skin excisions. Avoiding adrenaline spares a cardiac patient its tachycardia and hypertension, and the pinna is traditionally treated as an end artery site. A regional block or long acting agent adds risk without benefit for a small excision.
questions.kc: Small skin lesion excision = local infiltration with lidocaine; avoid adrenaline at end artery sites and in cardiac patients. Lidocaine: fast onset, standard for minor procedures Adrenaline: prolongs action and reduces bleeding, but avoid in cardiac disease and classic end artery sites (fingers, toes, penis, nose tip, ear) Bupivacaine: long acting, most cardiotoxic Regional blocks: for larger areas or longer procedures
questions.ep: In 'safest' anesthesia questions with heart disease, pick the plain short acting local over anything with adrenaline or bupivacaine.

questions.stem: Female in her 30s underwent carpal tunnel syndrome surgery, when the surgeon applied lidocaine with adrenaline injection she started to have severe Hand pain and numbness & Pallor . What is the most appropriate initial step?

opts.A: Monitor blood pressure and heart rates
opts.C: Assess her hand for signs of ischemia

why.A: Monitoring BP and heart rate checks for systemic adrenaline effects, but her complaint is local hand ischaemia, which needs direct assessment.
why.B: Doppler ultrasound is not needed first; bedside clinical assessment of perfusion comes before imaging.
why.D: IV phentolamine is the tempting distractor: local phentolamine reverses adrenaline vasoconstriction, but it is given after ischaemia is confirmed on examination, and it is infiltrated locally rather than given IV.

questions.right: Severe pain, numbness and pallor after injecting lidocaine with adrenaline suggest adrenaline-induced vasospasm and possible digital or hand ischaemia. The lead-in asks for the initial step, and no examination has been done yet, so the first action is to assess the hand for signs of ischaemia (colour, capillary refill, temperature, pulses) before choosing treatment.
questions.kc: Adrenaline-induced hand or digital ischaemia: assess, then reverse. Step 1: examine colour, capillary refill, temperature, pulses Persistent ischaemia: local phentolamine infiltration Adjuncts: warming, monitor recovery Adrenaline with lidocaine is safe in fingers in most patients, but ischaemia must be recognised
questions.ep: "Initial" step with no examination yet = assess; treatment (phentolamine) comes after.

questions.stem: A woman with follicular thyroid cancer and hypertension controlled with one medication is scheduled for surgery to remove the cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis?

why.A: Cefazolin is the standard prophylactic agent for clean procedures with implants or high- risk patients and for clean-contaminated surgery; uncomplicated thyroidectomy needs none.
why.B: Cefuroxime plus metronidazole covers bowel anaerobes and suits colorectal (clean- contaminated or contaminated) surgery, not a clean neck operation.

questions.right: Thyroidectomy is a clean procedure (no entry into respiratory, alimentary or urinary tracts) with a very low wound infection rate, so routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated. Controlled hypertension on one drug is not a risk factor that changes this.
questions.kc: Surgical prophylaxis follows wound class. Clean (thyroid, hernia repair without mesh): none routinely Clean with prosthesis or high risk: cefazolin Clean-contaminated: single dose within 60 min before incision Colorectal: add anaerobic cover (e.g. metronidazole)
questions.ep: Thyroidectomy = clean surgery = no prophylaxis, unless implant or specific high risk.

questions.stem: 60 year old woman is admitted to the surgical ward for colorectal surgery due to cancer , during preoperative She reports 10% wight loss , loss of appetite and fatigue during the past three months. The dietitian notes inadequate protein and caloric intake. Which one of the following is the most important preoperative nutritional intervention?

why.B: Fluid restriction has no role in correcting malnutrition and risks dehydration before bowel surgery. It applies to fluid overload states such as heart failure or SIADH.
why.C: TPN is for a non-functioning or inaccessible gut (obstruction, short bowel, severe ileus) or when enteral feeding cannot meet needs. It carries line sepsis and refeeding risks that are not justified when she can eat.
why.D: Nasogastric feeding is used when oral intake is inadequate or unsafe (dysphagia, coma, unable to meet targets orally). She can eat, so oral supplementation comes first.

questions.right: She is malnourished (10% weight loss, poor intake) but has a functioning gut and can eat. The first and most important preoperative intervention is oral nutritional support with a high protein diet or oral supplements, ideally for 1 to 2 weeks before surgery. The rule is to use the least invasive route that works: oral, then tube, then parenteral only if the gut cannot be used. The compiler notes this was long debated (TPN was favoured by many), but a high scoring examiner answered oral.
questions.kc: Route of nutrition ladder. Step 1: is the gut functioning? No: parenteral nutrition Gut works and patient can swallow: oral diet plus supplements Gut works but cannot eat, short term (<1 month): nasogastric tube; aspiration risk: nasojejunal Long term (>1 month): gastrostomy; aspiration risk: jejunostomy Severely malnourished starting feeds: watch for refeeding (low K, Mg, phosphate)
questions.ep: If the gut works, use it, and if the mouth works, use that first.

questions.stem: An elder patient going for CRC surgery. Pre operative found out he has 10% weight loss and loss of appetite for 3 months. He is low on carbohydrate and protein. What's next?

why.A: A feeding tube is for a working gut when the patient cannot or will not eat enough orally (dysphagia, coma, aspiration risk); nothing here prevents oral intake.
why.C: TPN is reserved for a non functioning or inaccessible gut (obstruction, ileus, short bowel) and carries line sepsis and refeeding risks; this gut works.
why.D: IV fluids correct volume, not protein energy malnutrition, so they do not address the problem described.

questions.right: This patient is malnourished before major surgery ( 10% weight loss over 3 months , poor appetite, low protein), so he needs preoperative nutritional support. Nothing suggests a non functioning gut or inability to swallow, and the rule is to use the simplest route that works: oral nutritional (protein) supplementation first. Tube feeding or parenteral nutrition comes only if oral intake fails or the gut cannot be used.
questions.kc: Feeding route ladder: if the gut works, use it. Can eat: oral diet plus oral protein supplements Gut works but cannot eat, short term: nasogastric tube (nasojejunal if aspiration risk) Gut works, long term (>1 month): gastrostomy (jejunostomy if aspiration risk) Gut not functioning: parenteral nutrition Severe malnutrition: watch for refeeding (low K, Mg, PO4)
questions.ep: Malnutrition alone does not mean TPN; the deciding question is whether the gut works and the patient can eat.

questions.stem: A 70y old male patient with prostate cancer undergoing robotic surgery. He is known case of hypertension and had a previous stroke. He is on anticoagulant which was stopped 5 days ago . Which of the following enhances safety of the surgery?

opts.C: Check medication cessation and monitor bleeding

why.A: Skipping the team briefing removes a key safety check (identity, procedure, anticoagulation, expected blood loss). The WHO surgical safety checklist requires it.
why.B: Anesthesia is dosed to the patient and procedure, never randomly; random underdosing risks awareness and instability.
why.D: Restarting anticoagulation right before surgery greatly increases bleeding risk. Anticoagulation is resumed after surgery once hemostasis is secure, with bridging only in selected high risk patients.

questions.right: This is a patient safety question. The patient takes an anticoagulant for stroke prevention that was "stopped 5 days ago" before major robotic surgery. Confirming that the drug was actually stopped (and checking coagulation) and monitoring bleeding during and after the operation is the step that directly reduces his risk. It fits the safe surgery checklist logic: verify critical patient factors before starting.
questions.kc: Perioperative anticoagulation and surgical safety. Before surgery: confirm the drug was held for the right number of days and check coagulation if needed Bridging: only for selected very high thrombotic risk patients Restart after surgery once bleeding risk allows WHO checklist: sign in, time out, sign out Team briefing covers anticoagulation, blood loss and allergies
questions.ep: Safety answers verify and monitor; they never skip steps or act at random.

questions.stem: 32 years old male admitted for motor vehicle accident, after initially stabilization and multiple surgical interventions for fractures . He is in post-op care Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measures?

why.A: Prolonged bed rest increases the risk of DVT/PE, atelectasis, pneumonia and pressure ulcers; it is the problem, not the prevention.
why.B: High-dose corticosteroids have no preventive role after orthopedic trauma surgery; they impair wound healing and increase infection risk.
why.D: Empirical 5-day antibiotics are not indicated; surgical prophylaxis is a single dose (or up to 24 hours), and longer courses only promote resistance and C. difficile.

questions.right: A young trauma patient after multiple fracture operations is at high risk of postoperative complications from immobility: DVT and PE, atelectasis and pneumonia, pressure sores and muscle wasting. Of the options, early mobilization and physiotherapy is the preventive measure that addresses these (alongside pharmacological VTE prophylaxis, which is not listed).
questions.kc: Postoperative prevention after major trauma or orthopedic surgery: Early mobilization and physiotherapy VTE prophylaxis: LMWH plus mechanical methods Incentive spirometry, chest physiotherapy (atelectasis) Pressure area care Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis: single dose within 1 hour before incision, not prolonged
questions.ep: If the options include LMWH and the question asks specifically about DVT prevention, pharmacological prophylaxis is the answer.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man was hit by a car 2 hours ago . On examination, his abdomen is distended, tense, and tender . (Blood pressure: 100/70 mmHg; Respiratory rate: 30/min; Oxygen saturation: 90 %; Heart rate: 120/min ; Temperature: 35 °C ) What type of shock is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Spinal (neurogenic) shock gives hypotension with BRADYCARDIA and warm, vasodilated peripheries plus a neurological deficit; this patient is tachycardic with an acute abdomen.
why.B: Cardiogenic shock needs pump failure signs (raised JVP, pulmonary edema, arrhythmia); after trauma it comes from blunt cardiac injury, whereas a distended tense abdomen means bleeding.
why.D: Anaphylactic shock follows an allergen exposure with urticaria, angioedema and bronchospasm, not trauma.

questions.right: A trauma victim with a distended, tense, tender abdomen has intra-abdominal bleeding. Tachycardia (120), tachypnea and hypothermia (35 °C) are features of blood loss, and a still-acceptable BP of 100/70 fits compensated hemorrhage. This is hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock, the commonest shock after trauma.
questions.kc: Shock after trauma: Hemorrhagic: tachycardia, cold, pale, source (abdomen, chest, pelvis, long bones) Neurogenic: hypotension + bradycardia + warm skin + cord injury Obstructive: raised JVP (tension pneumothorax, tamponade) Hypothermia worsens bleeding (lethal triad: hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy)
questions.ep: Hypotension with tachycardia = bleeding; hypotension with bradycardia after trauma = spinal.

questions.stem: Case of patient presented with signs and symptoms of bowel perforation with air under diaphragm and the patient is being prepared for laparotomy, The patient is hypotensive 88/55 Best next action is?

opts.B: IV crystalloid through a peripheral line
opts.C: IV colloid through a central line

why.A: Intubating a hypotensive, under-filled patient can cause cardiovascular collapse, and inotropes do not fix hypovolemia. Vasopressors are added in septic shock only after adequate fluid fails to restore pressure.
why.C: Colloids have no survival advantage over crystalloids and cost more, and a central line takes time and gives slower flow than short, wide peripheral cannulas. A central line fits vasopressor infusion or poor peripheral access.

questions.right: A patient with perforation who is "hypotensive 88/55" while being prepared for laparotomy needs immediate volume resuscitation. The best next action is an isotonic crystalloid bolus through large bore peripheral cannulas, which are faster to place and allow higher flow than a central line. Restoring perfusion before induction also reduces the risk of collapse at anesthesia.
questions.kc: Initial resuscitation of shock before surgery. Two large bore peripheral cannulas First fluid: isotonic crystalloid (Ringer lactate or normal saline) Hemorrhage: blood products early Septic shock not responding to fluid: vasopressor (norepinephrine) Then source control: laparotomy for perforation
questions.ep: Flow depends on cannula length and width: short and wide peripheral beats a long central line.

questions.stem: 59 years old patient came to ED with fever, chills and worsening cough with yellow to greenish phlegm which started 4-5 days before the presentation. The patient is a known case of COPD, DM and OA (knee). On examination respiratory distress and crackles in all lungs fields. GCS 12/15 BP 90/50 Chest X-Ray: hyperinflated lung with lower lobe infiltration and air bronchogram What is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.B: Vasopressor (norepinephrine) is added when hypotension persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation (target MAP ≥65); it is not started before fluids in this picture.
why.C: Blood transfusion has no role without significant anaemia or bleeding; nothing here suggests blood loss.
why.D: Antibiotics are essential and time critical (within 1 hour), but in an exam 'next step' with shock the haemodynamic resuscitation comes first; antibiotics would be the answer for a normotensive pneumonia.

questions.right: This is septic shock from community-acquired pneumonia: fever, purulent sputum, lobar infiltrate with air bronchogram, plus BP 90/50 and GCS 12 (hypoperfusion of the brain). Following ABC priorities, the first action is to restore perfusion with rapid IV crystalloid resuscitation (about 30 mL/kg), while cultures are drawn and antibiotics given within the first hour.
questions.kc: Sepsis hour-1 bundle: Measure lactate, take blood cultures Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4 Vasopressors if still hypotensive after fluids (MAP ≥65)
questions.ep: Pneumonia + hypotension + confusion = septic shock: fluids first, antibiotics in parallel, pressors only if fluids fail.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic hepa88s C and liver cirrhosis presented to Emergency Room with perforated pep;c ulcer that requires urgent laparotomy (see lab results). (Labs: Hb 90 [130-170 g/L male]; Platelets 90 [150-400 × 10⁹/L]; INR 2 [0.8-1.2]; Prothrombin time 17 [10-13 sec]) which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management prior to the procedure?

why.A: Platelet transfusion before major surgery is indicated when the count is below about 50 × 10⁹/L; 90 is adequate.
why.B: Cryoprecipitate supplies fibrinogen, factor VIII and von Willebrand factor; it is right for hypofibrinogenaemia (for example fibrinogen below about 1.5 g/L) or DIC, not for a raised INR.
why.D: Packed red cells correct anaemia and would be given for active bleeding or a low Hb, but they do not correct coagulopathy; Hb 90 is not the priority problem.

questions.right: The cirrhotic patient needs urgent laparotomy and has an INR of 2 and PT 17 from impaired hepatic synthesis of clotting factors. Fresh frozen plasma replaces all coagulation factors and is the product that corrects this coagulopathy before major surgery. As the compiler notes, platelets of 90 do not need transfusion and FFP is preferred over cryoprecipitate here.
questions.kc: Pick the blood product by the abnormal test. High PT/INR (liver disease, factor deficiency): FFP Warfarin reversal with bleeding: vitamin K + PCC (or FFP) Low fibrinogen: cryoprecipitate Platelets <50 before surgery (<100 for neurosurgery): platelets Anaemia: packed RBCs
questions.ep: Raised INR = FFP; platelets only when below 50.

questions.stem: A 45-years old female in 5th day post-hysterectomy the patient have fever, she does not complain of anything and the wound is clean . What is your next step of measurement?

why.A: CBC and blood culture are reasonable if she looks septic or has rigors; with no symptoms they rarely change management and are not the first step here.
why.B: UTI is a common cause of fever around days 3 to 5, but it is almost always accompanied by urinary symptoms; testing an asymptomatic patient yields bacteriuria that may not explain the fever.
why.C: Chest X-ray is for respiratory symptoms (cough, dyspnea, crackles) suggesting pneumonia; she has none.

questions.right: On post-op day 5 she has fever but no complaints at all and a clean wound . Investigations should be guided by symptoms and signs, and with nothing pointing to a site, the compiler's reasoning is to start by reviewing her medications: drug fever (the 'wonder drugs' of the 5 Ws) can occur any time from day 1 to 30 and is a common cause of isolated fever. A positive culture in an asymptomatic patient does not prove the source.
questions.kc: Post-op fever: think 5 Ws by day, but let symptoms choose the test. Day 1: atelectasis (wind) Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, thrombophlebitis, UTI (water) Days 4 to 5: surgical site infection, DVT (wound, walking) Day 6 onward: wound dehiscence, abscess Any day (1 to 30): drug fever ('wonder drugs')
questions.ep: If the stem gives dysuria, cough or a red wound, test that site; truly isolated fever with a clean wound points to medication review.

questions.stem: An elderly diabetic underwent major upper abdominal surgery 72 hours ago . Temperature: 38 °C . Oxygen saturation: 80% . Which of the following is the most likely cause?

why.B: Basal atelectasis is the classic cause of hypoxia and low grade fever in the first 24 hours, especially in a young patient after upper abdominal surgery. By 72 hours with fever it has usually progressed to pneumonia.
why.C: Pulmonary embolism is favored when there is a hypercoagulable profile (cancer, pelvic or orthopedic surgery, immobility) and sudden dyspnea, typically later in the first week. Fever is not its main feature.
why.D: A subphrenic collection usually appears around the end of the first week with swinging fever and abdominal signs. It is too early at 72 hours.

questions.right: Timing and fever decide this one. At "72 hours" after upper abdominal surgery with a temperature of 38 °C and marked hypoxia in an "elderly diabetic", the most likely cause is pneumonia, the usual day 2 to 3 complication when basal atelectasis is not reversed. Upper abdominal incisions splint the diaphragm, and age and diabetes add infection risk.
questions.kc: Postoperative fever and hypoxia by timing. Day 1: atelectasis Days 2 to 3: pneumonia Days 3 to 5: UTI, thrombophlebitis Days 4 to 5: surgical site infection, DVT Day 5 to 7 onwards: anastomotic leak, abscess, PE Young man, upper abdominal surgery, 24 h hypoxia: atelectasis Elderly woman with cancer, pelvic surgery, hypoxia: PE
questions.ep: Same question at 24 hours answers atelectasis; at 72 hours with fever it answers pneumonia.

questions.stem: 40 years old underwent appendectomy postoperative day 4 he developed a fever it's 38.7 C most appropriate next step ?

why.A: Reviewing medication looks for drug fever, which is a diagnosis of exclusion once infective and thrombotic causes are ruled out; it is the right first step in preconception or booking visits of women with chronic disease, not in postoperative fever.

questions.right: A fever of 38.7 on "postoperative day 4" after an appendectomy (a contaminated operation) is approaching the window when surgical site infection becomes the leading cause. The "most appropriate next step" in any postoperative fever is a focused assessment, and after an abdominal operation the first place to look is the surgical site for redness, swelling, tenderness or discharge.
questions.kc: Postoperative fever by timing (the 5 Ws guide the first examination). Wind (days 1 to 2): atelectasis, aspiration, pneumonia Water (days 3 to 5): urinary tract infection Wound (days 5 to 7): surgical site infection Walking (day 5 onward): DVT and PE Day 5 to 10 after abdominal surgery: intra-abdominal collection or anastomotic leak Wonder drugs: drug fever, a diagnosis of exclusion
questions.ep: Fever after abdominal surgery: examine the wound first; drug fever is only considered once infection and thrombosis are excluded.

questions.stem: A female patient underwent a cesarean section . On the 2nd day postoperative (written like this) she got SOB. O2 sat was in the 80s Temp 37.8 celsius (100% sure) Normal HR

why.A: Pneumonia: expect productive cough, higher fever and focal crackles/consolidation, usually from day 3 onward as untreated atelectasis progresses; nothing here points to infection.
why.B: Atelectasis: classic cause of low-grade fever on day 1, typically after UPPER abdominal or thoracic surgery (splinting, poor expansion) in a young man; it rarely drops saturation into the 80s, and a C-section is lower abdominal surgery in a hypercoagulable patient.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: A woman after caesarean section is doubly hypercoagulable (pregnancy/postpartum state plus pelvic surgery), so sudden SOB with O2 sat in the 80s on day 2 is pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise. A normal HR does not exclude PE, since many patients with PE are not tachycardic, and a low-grade temperature (37.8) can accompany PE. The degree of hypoxia is out of proportion to what simple atelectasis usually causes.
questions.kc: Postoperative hypoxia: match the PATIENT and the OPERATION, not just the day. Young man, upper abdominal surgery, mild hypoxia day 1: basal atelectasis Postpartum/pelvic or cancer surgery, sudden marked hypoxia: PE Day 1 fever: atelectasis; days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, thrombophlebitis Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT Normal HR does not rule out PE
questions.ep: Do not let the 'day 2 low-grade fever = atelectasis' rule override a postpartum woman with saturation in the 80s: that is PE.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man underwent abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 8 hours ago . His total urine output since the operation is only 50 mL . What is the most appropriate INITIAL step?

why.A: Dialysis is for established AKI with refractory complications (hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload, uremia); it is never the first response to low urine output.
why.C: Monitoring fluids and electrolytes is part of ongoing care but is not an initial action; it delays fixing a possible blocked catheter.
why.D: Ensuring hydration (fluid challenge) is the next step once the catheter is shown to be patent and the patient is hypovolemic; it comes second.

questions.right: Only 50 mL of urine in 8 hours after AAA repair is post-operative oliguria. The INITIAL step is always to exclude a mechanical cause: check that the Foley catheter is not blocked, kinked or displaced (flush it). This is quick, harmless and avoids treating a 'renal' problem that is really a blocked tube; only then assess volume status and give a fluid challenge.
questions.kc: Post-operative oliguria ladder: Step 1: check / flush the catheter (post-renal, mechanical) Step 2: assess volume status and give a fluid bolus if dry (pre-renal, commonest) Step 3: check urea, creatinine, potassium; review nephrotoxic drugs After aortic surgery: consider renal ischemia (clamp time) as a cause of AKI Dialysis: only for refractory complications
questions.ep: Before treating the kidney, check the tube.

questions.stem: A 60 year old patient known case of prostate cancer presents with an acute urinary retention. Foley catheter insertion failed . What is the next step?

why.A: Retrograde urethrogram is the first test when urethral injury is suspected (pelvic fracture, blood at the meatus), before any catheter; it does not drain the bladder and there is no trauma here.
why.C: TURP (a channel TURP when prostate cancer is the cause) is definitive relief of outflow obstruction once the patient is stable, not emergency decompression of a retained bladder.
why.D: Alpha blockers are the initial medical therapy for BPH symptoms and aid a trial without catheter, but they do not relieve an already distended bladder.

questions.right: Acute urinary retention needs immediate bladder decompression, and the first attempt is a Foley catheter. When urethral catheterization fails (here from an obstructing prostate cancer), the bladder is drained through the abdominal wall with a suprapubic catheter, which bypasses the obstructed prostatic urethra. Definitive treatment of the prostate comes later.
questions.kc: Acute retention: Foley first; if it fails or urethral injury, suprapubic catheter. Retention: Foley catheter plus urine culture Failed Foley (obstructing prostate, stricture): suprapubic catheter Suspected urethral injury: retrograde urethrogram first, no Foley, then suprapubic catheter BPH: alpha blocker initially, TURP definitively Prostate cancer metastasis: bone, especially spine
questions.ep: Retrograde urethrogram belongs to trauma (blood at meatus); in non traumatic failed catheterization go suprapubic.

questions.stem: 41 old male presents with lower abdominal distended after hernia repair under spinal anesthesia , he unable to void ? What is management

why.A: Reassurance only leaves an overdistended bladder untreated, which risks detrusor damage and prolonged retention. It is acceptable only in the first few hours when the patient is comfortable and the bladder is not yet full.
why.B: A bladder scan confirms the residual volume when retention is in doubt (no palpable bladder, obese patient). Here the distended lower abdomen already makes the diagnosis, so scanning would only delay the treatment.
why.C: An IV bolus treats oliguria from hypovolemia, where the bladder is empty. Giving fluid to a patient who cannot empty a full bladder makes the distension worse.

questions.right: Inability to void with a "distended" lower abdomen after hernia repair under "spinal anesthesia" is postoperative acute urinary retention: the spinal block and the groin surgery both impair detrusor function and reflex voiding. The bladder is clinically full, so the treatment is immediate decompression with a urethral catheter, which relieves pain and prevents overdistension injury to the detrusor.
questions.kc: Postoperative urinary retention = catheterize the full bladder. Risk factors: spinal anesthesia, groin or perineal surgery, opioids, older men with BPH Unable to void + distended suprapubic area: urethral (Foley) catheter Uncertain whether bladder is full: bladder scan first Low urine output with empty bladder: think hypovolemia, give fluid Failed urethral catheter: suprapubic catheter
questions.ep: Empty bladder with low output = fluids; full bladder that will not empty = catheter.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with nausea, vomiting, and muscle aches . She is 6 days post-operative and is unable to pass stool, and has abdominal distension (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.B: Urine potassium helps find the cause (renal vs extrarenal loss) once the patient is safe; it does not address the immediate arrhythmia risk.
why.C: Stool potassium has no role in routine assessment of hypokalaemia; GI loss is inferred from history and a low urine potassium.
why.D: Urine osmolality is used to work up hyponatraemia (for example SIADH), not hypokalaemia.

questions.right: Six days post-op with nausea, vomiting, muscle aches , inability to pass stool and abdominal distension (ileus) fits hypokalaemia . The immediate danger of hypokalaemia is cardiac arrhythmia, so the most appropriate next step is an ECG to look for flattened T waves, U waves or arrhythmia, which also dictates how urgently potassium must be replaced.
questions.kc: Electrolyte emergency order: protect the heart first, then find the cause. Hypokalaemia features: weakness, cramps, ileus, flattened T waves, U waves, arrhythmia Post-op causes: vomiting, NG losses, diuretics, inadequate replacement Next: ECG, then replace K (and correct magnesium) Hyperkalaemia: ECG, then calcium gluconate if ECG changes
questions.ep: Any significant potassium disturbance: ECG before the cause hunt.

questions.stem: A post-operative patient who underwent a subtotal colectomy has a nasogastric tube with high suction . Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum potassium level of 2.8 mmol/L. What is the cause of this patient's hypokalemia?

why.A: The NG tube is the trigger, but gastric juice contains only a small amount of potassium; direct loss in the aspirate accounts for a minor part of the deficit. Lower GI losses (diarrhea, fistula) are the ones where the gut itself is the main route of potassium loss.

questions.right: Gastric fluid removed by high NG suction contains little potassium. Loss of HCl causes metabolic alkalosis and volume loss; the volume loss activates aldosterone and the high bicarbonate load delivered to the distal tubule drives potassium secretion into the urine. So most of the potassium deficit is renal potassium wasting , which is why urine potassium is high in these patients.
questions.kc: Vomiting / NG suction: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. H+ and Cl− lost from stomach → alkalosis Volume depletion → aldosterone → distal K+ secretion Bicarbonaturia increases K+ loss in urine Urine K+ high (renal loss); urine Cl− low (saline responsive) Treat with normal saline plus KCl Hypokalemia post op causes ileus; check ECG
questions.ep: Upper GI loss = kidney loses the potassium; lower GI loss (diarrhea) = gut loses it directly, with metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 55-year-old man undergoes elective right hemicolectomy for a stage I (T2N0M0) cancer of the cecum. His postoperative ileus is somewhat prolonged, and on the fifth postoperative day his nasogastric tube is still in place . Physical examination reveals diminished skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension. Pertinent laboratory values are as follows: (ABG: pH 7.56 ; PCO2 50 mm Hg ; PO2 85 mm Hg) (Serum electrolytes mEq/L: Na+ 132; K+ 3.1; Cl− 80; HCO3− 42 ) (Urine electrolytes mEq/L: Na+ 2; K+ 5; Cl− 6) What is the patient’s acid–base abnormality?

opts.E: Mixed respiratory acidosis and respiratory alkalosis

why.A: "Uncompensated" would require a normal PCO2 (about 40); here PCO2 has risen to 50, which is the expected respiratory compensation.
why.B: Respiratory acidosis would give a low pH; this pH is 7.56 (alkalemia), so the raised PCO2 is compensatory, not primary.
why.C: A combined respiratory alkalosis needs a LOW PCO2 (hyperventilation); the PCO2 here is high.
why.E: One patient cannot simultaneously hypoventilate and hyperventilate; a mixed respiratory acidosis and respiratory alkalosis is not a valid combination.

questions.right: Prolonged nasogastric suction removes gastric HCl, giving pH 7.56 with HCO3 42 : a primary metabolic alkalosis. The PCO2 of 50 is the lungs hypoventilating to compensate; the expected PCO2 (about 0.7 × HCO3 + 20) is roughly 49, so the compensation is appropriate. Low urine chloride (6) and sodium (2) confirm volume depletion, so this is a chloride-responsive (saline- responsive) alkalosis.
questions.kc: Read pH first, then which value moved in the same direction, then check compensation. pH > 7.45 with high HCO3: metabolic alkalosis Expected PCO2 in metabolic alkalosis ≈ 0.7 × HCO3 + 20 Measured PCO2 = expected: appropriately compensated; higher: added respiratory acidosis; lower: added respiratory alkalosis Urine Cl low (< 20): vomiting/NG loss, saline responsive Treatment: normal saline plus potassium replacement
questions.ep: A raised PCO2 in an alkalemic patient is compensation, not a second disorder, as long as it matches the expected value.

questions.stem: A 34 years old male underwent surgery after a few days he developed redness and swelling and tenderness . Is the same site of surgery the best next step ?

why.B: Tracheostomy is for prolonged ventilation or upper airway obstruction that cannot be bypassed by intubation; nothing here involves the airway. Even after thyroidectomy, a compressive neck hematoma is managed by opening the wound at the bedside, not by tracheostomy.

questions.right: Redness, swelling and tenderness at the surgical site "a few days" after surgery describe a surgical site infection. Superficial SSI is managed by opening the wound to drain it, followed by dressings (and assessment for deeper infection if the patient does not settle), so opening the wound is the best next step.
questions.kc: Postoperative wound problems. SSI (red, swollen, tender): open the wound, then image for deep infection if needed Wound abscess with pus: incision and drainage Seroma (painless, afebrile serous swelling): explore, leave open, dress Small intra-abdominal collection: antibiotics; 4 x 4 cm or more: percutaneous drainage Neck swelling with stridor after thyroidectomy: open the wound at the bedside
questions.ep: Antibiotics alone do not treat an infected wound with a collection; opening the wound is the key step.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old underwent an open appendectomy for a perforated appendix 8 days ago and returns for follow-up. On examination, there is a seroma formation at the wound site, which is draining freely through a gaping wound . There are no signs of surrounding inflammation . (Vitals: BP 110/70 mmHg; HR 76 /min; RR 18 /min; Temp 36.6 °C) Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

why.A: No fever, no erythema, normal heart rate: there is no infection, so antibiotics are not indicated for a sterile seroma.
why.B: CT is for suspected deep intra-abdominal collection (spiking fever, ileus, tenderness); this is a superficial wound problem in a well patient.
why.D: Image guided drainage is for a closed collection; this one is already decompressing through the open wound.

questions.right: A seroma is a sterile serous collection. Here it is already draining freely through a gaping wound , there is no surrounding inflammation and the vital signs are normal (temperature 36.6). Nothing needs draining and nothing needs antibiotics, so local care with regular wound dressings is all that is required.
questions.kc: Postoperative wound fluid: decide by inflammation and depth. Seroma (no pain, fever or redness): open, irrigate, leave open, regular dressings Wound abscess (redness, pus, fever): incision and drainage Deep collection under 4 x 4 cm: antibiotics Deep collection 4 x 4 cm or more: percutaneous drainage Generalized peritonitis or unstable: laparotomy
questions.ep: Add redness, purulent discharge and fever and the answer flips to open drainage of a wound abscess.

questions.stem: Male patient came with scalp open wound, after 6h assault, what wound management?

why.A: Secondary or delayed closure (wound left open with dressings for several days, then closed once clean) is for heavily contaminated wounds, bites or late presentations; a fresh 6-hour scalp wound does not need it.
why.C: Debridement with healing by granulation suits wounds with tissue loss, infection or gross contamination where edges cannot be apposed, which is not described here.
why.D: Leaving a fresh scalp laceration to granulate gives prolonged bleeding, slow healing and a poor scar; secondary intention is for infected wounds, abscess cavities or pressure ulcers.

questions.right: A scalp laceration seen 6 hours after an assault is a fresh wound within the window for primary closure. The scalp has an excellent blood supply, so it resists infection and heals well; the wound is irrigated and debrided of devitalised tissue and foreign material, then closed primarily, which also controls the brisk scalp bleeding.
questions.kc: Wound closure choice: Fresh, clean or clean-contaminated (face and scalp even several hours later): debridement/irrigation + primary closure Heavily contaminated, bites (except face), late presentation: delayed primary closure Tissue loss, infected cavity: secondary intention (granulation), or VAC Degloving or crush with contamination: debridement, later grafting Always check tetanus status
questions.ep: Face and scalp tolerate later primary closure because of their rich blood supply; a dirty limb wound or a bite would push toward delayed closure.

questions.stem: 59 YO male post colostomy came after 10 days, during examination the wound is 10 cm , clean with healthy granulation tissue , without oozing pus or any discharge What is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.D: Primary closure and Vacuum-assisted wound dressing

why.A: Simple dressing lets the wound heal by secondary intention, which is acceptable for small wounds but very slow for a 10 cm defect. It fits a small or still contaminated wound not yet ready for closure. B. This option was not recalled by the examiner (left blank in the source), so it cannot be judged.
why.C: Antibiotics treat infection: cellulitis, pus or systemic signs. A clean, granulating wound without discharge is not infected.

questions.right: Ten days after surgery the wound is large ("10 cm") but "clean with healthy granulation tissue" and no pus or discharge, so the infection phase is over and it is ready to be closed. Closing it (delayed or secondary closure) and supporting it with vacuum assisted (negative pressure) dressing speeds healing of a large wound that would otherwise take weeks to heal by secondary intention. The recaller is certain option D combined closure and VAC.
questions.kc: Wound management by wound state. Clean fresh laceration: primary closure Contaminated or infected: leave open, debride, dressings Clean granulating wound after the infection settles: delayed primary or secondary closure Large or at risk of non-healing (diabetic foot, pressure sore): VAC Necrotic tissue: debridement first, then closure or graft
questions.ep: Healthy granulation with no discharge means the wound is ready to close, not to be treated.

questions.stem: 35-year-old patient, 16 days post-cesarean section , presents with a fever that is not responding to antipyretics and antibiotics. She had four previous cesareans, and during surgery, extensive adhesions were found. She is passing urine, flatus, and stool . Examination reveals abdominal tenderness (see report). Contrast CT scan confirms the diagnosis of a small bowel fistula . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.B: Restrict intake to a soft diet
opts.D: NPO and start pancreatic and gastric secretion inhibitors

why.A: A colostomy diverts the colon, which does not help a small bowel fistula and adds an unnecessary operation.
why.B: A soft diet keeps stimulating secretions and fistula output; the gut needs rest, not continued oral intake.
why.C: Early resection in a hostile, inflamed abdomen with dense adhesions is dangerous; definitive repair is delayed (often months) for fistulas that fail to close.

questions.right: A small bowel fistula after a difficult repeat cesarean ( extensive adhesions ) in a patient who is passing urine, flatus and stool has no distal obstruction, so most such fistulas close with conservative care. The first step is bowel rest (NPO), drugs that reduce gastric and pancreatic secretions (PPI, somatostatin analogue) to cut fistula output, plus fluid, electrolyte and parenteral nutrition support and control of sepsis.
questions.kc: Enterocutaneous fistula: SNAP before surgery. Sepsis control: drain collections, antibiotics Nutrition: NPO with TPN (enteral if output allows) Anatomy: define the tract with contrast CT or fistulogram Protect skin and plan: reduce output with PPI and octreotide Failure to close (FRIENDS): foreign body, radiation, inflammatory bowel disease or infection, epithelialisation, neoplasm, distal obstruction, short tract or sepsis Definitive surgery only after the abdomen settles (often months)
questions.ep: Passing flatus and stool means no distal obstruction, so the fistula should close conservatively.

questions.stem: A patient had a patch repair of perforated duodenal ulcer presents 3 weeks later with fever, RUQ pain & tenderness . There is decreased breath sounds on the right side & dullness on percussion. The patient is vitally stable. CXR Shows: Basal atelectasis & mild pleural effusion. What's the most appropriate INITIAL investigation?

why.A: CT: the most accurate test overall and the choice for left subphrenic or deep pelvic/interloop collections, or if US is non-diagnostic; for a right-sided collection the initial test is US.
why.C: Laparotomy: for an unstable patient with generalized peritonitis or a collection that cannot be drained percutaneously; never the first investigation in a stable patient.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: Three weeks after repair of a perforated ulcer, fever, RUQ pain and tenderness with a right basal effusion/atelectasis point to a right subphrenic (subhepatic) abscess. The lead-in asks for the INITIAL investigation in a vitally stable patient: ultrasound is quick, bedside, radiation- free and good at seeing the right upper quadrant through the liver window. As the compiler notes, right-sided collections are well seen on US, while left subphrenic collections (gas-filled bowel and stomach in the way) need CT.
questions.kc: Postoperative intra-abdominal abscess: fever 1 to 3 weeks after laparotomy, plus local signs. Right subphrenic/subhepatic: US first Left subphrenic, pelvic, interloop: CT Clue to subphrenic: ipsilateral basal effusion/atelectasis Treatment: image-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics
questions.ep: 'Initial' plus right side means US; if the question says 'best/most accurate' or the collection is left-sided, the answer becomes CT.

questions.stem: Pt present after a MVA with loss of consciousness multiple fracture with severe bleeding and his mouth is FULL of blood Best way to insure patent airway

why.A: Tracheostomy is a slower, more complex surgical airway done electively or semi- electively; it is not the emergency trauma airway.
why.C: Orotracheal intubation is the usual first-line definitive airway, but with the mouth full of blood the cords may be impossible to see and the recall key favours going straight to a surgical airway.
why.D: A nasopharyngeal airway only relieves soft tissue obstruction; it does not protect the lungs from aspirated blood, and it is unsafe if a base of skull fracture is possible.

questions.right: This recall's key is cricothyroidotomy: the patient is unconscious after a crash, so he needs a definitive airway, and his mouth is full of blood , which obscures the view for oral intubation. The compiler, following the trauma teaching, holds that when oral intubation is not feasible a surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy) is the fastest secure route.
questions.kc: Trauma airway: who needs one, and which one. Indications: GCS 8 or less, unconscious, SpO2 below 88%, aspiration risk (blood, vomit) First line: orotracheal intubation with suction and in-line C-spine stabilisation Oral route impossible or failed (massive facial or mandibular injury, blood obscuring view): surgical cricothyroidotomy Tracheostomy: not the emergency route Children under 12: needle cricothyroidotomy instead of surgical
questions.ep: Intubation indication + oral route not possible (facial fractures, blood) = cricothyroidotomy; otherwise orotracheal tube.

questions.stem: Pt present after a MVA with loss of consciousness multiple fracture with severe bleeding and his mouth is FULL of blood which if the following is the Best way to secure the airway

why.A: Tracheostomy is a slower, more complex surgical airway done electively or semi- electively; it is not the emergency trauma airway.
why.C: Orotracheal intubation is the usual first-line definitive airway, but with the mouth full of blood the cords may be impossible to see and the recall key favours going straight to a surgical airway.
why.D: A nasopharyngeal airway only relieves soft tissue obstruction; it does not protect the lungs from aspirated blood, and it is unsafe if a base of skull fracture is possible.

questions.right: This recall's key is cricothyroidotomy: loss of consciousness means a definitive airway is needed, and a mouth FULL of blood makes oral intubation hazardous and the view poor. The compiler, citing trauma (ATLS) teaching, favours a surgical airway when oral intubation is not feasible.
questions.kc: Trauma airway: who needs one, and which one. Indications: GCS 8 or less, unconscious, SpO2 below 88%, aspiration risk (blood, vomit) First line: orotracheal intubation with suction and in-line C-spine stabilisation Oral route impossible or failed (massive facial or mandibular injury, blood obscuring view): surgical cricothyroidotomy Tracheostomy: not the emergency route Children under 12: needle cricothyroidotomy instead of surgical
questions.ep: Intubation indication + oral route not possible (facial fractures, blood) = cricothyroidotomy; otherwise orotracheal tube.

questions.stem: Pt present after a MVA with loss of consciousness multiple fracture with severe bleeding and his mouth is FULL of blood which if the following is the Best way to secure the airway?

why.A: Tracheostomy is too slow for an emergency; it is a planned procedure (or for laryngeal fracture in some cases), not the way to secure a bleeding trauma airway.
why.B: Cricothyroidotomy is the surgical airway when intubation fails or is impossible, classically severe maxillofacial injury (mandibular fracture) with profuse oral bleeding; it is the key in the other versions of this recall.
why.D: A nasopharyngeal airway only keeps the tongue off the pharynx; it does not protect against aspiration of blood and is contraindicated with suspected base of skull fracture.

questions.right: Loss of consciousness and a mouth full of blood (aspiration risk) are clear indications for a definitive airway. This recall's key is endotracheal intubation because orotracheal intubation with suction is the standard first-choice definitive airway in trauma, and the stem as recalled mentions no facial fracture that would make intubation impossible.
questions.kc: Trauma airway ladder: Indications for definitive airway: GCS ≤8, unable to protect airway, aspiration risk (oral bleeding), hypoxia First choice: orotracheal intubation with in-line C- spine stabilization Intubation needed but impossible (severe facial / mandibular injury): cricothyroidotomy Child under about 12: needle cricothyroidotomy rather than surgical Tracheostomy: not an emergency airway
questions.ep: Blood in the mouth alone = intubate; blood plus a smashed face = cricothyroidotomy.

questions.stem: A pt was in motorcycle accident and not wearing a helmet GCS 14 and profuse bleeding from nose and mouth and decreased breath sounds in right hemithorax what is the most appropriate next step?

opts.B: intubation with in line cervical traction

why.A: A chest tube treats the hemothorax or pneumothorax suggested by decreased right breath sounds, but that is the B step. It would be first only if the airway were safe, or needle decompression first if there were signs of tension (hypotension, hyperresonance, tracheal shift).

questions.right: Airway comes before breathing. The "profuse bleeding from nose and mouth" puts the airway at immediate risk of aspiration, which is an indication for definitive airway even though GCS is 14. In an unhelmeted motorcyclist a cervical spine injury must be assumed, so intubation is done with manual in-line stabilization of the neck (the recall's "traction" means this; true axial traction is not used). The right hemithorax is addressed after the airway is secured.
questions.kc: ABCDE order decides the next step in trauma. Intubation indications: GCS ≤8, SpO2 <88%, unconsciousness, risk of aspiration (profuse oral bleeding) Head or neck trauma: assume C- spine injury, in-line stabilization during intubation Needs intubation + major facial injury preventing oral route: cricothyroidotomy Tension pneumothorax + needs intubation: intubate first, then decompress Simple pneumothorax or hemothorax: chest tube after airway
questions.ep: A GCS of 14 does not protect an airway that is filling with blood.

questions.stem: 33-year-old man was involved in a motor vehicle crash. On arrival to the Emergency Department, he was conscious and alert . Examinaon showed an open wound to the anterior surface of the neck with devitalized ssue. (Vitals: BP 100/60 mmHg; HR 104 /min; RR 28 /min; Oxygen saturaon 87% ) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

why.A: An oxygen mask is a temporising measure that does not secure a threatened airway in a hypoxic patient with a penetrating neck wound.
why.B: Tracheostomy is a planned, slower procedure for a prolonged airway; it is not the emergency first choice in the trauma bay.
why.C: Cricothyroidotomy is the rescue when intubation fails or is impossible, for example severe maxillofacial injury; it is not the first line here.

questions.right: Airway comes first in trauma. An open anterior neck wound threatens the airway and the patient is already hypoxic ( SpO2 87% , RR 28), and saturation below 88% is an indication for a definitive airway. Orotracheal (endotracheal) intubation is the first choice for a definitive airway; a surgical airway is kept for failed or impossible intubation.
questions.kc: Trauma airway: definitive airway indications and choice. Indications: SpO2 <88% despite oxygen, GCS ≤8, airway threat (burns, neck wound, expanding hematoma), aspiration risk First choice: orotracheal intubation with cervical spine protection Cannot intubate (major facial trauma, failed attempts): surgical cricothyroidotomy Children under about 12: needle cricothyroidotomy Tracheostomy: elective, not the emergency step
questions.ep: Facial injury that prevents intubation flips the answer to cricothyroidotomy.

questions.stem: A Trauma Patient Who Is Actively Bleeding , His GCS Is 8 , What's Most Appropriate INITIAL Step In Management

why.A: A tourniquet controls catastrophic bleeding from a limb; it is the right first step when exsanguinating limb haemorrhage is the main threat and the airway is protected, or done simultaneously by another team member.

questions.right: The lead-in asks for the INITIAL step and the patient has a GCS of 8 (7 or 8 in other versions). GCS 8 or less means he cannot protect his airway, which is a definite indication for endotracheal intubation. Following the ABC order, securing the airway comes before circulation measures, so intubation is the initial step.
questions.kc: Trauma ABC: airway with C-spine protection first. Intubate: GCS ≤8, unable to protect or maintain the airway, aspiration risk, refractory hypoxia Intubation impossible (severe maxillofacial trauma, failed attempts): surgical cricothyroidotomy Circulation: direct pressure, tourniquet for limbs, pelvic binder, blood products Catastrophic limb bleeding with a second rescuer: tourniquet is applied at the same time as airway care
questions.ep: GCS 8 = intubate; 'initial' follows ABC order.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old unconscious female after a road traffic accident, not wearing a helmet, presents with nasal and oral bleeding , decreased breath sounds on the right side, and hypotension. What is the first step in management?

opts.A: Tube thoracostomy on the right side
opts.B: Endotracheal intubation with cervical spine stabilization
opts.C: Packing for anterior and posterior nosebleed
opts.D: Obtain IV access and start emergency O-negative transfusion

why.A: The decreased right breath sounds (likely hemo/pneumothorax) need a chest tube, but Breathing is addressed after the Airway is secured.
why.C: Nasal packing controls epistaxis but does not protect an unconscious patient's airway from blood aspiration; it is not the first step.
why.D: IV access and O-negative blood treat the hypotension (Circulation), which comes after Airway and Breathing in the ABC sequence, although done in parallel by a team.

questions.right: ATLS priorities are Airway with cervical spine protection first. This patient is unconscious after a road traffic accident without a helmet, with nasal and oral bleeding threatening aspiration, so the airway is not protected. Definitive airway (endotracheal intubation) with in-line cervical stabilization comes before addressing breathing (the right chest finding) or circulation (hypotension).
questions.kc: ATLS order: A (with C-spine) then B then C then D then E. Intubate for: unconscious/GCS ≤ 8, inability to protect airway, profuse oral bleeding or secretions, severe hypoxia Severe facial injury preventing intubation: surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy) Breathing: tension pneumothorax: decompress; hemothorax: chest tube Circulation: two large-bore IV lines, blood, stop bleeding
questions.ep: When several life threats coexist, the one earliest in ABC is the "first step", even if another looks more dramatic.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man brought to ER after a motorcycle accident . He complain of abdominal pain and has suprapubic tenderness. His vital signs are all within normal limits . What is the next best step in management?

why.A: FAST is an adjunct to the primary survey, used mainly in unstable blunt trauma to look for free fluid; it follows, not replaces, initial assessment.
why.C: Contrast CT is the right imaging for a stable patient with abdominal trauma, but only after the primary survey and resuscitation are done.
why.D: Plain abdominal X-ray adds little in blunt abdominal trauma; pelvic X-ray is the useful plain film as a primary-survey adjunct.

questions.right: Every trauma patient starts with the primary survey and resuscitation (ABCDE) before any imaging, regardless of how the vitals look. A normal blood pressure does not exclude significant injury or the need for resuscitation. The lead-in asks for the next best step in a just- arrived motorcycle crash patient, so initial trauma assessment comes before FAST or CT.
questions.kc: Trauma sequence: primary survey first, then imaging by stability. Step 1: ABCDE and resuscitation in every patient Stable blunt abdomen: CT with contrast Unstable blunt: FAST; positive and unstable = laparotomy Unstable stab wound: laparotomy
questions.ep: If "initial assessment/resuscitation" is an option for a fresh trauma arrival, it beats every imaging test, even with normal vitals.

questions.stem: A patient brought by the red crescent following MVA. He is vitally stable . e-FAST was negative . What is the next step? (Type of trauma not mentioned)

why.A: Laparoscopy: used in stable penetrating trauma to assess diaphragm or peritoneal breach (e.g. left thoracoabdominal stab); not a routine step after blunt MVA.
why.C: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage: for an UNSTABLE patient with an equivocal or negative FAST, where the patient cannot go to CT.
why.D: Observation: acceptable for a stable patient with a negative FAST and a low-risk mechanism and reliable serial examination; with a high-energy MVA, injuries must be excluded by CT first.

questions.right: This recall's key is CT because the patient is vitally stable after a motor vehicle accident , a high-energy mechanism. A negative e-FAST does not exclude solid organ, hollow viscus, retroperitoneal or pelvic injury, so a stable patient with a significant mechanism is evaluated with CT, which is the main rule for stable abdominal trauma.
questions.kc: Blunt abdominal trauma algorithm. Unstable, FAST positive: laparotomy Unstable, FAST negative/equivocal: DPL or look for other bleeding source Stable (FAST positive or negative, significant mechanism): CT Stable, negative FAST, low-risk mechanism: observation and serial exams Positive CT findings or peritonitis: laparotomy
questions.ep: Hemodynamics decide first: unstable goes to theatre or DPL, stable goes to CT.

questions.stem: Blunt trauma, stable patient , FAST showed intraperitoneal fluid . What is the next step?

why.B: Exploratory laparotomy is for positive FAST in an UNSTABLE patient, peritonitis, or evisceration; in a stable patient it risks a non-therapeutic operation.
why.C: DPL is for an unstable patient with an equivocal or negative FAST when bleeding into the abdomen must be confirmed; FAST is already positive here.
why.D: Observation alone is for a stable patient with a negative FAST; free fluid needs anatomical characterization first.

questions.right: In blunt abdominal trauma, FAST detects free fluid but not which organ is injured. A stable patient with a positive FAST goes to CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to identify and grade solid organ injury, since many (liver, spleen) are then managed non-operatively. Hemodynamic status, not the FAST result alone, decides laparotomy.
questions.kc: Blunt abdominal trauma algorithm: Stable: CT abdomen Unstable: FAST FAST positive, stable: CT FAST positive, unstable: laparotomy FAST negative, unstable: DPL (look for other bleeding sources) FAST negative, stable: observe, serial exams
questions.ep: Change "stable" to "unstable" with the same positive FAST and the answer becomes laparotomy.

questions.stem: 33 years old had MVA came with sever diffuse lower abdominal pain, his WB were 16 with no other vitals, what you will order for him?

why.A: Diagnostic laparoscopy is reserved for selected stable patients with equivocal findings (for example suspected diaphragmatic injury after penetrating trauma); it is invasive and not the first study after blunt trauma.
why.C: Ultrasound (FAST) is the bedside test for the unstable blunt trauma patient to look for free fluid; it misses hollow viscus, retroperitoneal and many solid organ injuries, so it is not the test of choice in a stable patient. D. Option D was not recalled by the examinee, so it cannot be assessed; the decision here is between CT (stable) and FAST or laparotomy (unstable).

questions.right: After an MVA with "severe diffuse lower abdominal pain" and no instability described, the standard pathway is CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast: in a hemodynamically stable blunt trauma patient it is the most accurate study for solid organ, hollow viscus, mesenteric and pelvic injuries. The raised WBC is a nonspecific stress response. The compiler notes the answer stays CT whether the stem said "next" or "most appropriate", as long as the patient is stable.
questions.kc: Blunt abdominal trauma: stability decides the test. Stable: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast Unstable: FAST Unstable + FAST positive: laparotomy Unstable + FAST negative: DPL or look for another source Laparotomy: peritonitis, evisceration, unstable with positive FAST
questions.ep: If the stem adds hypotension or peritonitis, the answer flips from CT to FAST or laparotomy.

questions.stem: A man brought to ER after a motorcycle accident. He complains of mild abdominal tenderness . His vital signs are all within normal limits . What is the most diagnostic study?

why.A: FAST is the rapid bedside test for free fluid in unstable patients or during the primary survey; it is less sensitive and cannot define the organ or grade the injury.
why.B: Retrograde urography (retrograde pyelography via cystoscopy) images the ureters and collecting system and is not a trauma screening test; if a retrograde urethrogram was meant, that is for suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus, pelvic fracture, high-riding prostate), which nothing in this stem suggests.
why.D: Abdominal X-ray has little role in blunt abdominal trauma; erect films are used to look for free air in a suspected perforation.

questions.right: The patient has "mild abdominal tenderness" after a motorcycle accident and "vital signs all within normal limits". In a hemodynamically stable blunt trauma patient, contrast- enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the most diagnostic study: it grades solid organ injury, shows active bleeding, and detects retroperitoneal and hollow viscus injury. The lead-in "most diagnostic" favours the most accurate test, not the quickest bedside one.
questions.kc: Blunt abdominal trauma imaging: Stable: contrast CT abdomen and pelvis (most diagnostic) Unstable: FAST in the primary survey Unstable + positive FAST: laparotomy Blood at meatus: retrograde urethrogram before catheter A related version asking for the first action is answered by the primary survey and resuscitation (ATLS)
questions.ep: "First thing to do" = ABCDE; "most diagnostic" in a stable patient = contrast CT.

questions.stem: A hemodynamically stable patient presents with a 2 cm penetrating stab wound to the abdomen with minimal bleeding and partially exposed omentum . An abdominal CT scan shows no internal injuries. What is the next step in management?

why.A: Observation alone fits a stable stab wound without peritonitis or evisceration and a negative CT. Visible omentum removes this option.
why.B: Closing the wound over eviscerated omentum ignores the peritoneal breach. Closure is for wounds where exploration shows no fascial or peritoneal penetration.
why.C: Leaving the wound open is a wound care choice for contaminated wounds, not a management of a peritoneal breach with exposed omentum.

questions.right: "Partially exposed omentum" through a stab wound is omental evisceration, which proves the peritoneum is breached and is a classic indication for laparotomy regardless of stability. A normal CT does not overrule evisceration. The compiler notes that the alternative strategy (closing the wound and observing in a stable patient) is not offered as a combined option, so laparotomy remains the answer.
questions.kc: Laparotomy indications in abdominal trauma. Hemodynamic instability with a stab wound Unstable + positive FAST Peritonitis Evisceration (omentum or bowel in the wound) Positive CT findings needing repair Stable, no peritonitis, no evisceration: CT abdomen
questions.ep: Omentum in the wound = laparotomy, even with a clean CT.

questions.stem: An unstable trauma patient has confirmed multiple liver lacerations . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

why.A: Formal right hepatectomy is a long major resection that an unstable, coagulopathic patient cannot tolerate; resection is reserved for when packing fails.
why.C: Selective hepatic artery ligation does not control portal or hepatic venous bleeding from multiple lacerations and risks ischaemia; angioembolisation is the modern adjunct.
why.D: Ligating individual bleeders suits a single accessible bleeding point; with multiple lacerations in a shocked patient it takes too long.

questions.right: An unstable patient with multiple liver lacerations needs damage control surgery. Perihepatic packing compresses diffuse hepatic bleeding quickly, after which the patient is warmed and resuscitated in ICU (correcting hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy) and returned for a relook in 24 to 48 hours.
questions.kc: Liver trauma: stability decides. Stable: non-operative management (CT, observation, angioembolisation if blush) Unstable: laparotomy with perihepatic packing (damage control) Temporary inflow control: Pringle manoeuvre Packing fails: resection or angioembolisation Unstable splenic injury: splenectomy
questions.ep: Unstable + liver = pack, not resect; damage control before definitive repair.

questions.stem: trauma and have extravasation around kidney in the scenario he mentioned patient is hypotensive despite resuscitation but the vitals provided were normal like 100/80 and options were:

why.B: Nephrectomy (via laparotomy) is for the persistently unstable non responder, renal pedicle avulsion or a shattered kidney, or when angioembolization is unavailable or fails; it sacrifices a kidney that might be salvaged.
why.C: CT and observation alone suits a stable patient with low grade injury and no active extravasation; a blush with hypotension needs the bleeding controlled.

questions.right: The CT shows contrast extravasation around the kidney , meaning active arterial bleeding from a renal injury, and the patient is hypotensive or only partially responsive to resuscitation, yet the recalled vitals (about 100/80 ) allow transfer to the angiography suite. Selective angioembolization stops the bleeding vessel while preserving the rest of the kidney, and is the preferred step for active extravasation in a patient who can tolerate it. Most renal injuries are managed non operatively, with embolization as the bridge when there is bleeding.
questions.kc: Renal trauma: stable = non operative; active extravasation = angioembolization; unstable non responder = surgery. Stable abdominal trauma: CT abdomen Stable, no blush: observation, serial Hb, bed rest Contrast blush or extravasation, can go to angio: angioembolization Persistent instability despite resuscitation, pedicle injury: laparotomy, repair or nephrectomy Unstable blunt trauma: FAST first
questions.ep: If the stem stresses a truly unstable non responder with no time for angio, the answer flips to surgery; a measurable BP of 100/80 keeps embolization in play.

questions.stem: A 40-something-year-old woman presents after blunt abdominal trauma . She is initially hypotensive despite resuscitation, but her blood pressure is now 100/80 mmHg and IMPROVED . A CT scan shows contrast extravasation near the left kidney with a perirenal hematoma . What is the most appropriate management?

why.A: Emergent nephrectomy (via laparotomy) is for the patient who stays unstable despite resuscitation or has a shattered kidney or renal pedicle avulsion; this patient has responded.
why.B: Repeat CT months later is follow-up for a managed injury, not a treatment for active extravasation now.
why.D: Catheter and monitoring is conservative care for low grade renal injury without active bleeding; contrast extravasation means ongoing hemorrhage that needs control.

questions.right: After blunt trauma the patient was hypotensive but has responded to resuscitation (now 100/80 and improved), so she is stable enough for CT. CT shows a renal injury with active contrast extravasation and a perirenal hematoma: in a responding patient the standard treatment is angioembolization , which stops the bleeding and preserves the kidney.
questions.kc: Blunt solid organ injury: hemodynamics decide, CT findings refine. Unstable, not responding: laparotomy (FAST positive) or nephrectomy/repair Stable or responder with active contrast blush: angioembolization Stable, no blush, low grade injury: non operative management and observation Stable blunt abdominal trauma: CT abdomen
questions.ep: The word "improved" turns a laparotomy question into an angioembolization question; a non responder goes to theatre.

questions.stem: 28 years old male after gun shot in the upper abdomen with severe Shortness of Breath and absent breath sound in the right , the vitals: BP 69/40 Heart rate 125 RR 30 What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.D: Not correct at all (i think it was CT)

why.A: Chest X-ray delays treatment; a tension pneumothorax or massive hemothorax in a shocked patient is treated on clinical grounds, and imaging is for stable patients.
why.B: FAST looks for abdominal free fluid and is part of the circulation assessment, but breathing (B) is fixed before circulation (C); the absent breath sounds must be decompressed first.
why.D: CT is only for hemodynamically stable patients; taking a patient with BP 69/40 to the scanner is unsafe.

questions.right: A gunshot to the upper abdomen can cross the diaphragm. Severe dyspnea, absent breath sounds on the right and shock ( BP 69/40, HR 125 ) point to a tension pneumothorax or massive hemothorax, both clinical diagnoses. With no needle decompression offered, the chest tube treats both and must come before any imaging.
questions.kc: ATLS order: airway, breathing, circulation; treat life threats as you find them. Tension pneumothorax: needle (or finger) decompression, then chest tube Massive hemothorax: large bore chest tube, thoracotomy if big initial drainage or ongoing loss Simple pneumothorax: chest tube Thoracoabdominal penetrating injury: assume both cavities are involved
questions.ep: Absent breath sounds plus shock means decompress the chest now; if needle decompression is an option and the trachea is shifted with hyperresonance, needle comes first.

questions.stem: 21 years old is involved in a head-on collision as the driver of a motor vehicle. He is note to be severely tachypnea and hypotension . His trachea is deviated to the left , with palpable subcutaneous emphysema and reduced air entry in the right hemithorax . BP: 80/60 . The most appropriate management?

opts.A: Arterial puncture to measure blood gases.

why.A: Arterial blood gas only measures the problem; it delays life-saving decompression in a hypotensive patient.
why.B: Waiting for a chest X-ray is the classic error in tension pneumothorax; the diagnosis is clinical and imaging is done after decompression.
why.C: Intubation is not the fix here, and positive-pressure ventilation can worsen a tension pneumothorax; intubation comes first only when there is a separate airway indication (for example GCS 8 or less), followed straight away by decompression.

questions.right: "Trachea deviated to the left" , "reduced air entry in the right hemithorax" , "severely tachypneic" and "BP 80/60" after blunt chest trauma is tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis. It causes obstructive shock and can kill within minutes, so immediate needle decompression on the right is required, followed by a chest tube.
questions.kc: Tension pneumothorax = clinical diagnosis, treat before imaging. Signs: hypotension, tracheal shift away, absent/reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance, distended neck veins Step 1: needle decompression (or finger thoracostomy) Step 2: chest tube Needs intubation as well: intubate, then decompress immediately Never wait for CXR or ABG
questions.ep: Any option that delays decompression for an X-ray or a blood gas is wrong in an unstable patient.

questions.stem: 25 years old patient with reduced breath sound and tracheal deviation the most appropriate next step ?

why.A: Chest tube is the definitive step that follows decompression, and it is the first step for a simple (non tension) pneumothorax or hemothorax without tracheal shift; inserting it first delays relief in a tension picture.

questions.right: "Reduced breath sound" with "tracheal deviation" is a tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise: air trapped under pressure pushes the trachea and mediastinum away from the affected side. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis treated immediately, and the first step is needle decompression, which converts it into a simple pneumothorax before a chest tube is placed.
questions.kc: Tension pneumothorax: decompress first, drain second. Signs: absent or reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance, trachea shifted to the opposite side, raised JVP, hypotension Step 1: needle decompression (no imaging first) Step 2: chest tube Simple pneumothorax: chest tube directly Massive hemothorax: dull percussion, chest tube
questions.ep: Never order a chest X-ray to confirm a tension pneumothorax; tracheal deviation with reduced breath sounds means decompress now.

questions.stem: Car accident case of man and was transferred by Red Crescent to the hospital. There was no external bleeding. On examination there's reduced air entry to the right chest and resonance on percussion . (See Report) (Vitals: BP 90/40 mm Hg ; O2 sat 70% on room air) What is the next appropriate management?

why.A: Chest tube insertion: definitive treatment and the answer for a simple (non-tension) pneumothorax or haemothorax in a stable patient; in tension it follows needle decompression.
why.C: Pericardiocentesis: for cardiac tamponade (Beck triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) with normal, equal air entry; here breath sounds are reduced on one side.
why.D: Tracheostomy: a planned surgical airway (in emergencies a failed airway is managed by cricothyroidotomy); the airway is not the problem here, the collapsed lung is.

questions.right: After an MVA, reduced air entry with resonance (hyperresonance) on one side, hypotension 90/40 and O2 sat 70% is tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis that must not wait for X-ray. The immediate treatment is needle thoracostomy (decompression) , followed by a chest tube.
questions.kc: Chest trauma with shock: read breath sounds and percussion. Reduced air entry, hyperresonant, hypotension: tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube Reduced air entry, DULL: massive haemothorax: chest tube plus resuscitation Normal air entry, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds: tamponade: pericardiocentesis Needle site in adults (ATLS 10th ed): 4th/5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line
questions.ep: Hyperresonant = air = needle; dull = blood = chest tube.

questions.stem: A Trauma Patient With Shortness Of Breath Chest Pain Distended Neck Veins & Absent Breath Sounds On The Right . Diagnosis?

why.A: Cardiac tamponade also raises the JVP (with hypotension and muffled heart sounds, Beck's triad), but breath sounds are equal on both sides.
why.C: A massive right haemothorax gives absent breath sounds with dullness to percussion, but the neck veins are usually flat from blood loss.

questions.right: After trauma, absent breath sounds on the right together with distended neck veins and dyspnoea means air under tension compressing the mediastinum and obstructing venous return: a right (tension) pneumothorax. Absent unilateral breath sounds localize the problem to that pleural space, and raised JVP separates it from a haemothorax.
questions.kc: Chest trauma: neck veins + breath sounds sort the diagnosis. Raised JVP + absent unilateral breath sounds + hyperresonance: tension pneumothorax Raised JVP + equal breath sounds + hypotension: tamponade Flat veins + absent breath sounds + dullness: massive haemothorax Tension: needle decompression then chest tube (intubate first if indicated)
questions.ep: Distended neck veins with unilateral silence = tension pneumothorax, not haemothorax.

questions.stem: Trauma to axilla and lateral chest wall, fractured 4th and 5th ribs, during examination, suction sound was sourced from a lacerated wound on fractured ribs. What is the most appropriate next step?

why.B: Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax (hypotension, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins, hyperresonance); none of these are described here.
why.C: A chest tube is needed, but only after the wound is sealed; inserting it first leaves the sucking wound open. It is the definitive step, not the next one.
