why.D: Imaging delays treatment of an immediately life-threatening breathing problem identified in the primary survey; it is done after stabilization.

questions.right: A "suction sound" from a chest wall laceration is a sucking chest wound (open pneumothorax). The immediate step is a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides , which acts as a flutter valve: it stops air entering on inspiration but lets air escape on expiration, preventing conversion to tension pneumothorax. A chest tube placed away from the wound follows, then definitive wound closure.
questions.kc: Chest trauma breathing problems are treated clinically, before imaging. Open (sucking) pneumothorax: 3-sided occlusive dressing, then chest tube Tension pneumothorax: needle (or finger) decompression, then chest tube Simple traumatic pneumothorax: chest tube Massive hemothorax: chest tube, thoracotomy if large initial or ongoing drainage Flail chest: analgesia, oxygen, ventilation if hypoxic
questions.ep: Sealing the wound on all four sides can create a tension pneumothorax; three sides is the point.

questions.stem: An RTA presented to ER with shortness of breath. Dullness on percussion of right side. Vitals: BP 95/60 , tachycardia (120), tachypnea , Sp02 89%. What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Pneumothorax gives a hyper resonant percussion note with reduced breath sounds; tension pneumothorax adds tracheal deviation and distended neck veins. Dullness rules it out.
why.B: Pulmonary contusion causes hypoxia that develops over hours with patchy opacities on CXR; it does not produce marked dullness and does not explain hemorrhagic shock.

questions.right: After trauma, "dullness on percussion of right side" means fluid in the pleural space, and blood is the fluid in an RTA. Shock ( "BP 95/60, tachycardia 120" ) with hypoxia ( "SpO2 89%" ) shows a large volume of blood lost into the chest, which is massive hemothorax. Treatment is fluid/blood resuscitation and a large-bore chest tube; massive initial output (classically 1500 mL or more) indicates thoracotomy.
questions.kc: Chest trauma + shock: percussion and neck veins sort the diagnosis. Dull + reduced breath sounds + shock + flat neck veins: massive hemothorax Hyperresonant + tracheal shift + distended neck veins: tension pneumothorax Equal breath sounds + distended neck veins + hypotension: cardiac tamponade (Beck triad) Massive hemothorax: chest tube; thoracotomy if initial drain about 1500 mL or ongoing bleeding
questions.ep: Dull = blood, hyperresonant = air; both cause shock, the percussion note decides.

questions.stem: Hx of trauma (2 days or 1 week), patient presents with dyspnea, physical examination ( decreased breath sounds over the right chest + dullness on percussion ), vitally stable, slight anemia on labs. X-ray: Pleural effusion of the right hemithorax . most appropriate?

why.B: Needle aspiration does not drain clotting blood adequately and cannot monitor ongoing bleeding; needle decompression is used for tension pneumothorax, and diagnostic aspiration for nontraumatic effusions.
why.C: Thoracic surgery referral or thoracotomy is indicated when the initial chest tube drains a large volume (about 1500 ml) or there is continued brisk drainage or instability; it is not the first step in a stable patient.

questions.right: A post-traumatic pleural effusion with dyspnea, "dullness on percussion" and "slight anemia" is a hemothorax until proven otherwise. A hemothorax visible on chest X-ray needs a large-bore chest tube (tube thoracostomy) to evacuate the blood, re-expand the lung, measure ongoing bleeding and prevent a retained clot or empyema. The patient is "vitally stable", so drainage rather than immediate surgery is appropriate.
questions.kc: Traumatic hemothorax pathway: Dullness + low breath sounds after trauma: hemothorax Seen on CXR: large-bore chest tube Thoracotomy: initial output ~1500 ml, ongoing about 200 ml per hour for 2 to 4 hours, or instability Retained clot after tube: VATS evacuation Hyperresonance + hypotension: needle decompression then chest tube
questions.ep: Needle first only for tension pneumothorax; blood in the chest always gets a tube.

questions.stem: A patient (around 30-40) came to the ER after MVA with no initial SOB or respiratory distress. After an hour , the patient developed respiratory distress. Initial CXR showed 3-7 rib fractures with no hemothorax or pneumothorax . A repeated CXR shows right lung infiltration . What is the most probable diagnosis?

why.A: Flail chest is a clinical diagnosis: two or more ribs fractured in two or more places with a segment moving paradoxically; it would cause distress from the start and is not defined by a new infiltrate. Contusion often accompanies flail chest, but the finding asked about here is the infiltrate.

questions.right: After blunt chest trauma with rib fractures, the patient was initially comfortable, then developed respiratory distress after an hour , and the repeat CXR shows a new lung infiltrate with no pneumothorax or hemothorax. A delayed, evolving opacity that was not on the first film is the hallmark of pulmonary contusion (alveolar hemorrhage and edema that blossoms over hours).
questions.kc: Blunt chest trauma, delayed findings: Pulmonary contusion: hypoxia and infiltrate developing over hours, not respecting lobar boundaries Flail chest: paradoxical segment, treat with analgesia, oxygen, ventilation if hypoxic Tension pneumothorax: absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, raised JVP, hypotension Hemothorax: dullness, fluid on CXR; thoracotomy if over 1500 ml initially Contusion management: oxygen, analgesia, avoid fluid overload
questions.ep: If the stem describes paradoxical chest wall movement, the answer becomes flail chest even with an infiltrate.

questions.stem: A Patient Post MVA Presented With Paradoxical Chest Movement And Crepitus After A Motor Vehicle Accident. He Is Hypotensive . What Is The Likely Diagnosis?

why.A: Pneumothorax gives reduced breath sounds and hyperresonance (tension adds tracheal shift, raised JVP and hypotension); it does not cause paradoxical movement of a chest wall segment.
why.C: Pulmonary contusion is the lung injury that usually lies under a flail segment and causes hypoxia hours later; it has no external sign such as paradoxical movement.
why.D: Hemothorax gives dullness to percussion, reduced breath sounds and shock; it would be the answer if dullness, not paradoxical movement, were the clue.

questions.right: Paradoxical chest movement is the defining sign of flail chest: a segment of chest wall with two or more adjacent ribs each fractured in two or more places moves inward on inspiration. Crepitus from the rib fractures supports it. Hypotension does not change the diagnosis; it reflects associated injury or blood loss and prompts a search for hemothorax or other bleeding.
questions.kc: Chest trauma: match the sign to the injury. Paradoxical movement + rib crepitus: flail chest Hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal shift, raised JVP: tension pneumothorax Dullness + shock: massive hemothorax Raised JVP, muffled heart sounds, equal breath sounds: tamponade Flail chest treatment: analgesia, oxygen, ventilation if needed
questions.ep: The real danger in flail chest is the underlying pulmonary contusion, not the loose segment itself.

questions.stem: A 25 years old presented to the ER after MVA. He is setting well not in any distress an initial X-ray was taken and only showed T3-T7 rib fractures no pneumothorax or hemothorax (literally written) after 2 hours he experienced difficulty breathing and a second CXR was taken which showed a distinct right lung infiltration . Which of the following is the diagnosis?

why.A: Pulmonary embolism after trauma usually occurs days later from DVT, and the CXR is typically clear or nonspecific rather than showing a new infiltrate at 2 hours.
why.C: Tamponade presents with hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds (Beck triad), not a lung infiltrate.
why.D: Flail chest is a clinical diagnosis of paradoxical chest wall movement from ≥3 ribs each broken in ≥2 places; it often coexists with contusion but is not what a new parenchymal infiltrate represents.

questions.right: Multiple rib fractures (T3 to T7) without pneumothorax or hemothorax, followed "after 2 hours" by difficulty breathing and a new "distinct right lung infiltration", is pulmonary contusion. Contusion is bruising of the lung parenchyma with alveolar hemorrhage and edema; it typically appears or enlarges on CXR within the first hours after blunt chest trauma and is not limited to anatomic lobes or segments.
questions.kc: Chest trauma keywords: Infiltrate within hours of blunt trauma, not following lobes: lung contusion Paradoxical segment: flail chest Hyperresonance, tracheal shift, hypotension: tension pneumothorax Dullness, low breath sounds: hemothorax Raised JVP, hypotension, equal air entry: tamponade Days later with hypoxia and clear CXR: think PE or fat embolism
questions.ep: Same rib fractures, but new opacity within hours = contusion; paradoxical movement = flail.

questions.stem: A 20 years old patient presents after trauma (tennis-related accident) complaining of pain and SOB. He is conscious and Alert, with normal breath sounds . Chest X-ray shows multiple rib fractures (ribs 3,4,5,6) and a lung contusion . What is the next best step?

why.B: Surgical rib fixation is considered for selected flail chest or severely displaced fractures, usually after failed conservative care or failure to wean from the ventilator, not as a first step.
why.C: Intubation is for respiratory failure (hypoxia despite oxygen, exhaustion, reduced consciousness); prophylactic intubation for contusion increases complications.
why.D: A chest tube treats a pneumothorax or hemothorax; normal breath sounds and no pleural collection on X-ray mean there is no indication.

questions.right: This patient has multiple rib fractures and a lung contusion but is "conscious and alert, with normal breath sounds", with no hypoxia or respiratory failure described. Pain from rib fractures causes splinting and poor cough, which worsens the contusion, so effective analgesia (IV, often multimodal or regional) with oxygen and physiotherapy is the next step. As the compiler notes (EAST guidelines), intubation is avoided unless respiratory failure develops despite analgesia and noninvasive support.
questions.kc: Rib fractures and contusion: analgesia first. Analgesia: IV multimodal, consider epidural or nerve blocks for multiple fractures Plus oxygen, incentive spirometry, physiotherapy, judicious fluids Hypoxia despite this: noninvasive ventilation, then intubation if failing Pneumothorax or hemothorax: chest tube Rib fixation: selected flail or failure to wean
questions.ep: Add SpO2 84% or paradoxical movement with hypoxia, and the answer moves to assisted ventilation.

questions.stem: Following a head-on motor vehicle collision, a 21-year-old unrestrained passenger presents to ER with dyspnea and respiratory distress. She is intubated and physical examination reveals subcutaneous emphysema and decreased breath sounds. Chest x-ray reveals cervical emphysema, pneumomediastinum , and a right-sided pneumothorax. What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Tension pneumothorax adds hypotension, distended neck veins and tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and would be treated clinically before a CXR; it does not explain the pneumomediastinum and cervical emphysema.
why.B: Open pneumothorax requires an open chest wall wound (sucking chest wound); none is described after this blunt injury.
why.D: Pulmonary contusion shows patchy alveolar opacities with gradually worsening hypoxia; it does not cause pneumomediastinum or extensive cervical emphysema.

questions.right: A high-energy deceleration injury ( "head-on collision, unrestrained" ) with a pneumothorax plus extensive air tracking into the neck and mediastinum ( "cervical emphysema, pneumomediastinum" , "subcutaneous emphysema" ) means air is leaking from a central airway. This combination points to tracheobronchial injury rather than a simple lung or pleural injury. A large persistent air leak and failure of the lung to re-expand after a chest tube confirm it; diagnosis is by bronchoscopy.
questions.kc: Pneumothorax + pneumomediastinum + extensive subcutaneous/cervical emphysema after blunt trauma = tracheobronchial injury. Clue: persistent large air leak after chest tube, lung fails to re-expand Diagnosis: bronchoscopy Tension pneumothorax: hypotension + raised JVP + tracheal shift Open pneumothorax: chest wall defect, 3-sided dressing then chest tube Pneumomediastinum after vomiting (not trauma): think Boerhaave
questions.ep: Decreased breath sounds and pneumothorax are shared distractors; mediastinal and cervical air is the clue that points to the airway.

questions.stem: A 32 years old female presented with severe pelvic pain after MVA. CT showed multiple pelvic injury with severe hematoma Bp 88/55 What Is Most Appropriate management?

why.A: Bed rest and analgesia is for a stable, isolated, minor pelvic fracture; this patient is in shock.
why.B: Emergency laparotomy is for intraperitoneal bleeding (positive FAST in an unstable patient); pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal and laparotomy can release tamponade and worsen it.
why.C: IV fluid and observation underestimates the shock; aggressive crystalloid dilutes clotting factors, and a hypotensive patient with pelvic hematoma needs blood, not watching.

questions.right: A pelvic fracture with a large hematoma and BP 88/55 is hemorrhagic shock from a pelvic (retroperitoneal) bleed. The priority is damage-control resuscitation with blood products (balanced transfusion) rather than large volumes of crystalloid. As the compiler notes, pelvic binder and angio-embolization were not offered; among the listed options, transfusing blood is the most appropriate step.
questions.kc: Unstable pelvic fracture ladder: ABCDE + early blood products (massive transfusion protocol) Pelvic binder to close the pelvic volume Angio-embolization (arterial) or preperitoneal packing / external fixation Laparotomy only if FAST shows intraperitoneal blood Blood at meatus: retrograde urethrogram before catheter
questions.ep: If 'pelvic binder' or 'angio-embolization' is offered, it competes strongly with transfusion as the answer.

questions.stem: patient after RTA with pelvic instability and hypotensive , asking about initial?

why.A: Laparotomy does not control retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding and opening the abdomen can release the tamponade. It is for an unstable patient with intraperitoneal bleeding (positive FAST) or a penetrating wound.
why.B: Transfusion is needed, but replacing blood while the source keeps bleeding is not the initial priority. It is the answer when the question asks about resuscitation of shock once the source is controlled or with no mechanical option offered.

questions.right: "Pelvic instability" with "hypotension" after an RTA means hemorrhagic shock from a pelvic fracture, mostly venous bleeding from the pelvic plexus. The initial step is to stop the bleeding by closing the pelvic volume with a pelvic binder, which tamponades the bleeding and is applied as part of circulation control while resuscitation runs in parallel.
questions.kc: Bleeding control comes before volume replacement in trauma. External bleeding: direct pressure Unstable pelvic fracture: pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters Persistent instability after binder: preperitoneal packing or angioembolization Unstable + positive FAST: laparotomy Unstable stab wound abdomen: laparotomy
questions.ep: Pelvic bleed = binder first; laparotomy is for the abdomen, not the pelvis.

questions.stem: A young male presents after a motorcycle trauma. On examination ,there is blood at the urethral meatus . Pelvic X-ray reveals a pelvic fracture . His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. What is the initial investigation?

why.A: MRI pelvis is slow, unsuitable in acute trauma and not the test for urethral integrity; it may be used later to plan delayed urethral reconstruction.
why.B: CT (incompletely recalled) is excellent for pelvic and visceral injury and bleeding, but it does not reliably assess the urethra; RUG remains the test for suspected urethral injury.
why.C: Pelvic angiography (with embolisation) is for ongoing pelvic arterial bleeding in an unstable patient; this patient is stable and the question is the urethra.

questions.right: Blood at the urethral meatus with a pelvic fracture means urethral injury until proven otherwise. A retrograde urethrogram must be done first, before any catheter, to show the injury. The patient is haemodynamically acceptable (BP 110/70), so there is time for this targeted study.
questions.kc: Suspected urethral injury: image before you catheterise. Clues: blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal or scrotal haematoma, inability to void Test: retrograde urethrogram Confirmed injury: suprapubic catheter (no Foley) Definitive repair: delayed urethroplasty Most commonly injured with pelvic fracture: membranous (posterior) urethra
questions.ep: Blood at meatus = no Foley; RUG first, then suprapubic catheter if injured.

questions.stem: A young male presents after a motorcycle trauma. On examination, there is blood at the urethral meatus . Pelvic X-ray reveals a pelvic fracture . His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. What is the initial investigation?

opts.B: CT ... (Not Sure If It Was CT Contrast Or Other Type Of CT)

why.A: MRI pelvis has no place in acute trauma assessment; it is slow and used later, for example to plan urethral reconstruction.
why.B: CT (with contrast) stages pelvic and abdominal injuries in a stable trauma patient but does not reliably show a urethral tear; some versions with CT contrast have no confirmed key.
why.C: Pelvic angiography with embolization is for a pelvic fracture with ongoing hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability; this patient is stable and the clue is urethral.

questions.right: Blood at the urethral meatus with a pelvic fracture in a young male means a posterior (membranous) urethral injury until proven otherwise. A Foley catheter must not be passed blindly, so the retrograde urethrogram is the initial investigation to show whether the urethra is intact. The patient is stable ( BP 110/70 ), so there is time for it.
questions.kc: Blood at meatus after pelvic trauma: image the urethra before any catheter. Other clues: high riding prostate on DRE, perineal or scrotal hematoma, inability to void Retrograde urethrogram first Urethral injury confirmed: suprapubic catheter (no Foley) Membranous urethra: commonest site with pelvic fracture Unstable pelvic fracture: binder, then angioembolization or packing
questions.ep: "Next step after the RUG shows a tear" is suprapubic catheter; inserting a Foley is the classic wrong answer.

questions.stem: A young male presents after a motorcycle trauma. On examination, there is blood at the urethral meatus . Pelvic X-ray reveals a pelvic fracture . His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. What is the initial investigation?

why.A: MRI has no role in acute trauma assessment; it is used later to plan delayed urethroplasty.
why.B: Contrast CT is used to evaluate a stable trauma patient's abdomen and pelvis overall, but it does not reliably image the urethra; the specific test for the meatal blood question is the urethrogram (the compiler notes a version featuring CT contrast has no confirmed answer).
why.C: Pelvic angiography with embolization is for an unstable patient with ongoing pelvic arterial bleeding; this patient is normotensive.

questions.right: Blood at the urethral meatus with a pelvic fracture means posterior (membranous) urethral injury until proven otherwise. Before any urethral catheter is passed, a retrograde urethrogram is the initial investigation to confirm or exclude urethral disruption. The patient is stable (BP 110/70), so there is time for it; if injury is shown, a suprapubic catheter drains the bladder.
questions.kc: Suspected urethral injury: urethrogram before catheter. Signs: blood at meatus, inability to void, perineal/scrotal hematoma, high-riding prostate Most commonly injured with pelvic fracture: membranous (posterior) urethra Straddle injury: bulbar (anterior) urethra Investigation: retrograde urethrogram Injury confirmed: suprapubic catheter, never a Foley
questions.ep: If the lead-in asks for the next step after a urethrogram shows disruption, the answer becomes suprapubic catheter.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man complains of pelvic pain after a motorcycle collision. Physical and radiologic examinations confirm a pelvic fracture . Urologic workup reveals a normal urethrogram and extraperitoneal bladder injury . Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his bladder injury?

opts.B: Placement of a permanent suprapubic tube
opts.C: Catheter drainage followed by definitive repair after 2 weeks
opts.D: Catheter drainage for 2 weeks followed by repeat imaging

why.A: Immediate surgical repair is for INTRAperitoneal rupture (urine leaks into the peritoneum causing peritonitis), or extraperitoneal injury with bladder neck involvement, bone fragments in the bladder, rectal injury, or when the pelvis is being opened for fixation anyway.
why.B: A permanent suprapubic tube is not needed for a healing bladder tear; temporary suprapubic drainage is used when the urethra is injured.
why.C: Planned definitive repair after 2 weeks is unnecessary: the tear usually heals with drainage alone, and imaging decides catheter removal; delayed repair applies to urethral strictures, not bladder tears.

questions.right: An extraperitoneal bladder rupture with a normal urethrogram (so a urethral catheter is safe) is managed conservatively: urethral catheter drainage for about 2 weeks, then a repeat cystogram to confirm healing before removal. Most extraperitoneal tears heal without surgery.
questions.kc: Bladder injury with pelvic fracture: Blood at meatus: retrograde urethrogram before any catheter Urethral injury: suprapubic catheter Extraperitoneal rupture: catheter drainage about 2 weeks, then cystogram Intraperitoneal rupture: surgical repair Diagnosis: CT or retrograde cystography
questions.ep: Extra = catheter; intra = theatre.

questions.stem: Patient with trauma to the thigh After Fall??? From High Place about 4cm with visible underline tissues and bone + There Was Fracture Of Distal Femur . What is the initial treatment?

opts.C: IV antibiotics within the first hour

why.A: A compressive dressing is used to control active bleeding; none is mentioned. The wound is covered with a sterile moist dressing, but that is not the definitive initial treatment asked for.
why.B: Analgesia and monitoring for swelling is the approach to a closed fracture at risk of compartment syndrome; an open fracture needs antibiotics and surgery.
why.D: Urgent surgical debridement, irrigation and stabilization is the next step after antibiotics, not before; it is chosen when antibiotics are not offered or already given.

questions.right: A 4 cm wound with visible underlying tissue and bone over a distal femur fracture is an open fracture. The lead-in asks for the initial treatment, and the time to first antibiotic dose is the main modifiable factor for infection, so IV antibiotics are given in the emergency department within the first hour, with tetanus prophylaxis. As the compiler notes, no bleeding is described, so hemorrhage control is not the priority.
questions.kc: Open fracture pathway: IV antibiotics (within 1 hour) and tetanus, then debridement and irrigation, then fixation. Open fracture: any wound communicating with the fracture, even small or oozing ED: IV antibiotics, tetanus, sterile dressing, splint, check pulses Then: surgical debridement and irrigation Then: stabilization (IM nail or external fixation) Active hemorrhage: direct pressure or compressive dressing first
questions.ep: If the stem describes active bleeding, control of hemorrhage comes first; with no bleeding, antibiotics are the initial step.

questions.stem: 17 year old male presenting with supracondylar fracture , then developed pallor paresthesia and pulselessness Initial management?

why.A: Steroids have no role in compartment syndrome or fracture related ischemia; they do nothing to lower compartment pressure, and time spent on them costs the limb.

questions.right: A fracture followed by pallor, paresthesia and pulselessness means the limb is ischemic, and this is a limb threatening emergency. Of the two recalled options, immediate fasciotomy is the only one that relieves compartment pressure and restores perfusion; it should not wait for a pressure reading when the clinical picture is this clear.
questions.kc: Ischemic signs after a fracture = surgical emergency, act on clinical grounds. Compartment syndrome order: pain first (pain on passive stretch), then paresthesia, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis Compartment pressure above 30 mmHg is diagnostic, but measuring it is optional when suspicion is high Supracondylar fracture, pink warm hand: reduction and K-wire fixation Supracondylar fracture, pale cold pulseless hand: urgent reduction and vascular exploration Established forearm compartment syndrome: urgent fasciotomy (prevents Volkmann ischemic contracture)
questions.ep: Pulselessness is a late sign; if the options include surgical exploration for a pale pulseless hand after a supracondylar fracture, that is the vascular answer, while fasciotomy is the compartment syndrome answer.

questions.stem: A mechanic had an accidental injection of high-pressure oil dissolving injection in his index finger. Finger is red and swollen with mild tenderness O/E uncomfortable joint movement, sensation is intact what to give?

opts.D: Elevate the hand and ice packing

why.A: Oral antibiotics alone ignore the retained foreign material and tissue destruction; antibiotics are an adjunct to surgery, not the treatment.
why.B: Steroids have been tried as adjuncts for inflammation, but with antibiotics and no debridement the injected material remains and the finger is lost.
why.D: Elevation and ice suit simple soft tissue sprains or contusions; the benign early appearance of an injection injury is misleading and conservative care leads to high amputation rates.

questions.right: A "high-pressure" injection of oil or solvent into the "index finger" is a surgical emergency, however mild it looks. The small entry wound hides material spreading along tendon sheaths and fascial planes, causing chemical inflammation, ischemia and infection; solvents and oils cause severe damage. Urgent surgical exploration with debridement and removal of the injected material is the only treatment that prevents necrosis and amputation.
questions.kc: High-pressure injection injury of the hand = emergency surgical debridement. Small entry wound, deceptively mild early signs Material tracks along tendon sheaths and fascial planes Paint, solvents and oils: worst outcomes Management: urgent exploration, debridement and decompression + IV antibiotics + tetanus Delay increases amputation risk
questions.ep: "Mild tenderness, intact sensation" is the trap: injection injuries look benign at first and still go to theatre.

questions.stem: Male burned his hand while cooking. Total surface area of burn is 4%. Burn with Painful , erythema , moist , swelling, blisters . Type of burn:

why.A: First-degree (superficial) burns are painful and red but dry and without blisters, like sunburn.
why.C: Deep partial-thickness burns reach the deep dermis; they look mottled or white, are drier, blanch poorly and have reduced pain sensation.
why.D: Third-degree (full-thickness) burns are white, leathery or charred, dry and painless because nerve endings are destroyed.

questions.right: Burn depth is judged by the clinical features: a painful , red, moist burn with blisters and swelling is a superficial partial-thickness (superficial second-degree) burn. It involves the epidermis and superficial dermis, blanches with pressure, and heals in about 2 to 3 weeks with little scarring. The compiler highlights "moist" as the decisive word.
questions.kc: Burn depth: Superficial (1st): red, dry, painful, no blisters Superficial partial (2nd): red, moist, blisters, very painful, blanches Deep partial (2nd): mottled or white, less moist, reduced pain, poor blanching Full thickness (3rd): white or leathery, painless, needs grafting Hand burns are a referral criterion to a burn centre regardless of size
questions.ep: Blisters plus moist plus pain = superficial partial; lose the pain and it becomes deeper.

questions.stem: A 37y patient suffered from circumferential right forearm burn + weak distal pulsation + oxygen saturation 86% in right arm ,what is most appropriate next step

opts.C: IV fluids , burn dressing , limb elevation

why.A: IV vasodilators do nothing for a mechanical constriction; the vessels are compressed from outside by the eschar.
why.C: Fluid resuscitation, dressing and elevation are part of standard burn care, but with ischemia already present they do not relieve the constriction, and escharotomy must not be delayed.
why.D: Compartment pressure measurement is used when compartment syndrome is uncertain; a circumferential burn with distal ischemia is a clinical indication for escharotomy. Fasciotomy is considered if perfusion is still poor after escharotomy (for example electrical or crush injury).

questions.right: A "circumferential" full-thickness burn forms a rigid, inelastic eschar that acts like a tourniquet as the tissue swells with burn edema. "Weak distal pulsation" and "oxygen saturation 86%" in that arm show distal circulation is already compromised. The treatment is immediate escharotomy (incising the eschar) to release the constriction and restore perfusion.
questions.kc: Circumferential full-thickness burn + signs of distal ischemia = immediate escharotomy. Limb: weak/absent pulses, low pulse oximetry, cold pale limb, pain Chest: restricted ventilation, high airway pressures: chest escharotomy Escharotomy cuts the eschar; fasciotomy opens the fascia (deeper) Fasciotomy: persistent compartment syndrome after escharotomy, electrical burns Supportive: elevation, fluids per Parkland
questions.ep: "Circumferential" is the trigger word: think tourniquet-like eschar and cut it.

questions.stem: A patient was in a house fire. in the ER, burned nose hair is observed and while taking, the patient is starting to get confused . What is the most appropriate next step?

why.B: ICU observation suits a patient with possible inhalation exposure but no high-risk signs; with singed hair and confusion, waiting risks losing the airway as edema develops.
why.C: Analgesia is needed in burns but does not address the threatened airway; Airway always comes first.
why.D: Option not recalled. Other options a student might consider are 100% oxygen by mask (given anyway, but does not secure the airway) and bronchoscopy (confirms airway injury but delays securing it).

questions.right: Burned nasal hair after a house fire signals inhalation injury, and new confusion (altered mental status, possibly from CO toxicity or hypoxia) is a further intubation indication. Airway edema progresses over hours and can make later intubation impossible, so early elective intubation while the airway is still manageable is the next step, with 100% oxygen.
questions.kc: Inhalation injury: intubate early when any high-risk sign is present. Facial burns, singed facial or nasal hair Soot in mouth/nose, carbonaceous sputum Hoarseness, stridor, airway edema Altered mental status Respiratory failure (hypoxia, hypercapnia), extensive burns Also: 100% oxygen for possible CO poisoning
questions.ep: An alert patient with only smoke exposure and no airway signs can be observed; any hoarseness, soot or confusion flips it to intubation.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man presented to the Emergency Department after a motor vehicle accident. Initially he was stable then he lost consciousness . Dilated pupils were noted on examination. GCS was 6/15. CT brain shows convex hematoma in the temporal region . What is the appropriate management?

why.B: High-flow oxygen is supportive only and does not relieve the mass effect of an expanding arterial bleed; a GCS of 6 also needs a definitive airway, not just oxygen.
why.C: Steroids have no role in traumatic brain injury and are associated with worse outcomes; they help vasogenic edema around tumors, not traumatic hematoma.
why.D: A shunt treats hydrocephalus (CSF diversion); it does nothing for an acute extra-axial blood collection.

questions.right: "Initially stable then lost consciousness" is a lucid interval, and a "convex hematoma in the temporal region" is the lens-shaped collection of an epidural hematoma from the middle meningeal artery. With "GCS 6/15" and "dilated pupils" the brain is herniating, so the hematoma must be evacuated immediately (craniotomy). The compiler notes intubation was not among the options; airway protection happens alongside, but of the listed choices only evacuation treats the cause.
questions.kc: Epidural hematoma with deterioration = emergency surgical evacuation. Epidural: convex/lens shaped, middle meningeal artery, temporal fracture, lucid interval Subdural: concave/crescent, bridging veins, elderly and alcoholics Dilated pupil = uncal herniation (CN III compression), usually same side as the clot GCS ≤ 8 = secure the airway Steroids: not used in head trauma
questions.ep: Lucid interval + convex temporal clot + falling GCS: the cure is the knife, not medical measures.

questions.stem: child fells from 2 meters now he is vomiting multiple times and sleepy. He has left side weakness , CT shows extradural hemorrhage . BEST MANAGEMENT?

why.B: Securing the airway comes first when the airway is threatened or GCS is 8 or less; the stem describes a sleepy but not comatose child, so the question is aiming at the definitive treatment of a symptomatic extradural hematoma.

questions.right: A fall from height followed by repeated vomiting, drowsiness ("sleepy") and a lateralizing deficit ("left side weakness") with a CT-proven extradural hemorrhage indicates a symptomatic, expanding hematoma with mass effect. The definitive and best management is urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the hematoma, as outcome depends on how fast the clot is removed.
questions.kc: Extradural (epidural) hematoma. Source: middle meningeal artery, often with temporal bone fracture Classic course: lucid interval then rapid deterioration CT: biconvex (lens shaped) hyperdensity that does not cross sutures Symptomatic, large or lateralizing: urgent craniotomy and evacuation Small, asymptomatic, no shift: close observation with repeat CT Always ABC first if GCS 8 or less
questions.ep: If the stem gives GCS 8 or less or a compromised airway, the answer flips to intubation before evacuation.

questions.stem: Old man fell down and then came to the ER confused, CT brain showed: crescent shaped lesion , most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Epidural hematoma is a biconvex (lens-shaped) collection limited by sutures, usually from a temporal bone fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery, classically with a lucid interval in a younger patient.
why.C: Subarachnoid hemorrhage shows blood in the sulci, fissures and basal cisterns, not a crescent extra-axial collection, and classically presents with a thunderclap headache.

questions.right: An elderly patient after a fall with confusion and a crescent-shaped (concave) collection on CT has a subdural hematoma. Tearing of bridging veins, which are stretched by brain atrophy in the elderly and alcoholics, produces blood that spreads along the brain surface and crosses suture lines, giving the crescent shape.
questions.kc: Head CT shapes: Crescent (concave), crosses sutures: subdural, bridging veins, elderly, alcoholics, anticoagulated Biconvex (lens), stops at sutures: epidural, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval Blood in cisterns and sulci: subarachnoid, berry aneurysm, worst headache Chronic subdural: days to weeks of fluctuating confusion after minor fall
questions.ep: SuB = Banana shape (subdural); Epidural = Egg/lens shape.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ER for a severe head injury after a fall. He was intubated in the field for his decreased level of consciousness. He is tachycardic and hypotensive. On examination, he is noted to have an obvious skull fracture and his right pupil is dilated . Which of the following is the next best management?

why.A: Brief hyperventilation is a temporizing bridge for herniation signs; it lowers ICP by cerebral vasoconstriction but risks ischemia and does not remove the clot. Another version of this question (asking the initial step, or without craniotomy listed) is keyed to it.
why.C: Mannitol is another temporizing ICP measure and is relatively unwise in a hypotensive patient because of its diuretic effect (hypertonic saline is preferred); it buys time but is not definitive.
why.D: Head elevation to about 30 degrees is a basic supportive ICP measure; it is far from adequate for a herniating patient with a surgical lesion.

questions.right: A skull fracture with a dilated right pupil and depressed consciousness indicates an expanding intracranial hematoma (typically extradural) causing uncal herniation. The airway is already secured, and the lead-in is "next best" , so definitive treatment is surgical decompression: craniotomy and evacuation. The compiler agrees: ICP-lowering measures are bridges given on the way to theatre, not substitutes.
questions.kc: Head injury with herniation signs: temporize, then evacuate. Airway (GCS ≤ 8: intubate), avoid hypoxia and hypotension Bridges: head up 30 degrees, osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), brief hyperventilation Definitive: craniotomy and evacuation of the hematoma Lucid interval + temporal fracture + fixed dilated pupil: extradural hematoma Hypotension in head injury: look for bleeding elsewhere
questions.ep: "Initial" step with no craniotomy option points to a temporizing measure such as hyperventilation; "next best" with craniotomy listed points to surgery.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset severe headache described as " the worst headache . Which of the following is the BEST diagnostic test?

opts.C: Non-contrast CT scan of the head

why.B: MRI brain is not the standard test for acute SAH; it is used later or for other causes when CT and LP are unrevealing.
why.C: Non-contrast CT head is the FIRST test for thunderclap headache and is highly sensitive within 6 hours; it is the answer whenever the lead-in says initial, first or next step.
why.D: Cerebral angiography (CTA or catheter) is done after SAH is confirmed, to find the aneurysm and plan treatment, not to diagnose the bleed.

questions.right: A sudden 'worst headache' is subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise. This recall's key is lumbar puncture because the examiner was sure the lead-in was BEST diagnostic test: LP looking for xanthochromia and a persistently high RBC count across tubes is the most sensitive test and the one that confirms or excludes SAH when CT is negative, particularly beyond 6 hours from onset.
questions.kc: Thunderclap headache pathway: Step 1: non-contrast CT head CT positive: SAH; then CT angiography to find the aneurysm CT negative within 6 h: SAH effectively excluded CT negative after 6 h: lumbar puncture (xanthochromia, RBCs not clearing from tube 1 to 4) LP abnormal: CT angiography
questions.ep: The verb decides: initial/next = CT; most sensitive/confirm after negative CT = LP.

questions.stem: A Case Of subarachnoid hemorrhage The stem was what is the most diagnostic step?

why.A: Contrast enhanced CT can mimic or obscure blood, because contrast is also hyperdense; CT angiography is added after SAH is confirmed, to locate the aneurysm.
why.C: MRI (FLAIR) can detect subarachnoid blood, especially later, but it is less available, slower and harder in an unwell patient; it is not the first choice.

questions.right: For suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage the first and key diagnostic test is non contrast CT of the head, which shows fresh blood in the basal cisterns and sulci as hyperdensity and is most sensitive in the first hours. The lead-in "most diagnostic step" among these options therefore points to CT without contrast; the compiler notes lumbar puncture was probably not offered.
questions.kc: SAH workup. Thunderclap (worst ever) headache, neck stiffness, possible third nerve palsy Step 1: non contrast CT head CT normal but suspicion high: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia Confirmed SAH: CT angiography (or catheter angiography) for the aneurysm Treat: nimodipine, secure aneurysm (coiling or clipping)
questions.ep: If the stem says CT is normal, the answer becomes lumbar puncture.

questions.stem: A Patient Presents With Back Pain And Hypesthesia Localized To The Left Lateral Calf And Left Lateral Foot . Which Of The Following Nerve Root Levels Is Most Likely Affected?

why.A: L3-L4 affects the L4 root: medial leg and medial malleolus, reduced knee reflex, weak knee extension.
why.B: L4-L5 affects the L5 root: lateral leg and dorsum of the foot including the first web space, weak great toe extension and foot dorsiflexion; the lateral foot is S1, not L5.
why.D: S1-S2 is not a usual disc herniation level; S2 supplies the posterior thigh and calf, not the lateral leg and foot.

questions.right: Sensory loss over the lateral calf (L5 dermatome) extending to the lateral foot (S1 dermatome) points to the lumbosacral junction. A disc herniation at the L5-S1 level typically compresses the S1 root (lateral foot, sole, reduced ankle reflex, weak plantar flexion), and the combined L5/S1 distribution makes L5-S1 the best fit.
questions.kc: Lumbar radiculopathy map (posterolateral disc compresses the lower root): L3-L4 disc → L4: medial leg, knee jerk reduced L4-L5 disc → L5: lateral leg and dorsum of foot, big toe extension weak, no reflex change L5-S1 disc → S1: lateral foot and sole, ankle jerk reduced, plantar flexion weak Red flags (saddle anesthesia, retention): cauda equina, urgent MRI
questions.ep: Dorsum of foot and big toe = L5 (L4-L5); lateral border of foot and little toe = S1 (L5-S1).

questions.stem: A 38-Year-Old Woman Has Weakness Of The Right Arm With Neck Extension . MRI Brain Done And Reported Normal . What Is The .... Investigation?

why.A: EEG is for seizures; focal weakness that is reproduced by a neck posture is mechanical, not epileptic.
why.B: C-spine X-ray shows bone alignment and degenerative changes but not the disc, nerve roots or cord; it is a cheap first look, not the diagnostic test for radiculopathy.
why.D: Carotid ultrasound is for TIA or stroke of anterior circulation origin (transient weakness, risk factors, bruit); weakness triggered by neck extension is a compressive spinal problem.

questions.right: Arm weakness provoked by neck extension points to the cervical spine (cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy from disc prolapse or spondylosis narrowing the foramina), and a normal MRI brain removes an intracranial cause. MRI of the cervical spine is the investigation of choice because it shows the discs, nerve roots and spinal cord directly, which plain films cannot.
questions.kc: Neurological symptom provoked by neck movement = cervical spine. Radiculopathy: dermatomal pain, numbness, weakness, lost reflexes in the arm Myelopathy: hand clumsiness, gait problems, upper motor neuron signs Investigation of choice: MRI cervical spine Transient weakness with vascular risk factors: carotid duplex
questions.ep: Normal brain MRI plus a posture-triggered arm deficit means you image the neck, not the vessels.

questions.stem: 26 years old primigravida presented 10 days after vaginal delivery complaining of fever and back pain. On examination, lower back tenderness lower limb weakness, and incontinence . Diagnosis of spinal epidural abscess was made. Most appropriate management?

why.A: IV antibiotics are always given, but antibiotics alone are reserved for patients with no neurological deficit, poor surgical candidates or longstanding complete paralysis; with progressive weakness and incontinence they are not sufficient alone.
why.C: CT-guided needle aspiration can be used for selected small collections in neurologically intact patients; it does not decompress the cord adequately when deficits are present.
why.D: Observing a patient with established motor and sphincter deficits risks irreversible paralysis; observation with antibiotics is only for neurologically intact patients under close monitoring.

questions.right: A spinal epidural abscess with "lower limb weakness and incontinence" means the cord or cauda equina is already compressed. New or progressing neurological deficit is an indication for urgent surgical decompression and evacuation of the abscess (with IV antibiotics) as soon as possible, because delay leads to permanent paralysis. The compiler notes the precise term is surgical evacuation or decompression and that "surgical exploration" is the closest option.
questions.kc: Spinal epidural abscess: Classic triad: back pain, fever, neurological deficit Risk: epidural anesthesia, IV drug use, diabetes, bacteremia Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus Diagnosis: MRI spine with gadolinium Deficit present: urgent surgical decompression + IV antibiotics No deficit: IV antibiotics with close neurological monitoring
questions.ep: Spinal epidural abscess with weakness or incontinence: decompress surgically plus antibiotics, not antibiotics alone.

questions.stem: (Don't recall age ) MALE came to ER with 3 days history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and brisk reflexes in both legs, with urinary retention , inability to walk, and a sensory level of T10 . What is the diagnosis?

why.A: Transverse myelitis gives the same picture (sensory level, weakness, bladder involvement), usually after a viral illness or with MS/NMO; it is diagnosed after MRI excludes compression, and it was the examiner's own answer.
why.B: GBS causes ascending weakness with areflexia (lower motor neuron) and no sensory level; bladder function is usually spared early.
why.C: Cauda equina syndrome is a lower motor neuron lesion: reduced reflexes, saddle anesthesia, and no thoracic sensory level, because the cord ends at about L1-L2.

questions.right: "Progressive bilateral leg weakness" with "brisk reflexes", "urinary retention" and a "sensory level of T10" is an upper motor neuron spinal cord syndrome (myelopathy). The compiler's answer is cord compression, the cause that must be assumed and excluded first with urgent whole-spine MRI because delay causes permanent paralysis (e.g. metastatic disease, abscess, disc).
questions.kc: Myelopathy (sensory level + UMN signs + sphincter involvement): First: urgent MRI whole spine to exclude compression Compression: tumor/metastasis, epidural abscess, disc, trauma Malignant compression: dexamethasone, surgery or radiotherapy No compression: think transverse myelitis (inflammatory) Cauda equina: LMN, saddle anesthesia; GBS: areflexia, no sensory level
questions.ep: A sensory level puts the lesion in the cord, which rules out GBS and cauda equina; then exclude compression first.

questions.stem: Patient with atrial fibrillation presents with severe abdominal pain out of proportion . What is the initial investigation?

why.A: Ultrasound is limited by bowel gas in an ileus-prone ischemic abdomen and cannot reliably show mesenteric vessel occlusion; it is first line for biliary or pelvic causes, not for suspected mesenteric ischemia.
why.B: Catheter mesenteric angiography is invasive and is reserved for when CT is equivocal or when endovascular therapy (thrombolysis, embolectomy, stenting) is planned; it is not the first test.
why.C: A plain X-ray is often normal early and only shows late signs (ileus, thumbprinting, pneumatosis); it can exclude free air but cannot diagnose mesenteric ischemia.

questions.right: AF (an embolic source) plus "pain out of proportion" to the examination is acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise. The lead-in asks for the initial investigation, and the first test is a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (performed as a CT angiogram), which is fast, non-invasive and shows the embolus or thrombus, bowel wall thickening and complications. Examinees confirmed the option was plain "CT with contrast", not catheter angiography.
questions.kc: Pain out of proportion + embolic source (AF, recent MI, valve disease) = acute mesenteric ischemia. Initial/confirmatory test: CT with IV contrast (CT angiography) Catheter angiography: when CT is inconclusive or for endovascular treatment Labs: leukocytosis, lactic acidosis (late) Peritonitis or unstable: laparotomy Elderly + bloody diarrhea + LLQ pain + thumbprinting = ischemic colitis instead
questions.ep: If the stem says "gold standard" or "definitive and therapeutic", the answer shifts to mesenteric angiography; "initial" means CT.

questions.stem: 45 years old with AF came with severe abdominal pain . What is the initial investigation?

why.B: Ultrasound is limited by gas filled, distended bowel and cannot reliably show the mesenteric vessels or bowel ischemia in this emergency.
why.C: Plain X ray is usually normal early in mesenteric ischemia and only shows late signs such as ileus or pneumatosis; it is the first test for suspected perforation, not ischemia.

questions.right: Atrial fibrillation plus severe abdominal pain is embolic acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise; pain is typically out of proportion to examination. CT angiography is the investigation of choice because it shows the embolus or thrombus in the mesenteric vessels and signs of bowel ischemia, and it should be done promptly since bowel viability is time dependent.
questions.kc: Acute mesenteric ischemia: think vascular when the pain outweighs the signs. Causes: embolus (AF, recent MI, valve disease), thrombosis, venous thrombosis, non occlusive Pain out of proportion to examination, later bloody diarrhea Labs: leukocytosis, raised lactate, metabolic acidosis Diagnosis: CT angiography Treatment: heparin, fluids, then revascularisation and resection of dead bowel
questions.ep: AF (at any age) with severe abdominal pain: CT angiography, not plain films.

questions.stem: Patients with atrial fibrillation presents with severe abdominal pain out of proportion . What is the most appropriate investigation?

why.A: Ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and cannot reliably show mesenteric occlusion; it fits gallbladder or gynecological pain.
why.B: Conventional mesenteric angiography was the old gold standard but is invasive; it is now used when CT is equivocal or when endovascular treatment is planned, not as the first investigation.
why.C: Plain X-ray is often normal early in mesenteric ischemia; late findings such as thumbprinting or pneumatosis appear only after infarction.

questions.right: "Atrial fibrillation" (embolic source) with "severe abdominal pain out of proportion" to examination is acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise. The most appropriate investigation is contrast enhanced CT (CT angiography), which is fast, widely available and shows the embolus or thrombus, bowel wall thickening and complications.
questions.kc: Acute mesenteric ischemia. Clues: AF, recent MI, valvular disease, old age Pain out of proportion to exam, later bloody diarrhea Labs: leukocytosis, lactic (metabolic) acidosis Diagnosis: CT angiography Peritonitis or infarcted bowel: laparotomy with resection
questions.ep: AF plus pain out of proportion means CT angiography, not a plain film that will look normal.

questions.stem: 71-year-old man known case of IHD , complaining of severe central abdominal pain for 10 hours, and has vomited 3 times. On examination there is mild tenderness , and bowel sounds are sluggish. (See report) (Labs: Amylase 400 IU/L [24 – 151 IU/L]; WBC 22 × 10⁹/L [4.5 – 10.5 × 10⁹/L]) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Acute pancreatitis typically gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with amylase or lipase at least 3 times normal; here amylase is under 3 times the upper limit and the cardiac background points to ischemia.
why.C: Bowel perforation causes peritonitis: a rigid, diffusely tender abdomen with guarding and free air; this exam shows only mild tenderness.
why.D: Diverticulitis presents with left lower quadrant pain, fever and localized tenderness, not severe central pain with a benign exam.

questions.right: An elderly man with IHD and severe central abdominal pain for 10 hours but only mild tenderness has pain out of proportion to examination, the hallmark of acute mesenteric ischemia. The marked leukocytosis (WBC 22 ) reflects bowel ischemia, and a modest amylase rise (400) occurs in ischemic bowel and does not by itself mean pancreatitis. Confirm with CT angiography.
questions.kc: Old age + cardiovascular disease (AF, MI, IHD) + severe pain with minimal signs = acute mesenteric ischemia. Labs: leukocytosis, lactic acidosis, mildly raised amylase Late: bloody diarrhea, peritonitis Diagnosis: CT angiography Treatment: resuscitation, heparin, revascularization, resection of dead bowel
questions.ep: A raised amylase does not make it pancreatitis: below 3 times normal with pain out of proportion in a cardiac patient is ischemia.

questions.stem: A patient with a known history of atrial fibrillation presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset severe abdominal pain . What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

why.A: MRI (MRA) is too slow and less available for an emergency; it can image mesenteric vessels electively but delays management of a time-critical ischemic bowel.
why.C: Abdominal ultrasound is limited by gas-filled bowel in ischemia and cannot reliably assess the SMA; it is first line for biliary pathology or in children and pregnancy.
why.D: Laparoscopy is a treatment/assessment tool for bowel viability once the diagnosis is made or the patient has peritonitis; it is not the initial investigation.

questions.right: Atrial fibrillation plus sudden severe abdominal pain is embolic acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise. The initial investigation of choice is CT (CT angiography with IV contrast), which shows the embolus or thrombus in the superior mesenteric artery and the state of the bowel. Other versions of this recall are keyed to "CT abdomen with contrast".
questions.kc: Acute mesenteric ischemia: CT angiography first. Embolic: AF, recent MI, valve disease: sudden onset Thrombotic: atherosclerosis, prior post-prandial pain (intestinal angina) Hallmark: pain out of proportion to examination Labs: leukocytosis, lactic acidosis Peritonitis: straight to laparotomy
questions.ep: Same AF patient with sudden leg pain and paralysis flips to embolectomy without imaging.

questions.stem: Elderly (smoker k/c of hypertension and DM) presents with diminished right leg pulse (maybe with calf pain), there is popliteal bypass scar on his left leg. Which of the following indicates acute limb ischemia ?

why.A: Intermittent claudication (pain on walking, relieved by rest) indicates chronic, stable peripheral arterial disease, not an acute threatened limb.
why.C: The left popliteal bypass scar is a history of prior arterial disease in the other leg; it is a risk factor, not a sign of acute ischemia in the right leg.
why.D: Smoking is a risk factor for atherosclerosis, not a clinical indicator of acute limb ischemia.

questions.right: Among the options, only pain at rest reflects ischemia severe enough to threaten the limb; a new onset of rest pain with a diminished pulse in the right leg signals an acute (or acute-on-chronic) ischemic event, consistent with the 6Ps where pain is the first P. The recaller stressed the scenario was acute, not chronic.
questions.kc: Acute limb ischemia (6Ps): pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis. Step 1: IV heparin Imaging: duplex, then CT angiography; paralysis = threatened limb, go straight to revascularization Embolic (AF, sudden, normal other leg): embolectomy Thrombotic on atherosclerosis (claudication history): catheter-directed thrombolysis Chronic PAD: claudication, then rest pain (critical ischemia), then ulcer/gangrene
questions.ep: Rest pain alone without sudden onset is chronic critical limb ischemia; it is the acute onset that makes it ALI.

questions.stem: Patient with pain, parasthesia and pulselessness for 3 hours ? Deplex signals were undetectable Most appropriate Next step

why.A: Aspirin and reassessment is the approach to chronic stable claudication; acute limb ischemia needs full anticoagulation with heparin and urgent revascularisation.
why.B: MR angiography is slow and not used in an emergency threatened limb; if imaging is needed for planning, CT angiography is done after the vascular team is involved.
why.D: Doppler has already shown absent signals, so repeating it only wastes time in a limb that loses viability with every hour.

questions.right: Pain, paresthesia and pulselessness for 3 hours describe acute limb ischemia, and undetectable Doppler signals with sensory change mean the limb is threatened. This is a time critical emergency: start IV heparin and obtain an urgent vascular surgery consultation for revascularisation (embolectomy, thrombolysis or bypass). The Doppler has already been done, so further imaging must not delay the specialist.
questions.kc: Acute limb ischemia: the 6 Ps and the clock. Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia (perishing cold) Immediately: IV unfractionated heparin plus urgent vascular surgery Viable (Doppler signals present, no sensory loss): imaging then revascularise Threatened (absent arterial Doppler, sensory loss, weakness): urgent revascularisation Irreversible (paralysis, rigor, no signals at all): amputation Look for the source: AF (embolus) vs known PAD (thrombosis)
questions.ep: Paresthesia and paralysis mark a threatened limb; go to the vascular surgeon, not to more imaging.

questions.stem: Patient with intermittent claudication before few months known case of hypertension and diabetes present with pain and paralysis . Intact distal pulse . What is the most appropriate diagnostic study ?

why.A: Ultrasound (arterial Doppler with ABI) is the first, non invasive test for chronic PAD and arterial ulcers; it does not give the full anatomic road map needed in an acutely ischemic, paralysed limb.
why.C: Plain X-ray has no role in diagnosing arterial occlusion; it is for fractures or gas in tissue.

questions.right: A diabetic, hypertensive patient with months of "intermittent claudication" who now has acute "pain and paralysis" has acute on chronic limb ischemia; paralysis marks a threatened limb. The lead-in asks for the "most appropriate diagnostic study", which is the confirmatory test that maps the occlusion for revascularization: CT angiography. The "intact distal pulse" in the recall does not fit acute limb ischemia and is likely a recall error; the keyed reasoning rests on the ischemic picture.
questions.kc: Limb ischemia investigation ladder. Chronic PAD: ABI, then duplex ultrasound, then CT angiography before intervention Acute limb ischemia (6 Ps): heparin first, then CT angiography Paralysis or sensory loss: limb threatened, urgent revascularization Embolic source (AF): embolectomy; in situ thrombosis on atherosclerosis: catheter directed thrombolysis Ulcer with intact pulses: think venous, venous duplex
questions.ep: "Most appropriate diagnostic" in acute limb ischemia means CT angiography; "next step" means heparin.

questions.stem: 45 YO Male patient diabetic and smoker presented with ulcer on 2nd , 3rd and 4th left foot toes . He gave a history of superficial thrombophlebitis . Upon examination: he has absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis pulse in both limbs , while the popliteal pulse was intact . What is the initial management ?

opts.D: Ask patient to stop smoking with lifestyle modifications

why.A: Amputation is reserved for gangrene or non healing ulcers despite smoking cessation and maximal therapy; it is not the initial step.
why.B: Long term anticoagulation has no proven role in Buerger disease, since the process is inflammatory and occlusive rather than embolic; it fits atrial fibrillation with limb embolism or recurrent DVT.
why.C: Surgical revascularization is rarely possible because the disease is distal and segmental with poor run off; it is considered for atherosclerotic PAD with suitable targets, not as first line here.

questions.right: A young male smoker with ischemic ulcers of several toes, a history of (migratory) superficial thrombophlebitis, and absent distal pulses with a preserved popliteal pulse describes thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease), a small and medium vessel disease of distal arteries. The single most effective initial management, and the only one that halts progression, is complete smoking cessation with lifestyle measures.
questions.kc: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans). Young male heavy smoker, usually under 45 to 50 Distal ischemia: digital ulcers or gangrene, claudication of the foot Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis, Raynaud phenomenon Distal pulses absent, proximal (popliteal) intact Treatment: absolute smoking cessation; amputation only for gangrene
questions.ep: Superficial thrombophlebitis plus distal toe ulcers in a young smoker equals Buerger; the answer is stop smoking, not anticoagulate.

questions.stem: Patient came with medial leg ulcers . Which of following is highest risk factor?

why.A: Diabetes causes neuropathic ulcers on pressure points of the foot (plantar metatarsal heads, heel), not typical medial gaiter ulcers.
why.C: Atherosclerosis causes arterial ulcers: painful, punched-out lesions on toes, heel and pressure areas with absent pulses, not the medial gaiter region.

questions.right: Ulcers on the medial lower leg (gaiter area above the medial malleolus) are classic venous ulcers. They result from chronic venous hypertension due to valvular incompetence or prior DVT, so venous hypertension is the strongest risk factor here.
questions.kc: Leg ulcer by site: Medial gaiter area, shallow, irregular, granulating base: venous (venous hypertension) Toes, heel, pressure areas, punched out, painful, absent pulses: arterial Plantar pressure points, painless, diabetic: neuropathic First step: check pulses (and ABPI before compression) Venous ulcer: duplex ultrasound, then compression therapy
questions.ep: A lateral malleolus or toe ulcer with absent pulses flips the answer to atherosclerosis.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with an erythematous, oozing , painful lesion on her left arm. She has a history of burn injury on the same side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: A neuropathic ulcer occurs over pressure points in insensate skin (e.g. diabetic foot) and is typically painless; nothing links it to a burn scar.
why.B: "Ulcer" is only a description, not a diagnosis; a non-healing ulcer in a burn scar must be presumed malignant (Marjolin) until biopsy proves otherwise.

questions.right: A chronic, oozing, painful lesion arising in an old burn scar in an older patient is a Marjolin ulcer : an aggressive malignancy (usually squamous cell carcinoma) developing in chronic wounds or scars, often decades after the burn. The history of a burn "on the same side" is the decisive clue; biopsy confirms it.
questions.kc: Chronic non-healing wound in an old scar = suspect Marjolin ulcer. Arises in burn scars, chronic osteomyelitis sinuses, venous ulcers Usually squamous cell carcinoma; long latency Clues: new pain, bleeding, raised everted edges, change in an old scar Diagnosis: biopsy of the edge; treatment: wide excision
questions.ep: Burn scar + new non-healing ulcer = biopsy for SCC (Marjolin).

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes presents with swelling of the big toe and warmth and tenderness of the (calf) for 4 days. There is 2 cm ulcer over ... . No discharge is noted. Distal pulses are intact . What is the most appropriate investigation?

why.B: Conventional angiography is invasive and reserved for planning revascularization in arterial disease with absent or reduced pulses; pulses here are intact.
why.C: MRI is the best test for suspected osteomyelitis or deep foot infection (e.g. discharging ulcer over bone, positive probe to bone); the leading problem here is calf signs suggesting a venous cause.
why.D: CT with contrast (CT angiography) is used for acute limb ischemia with absent pulses or when MRI is unavailable for deep infection; it adds radiation and contrast load in a diabetic without need.

questions.right: The examiner recalls calf warmth, tenderness (and swelling) for 4 days with intact distal pulses and no discharge . Intact pulses exclude significant arterial disease, and a warm tender calf raises deep vein thrombosis, so the most appropriate investigation is duplex ultrasound of the leg. Duplex is non invasive, fast and also assesses arterial flow if needed.
questions.kc: Leg or foot problem: check the pulse first, then choose the vascular test. Intact pulse + swelling or calf tenderness: venous duplex (DVT, venous ulcer) Absent pulse, chronic: ABI then arterial duplex Acute ischemia with absent pulses: CT angiography (straight to embolectomy if motor deficit) Suspected osteomyelitis: X-ray first, MRI best Non pitting edema with thick skin: lymphoscintigraphy
questions.ep: Do not confuse with the discharging big toe ulcer over the first metatarsal recall (osteomyelitis, cross sectional imaging); calf signs with intact pulses point to duplex.

questions.stem: Patient with diabetes presented with big toe swelling and discharge for 4 days. There was an ulcer 2cm on the first metatarsal Bone . Distal pulses intact. What's the most appropriate way to assess?

why.A: Duplex ultrasound assesses arterial or venous flow; with intact distal pulses perfusion is adequate and duplex does not evaluate bone.
why.B: Conventional angiography is invasive and used to plan revascularization in arterial insufficiency, which intact pulses argue against.
why.C: MR angiography images the vessels, not the bone marrow; plain MRI (not angiography) would be the best test for osteomyelitis and would be chosen if it were offered.

questions.right: A diabetic with big toe swelling, discharge and an ulcer over the first metatarsal bone, with intact pulses , is suspected of underlying osteomyelitis rather than a vascular problem. The best test for osteomyelitis is plain MRI, but the recalled option is MR angiography , a vascular study. The compiler therefore keys CT with contrast as the best available cross sectional test to show bone destruction, sequestra and a deep abscess.
questions.kc: Diabetic foot ulcer over bone with discharge = think osteomyelitis: X-ray first, MRI best, CT when MRI not available. Probe to bone positive or ulcer over bone: suspect osteomyelitis Plain X-ray: initial, may be normal early MRI: most sensitive and specific CT: alternative when MRI unavailable or contraindicated Bone biopsy and culture: confirms organism Absent pulses: add arterial assessment (ABI, duplex)
questions.ep: Read the option exactly: 'MR angiography' is a vessel study, not the MRI that diagnoses osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: Diabetic patients with pus discharge from ulcer in the Lateral foot ulcer with granulation tissue and pus, pulses are present . What's the underlying etiology?

why.A: Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area of the leg, classically above the medial malleolus, with edema, hemosiderin pigmentation and lipodermatosclerosis. This ulcer is on the foot.
why.B: Arterial ulcers are painful, punched out, on toes or heel, with absent or weak pulses and a pale, poorly granulating base. Here pulses are present and the bed is granulating.
why.D: A malignant (Marjolin) ulcer arises in a long standing scar or chronic ulcer, with rolled everted edges and progressive growth. Nothing here suggests it; biopsy would be needed if it did.

questions.right: In a "diabetic" patient an ulcer on the FOOT at a pressure area (the lateral border, over the fifth metatarsal) with "pulses present" is a neuropathic ulcer: loss of protective sensation lets repeated pressure break the skin. Infection with pus and granulation tissue is common on top of it. The compiler stresses that a lateral or medial FOOT ulcer is neuropathic, while a lateral or medial LEG (malleolar, gaiter) ulcer is venous.
questions.kc: Lower limb ulcer: site plus pulses. Diabetic foot, pressure point (plantar metatarsal heads, lateral foot), pulses present: neuropathic Toes or heel, painful, absent pulses: arterial, arterial Doppler Gaiter area of the leg, pigmentation, pulses present: venous, venous duplex Non- healing ulcer in an old scar with rolled edges: Marjolin, biopsy First step in any ulcer: check distal pulses
questions.ep: Foot is not leg: a malleolar ulcer with pulses is venous, a foot ulcer in a diabetic with pulses is neuropathic.

questions.stem: 45 diabetic patients came with bad smelling ulcer . What is the initial step in the management?

why.A: Antibiotics are needed for an infected diabetic ulcer and are started alongside debridement, but they cannot sterilise necrotic tissue on their own; they would be the main answer for cellulitis without necrosis or slough.
why.B: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is an adjunct for selected non-healing ischaemic diabetic ulcers that fail standard care; it is never the initial step.
why.C: Negative pressure wound therapy is used after debridement to promote granulation in a clean wound; applying it over necrotic, foul tissue is contraindicated.

questions.right: A bad-smelling diabetic ulcer signals infected, necrotic (often anaerobic) tissue. Dead tissue harbours bacteria, blocks antibiotic penetration and prevents healing, so the initial step is surgical debridement of all necrotic and infected tissue back to bleeding, viable tissue (with deep tissue taken for culture). Antibiotics, offloading and advanced dressings are then built on a clean wound bed.
questions.kc: Diabetic foot ulcer basics: Necrotic/foul/slough: sharp surgical debridement first, deep tissue culture Infection: empirical antibiotics, adjusted to culture Offloading and glycaemic control for every ulcer Check perfusion (pulses, ABI); revascularise ischaemic limbs Clean wound: then NPWT/dressings; HBOT only as adjunct
questions.ep: Necrotic or foul-smelling wound: debride first; NPWT only goes on a clean, debrided bed.

questions.stem: 70 years old male with history of dyslipidemia, on atorvastatin. He also has a history of recurrent TIA , but now he is asymptomatic. He came complaining of his last TIA symptoms. His labs are all normal except for LDL (slightly above the normal range) He did carotid US and showed narrowing 70-90% . What is your management?

why.A: Repeat ultrasound surveillance is for asymptomatic or mild to moderate stenosis; delaying surgery in recurrent TIA with severe stenosis leaves him at high early stroke risk.
why.C: Intensifying the statin (e.g. switching to rosuvastatin) is part of best medical therapy and can be added, but it does not treat a symptomatic 70 to 90% stenosis.
why.D: Unrecalled option. Alternatives a student might meet: carotid stenting (for patients at high surgical risk or with a hostile neck) and antiplatelet therapy alone (for stenosis below 50%); neither beats endarterectomy in a fit 70-year-old.

questions.right: Recurrent TIAs with carotid US showing 70 to 90% stenosis make this a symptomatic severe carotid stenosis, even though he is asymptomatic between episodes. Symptomatic 70 to 99% stenosis in a fit patient is the strongest indication for carotid endarterectomy, ideally soon after the event, on top of antiplatelet and statin therapy. The slightly raised LDL is managed medically but does not replace revascularization.
questions.kc: Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70 to 99% = carotid endarterectomy (plus antiplatelet and statin). TIA work up: brain imaging, carotid duplex (initial neurovascular test), ECG and cardiac evaluation Symptomatic 70 to 99%: endarterectomy, early (within about 2 weeks) Symptomatic 50 to 69%: consider surgery case by case Below 50%: medical therapy only Complete (100%) occlusion: no endarterectomy
questions.ep: 'Now asymptomatic' does not make the stenosis asymptomatic; previous TIAs in that territory define it as symptomatic.

questions.stem: 70 years old male with history of dyslipidemia which he is taking atorvastatin for he also has history recurrent TIA but now he is asymptomatic he came complaining of his last TIA symptoms his labs all are normal except for LDL (slightly above the normal range) he did carotid US and showed narrowing 70- 90% . Your management is

why.B: Intensifying the statin is part of best medical therapy and he should continue it, but changing statins does not treat a severe symptomatic stenosis. Medical therapy alone fits stenosis under 50%.
why.C: Follow up in 6 months leaves him at high early risk of stroke after recurrent TIAs. Surveillance fits asymptomatic moderate stenosis.

questions.right: This man has "recurrent TIA" symptoms and carotid narrowing of "70-90%", which is symptomatic severe carotid stenosis. Carotid endarterectomy on the symptomatic side, ideally within 2 weeks of the event, gives a clear stroke risk reduction on top of best medical therapy. Being asymptomatic at the time of the visit does not change his symptomatic status.
questions.kc: Carotid stenosis management (NASCET degree). Symptomatic 70 to 99%: endarterectomy, best within 2 weeks Symptomatic 50 to 69%: endarterectomy can be considered Symptomatic <50%: medical therapy only Near or complete occlusion: no endarterectomy Always: antiplatelet, high intensity statin, BP and diabetes control
questions.ep: Symptomatic means a TIA or stroke in that territory, even if he is well today.

questions.stem: Elderly (70 maybe) come with severe Abdominal pain above umbilicus What will you order ?

why.A: Chloride level does not help separate an aneurysm from pancreatitis or any other cause of epigastric pain.
why.C: Calcium is used in pancreatitis severity scoring (and hypocalcemia is a complication), not as the test that establishes or excludes the diagnosis.
why.D: Option not recalled; in the full version it was an arterial blood gas, which is not needed in a stable patient.

questions.right: In an elderly patient with severe pain above the umbilicus , the fuller version of this recall describes a tender pulsatile supraumbilical mass, so the leading concern is an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acute pancreatitis can present almost identically (epigastric pain radiating to the back), so amylase is ordered to exclude it before labelling the pain as aneurysmal.
questions.kc: Epigastric or supraumbilical pain in an elderly patient: think AAA, but exclude pancreatitis. Pancreatitis mimics AAA: check amylase/lipase Normal amylase/lipase plus pulsatile mass: image the aorta AAA: ultrasound is the initial test, CT angiography is the definitive test Unstable with known or suspected ruptured AAA: straight to theatre
questions.ep: If the stem already gives a normal amylase and lipase, the next answer is aortic imaging (US first, CT angiogram as the diagnostic test), not another enzyme.

questions.stem: 65 years old woman came to the ER complaining of sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back Xray: widened mediastinum Dx?

why.B: Esophageal rupture (Boerhaave) follows forceful vomiting or endoscopy and shows pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema; no vomiting or instrumentation is described.
why.C: GERD causes chronic burning retrosternal pain related to meals and lying down; it is not sudden and has a normal chest X-ray.
why.D: Acute pancreatitis also causes epigastric pain radiating to the back, but it is diagnosed by raised lipase/amylase and does not widen the mediastinum.

questions.right: "Sudden" severe pain radiating "to the back" in an older patient, together with a "widened mediastinum" on X-ray, is aortic dissection. Dissection can present with epigastric rather than chest pain when it involves the descending aorta. A stable patient is confirmed by CT angiography; an unstable one by echocardiography (TEE).
questions.kc: Pain radiating to the back: the extra clue picks the diagnosis. Sudden tearing pain + widened mediastinum (+ unequal arm BP, pulse deficit): aortic dissection Epigastric pain to back + raised lipase, gallstones/alcohol: pancreatitis Pulsatile epigastric mass: abdominal aortic aneurysm Vomiting + chest pain + subcutaneous emphysema: Boerhaave Dissection imaging: CT angiography (stable), TEE (unstable)
questions.ep: Epigastric pain to the back tempts you toward pancreatitis; the widened mediastinum makes it aortic.

questions.stem: A patient has a suspicious thyroid nodule measuring 3×4 cm with both solid and cystic components seen on imaging. What is the next step?

opts.B: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the solid Component
opts.C: FNA of both solid and cystic components

why.A: Core needle biopsy is not the first line test for a thyroid nodule; it is reserved for repeatedly nondiagnostic FNA or suspected lymphoma or anaplastic cancer.
why.C: Sampling the cystic part adds mostly fluid and debris with few follicular cells, lowering the diagnostic yield; a pure cyst can be drained, but a mixed nodule is sampled at its solid portion.

questions.right: A suspicious nodule of 3×4 cm is far above the size threshold for tissue diagnosis, so the next step is ultrasound guided FNA. Because it is mixed solid and cystic , the needle must target the solid component : that is where the cells are, while cyst fluid is usually acellular and gives a nondiagnostic sample.
questions.kc: Thyroid nodule work up: TSH first, then ultrasound, then FNA if criteria are met. TSH normal or high: ultrasound; suspicious features and ≥1 cm → FNA TSH low: thyroid scan; hot nodule → no FNA, cold nodule → back to the ultrasound/FNA pathway Mixed solid cystic nodule → FNA aimed at the solid part Nodule <1 cm with no high risk features → follow up imaging Repeated nondiagnostic FNA → repeat under US or core biopsy
questions.ep: Cyst fluid alone is nondiagnostic: in a complex nodule always aim at the solid wall component.

questions.stem: A 32 years old male with neck mass and dysphagia, US done and showed mass 2*3 cm, FNA cytology revealed hypercellular of large poorly cohesive spindle-like shape cells . Labs showed high calcitonin and CEA . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Papillary cancer shows papillae, nuclear grooves and Orphan Annie eye nuclei with psammoma bodies, and is followed with thyroglobulin, not calcitonin.
why.C: Anaplastic cancer is a rapidly enlarging hard mass in an elderly patient with pleomorphic giant and spindle cells, but it does not secrete calcitonin or CEA.
why.D: Follicular cancer shows follicular cells (diagnosed by capsular or vascular invasion on histology), spreads by blood and is followed with thyroglobulin.

questions.right: High calcitonin together with raised CEA is the biochemical signature of medullary thyroid carcinoma, which arises from the calcitonin producing parafollicular C cells. Its cytology classically shows poorly cohesive spindle shaped or plasmacytoid cells, matching this FNA. Treatment is total thyroidectomy and calcitonin is the follow up marker.
