questions.kc: Thyroid cancer: match the marker to the cell of origin. Papillary: most common, lymphatic spread, thyroglobulin Follicular: hematogenous spread, thyroglobulin Medullary: C cells, calcitonin and CEA, MEN 2, total thyroidectomy Anaplastic: elderly, rapid growth, very poor prognosis Lymphoma: long standing Hashimoto with rapidly growing goiter
questions.ep: Calcitonin in the stem means medullary; screen for MEN 2 (RET, pheochromocytoma) before surgery.

questions.stem: What is the most suggestive indication for surgical intervention in a patient with a thyroid nodule?

opts.B: Positive family history of thyroid cancer
opts.C: 10% increase in nodule size within 6 months

why.B: Family history of thyroid cancer raises suspicion and lowers the threshold for FNA, but it does not by itself mandate surgery.
why.C: A 10% increase over 6 months is within measurement variation; significant growth (about 20% in two dimensions or 50% in volume) leads to repeat FNA, not straight to surgery.
why.D: Hyperthyroidism points to a hot (toxic) nodule, which is rarely malignant and is treated with antithyroid drugs then radioactive iodine or surgery; it is not the strongest indication here.

questions.right: Bethesda IV (follicular neoplasm or suspicious for follicular neoplasm) cannot be called benign or malignant on cytology, because follicular carcinoma is defined by capsular or vascular invasion seen only on histology. It is therefore managed with diagnostic hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy). Of the options, it is the only finding that directly indicates surgery.
questions.kc: Bethesda categories and their action. I nondiagnostic: repeat FNA under ultrasound II benign: ultrasound follow up III atypia of undetermined significance: repeat FNA or molecular testing IV follicular neoplasm: diagnostic hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy) V suspicious for malignancy: surgery as for VI VI malignant: thyroidectomy (total, or lobectomy for small low risk tumors)
questions.ep: Follicular lesions cannot be diagnosed on FNA, which is exactly why Bethesda IV goes to lobectomy.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old patient presented with a neck mass that has been present for 3 years. Physical examination confirmed a palpable left thyroid gland, with no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Neck Ultrasound: Left thyroid nodule occupying most of the left lobe, measures 3.4 x 3.8 cm and has mixed cystic and solid components, the right lobe is normal . Fine Needle Aspiration: Finding is coded as Bethesda IV (suspicious for follicular neoplasm). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

why.A: A thyroid scan is the next step for a nodule with LOW TSH (possible hot nodule); TSH status is not given and cytology already places this in a surgical category.
why.B: Total thyroidectomy is for Bethesda VI (malignant), bilateral disease, nodal spread or a large confirmed cancer; for an indeterminate unilateral nodule it overtreats and adds bilateral nerve and parathyroid risk.
why.D: Repeat FNA is for Bethesda I (nondiagnostic) and Bethesda III (AUS/FLUS); repeating it in Bethesda IV cannot answer the invasion question.

questions.right: FNA Bethesda IV (follicular neoplasm or suspicious for follicular neoplasm) cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from carcinoma on cytology, because carcinoma is defined by capsular or vascular invasion seen only on histology. With a unilateral nodule, a normal right lobe and no nodes , the standard is diagnostic lobectomy: left hemithyroidectomy. Completion thyroidectomy follows only if histology shows carcinoma needing it.
questions.kc: Bethesda category to action: I nondiagnostic: repeat FNA (ultrasound guided) II benign: ultrasound follow-up III AUS/FLUS: repeat FNA or molecular testing IV follicular neoplasm: lobectomy (hemithyroidectomy) V suspicious for malignancy: lobectomy or total VI malignant: total (near-total) thyroidectomy
questions.ep: Follicular carcinoma is a histology diagnosis (capsular/vascular invasion), which is why Bethesda IV goes to lobectomy, not repeat FNA.

questions.stem: Patient With Thyroidectomy Due To Multi-Nodular Goiter. After Surgery He Developed Peri-Oral Numbness, Chvostic Signs, Torrous Sign + Other S&S Of Hypo-Calcemia. What's Most Diagnostic Test

why.A: Serum albumin only helps correct total calcium for protein level; it does not diagnose the cause.
why.B: Serum magnesium is checked when hypocalcemia is refractory to adequate calcium replacement, because low magnesium impairs PTH secretion; that is a later step.
why.C: Serum total calcium (or ionized calcium) is the first, 'next step' test to confirm hypocalcemia, but it does not show why; it would be the answer for 'next step'.

questions.right: Perioral numbness, Chvostek and Trousseau signs after thyroidectomy are hypocalcemia, almost always from injury, devascularization or removal of the parathyroids. The lead-in asks for the most diagnostic test (the recaller is sure it did not say 'next'), so the test that confirms the cause is serum intact PTH: a low or inappropriately normal PTH with low calcium proves post-operative hypoparathyroidism. Early PTH levels also predict who needs calcium and active vitamin D.
questions.kc: Post-thyroidectomy tetany: calcium confirms it, PTH diagnoses the cause, magnesium if refractory. Next step: check calcium Most diagnostic of hypoparathyroidism: intact PTH (low) Refractory hypocalcemia: check magnesium Neck swelling with stridor hours post-op: open wound at bedside (hematoma) Hoarseness: recurrent laryngeal nerve; loss of high pitch: superior laryngeal nerve
questions.ep: 'Next step' = calcium; 'most diagnostic' = PTH; 'not responding to calcium' = magnesium.

questions.stem: Presents with a painless midline neck swelling that moves up and down with swallowing . What is the management? (They mentioned that on biopsy there was mucoid fluid)
questions.kc: Midline neck mass moving with swallowing AND tongue protrusion = thyroglossal cyst, treated with Sistrunk excision. Thyroglossal cyst: midline, at or below hyoid, moves with tongue protrusion, mucoid fluid; treatment surgery (Sistrunk) Thyroid nodule or goiter: moves with swallowing only, not tongue protrusion Cystic hygroma: lateral (posterior triangle), transilluminates, lymphatic fluid; sclerotherapy then surgery Branchial cyst: lateral, anterior border of sternocleidomastoid Dermoid cyst: midline but does not move with swallowing
questions.ep: Moves with tongue protrusion separates a thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule; both move with swallowing.

questions.stem: A 14-year -old patient presented with a painless neck swelling. Examination confirmed a midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone that moves up and down with swallowing . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Cystic hygroma is a soft, transilluminating lymphatic malformation of the lateral neck (posterior triangle), usually seen in infancy, and does not move with swallowing.
why.C: A midline dermoid cyst sits in the midline too, but it is attached to the skin rather than the hyoid, so it does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.
why.D: Submental lymph nodes lie above the hyoid under the chin, are often tender with an infective source, and do not move with swallowing.

questions.right: A painless midline neck swelling just below the hyoid that moves with swallowing in a teenager is a thyroglossal duct cyst. Its tract is attached to the hyoid and foramen caecum, which is also why it rises on tongue protrusion. Treatment is surgical excision with the central part of the hyoid (Sistrunk).
questions.kc: Midline neck mass: movement tells the attachment. Moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst Moves with swallowing only: thyroid swelling Midline, no movement, skin attached: dermoid cyst Lateral, transilluminates: cystic hygroma Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid: branchial cyst
questions.ep: Movement on tongue protrusion separates a thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule, which moves only on swallowing.

questions.stem: 32 -year-old came to the clinic requesting screening for breast cancer. She doesn't have any lump or discharge. She is on oral contraceptive pills. Her mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at 45. Her menarche started at 11. She did BRCA and it was positive for BRCA1 .

why.A: Six-monthly ultrasound is not a recognised screening strategy; ultrasound is an adjunct for symptoms or dense breasts, not a substitute for MRI.
why.B: Clinical breast examination alone is insufficient for a BRCA1 carrier; imaging surveillance is required.
why.D: Waiting until 35 for mammography delays screening in a very high-risk woman, and mammogram alone is less sensitive than MRI at her age.

questions.right: A woman with a proven BRCA1 mutation is high risk, so average-risk rules (mammogram from 40) do not apply. High-risk screening uses annual breast MRI , the most sensitive test in young dense breasts, beginning from about age 25. At 32 she is already overdue, so MRI should start now (with annual mammography added from 30).
questions.kc: Breast screening by risk. Average risk: screening mammogram starting at 40 to 50 depending on the guideline Strong family history: start mammogram earlier BRCA carrier: annual MRI from about 25, add annual mammogram from 30 Consider risk-reducing surgery after childbearing
questions.ep: BRCA positive = MRI, and start now; mammogram-first answers are for average risk.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presented for her first screening mammography . She has no past medical history, and no family history of cancer (see reports). Bilateral breast mammogram: Bilateral dense breast with multiple fibro-glandular opacities, no suspicious microcalcifications or speculated lesions. Breast ultrasound: Bilateral multiple variable sizes cysts. Findings coded as BIRADS III (Probably benign) . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.A: Routine annual screening is for BI-RADS 1 (negative) and 2 (benign). A BI-RADS 3 finding needs a closer look before returning to routine screening.
why.B: Core needle biopsy is for BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) and 5 (highly suggestive of malignancy), or a solid palpable mass with worrying features. Probably benign findings do not need tissue.

questions.right: The findings were "coded as BIRADS III (Probably benign)", and the management of BI-RADS 3 is short interval follow-up imaging (about 6 months), because the malignancy risk is at most 2%. The rest of the stem (dense breasts, multiple cysts, no microcalcifications or spiculated lesions, no family history) supports a benign picture.
questions.kc: BI-RADS category decides the next step. 0: incomplete, additional imaging 1 and 2: negative or benign, routine screening 3: probably benign (≤2% cancer), short interval follow-up at 6 months 4: suspicious, core needle biopsy 5: highly suggestive of malignancy, core needle biopsy 6: known biopsy proven cancer, treat
questions.ep: BI-RADS 3 is the only category answered by follow-up imaging rather than routine screening or biopsy.

questions.stem: A woman with a left breast mass for months. Mammogram: speculated mass with suspicious microcalcification and axillary lymph node involvement, BI-RAD V (probable malignancy), next step?

why.A: Excisional biopsy is not the first diagnostic step for a likely cancer; it removes the lesion without a planned margin and can complicate definitive surgery. It is used when core biopsy is non- diagnostic or discordant, or for lesions such as atypical ductal hyperplasia.
why.C: Modified radical mastectomy is a treatment, and no surgery is planned before histological confirmation and receptor status; some patients will be offered neoadjuvant therapy first.

questions.right: "BI-RADS V" with a spiculated mass, suspicious microcalcification and axillary nodes is highly suggestive of malignancy, but treatment can never start without a tissue diagnosis. The next step is image-guided core needle (Tru-cut) biopsy, which gives histology, grade and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) to plan treatment. The node should also be sampled.
questions.kc: BI-RADS guides the next step. BI-RADS 1 to 2: routine screening BI-RADS 3: short- interval follow-up (about 6 months) BI-RADS 4 to 5: core needle (Tru-cut) biopsy BI-RADS 6: biopsy- proven malignancy, plan treatment Cystic mass: fine needle aspiration; solid mass: core biopsy
questions.ep: Even BI-RADS 5 needs core biopsy before any surgery; "no tissue, no treatment".

questions.stem: A 40 year old female underwent breast cancer screening due to positive family history of breast cancer. Bilateral mammogram showed very dense tissue with no suspicious lesions What is the appropriate next step?

why.A: Annual mammogram alone is routine screening for average-risk women; it ignores the reduced sensitivity of mammography in very dense breasts in a woman with a family history.
why.C: BRCA testing is offered based on the pedigree (e.g. multiple relatives, young onset, ovarian or male breast cancer), not because a mammogram showed dense tissue; it does not replace imaging.
why.D: Ultrasound is the supplemental option when MRI is unavailable or not tolerated, and the first imaging for women under about 30, pregnant women or to characterise a palpable lump; it is less sensitive than MRI for screening.

questions.right: The key clues are positive family history (higher than average risk) and very dense breast tissue on mammography. Dense tissue masks tumours, so a negative mammogram is less reassuring; for women at increased risk with dense breasts, supplemental screening with breast MRI is the most sensitive next step.
questions.kc: Supplemental breast screening: Dense breasts + increased risk (family history, genetic, prior chest radiation): add MRI MRI not possible: whole-breast ultrasound Average risk: mammography alone Mammogram finding: manage by BI-RADS (III = short interval follow-up, IV/V = biopsy)
questions.ep: Negative mammogram + very dense breasts + family history = MRI, not just repeat mammography next year.

questions.stem: 55 years old female presented to Women Health Care Clinic with bilateral breast pain and bilateral green discharge from multiple ducts . Imaging shows multiple dilated ducts, not suspicious . What to do?

why.A: Needle biopsy is for a suspicious lesion (BI-RADS 4 or 5) or a solid intraductal mass; nothing suspicious was seen.
why.C: Galactography (ductography) evaluates single-duct, spontaneous, bloody or serous discharge to localise an intraductal lesion such as a papilloma; it is not used for bilateral multi-duct green discharge.
why.D: Breast MRI is reserved for problem solving in suspicious discharge with negative standard imaging, high-risk screening or staging; it adds nothing to a benign multi-duct picture.

questions.right: "Bilateral" , "green" discharge from "multiple ducts" in a perimenopausal woman, with "multiple dilated ducts, not suspicious" on imaging, is duct ectasia, a benign process. Discharge that is bilateral, multi-duct and non-bloody is non-pathological and needs no tissue sampling. The compiler notes the ideal answer is reassurance with routine screening (benign finding); since that was not offered, interval follow-up imaging is the nearest non-invasive choice and the key.
questions.kc: Nipple discharge: pathological vs physiological. Pathological: unilateral, single duct, spontaneous, bloody or serous: imaging, then excision of the duct Physiological: bilateral, multiple ducts, expressed, green/milky: reassure Duct ectasia: perimenopausal, green discharge, nipple inversion, dilated ducts Intraductal papilloma: commonest cause of bloody discharge BI-RADS 2 benign: routine screening; BI-RADS 3: short-interval follow-up
questions.ep: Bilateral and multiple ducts = physiological; one duct and bloody = investigate.

questions.stem: Female non-pregnant with bloody nipple discharge .

why.A: Fibroadenoma presents as a mobile, painless, well-defined lump in a young woman and does not cause nipple discharge.
why.C: Breast cancer must always be excluded with bloody discharge, especially in older women or with a mass, but it is a less common cause than papilloma when discharge is the only finding.
why.D: Duct ectasia occurs around menopause and typically gives thick green or multicoloured discharge with nipple retraction (slit-like), not classically bloody discharge.

questions.right: In a "non-pregnant" (non-lactating) woman with "bloody nipple discharge" and no mass described, the most common cause is intraductal papilloma, a benign lesion in a large subareolar duct. It typically gives spontaneous, single-duct, unilateral bloody or serous discharge. Workup is ultrasound (and mammogram by age), and treatment is excision of the involved duct.
questions.kc: Nipple discharge by colour: Bloody, single duct, no mass: intraductal papilloma Green or multicoloured, perimenopausal, slit nipple: duct ectasia Milky, bilateral: galactorrhea (check prolactin, pregnancy) Bloody with mass or older age: carcinoma until excluded Papilloma management: imaging then duct excision
questions.ep: Bloody discharge with a hard mass or skin change, especially in an older woman, flips the answer to cancer.

questions.stem: A 36 y/o Female came with complaint of nipple ulceration, crusting, oozing and redness for 6 months . US and Mammography for bilateral breasts done and they were negative . What is the most appropriate thing to do?

opts.D: Follow up after 2 months or something like that

why.B: Dermatology referral treats it as eczema and delays diagnosis; nipple eczema is usually bilateral, itchy, starts on the areola and spares the nipple, and responds quickly to topical steroids.
why.C: A steroid trial is acceptable only for a short period when eczema is likely; after 6 months of a unilateral destructive lesion, steroids may give partial improvement and mask a cancer.
why.D: Further follow-up after 6 months of persistent symptoms only delays the diagnosis of a possible malignancy.

questions.right: Six months of nipple "ulceration, crusting, oozing and redness" that has not settled is Paget disease of the nipple until proven otherwise. As the compiler notes, Paget disease can have normal mammography and ultrasound and mimics eczema, so negative imaging does not exclude it. The diagnosis is made by full-thickness biopsy of the nipple (punch or wedge), which shows Paget cells; MRI may then look for an underlying cancer.
questions.kc: Paget disease of the nipple: Unilateral, starts on the nipple then spreads to the areola Eczema: often bilateral, itchy, starts on the areola, nipple spared, responds to steroids Imaging can be normal Diagnosis: full-thickness punch or wedge biopsy of the nipple Usually associated with underlying DCIS or invasive cancer Negative imaging: MRI to look for the underlying tumour
questions.ep: A nipple rash that does not heal is biopsied, even when mammogram and ultrasound are negative.

questions.stem: A 1 week postpartum female presents with fever, tenderness and a small fluctuant mass in the breast. US shows septations . What is the diagnosis and the management?

why.B: Mastitis with antibiotics: right for a tender, red, indurated breast WITHOUT fluctuation or a collection on US; once an abscess forms, antibiotics alone fail.
why.C: Inflammatory breast cancer with mastectomy: think of it when 'mastitis' does not respond to antibiotics, in a non-lactating woman, with peau d'orange and no fever; it is treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy first, not immediate mastectomy.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: A postpartum woman with fever, tenderness and a fluctuant mass has a breast abscess, and the US showing a septated (multiloculated) collection confirms a pus collection rather than diffuse inflammation. A collection must be drained; incision and drainage is the listed treatment, with antibiotics and continued milk removal.
questions.kc: Lactational breast infection. Mastitis (no fluctuation): flucloxacillin/dicloxacillin, continue breastfeeding Abscess (fluctuant mass or collection on US): drainage plus antibiotics Small, simple abscess: US-guided needle aspiration Large, multiloculated, thinned/necrotic skin: incision and drainage Not settling on antibiotics: US to look for abscess
questions.ep: Fluctuation or a collection on US means abscess; septations push toward formal incision and drainage.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman underwent surgical excision of a breast mass that was clinically and radiologically suspected to be a fibroadenoma. The final histopathology report reveals a benign fibroadenoma with an incidental finding of a single focus of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) with free surgical margins . What is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.A: Mastectomy is overtreatment for classic LCIS; bilateral risk reducing mastectomy is only considered in very high risk women such as BRCA carriers, and a unilateral one makes no sense for a bilateral risk marker.
why.B: Radiotherapy is used after breast conserving surgery for DCIS or invasive cancer, not for classic LCIS.
why.C: Cytotoxic chemotherapy is for invasive cancer; LCIS is non invasive, so the only drug option is endocrine chemoprevention.

questions.right: Classic LCIS is not a precancer that needs to be cut out: it is a marker of increased risk of invasive cancer in both breasts. Found incidentally as a single focus with free margins in a 28 year old, it needs no further surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy. The appropriate step is high risk screening and follow-up , with risk reduction (for example endocrine chemoprevention) discussed.
questions.kc: LCIS = risk marker; DCIS = precursor lesion. Classic LCIS: surveillance (clinical exam, imaging) plus chemoprevention discussion Margins do not need to be clear for classic LCIS Pleomorphic or florid LCIS: managed more like DCIS (excision to clear margins) DCIS: excision with clear margins, usually radiotherapy Atypical ductal hyperplasia on core biopsy: surgical excision
questions.ep: Swap LCIS for DCIS in the stem and the answer moves to excision with clear margins plus radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 60 YO male K/C of chronic GERD for several years, upper GI endoscopy done for him and showed metaplastic intestinal type mucosa , what is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Esophagitis is mucosal inflammation and erosion from reflux seen as erosions or ulcers on endoscopy; it does not change the epithelium into intestinal-type mucosa.
why.C: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is iron deficiency anemia with dysphagia from upper (postcricoid) esophageal webs, typically in middle-aged women; it is unrelated to GERD or metaplasia.
why.D: Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear at the gastro-esophageal junction causing hematemesis after forceful vomiting; it is an acute tear, not a chronic metaplastic change.

questions.right: Long-standing reflux ( "chronic GERD for several years" ) plus endoscopy showing "metaplastic intestinal type mucosa" is the definition of Barrett's esophagus. Chronic acid exposure makes the normal squamous lining of the distal esophagus change to columnar epithelium of intestinal type, which is a premalignant lesion for esophageal adenocarcinoma. The lead-in asks for the diagnosis, and only Barrett's names a metaplastic change.
questions.kc: Chronic GERD + intestinal (columnar) metaplasia of the distal esophagus = Barrett's esophagus. Barrett's: premalignant, risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma ; needs endoscopic surveillance with biopsies Esophagitis: erosions/ulcers, inflammation without metaplasia Plummer-Vinson: iron deficiency + dysphagia + upper esophageal web (squamous cell carcinoma risk) Mallory-Weiss: GEJ tear, hematemesis after repeated vomiting
questions.ep: Metaplasia is the keyword: "inflammation" points to esophagitis, "intestinal-type metaplasia" points to Barrett's.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with a 10-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease on pantoprazole is evaluated in the clinic because of a 4-month history of intermittent dysphagia for solids . What is the most appropriate next investigation?

why.B: Manometry confirms motility disorders such as achalasia, suggested by dysphagia to liquids as well as solids from the start; it is done after endoscopy has excluded a structural lesion.
why.C: Barium swallow is the first test for suspected motility disorders or a complex proximal stricture (after radiation or caustic injury); it cannot take a biopsy.
why.D: Fecal occult blood testing screens for colorectal bleeding, for example in iron deficiency anaemia; it does not evaluate dysphagia.

questions.right: Long-standing GERD (10 years) with new dysphagia for solids is an alarm symptom: it suggests peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus, eosinophilic oesophagitis or adenocarcinoma. Alarm features mandate upper endoscopy (EGD) , which visualizes the lesion, allows biopsy and can dilate a stricture.
questions.kc: GERD: treat empirically unless alarm features exist, then EGD. Alarm: dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding or anaemia, persistent vomiting, age >60 at onset Solids only, progressive: mechanical (stricture, cancer): EGD Solids and liquids from onset: motility: barium swallow then manometry
questions.ep: Any GERD patient who starts struggling to swallow solids gets a scope.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with 9-months history of worsening dysphagia for both solid and liquid . Recently she had episodes of ill defined central chest discomfort and nocturnal cough . Clinical examination was unremarkable (see lab results). (Labs: RBC 5 [4.7-6.1 x10^12/L male; 4.2-5.4 female]; Hb 11.8 [130-170 g/L male; 120-160 female]; Platelets 300 [150-400 x10^9/L]; WBC 7 [4.5-10.5 x10^9/L]; ESR 13 [2-10 mm/h male; 3-15 female]) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Esophageal web: intermittent dysphagia to SOLIDS only, classically with iron deficiency anaemia (Plummer-Vinson); the Hb here is only mildly low, and a web does not explain liquid dysphagia, chest discomfort or nocturnal cough.
why.C: Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker): elderly patient with oropharyngeal dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, gurgling neck swelling.
why.D: Squamous cancer of esophagus: progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids, rapid weight loss, older smoker/drinker; not equal solid and liquid dysphagia from the start.

questions.right: A 45-year-old woman with 9 months of dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset, ill-defined chest discomfort and nocturnal cough (aspiration of retained food) with near-normal labs has a motility disorder: achalasia. Dysphagia to liquids as well as solids is the decisive clue against a mechanical obstruction.
questions.kc: Dysphagia pattern tells the cause. Solids and liquids from onset: motility (achalasia) Solids then liquids, progressive, weight loss: cancer Intermittent solids, food bolus: ring/web, eosinophilic esophagitis Regurgitation of old food, halitosis: Zenker Achalasia: barium bird's beak; manometry is diagnostic
questions.ep: Liquids as hard to swallow as solids from day one = motility disorder, not a stricture.

questions.stem: A 34-Year-Old Woman With Progressive Dysphagia Diagnosed As A Case Of Achalasia . She Has No Medical Problem And Not On Any Medications. She Is Clinically Unremarkable. (Labs: RBC 4 [4.2-5.4 x 10¹²/L female]; Hb 10 [120-160 g/L female]; Platelets 455 [150-400 x 10⁹/L]; WBC 9 [4.5-10.5 x 10⁹/L]; Urea 5 [2.75-7.4 mmol/L]; Creatinine 98 [44-115 µmol/L]) Which Of The Following Is The Best Treatment Option?

why.A: Fundoplication alone treats GERD and would worsen achalasia by tightening the junction; it is only added to a Heller myotomy to prevent post-myotomy reflux.
why.C: Oral nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate) or calcium channel blockers relax the sphincter weakly and briefly; they are for patients unfit for or refusing dilatation and surgery.
why.D: Botulinum toxin injection is effective only for months and is reserved for elderly or high- risk patients who cannot tolerate dilatation or surgery.

questions.right: A young, healthy (34-year-old, no comorbidities) woman with confirmed achalasia needs a definitive treatment that disrupts the lower oesophageal sphincter. Heller myotomy (or POEM) is first line but is not offered , so pneumatic dilatation , the effective non- surgical definitive option, is best. The mild anaemia and slightly high platelets are distractors that do not change the plan.
questions.kc: Achalasia treatment ladder. Fit patient: Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication or POEM (first line) Pneumatic dilatation: definitive non-surgical option (second line) Unfit or elderly: botulinum toxin injection Last resort: nitrates or CCBs Diagnosis: barium swallow (bird's beak), confirm with manometry, endoscopy to exclude cancer
questions.ep: Young and fit = definitive therapy; Botox is for the frail.

questions.stem: A 70-Year-Old Male Complains Of Severe Chest Pain And Change In Voice After 8 Hours Of Pneumatic Dilatation Of Esophageal Stricture. What Is The Cause?

why.A: Aspiration after a procedure gives cough, fever, dyspnea and lung infiltrates, not severe chest pain with voice change.
why.B: Bleeding after dilatation presents with hematemesis or melena and is usually minor; it does not produce severe chest pain.
why.D: MI must be excluded with an ECG in any elderly patient with chest pain, but pain arising hours after esophageal instrumentation with voice change points to perforation.

questions.right: Severe chest pain hours after pneumatic dilatation of an esophageal stricture is iatrogenic esophageal perforation until proven otherwise; dilatation is the commonest cause of esophageal perforation. The voice change reflects air or inflammation tracking into the neck and mediastinum (subcutaneous emphysema, mediastinitis). Confirm with a water-soluble (Gastrografin) contrast study or CT.
questions.kc: Esophageal perforation: Causes: endoscopic dilatation (commonest), Boerhaave (vomiting), trauma, foreign body Clues: chest pain, fever, crepitus in neck, voice change, pneumomediastinum Confirm: water-soluble contrast swallow or CT Treatment: NPO, IV antibiotics, IV PPI; small contained leak in a stable patient may be managed nonoperatively, otherwise surgery
questions.ep: Mallory Weiss = mucosal tear with hematemesis; perforation = transmural with pain and emphysema.

questions.stem: 50 years old female presented to ER with sudden left lower chest pain and epigastric pain, after forceful vomiting . On examination there was decreased breath sound in the left lower chest . What is the most likely concern?

why.A: Pneumonia causes reduced breath sounds with fever, cough and crackles developing over days, not sudden pain immediately after retching.
why.B: A pneumothorax can be part of the picture, but a spontaneous pneumothorax would not explain the vomiting trigger and epigastric pain; when it follows forceful vomiting the underlying concern is esophageal rupture.
why.C: Aspiration follows vomiting in patients with reduced consciousness and causes cough, hypoxia and right lower lobe infiltrates, not sudden severe chest and epigastric pain in an alert patient.

questions.right: Sudden lower chest and epigastric pain "after forceful vomiting" is Boerhaave syndrome, a full-thickness rupture of the distal esophagus, most often on the left posterolateral wall. Leakage into the left pleural space causes a left effusion or hydropneumothorax, which explains the "decreased breath sound in the left lower chest". It is the most dangerous concern because mortality rises sharply if diagnosis and treatment are delayed.
questions.kc: Boerhaave = transmural esophageal rupture after forceful vomiting. Mackler triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema Usually left distal esophagus: left effusion or hydropneumothorax CXR: pneumomediastinum, effusion; confirm with water-soluble contrast swallow or CT with oral contrast Initial: NPO, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, PPI Large or uncontained: surgical repair Mallory Weiss: mucosal tear with hematemesis, no emphysema
questions.ep: Vomiting then hematemesis = Mallory Weiss; vomiting then chest pain and air or effusion = Boerhaave.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with vomiting blood after attacks of excessive vomiting (see lab results). (Vitals: BP 112/63 mmH; HR 89 /min; RR 21 /min; O2 sat 96 %) (Labs: Hb 135 [130-170 g/L male; 120-160 female]; WBC 7.8 [4.5-10.5 x10^9/L]) Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?

why.A: Upper GI endoscopy: confirms the tear and allows haemostasis; it is mandatory if bleeding continues, the patient is unstable or Hb falls, and many guidelines advise it for all upper GI bleeds.
why.C: Exploratory laparotomy: for Boerhaave perforation with peritonitis or failed endoscopic control; there is no sign of perforation here.
why.D: Sengstaken-Blakemore tube: a temporary bridge for uncontrolled variceal bleeding in liver disease; not for a mucosal tear in a stable patient.

questions.right: This recall's key is conservative treatment: haematemesis after excessive vomiting in a young man is a Mallory-Weiss tear, and he is haemodynamically stable (BP 112/63, HR 89) with a normal Hb of 135 . Most Mallory-Weiss tears stop bleeding on their own and heal within days with supportive care (fluids, antiemetics, acid suppression).
questions.kc: Vomiting then haematemesis. Mallory-Weiss: mucosal tear at GEJ, stable, self- limiting: supportive care Ongoing bleed or instability: endoscopy with haemostasis Boerhaave: full- thickness rupture, severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, shock: CT/contrast swallow and surgery Varices: liver disease stigmata: terlipressin, antibiotics, banding; balloon tamponade as bridge
questions.ep: Stable vitals with normal Hb = conservative; chest pain plus emphysema after vomiting = Boerhaave, not Mallory-Weiss.

questions.stem: Child with inhalation of alkaline fluid 3 h ago presented with oropharyngeal pain, difficulty swallowing, Drooling Of Saliva. Vitally stable , O/E orohpharngeal redness, mild tenderness . What to do?

opts.C: Exploration of the area in OR

why.B: Bronchoscopy examines the airway; it is used for stridor or suspected aspiration into the airway. The structure at risk after swallowing a caustic is the esophagus, assessed by upper endoscopy, not bronchoscopy.
why.C: Surgical exploration is reserved for perforation or full-thickness necrosis (peritonitis, mediastinitis, free air, shock); a stable child with mild oropharyngeal redness does not qualify.
why.D: Discharge is acceptable only for an asymptomatic child after a trivial exposure; drooling and dysphagia predict esophageal injury and mandate admission.

questions.right: The stem says "inhalation" , but oropharyngeal pain, "difficulty swallowing" and "drooling" describe a caustic (alkali) ingestion; drooling and dysphagia are markers of possible significant esophageal burn, so the child cannot be sent home. He is "vitally stable" with no airway compromise and no signs of perforation, so the correct path is admission, nil by mouth, IV fluids and supportive care with observation (and endoscopy to grade the burn). Admission is the key point of the answer; antibiotics are not routine and are added only if perforation or infection is suspected.
questions.kc: Caustic ingestion: symptoms decide admission; endoscopy grades the injury. Never induce vomiting, never give neutralising agents Symptomatic (drooling, dysphagia, vomiting, stridor): admit, NPO, IV fluids Upper endoscopy within the first 12 to 24 hours to grade esophageal burns Stridor or respiratory distress: secure the airway first Perforation (mediastinitis, peritonitis, free air): surgery Late complication: esophageal stricture
questions.ep: Alkalis cause deep liquefactive necrosis of the esophagus even when the mouth looks only mildly red; drooling means admit.

questions.stem: A patient presents with epigastric pain that worsens after eating. She has a history of NSAID use For Osteoarthritis. Endoscopy reveals a duodenal ulcer . What is the next step in management?

opts.D: change diet and take over the counter antacid

why.A: Elective surgery is not used for uncomplicated peptic ulcer; surgery is reserved for complications (perforation, uncontrolled bleeding, obstruction) or truly refractory disease.
why.B: Eradication therapy is given only once H. pylori is proven (biopsy urease test or urea breath test); here the stem gives NSAID use as the cause and no positive H. pylori test, so antibiotics are not the next step.
why.D: Diet change and over-the-counter antacids give symptomatic relief only and do not heal an endoscopically proven ulcer; they suit mild dyspepsia, not a confirmed duodenal ulcer.

questions.right: The ulcer is already confirmed on endoscopy and the clear cause is "NSAID use for osteoarthritis" . An uncomplicated peptic ulcer (no bleeding, perforation or obstruction mentioned) is treated medically: a proton pump inhibitor heals the ulcer by suppressing acid, together with stopping the NSAID where possible. The PPI is therefore the next step in management.
questions.kc: Uncomplicated peptic ulcer = medical treatment; the PPI is the core of it. NSAID ulcer: stop the NSAID if possible + PPI H. pylori positive: triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin) H. pylori is tested for in every ulcer; antibiotics only if positive Surgery: complications only (perforation, bleeding not controlled endoscopically, obstruction) NSAID must continue: keep a PPI as cover
questions.ep: Antibiotics need a positive H. pylori test; a known NSAID ulcer without that result goes to PPI.

questions.stem: Patient with peptic ulcer most significant risk factor ?

why.B: Smoking is a real but weaker contributor: it impairs healing and increases recurrence and complications, but it is not a primary cause of ulcers in the way NSAIDs and H. pylori are.

questions.right: The two leading causes of peptic ulcer disease are Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID use. H. pylori is not offered here, so between the listed options NSAIDs are the most significant risk factor, because they directly block prostaglandin mediated mucosal protection.
questions.kc: Peptic ulcer risk factors ranked. 1. H. pylori infection 2. NSAIDs and aspirin Others: smoking, physiological stress (ICU, burns), steroids combined with NSAIDs, Zollinger Ellison syndrome Duodenal ulcer: pain relieved by eating Gastric ulcer: pain worsened by eating, weight loss
questions.ep: If H. pylori appears in the options it beats NSAIDs; without it, NSAIDs win.

questions.stem: Old Female Patient Presents With UGIB Due To Peptic Ulcer , She Has Osteoarthritis & She Takes Ibuprofen For It. What's The Cause Of Her Condition?

why.A: Older age increases the risk of complications from NSAID ulcers, but age itself does not cause the ulcer; it would be the answer only to a question about a risk factor for bleeding.
why.C: Diabetes is not an established cause of peptic ulcer and there is no history of it here.
why.D: Female sex is not a cause of peptic ulcer disease.

questions.right: The lead-in asks for the cause . She has a peptic ulcer with UGIB and takes ibuprofen for osteoarthritis : NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 and prostaglandin synthesis, reducing mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow, and are the second commonest cause of peptic ulcer after H. pylori . Age and sex only modify risk; the NSAID is the causative agent here.
questions.kc: Peptic ulcer causes: H. pylori and NSAIDs account for most. Others: steroids with NSAIDs, smoking, stress (critical illness), Zollinger-Ellison NSAID ulcer bleeding risk rises with age >65, prior ulcer, anticoagulants, steroids Management: stop NSAID, PPI, test and treat H. pylori
questions.ep: Cause vs risk factor: the drug causes the ulcer; age only raises the risk.

questions.stem: 60 years old lady, have upper GI symptoms since 11mo , aggravated after meal and relived by calcium carbonate, Stool occult test: Positive , Colonoscopy normal . What the most appropriate action to do?

why.B: Empirical omeprazole is appropriate for a young patient with uncomplicated dyspepsia and no alarm features (often after an H. pylori test-and-treat), not for a 60-year-old with occult GI bleeding; PPIs can also mask and heal a malignant ulcer, delaying diagnosis.

questions.right: A 60-year-old with 11 months of dyspepsia and a "positive stool occult test" has red flags: age ≥60 with persistent symptoms and evidence of GI blood loss. Once "colonoscopy normal" has excluded a colonic source, the bleeding must be looked for in the upper GI tract, and EGD with biopsy is mandatory to exclude peptic ulcer and gastric cancer. Empirical treatment would delay a possible cancer diagnosis.
questions.kc: Dyspepsia + any alarm feature = endoscopy first. Alarm: age ≥60 (new or persistent symptoms), weight loss, dysphagia or odynophagia, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding or iron deficiency anemia, palpable mass No alarm features and young: H. pylori test and treat or PPI trial Positive FOBT: colonoscopy first; if negative and upper symptoms, EGD Both negative with ongoing bleeding: capsule endoscopy
questions.ep: Positive occult blood with a normal colonoscopy means the search moves upstream: EGD, not a PPI trial.

questions.stem: To Prevent Gastric Cancer , It's Recommended To?

why.A: Acetaminophen has no link with gastric cancer; NSAIDs and aspirin are linked with ulcers, not with cancer risk in this way.
why.B: Protein restriction has no role in preventing gastric cancer; it is a dietary measure in advanced CKD, not a cancer prevention strategy.
why.C: Increasing carbohydrates has no protective effect against gastric cancer.

questions.right: High intake of salt and salt-preserved foods (salted, pickled, smoked) is an established dietary risk factor for gastric cancer; salt damages the gastric mucosa and promotes atrophic gastritis, especially with H. pylori. Reducing salt is therefore a recommended preventive measure, together with eating fresh fruit and vegetables, stopping smoking and eradicating H. pylori.
questions.kc: Gastric cancer risk factors: H. pylori infection (most important; eradication is preventive) High salt, smoked, pickled and nitrate-rich foods Smoking Atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, partial gastrectomy Protective: fresh fruit and vegetables
questions.ep: If 'eradicate H. pylori' is among the options, it is the strongest preventive measure.

questions.stem: A 70 year old male admitted to ICU as a case of intracranial hemorrhage on mechanical ventilation , 3 days later he developed coffee ground emesis , what is the most likely cause?

why.A: H. pylori gastritis: a chronic cause of PUD in outpatients with dyspepsia; nothing links the acute bleed to the ICU stay.
why.B: Dyspepsia: a symptom (upper abdominal discomfort), not a cause of haematemesis.
why.D: NSAID-induced gastritis: right if there is a history of NSAID/aspirin use; no such drug is given here, and NSAIDs are usually avoided after intracranial haemorrhage.

questions.right: A critically ill patient (intracranial haemorrhage, on mechanical ventilation in ICU) who develops coffee-ground emesis a few days later has stress-related mucosal disease. Mechanical ventilation and major neurological injury are the classic risk factors, which is why such patients receive stress ulcer prophylaxis with a PPI or H2 blocker.
questions.kc: Stress ulcer = acute mucosal injury in critical illness. Main risk factors: mechanical ventilation, coagulopathy Also: shock, sepsis, burns (Curling ulcer), head injury/raised ICP (Cushing ulcer) Prevention: PPI or H2 blocker prophylaxis
questions.ep: Burns = Curling ulcer; head injury/neurosurgery = Cushing ulcer; both are stress ulcers.

questions.stem: A 55-Year-Old Male With A Medical History Of GERD And Osteoarthritis Presents To The Emergency Department 2 Hours After Sudden Onset Of Intense Epigastric Pain . He Takes Naproxen Almost Daily For Joint Pain. On Examination The Patient Is Pale. His Vital Signs Include: Blood Pressure Of 90/60 mmHg , A Pulse Rate Of 125 Beats/Min . He Is Exquisitely Tender To Palpation In His Abdomen, Particularly At The Epigastrium. There Is No Fluid Wave Or Hepatomegaly. You Do Not Note Any Obvious Stigmata Of Chronic Liver Disease. Which One Of The Following Tests Should Be Performed To Assist In The Diagnosis?

why.A: Aortic ultrasonography is the bedside test for a suspected ruptured AAA (pain radiating to the back, pulsatile mass, vascular risk factors); here NSAID use and epigastric peritonism point to a perforated ulcer.
why.C: CT abdomen and pelvis is more sensitive for small amounts of free air and is chosen in a STABLE patient with an equivocal X-ray; this patient is in shock.
why.D: Paracentesis is for ascites (fluid wave, chronic liver disease, suspected SBP); the stem specifically says no fluid wave and no stigmata of liver disease.

questions.right: Daily naproxen plus a sudden, intense epigastric pain of 2 hours with an exquisitely tender abdomen is a perforated peptic ulcer until proven otherwise. The patient is hypotensive and tachycardic , so the quick bedside test is plain radiography (erect chest or abdominal film) looking for free air under the diaphragm; it confirms perforation fast without moving an unstable patient to the CT scanner, and positive free air plus peritonitis goes straight to surgery.
questions.kc: Suspected perforated viscus: Risk: NSAIDs, steroids, smoking, H. pylori Picture: sudden severe epigastric pain, board-like rigidity, shock First test: erect chest X-ray (or abdominal film) for free air under the diaphragm Stable with negative or unclear film: CT abdomen Treatment: resuscitation, IV PPI, antibiotics, surgical repair (omental patch)
questions.ep: Unstable patient = bedside or quick test; stable patient with doubt = CT.

questions.stem: Male with Rheumatoid arthritis and on NSAD Complain of sever epigastric pain , vomiting and abdominal distention What is you're initial investigating?

why.B: A plain abdominal X-ray is useful for obstruction (dilated loops, air fluid levels) but is less sensitive than an erect chest film for free subdiaphragmatic air.
why.C: Endoscopy is contraindicated when perforation is suspected because insufflated air can enlarge the leak; it is for stable ulcer bleeding or dyspepsia workup.
why.D: CT abdomen is more sensitive and is used when the erect film is negative but suspicion remains; it is not the first, bedside test.

questions.right: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis on NSAIDs who develops severe epigastric pain has a perforated peptic ulcer until proven otherwise. The initial investigation is an erect chest X-ray , which quickly shows free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum); the examiner's own reasoning was exactly this.
questions.kc: Suspected perforated viscus: erect chest X-ray first. Clues: NSAID or steroid use, sudden severe epigastric pain, peritonitis Erect CXR negative but high suspicion: CT abdomen Endoscopy: avoid in suspected perforation Confirmed perforation: resuscitation, antibiotics, PPI and surgical repair
questions.ep: "Initial" picks the erect chest X-ray; "most sensitive" or "if X-ray is negative" picks CT.

questions.stem: 21-year-old male presents with generalized abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He is a heavy smoker . On examination, the abdomen is scaphoid and rigid . (See report) (Vitals: BP 110/70 mm Hg; Temperature 38.5°C; HR 105 bpm; O2 sat 95 on room air) What is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.B: Erect abdominal X-ray: shows air-fluid levels in bowel obstruction but is less sensitive than an erect CXR for free subdiaphragmatic air.
why.C: Abdominal ultrasound: first choice for biliary disease or appendicitis in children/pregnancy; poor at detecting free air.
why.D: Abdominal CT scan: most sensitive and used when the erect CXR is negative but suspicion remains, or the diagnosis is unclear; not the first step in a classic perforation picture.

questions.right: A young heavy smoker with generalized abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen , fever and tachycardia has generalized peritonitis, most likely from a perforated peptic ulcer (smoking is a PUD risk factor). The first imaging is an upright (erect) chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm, which is quick, cheap and diagnostic of perforation.
questions.kc: Suspected perforated viscus (sudden pain, board-like rigidity). Initial imaging: erect CXR for free air under the diaphragm Negative CXR, still suspected: CT abdomen Confirmed perforation: resuscitate, then laparotomy/omental patch
questions.ep: Rigid abdomen in a smoker or NSAID user: erect CXR first; CT only if it is negative or the picture is unclear.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man presented with sudden onset epigastric pain radiating to the back of 6 hours' duration. He has ischemic heart disease, on plavix and aspirin. Examination confirmed an ill looking and dehydrated patient, with generalized abdominal tenderness and absent bowel sounds (see report). Erect chest X-ray: Air under the left hemidiaphragm . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Gallstone disease: RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder, Murphy sign; does not produce free intraperitoneal air.
why.B: Acute pancreatitis: shares epigastric pain radiating to the back, but needs raised amylase/lipase or imaging and causes no pneumoperitoneum.
why.D: Gastric outlet obstruction: weeks of non-bilious projectile vomiting, succussion splash, hypochloraemic alkalosis; not sudden peritonitis with free air.

questions.right: An older man on aspirin and clopidogrel (ulcer risk) with sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back, generalized tenderness and absent bowel sounds (peritonitis) and air under the diaphragm on erect CXR has a perforated viscus, most likely a perforated peptic ulcer. Free air is the deciding clue.
questions.kc: Sudden epigastric pain: free air separates perforation from mimics. Free air under diaphragm: perforated viscus (PUD most common) Raised lipase/amylase more than 3x: pancreatitis RUQ, Murphy sign, US stones: cholecystitis Treatment of perforated PUD: resuscitation, then laparotomy with omental patch
questions.ep: Pain radiating to the back is not specific for pancreatitis; air under the diaphragm makes it perforation.

questions.stem: A 65-Year-Old Woman Underwent Elective Colon Resection. On Day 5 Post-Op , She Complained Of Abdominal Pain And Distention. While Preparing Her For CT Scan, She Had Fresh Blood And Coffee Ground In Her NGT Tube Bag. Her Vitals And Hgb Levels Are Normal . What Is The Most Appropriate Diagnostic Test?

why.A: Colonoscopy evaluates lower GI bleeding (fresh blood per rectum) and is risky early after a colon anastomosis; NGT blood means an upper source.
why.B: CT scan was planned for the pain and distension (to look for a leak or collection), but it cannot see a mucosal bleeding lesion or treat it; CT angiography is for brisk bleeding when endoscopy fails.
why.D: Abdominal ultrasound is for gallbladder, free fluid or collections; it has no role in localizing upper GI bleeding.

questions.right: Fresh blood and coffee-ground material in the NGT bag places the bleed proximal to the ligament of Treitz, most likely a stress ulcer or gastritis after major surgery. Her vitals and Hb are normal, so she is stable enough for upper GI endoscopy, which both diagnoses the source and allows endoscopic hemostasis. The colon anastomosis is not the source: it would bleed per rectum, not into the stomach.
questions.kc: Locate the bleed by where the blood appears: Hematemesis, coffee grounds, blood in NGT, melena: upper GI, do endoscopy (OGD) Fresh blood per rectum: lower GI, colonoscopy (if stable) Post-operative upper bleed: stress ulcer, think PPI prophylaxis Brisk bleed with negative endoscopy: CT angiography
questions.ep: A colon operation does not make every bleed colonic: the NGT tells you the level.

questions.stem: 48 y old k/c of hyperlipdia induced acute pancreatitis for 10y, came to er with hematwmsis for 6h Us show splenomegaly with normal portal vein Endoscopy show gastric antral ulcer

why.A: Angiography is a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure, not a diagnosis; it is used to find and embolize an arterial bleeder such as a pseudoaneurysm.
why.B: An AV fistula (e.g. splenic arteriovenous fistula) is rare and causes portal hypertension with a hyperdynamic portal flow, not a picture tied to chronic pancreatitis with a normal portal vein.
why.C: Splenic artery aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm complicates pancreatitis and can bleed into the gut or pancreatic duct (hemosuccus pancreaticus), but it does not cause splenomegaly.

questions.right: Long standing (10 year) pancreatitis , hematemesis , splenomegaly on ultrasound and a normal portal vein point to left sided (sinistral) portal hypertension. Inflammation of the pancreas thromboses the splenic vein that runs behind it; splenic blood then reroutes through the short gastric veins, causing splenomegaly and gastric (fundal) varices while the portal vein and liver stay normal. The recalled endoscopy shows an antral ulcer rather than varices, but the splenomegaly with a normal portal vein in a pancreatitis patient is what the key rests on. Definitive treatment is splenectomy.
questions.kc: Pancreatitis + splenomegaly + gastric (fundal) varices + normal portal vein = splenic vein thrombosis (sinistral portal hypertension). Mechanism: splenic vein thrombosis behind the pancreas Collaterals: short gastric veins, so isolated gastric varices Liver function and portal vein normal Treatment: splenectomy (curative) Esophageal varices with cirrhosis: generalized portal hypertension instead
questions.ep: Normal portal vein with splenomegaly and gastric bleeding in a pancreatitis patient: left sided, not cirrhotic, portal hypertension.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman underwent percutaneous trans-hepatic cholangiography for treatment of obstructive jaundice. 24 hours after the procedure , she started to have upper gastrointestinal bleeding (see lab results). (Vitals: BP 105/62 mmHg; HR 89/min; RR 22/min; O2 sat 94%) (Labs: Hb 103 g/L [130-170 male, 120-160 female]; WBC 7.8 x10^9/L [4.5-10.5]) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management plan?

why.A: CT scan (CT angiography) can show a pseudoaneurysm or clot in the ducts and is used as a non-invasive first look in stable patients, but it cannot stop the bleeding; catheter angiography is diagnostic and therapeutic.
why.B: Endoscopy is the first step for ordinary upper GI bleeding (ulcer, varices); in haemobilia it may only show blood coming from the ampulla and cannot treat the arterial source.
why.C: Ultrasound may show clot in the bile ducts or a haematoma but cannot identify or control the bleeding artery.

questions.right: Upper GI bleeding 24 hours after percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography means haemobilia: the needle tract injured a hepatic artery branch (often a pseudoaneurysm or arteriobiliary fistula) and blood is draining through the bile duct into the duodenum. Iatrogenic injury is the leading cause of haemobilia. Angiography is the gold standard because it both localises the bleeding vessel and treats it by transarterial embolisation in the same session.
questions.kc: Haemobilia = bleeding into the biliary tree, most often after liver/biliary instrumentation (PTC, liver biopsy, TIPS) or trauma. Quincke triad: upper GI bleeding, biliary colic (RUQ pain), jaundice Diagnosis and treatment: angiography with transarterial embolisation Surgery: only if embolisation fails
questions.ep: GI bleeding shortly after a hepatobiliary procedure is haemobilia until proven otherwise; go to angiography, not endoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient suspected to have appendicitis, the physician examined the left lower abdomen and that triggered pain in the RIF . What does this sign call?

why.A: Rebound tenderness is pain on sudden release of pressure at the same site (e.g. McBurney's point), showing peritonism; it is not pain referred from the left side.
why.C: Obturator sign is RIF pain on passive internal rotation of the flexed right hip, pointing to a pelvic appendix.
why.D: "Appendicular sign" is not a named eponymous sign; the specific left-to-right referral has its own name, Rovsing's.

questions.right: Pressing on the left lower abdomen and producing pain in the RIF is Rovsing's sign. Palpation displaces bowel and gas toward the inflamed appendix, irritating the right-sided peritoneum. It is one of the classic signs of acute appendicitis.
questions.kc: Appendicitis signs: know which manoeuvre each one is. Rovsing: LIF pressure gives RIF pain Psoas: pain on right hip extension (retrocaecal appendix) Obturator: pain on internal rotation of flexed hip (pelvic appendix) Rebound: pain on release (peritonitis)
questions.ep: Pain felt where you are NOT pressing (left press, right pain) = Rovsing's.

questions.stem: Patient suspected appendicitis we do abdominal examinations and there is a sign of pain referral to the RLQ when palpate the LLQ what is the name of the sign?

why.A: Psoas sign is RLQ pain on extension of the right hip (patient lying on the left side), suggesting a retrocecal appendix lying on the psoas.
why.B: Obturator sign is pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip, suggesting a pelvic appendix touching obturator internus.
why.D: Dunphy sign is increased abdominal pain with coughing, a sign of peritoneal irritation, not referral from the left side.

questions.right: Pain felt in the RLQ when the LLQ is "palpated" is Rovsing's sign. Pressure on the left pushes bowel gas and contents toward the inflamed right peritoneum, so the pain is referred to the side of the appendix.
questions.kc: Appendicitis signs: what you do and what it means. Rovsing: press LLQ, pain in RLQ Psoas: extend right hip, retrocecal appendix Obturator: internally rotate flexed right hip, pelvic appendix Dunphy: pain on coughing, peritonitis McBurney point tenderness: one third from ASIS to umbilicus
questions.ep: The sign is named by where you press (left) and where it hurts (right): Rovsing.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old man presented to Emergency Room with right lower quadrant pain and anorexia. Examination revealed tendemess and rebound tenderness at Mc Burney's point (see image, lab result and report). (HR 92 /min; Temp 38.2 °C. Labs: WBC 21.3 x 10^9/L [4.5-10.5]) Abdominal X-ray: Round 1.5 cm Radio opaque area at right iliac fossa . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

why.B: A urology consult would suit a ureteric stone (colicky loin to groin pain, hematuria), but stones do not cause McBurney rebound, fever and marked leukocytosis.
why.C: Non contrast CT is the test for renal colic; CT for appendicitis is used when the diagnosis is uncertain, which it is not here.
why.D: Gallbladder ultrasound evaluates RUQ pain; this is right lower quadrant pain.

questions.right: RLQ pain, anorexia, rebound tenderness at McBurney's point , fever 38.2 and WBC 21.3 are a clear clinical picture of acute appendicitis. The 1.5 cm round radiopaque density in the right iliac fossa is an appendicolith, which supports the diagnosis. With a confident clinical diagnosis, no more imaging is needed: proceed to appendectomy .
questions.kc: Appendicitis: clinical diagnosis first, imaging only if unclear. Migratory pain, anorexia, fever, McBurney rebound, leukocytosis Uncertain diagnosis in non pregnant adult: CT abdomen Children and pregnant women: ultrasound first Appendicolith: higher risk of perforation, favours surgery over antibiotics alone Appendicular mass or abscess: CT, antibiotics with or without percutaneous drainage
questions.ep: A right iliac fossa calcification with peritonism is an appendicolith, not a ureteric stone.

questions.stem: Female patient with periumbilical pain it was classical case of appendicitis what is the next step ?

opts.A: CT or US yes in one choice

questions.kc: Suspected appendicitis: imaging depends on who the patient is. Woman of reproductive age: pregnancy test, then ultrasound (transabdominal or transvaginal) Child or pregnant woman: ultrasound first, MRI if inconclusive in pregnancy Non pregnant adult, equivocal or obese: CT abdomen Classic picture with high clinical score: appendectomy, often laparoscopic Other options to expect: pregnancy test, laparoscopy, antibiotics
questions.ep: In any woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain, a pregnancy test precedes imaging and surgery.

questions.stem: A 24 year old complains of RLQ pain nausea and vomiting (symptoms of appendicitis). Examination shows right iliac fossa mass CT Scan: shows peri- appendicular collection 10x12 of abscess with fecalith and it extends down. What is the most appropriate next step?

why.A: Open appendectomy is for uncomplicated appendicitis, or for abscess not amenable to drainage or failure of drainage, not the first step for a large drainable abscess.
why.B: Laparoscopic appendectomy is the treatment of acute uncomplicated appendicitis; immediate surgery into an abscess or mass carries higher morbidity.
why.C: Non-intervention (antibiotics alone) suits an appendiceal phlegmon without a collection or a small abscess (under about 4 cm); a 10x12 collection needs drainage.

questions.right: RIF pain with a right iliac fossa mass and CT showing a large ( 10x12 ) peri- appendiceal abscess means complicated appendicitis with a walled-off abscess. Operating into an inflamed mass is hazardous (bowel injury, possible ileocaecal resection), so the standard is image- guided percutaneous drainage with IV antibiotics, followed by interval appendectomy if indicated.
questions.kc: Appendicitis by CT finding: Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy Phlegmon (mass, no pus): antibiotics, conservative Small abscess (< about 4 cm): antibiotics Large abscess: percutaneous drainage + antibiotics, then interval appendectomy Generalised peritonitis or perforation without walled-off collection: urgent surgery
questions.ep: Appendicitis with a walled-off abscess = drain first; with free perforation and peritonitis = operate.

questions.stem: During Laparoscopic surgery for appendicitis, a 2-cm carcinoid tumor is found at the base of the appendix. What is the most appropriate management?

why.A: Chemotherapy has little role in localized appendiceal carcinoid; it is for advanced or metastatic neuroendocrine disease.
why.B: Neuroendocrine tumors of the appendix are not treated with radiotherapy; surgery is curative.
why.D: Appendectomy alone is enough only for a small (<2 cm) tumor at the tip with no mesoappendix or node involvement.

questions.right: Appendiceal carcinoid needs right hemicolectomy when it is larger than about 2 cm , or when risk features are present: a tumor at the base (margin cannot be cleared), mesoappendix invasion or involved nodes. This tumor is 2 cm , at the threshold, and sits at the base , so appendectomy alone cannot give a clear margin or nodal clearance; a right hemicolectomy is the appropriate cancer operation.
questions.kc: Appendiceal carcinoid: size and site decide the operation. Small (under about 1 to 2 cm), at the tip, no mesoappendix or node invasion: appendectomy alone, then observe >2 cm: right hemicolectomy 1 to 2 cm with base involvement or positive margin, mesoappendix or node invasion: right hemicolectomy Appendiceal adenocarcinoma: right hemicolectomy
questions.ep: Tip and small means appendectomy only; size about 2 cm plus a base location means right hemicolectomy.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man underwent an open appendectomy for a perforated appendix. He presented to the Emergency Department on the 6th postoperative day complaining of severe abdominal pain, distension and an inability to pass stool. On examination, there is feculent discharge from the wound site with signs of peritonitis (BP 110/70 mmHg; HR 120/min; RR 18/min; Temp 38°C; SpO2 95%) (ABG: HCO3- 10 mmol/L [22-28]; PCO2 4.8 kPa [4.7-6.0]; pH 7.25 [7.36-7.45]; PO2 11 kPa [10.6-14.2]; Base excess -12 [-2 to 2]). Ultrasound abdomen: Moderate ascites with echoes and septtations. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

why.A: Wound care alone treats a superficial wound infection or seroma with a soft abdomen. Feculent discharge plus peritonitis means the problem is intra-abdominal.
why.B: IV antibiotics are needed but cannot control a fecal leak with generalized peritonitis. Antibiotics alone fit a small localized collection.
why.C: CT helps a stable patient with suspected localized collection or unclear diagnosis, guiding percutaneous drainage. Generalized peritonitis with sepsis is a clinical indication for laparotomy, and CT would only delay it.

questions.right: On the "6th postoperative day" after appendectomy for perforation, this man has "feculent discharge from the wound", generalized peritonitis, tachycardia, fever, metabolic acidosis (pH 7.25, HCO3 10, base excess -12) and septated ascites. This is a fecal leak (stump or bowel) with generalized peritonitis and sepsis, which needs source control by exploratory laparotomy.
questions.kc: Postoperative abdominal complications after appendectomy. Red, painful wound with pus, soft abdomen: wound abscess, open drainage Serous drainage, no inflammation: seroma, dressings Localized collection, stable: CT then percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics Generalized peritonitis or feculent discharge with sepsis: exploratory laparotomy Distension without tenderness days 2 to 4: ileus, check potassium
questions.ep: Feculent wound discharge plus generalized peritonitis = back to theatre.

questions.stem: A 27 years old female came to the ER with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. WBC is high. The doctor will order a CT for her. What should be done before the CT ?

why.A: CBC has already been done (the WBC is high) and does not change whether the CT is safe to perform.
why.B: Renal function matters before iodinated contrast in patients at risk of kidney injury, but in a healthy young woman the overriding safety step is excluding pregnancy.

questions.right: A 27 year old woman is of reproductive age, so pregnancy must be excluded before a CT to avoid radiation exposure of an early fetus. A pregnancy test also changes the differential, because ectopic pregnancy is a must not miss cause of severe abdominal pain with vomiting in her age group.
questions.kc: Before imaging any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain: β hCG. Positive: ultrasound first, think ectopic pregnancy Negative: CT is safe if indicated Ultrasound is first line in pregnancy and in suspected gynecologic causes Renal function: check before contrast if older, diabetic or known kidney disease
questions.ep: Every woman aged roughly 12 to 50 with abdominal pain gets a pregnancy test before radiation.

questions.stem: 28yo female came ER with left lower quadrant pain for 12h, physical examination revealed suprapubic and lower quadrant tenderness without rebound Wbc 12.5- 14 US: inconclusive What is the most appropriate next step?

why.A: CT is the next step in a non pregnant adult when ultrasound, including the pelvic study, is inconclusive or when diverticulitis or appendicitis is the leading concern; in a young woman it comes after the radiation free pelvic ultrasound.
why.C: Diagnostic laparoscopy is for persistent diagnostic uncertainty with worsening findings or peritonitis after imaging; it is not the next step in a stable patient without rebound.
why.D: Open appendectomy needs a confirmed or strongly suspected appendicitis, which usually presents in the right lower quadrant; here the pain is left sided and the diagnosis is not established.

questions.right: A "28yo female" with lower quadrant and "suprapubic" tenderness "without rebound" and mild leukocytosis has a broad differential in which gynecological causes (ovarian cyst, torsion, ectopic pregnancy, tubo-ovarian abscess) are prominent. When the initial (transabdominal) ultrasound is "inconclusive", transvaginal ultrasound is the radiation free next step that best images the ovaries and adnexa; the compiler holds TVUS as the answer for this reason.
questions.kc: Lower abdominal pain in a woman of reproductive age. First: pregnancy test Then: ultrasound, transabdominal plus transvaginal Inconclusive and not pregnant: CT abdomen and pelvis Pregnant and inconclusive: MRI Peritonitis or instability: surgery (laparoscopy)
questions.ep: If the stem says TVUS was already done and inconclusive, the answer moves to CT.

questions.stem: Long case patient with guarding and rigidity
questions.kc: Peritonitis means operate. Signs: guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness, silent abdomen Resuscitate first (IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesia), then laparotomy Unstable patient: straight to theatre, no CT Stable without peritonitis: imaging first (CT) Likely distractors: CT, observation, antibiotics alone, ultrasound
questions.ep: Guarding and rigidity are the words that turn "investigate" into "operate".

questions.stem: A patient developed severe abdominal pain after playing tennis 3 hours ago. The pain was progressive, associated with vomiting, and localized to the right lower quadrant. On examination, there is a localized mass in the right iliac fossa with tenderness and rebound. The patient is vitally stable . What is the appropriate next step in management?

why.B: Exploratory laparotomy is for an unstable patient or diffuse peritonitis; in a stable patient with a localized mass it may be unnecessary (for example a rectus sheath hematoma or an appendiceal mass is treated non-operatively).
why.C: Biopsy is irrelevant to an acute painful mass with peritoneal signs; it is for a chronic mass suspected to be neoplastic.
why.D: Discharge is unsafe with rebound tenderness and a tender mass; a surgical cause has not been excluded.

questions.right: Acute RLQ pain with a localized tender mass and rebound after exertion (tennis) has a differential that includes appendiceal mass/abscess and rectus sheath hematoma. Because the patient is vitally stable , the next step is CT abdomen to define the lesion before deciding on treatment. Stable patient = image first.
questions.kc: Acute abdomen: hemodynamic status chooses imaging vs theatre. Stable: CT abdomen Unstable or generalized peritonitis: laparotomy Exertion + sudden abdominal wall mass (does not cross midline, persists on tensing muscles): rectus sheath hematoma RIF mass after several days of appendicitis: appendiceal mass, conservative then interval care
questions.ep: "Vitally stable" in an acute abdomen usually points to CT before any operation.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of appendectomy 10 years ago presents abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation for 2 days. What is the most initial step in management?

why.A: Gastroscopy evaluates dyspepsia, upper GI bleeding or alarm symptoms; it has no role in suspected obstruction.
why.B: Colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute obstruction (risk of perforation) and the bowel cannot be prepared; it is for chronic change in bowel habits or bleeding.
why.C: Ultrasound is the first test for obstruction in young children (intussusception) but gas filled loops limit it in adults; plain X-ray comes first.

questions.right: Abdominal pain, vomiting and constipation in a patient with a previous appendectomy is adhesive small bowel obstruction until proven otherwise. The initial investigation is a plain abdominal X-ray (with an erect chest film), which shows dilated loops and air fluid levels; CT then confirms the level and looks for strangulation.
questions.kc: Suspected bowel obstruction in an adult. Commonest cause of small bowel obstruction: adhesions from previous surgery Initial imaging: abdominal X-ray (supine and upright) plus erect chest X-ray Confirmatory imaging: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast Treatment: drip and suck (IV fluids, NG tube), correct electrolytes Surgery: peritonitis, strangulation, failure of conservative care
questions.ep: "Initial" = plain X-ray; if the stem already gives air fluid levels, the next answer is CT.

questions.stem: Patient undergoes surgery developed small obstruction symptoms . No guarding , no rigidity was the most appropriate step?

why.A: Plain abdominal X-ray (with erect chest film) is the quick initial screen for dilated loops and free air, but it cannot reliably distinguish ileus from mechanical obstruction or show ischemia; it fits a lead-in asking for the initial imaging.
why.C: Ultrasound is limited by gas filled dilated bowel; it is used in pregnancy or children, not as the standard test for adult postoperative obstruction.

questions.right: After abdominal surgery, symptoms of small bowel obstruction may be adhesive or early postoperative obstruction or simply paralytic ileus. With "no guarding, no rigidity" there is no peritonitis to justify immediate laparotomy, so the patient is stable for imaging, and CT abdomen with IV contrast is the most appropriate study: it confirms obstruction, finds the transition point and cause, and shows signs of strangulation.
questions.kc: Bowel obstruction workup. Initial: erect chest X-ray plus supine and erect abdominal X-ray Confirmatory: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast Management: drip and suck (IV fluids, NG tube, electrolytes) Laparotomy: peritonitis, strangulation, failure of conservative care Ileus: dilated small and large bowel, no transition point
questions.ep: No guarding and no rigidity means image first; peritonitis means go to theatre.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man presented with a 12-hour history of sudden lower abdominal pain, associated with progressive abdominal distension , nausea, vomiting and absolute constipation . Physical examination confirmed a grossly distended abdomen, generalized discomfort with normal bowel sounds with an empty rectum (see report). Erect abdominal X-ray: Massively distended bowel loop pointing to the right upper quadrant . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Rectosigmoid cancer causes gradual obstruction preceded by change in bowel habit, weight loss or rectal bleeding. It shows distended colon proximal to a cut-off, not a single huge inverted U loop.
why.C: Volvulus is a type of closed loop obstruction, but the question asks for the most likely specific diagnosis, and the coffee bean loop names it.
why.D: Diverticulitis presents with LLQ pain, fever, tenderness and leukocytosis; obstruction is uncommon and develops gradually.

questions.right: A 75 year old man with sudden pain, gross distension, vomiting, "absolute constipation" and an "empty rectum" has large bowel obstruction. The X-ray clue "massively distended bowel loop pointing to the right upper quadrant" is the coffee bean sign of sigmoid volvulus, where the twisted sigmoid loop rises out of the pelvis toward the right upper abdomen.
questions.kc: Sigmoid volvulus. Elderly, institutionalized, chronic constipation Sudden pain, massive distension, absolute constipation X-ray: coffee bean loop pointing to RUQ Stable, no peritonitis: endoscopic (sigmoidoscopic) decompression Peritonitis or gangrene: laparotomy (Hartmann procedure) Cecal volvulus: loop pointing to the left upper quadrant
questions.ep: Loop pointing to the right upper quadrant = sigmoid; to the left upper quadrant = cecal.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal pain and absolute constipation for 2 days associated with nausea and vomiting. He has a significant past history of constipation requiring use of laxatives . On examination, his abdomen is distended, tense, tender all over with a palpable mass in the le\ lumbar and hypochondrium (see image). Which of the following is the most likely site of volvulus?

why.A: Caecal volvulus affects younger patients with a mobile caecum and behaves like a small bowel obstruction early on; it lacks the long history of chronic constipation and laxative use that defines sigmoid volvulus here.
why.B: The rectum is fixed in the pelvis and extraperitoneal, so it does not undergo volvulus.
why.D: Transverse colon volvulus is rare because the transverse colon has a short mesocolon and fixed flexures.

questions.right: Severe pain, absolute constipation , vomiting and a distended, tense abdomen indicate large bowel obstruction. In a 55-year-old with chronic constipation on laxatives , the redundant sigmoid loop twists on its long mesentery, and the twisted, dilated loop is felt as a mass in the left lumbar and hypochondrium . This is sigmoid volvulus, the commonest colonic volvulus.
questions.kc: Colonic volvulus. Sigmoid (most common): elderly, chronic constipation, laxatives, institutionalized; coffee bean sign pointing to RUQ Stable sigmoid: endoscopic detorsion, then elective sigmoid colectomy Peritonitis or ischaemia: sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy (Hartmann) Caecal: younger, needs surgery (right hemicolectomy)
questions.ep: Chronic constipation + obstruction in an older adult = sigmoid volvulus.

questions.stem: A male patient K/C of diverticulosis. Presents now with abdominal pain and fever. Imaging shows a thickened sigmoid wall with free intra-peritoneal air . How to manage?

why.B: Laparoscopy (laparoscopic lavage or resection) is used in selected stable patients in expert centres, but the classic exam answer for free perforation with peritonitis is laparotomy.
why.C: Colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute diverticulitis, especially with perforation, because insufflation worsens the leak; it is done 6 to 8 weeks after recovery to exclude cancer.

questions.right: Known diverticular disease with pain, fever, a thickened sigmoid wall and free intraperitoneal air means perforated diverticulitis. Free perforation causes peritonitis (purulent or feculent, Hinchey III to IV) and requires emergency laparotomy, usually sigmoid resection with end colostomy (Hartmann procedure) or resection with anastomosis in selected patients.
questions.kc: Diverticulitis management by severity: Uncomplicated: oral antibiotics (or observation in selected cases) Small pericolic abscess: IV antibiotics Larger abscess (about 4 cm or more): CT-guided percutaneous drainage Free air with purulent or feculent peritonitis: emergency laparotomy (Hartmann) Investigation of choice: CT with contrast; colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks later
questions.ep: Abscess = drain; free perforation = laparotomy.

questions.stem: 64 years old, male, sever abdominal pain with bloody diarrhea O / E: left lower abdominal tenderness , anorexia, significant abdominal tenderness with guarding Ct showed small collection 1x1 in the sigmoid

why.A: Sigmoidectomy (Hartmann's or resection with anastomosis) is for perforated diverticulitis with purulent or fecal generalized peritonitis, or failure of conservative treatment.
why.B: Colonoscopy is avoided in acute diverticulitis because of perforation risk; it is done after recovery (around 6 weeks) to exclude cancer.
why.D: Laparotomy with washout is for generalized purulent peritonitis; a small contained collection does not need it.

questions.right: An older patient with left lower abdominal pain and tenderness and a CT showing a small 1x1 collection by the sigmoid has complicated diverticulitis with a small pericolic abscess. Small abscesses resolve with IV antibiotics and bowel rest; as the compiler notes, localized guarding is a sign of localized peritonitis and is not by itself an indication for surgery. Surgery is reserved for generalized peritonitis, free perforation or failure of medical treatment.
