questions.kc: Diverticulitis by severity (CT based): Uncomplicated: oral antibiotics or supportive care Small abscess: IV antibiotics alone Larger abscess: CT-guided percutaneous drainage + antibiotics Generalized peritonitis / free perforation: surgery (Hartmann's) After recovery: colonoscopy to exclude cancer
questions.ep: Localized guarding is not generalized peritonitis; only diffuse peritoneal signs push you to the theatre.

questions.stem: 42 years old male can to the ER complaint of left lower quadrant pain and tenderness. WBC high . What’s the most appropriate next step ?

why.B: Ultrasound is operator dependent and limited by bowel gas in the left colon; it is preferred in children, pregnancy, or when gynecologic causes are suspected in young women.
why.C: Plain X ray only shows free air or obstruction (or the coffee bean of sigmoid volvulus) and cannot diagnose or stage diverticulitis.

questions.right: Left lower quadrant pain and tenderness with a high WBC in an adult is acute diverticulitis until proven otherwise. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast is the investigation of choice: it confirms the diagnosis, grades severity and detects abscess or perforation, which decides antibiotics versus drainage or surgery.
questions.kc: Imaging the acute abdomen depends on who and where. Adult with LLQ pain and fever or leukocytosis: CT with contrast (diverticulitis) Suspected perforation: erect chest X ray first for free air Child or pregnant woman: ultrasound first RUQ pain: ultrasound (gallbladder) AF with pain out of proportion: CT angiography (mesenteric ischemia) Colonoscopy after recovery, not during acute diverticulitis
questions.ep: Never scope acute diverticulitis; CT now, colonoscopy about 6 weeks later.

questions.stem: 38 year old obese male present with recurrent left lower quadrant pain associated with fever . Previous episodes resolved with antibiotics . DRE shows no blood. What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Crohn's disease usually presents in young patients with right lower quadrant pain, chronic diarrhea, weight loss and perianal disease; episodes do not simply resolve with short antibiotic courses.
why.C: Mesenteric ischemia affects older patients with AF or vascular disease, with sudden pain out of proportion to examination, acidosis and later bloody stool; not recurrent febrile episodes in a 38 year old.
why.D: This option was not recalled; consider the usual alternatives, such as colon cancer (older, weight loss, bleeding, change in bowel habit) or ulcerative colitis (bloody diarrhea with urgency).

questions.right: "Recurrent left lower quadrant pain" with "fever" whose "previous episodes resolved with antibiotics" is the textbook picture of recurrent sigmoid diverticulitis, and obesity is a known risk factor even in younger adults. "DRE shows no blood" argues against ischemic or inflammatory colitis.
questions.kc: LLQ pain differential. Diverticulitis: LLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis; CT with contrast to confirm Uncomplicated: antibiotics (or observation); abscess of 4 cm or more: percutaneous drainage Perforation with peritonitis: Hartmann procedure After an episode: colonoscopy to exclude cancer Bloody stool after hypotension in the elderly: ischemic colitis
questions.ep: Do not dismiss diverticulitis because the patient is under 40; obesity makes it more common in young men.

questions.stem: An old man presents with 2 days of worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever , and decreased appetite. He has mild nausea but no vomiting. On examination, the patient had bleeding per rectum . What is the most appropriate next step?

why.A: Colonoscopy: contraindicated in acute diverticulitis (risk of perforation) and not done during active bleeding with an inflamed colon; it is done 6 to 8 weeks after the attack to exclude cancer.
why.C: Exploratory laparotomy: reserved for generalized peritonitis (purulent/faecal) or failure of conservative treatment; this patient has no generalized peritonism and has not yet been imaged.
why.D: Percutaneous drainage: treats a diverticular abscess that has been shown on CT; it cannot come before the CT that finds it.

questions.right: An old man with LLQ pain, fever and anorexia for 2 days has acute diverticulitis until proven otherwise, and diverticular disease is also a common cause of rectal bleeding in the elderly. The investigation of choice is CT abdomen with contrast , which confirms diverticulitis and shows complications (abscess, perforation) that decide further management.
questions.kc: Acute diverticulitis: image first, then treat by complication. Suspected diverticulitis: CT abdomen with contrast Uncomplicated: antibiotics/conservative Abscess: image-guided percutaneous drainage Generalized peritonitis: surgery (Hartmann) Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks later to exclude cancer
questions.ep: Colonoscopy is the trap: it is never done in the acute phase of diverticulitis.

questions.stem: A 60 year old male presents to the Emergency Department with an acute abdomen. Imaging showed localized perforated diverticulitis , and a conservative treatment was started. Which of the following health promotion strategies is recommended?

opts.B: More high fiber into the diet

why.A: Low fibre diet: a low-residue diet is sometimes used briefly during the acute attack, but long term it raises colonic pressure and is the classic risk factor for diverticular disease.
why.C: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: Once the acute episode of diverticulitis settles, the recommended health promotion advice is a high-fibre diet . Fibre softens and bulks the stool, lowering colonic intraluminal pressure, and higher fibre intake is associated with fewer diverticular complications.
questions.kc: Diverticular disease prevention and follow-up. Long term: high fibre diet, fluids, exercise, weight loss, stop smoking Avoid NSAIDs and opioids where possible Nuts and seeds need not be avoided Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks after the attack to exclude cancer
questions.ep: Low fibre causes diverticular disease; high fibre prevents recurrence.

questions.stem: A 65-Year-Old Patient Presented With Fever 38.3 And Abdominal Left Lower Quadrant Tenderness, 1 Episode Of Bloody Diarrhea (They Mentioned That it STOPPED) CT Showed: Thickened Left Colon, Multiple Diverticuli , And Paracolonic Collection 1 × 1 cm . What Is Most Appropriate Next Step?

why.A: Colonoscopy is avoided in the acute phase because insufflation risks perforation; it is done 6-8 weeks after the episode to exclude cancer. The bloody diarrhoea (now stopped) is the trap that tempts you to scope early.
why.C: Exploratory laparotomy is for generalized peritonitis from free perforation (purulent or feculent), or failure of non-operative care.
why.D: Percutaneous CT-guided drainage is right for a larger abscess (roughly 3-4 cm or more) that is accessible; a 1 cm collection is too small to drain and responds to antibiotics.

questions.right: This is acute diverticulitis (LLQ tenderness, fever, thickened left colon with diverticula) complicated by a small paracolic abscess (1 × 1 cm) , with the bleeding having stopped and no sign of free perforation or peritonitis. Small abscesses (generally under about 3-4 cm) resolve with IV antibiotics, bowel rest and observation, so conservative management is the most appropriate next step.
questions.kc: Complicated diverticulitis: manage by abscess size and peritonitis. Uncomplicated or small abscess: antibiotics, bowel rest (conservative) Larger abscess: percutaneous drainage + antibiotics Free perforation with peritonitis: laparotomy (Hartmann or resection) CT with contrast is the investigation of choice; colonoscopy after 6-8 weeks
questions.ep: Never scope an acute diverticulitis; wait 6-8 weeks.

questions.stem: 65-year-old man presents with severe left lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever. A CT scan reveals diverticulitis with a 1x1 cm peri-colonic fluid collection . He is hemodynamically stable . What is the best management for this patient?

why.B: Colonoscopy is avoided in acute diverticulitis (perforation risk); it is done about 6 to 8 weeks after recovery to exclude cancer.
why.C: Laparoscopy (lavage or resection) is for purulent or feculent peritonitis or failure of non- operative care, not a small contained abscess.
why.D: Percutaneous drainage is for larger abscesses (about 4 cm or more) that are accessible; a 1 cm collection is not amenable to drainage.

questions.right: CT shows diverticulitis with a 1 × 1 cm pericolic collection in a hemodynamically stable man: complicated but with a tiny abscess. Small abscesses (under about 3 to 4 cm) are too small to drain and resolve with conservative management: IV antibiotics, bowel rest and fluids.
questions.kc: Diverticulitis: Hinchey stage guides treatment. Uncomplicated or small pericolic abscess (under about 3 to 4 cm): antibiotics (conservative) Larger abscess: CT-guided percutaneous drainage + antibiotics Purulent or feculent peritonitis: surgery (Hartmann or resection with anastomosis) Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks after resolution
questions.ep: Same scenario with a 5 cm abscess flips the answer to percutaneous drainage.

questions.stem: 60 y old make came to the ER with massive bleeding what is the most common cause ?

why.A: Colon cancer usually causes occult bleeding, iron deficiency anemia or a change in bowel habit with weight loss, rarely massive hematochezia.
why.C: Angiodysplasia is an important cause of bleeding in the elderly (often right colon, recurrent, low grade and painless), but it is second to diverticulosis for acute massive lower GI bleeding.
why.D: Not a clinical option (placeholder from a partial recall).

questions.right: In a 60-year-old with massive lower GI bleeding, the most common cause is diverticular bleeding from diverticulosis. Diverticular bleeding is typically sudden, painless and large volume, arising from a vasa recta at the neck of a diverticulum; the recaller notes no vitals were given, so the epidemiology of massive bleeding decides it.
questions.kc: Lower GI bleeding causes: Most common overall and massive in adults over 50: diverticulosis Elderly, recurrent, low grade, right colon, aortic stenosis association: angiodysplasia Occult bleeding, anemia, weight loss: colon cancer Bloody diarrhea with pain in an elderly vascular patient: ischemic colitis Young adult with bloody diarrhea: IBD
questions.ep: Diverticulitis (inflamed) rarely bleeds; diverticulosis (non-inflamed) is the bleeder.

questions.stem: Old Women Presented With Lower GI Bleeding . On Examination, Diffusely Tender Abdomen. PR Exam Showing Fresh Blood. Patient Is Hypotensive Despite Receiving Blood . What Is The Most Appropriate Next Step In Management?

why.A: FFP corrects coagulopathy (warfarin, massive transfusion) as part of resuscitation, but it does not stop an ongoing bleed in a patient who is still hypotensive.
why.B: Angiography (CT angiography then embolization) is the localizing and therapeutic step for brisk lower GI bleeding in a patient who responds to resuscitation; persistent shock despite blood pushes toward the operating room in this recall.
why.D: Emergency colonoscopy needs a stable patient and ideally bowel preparation; it is for stable or stabilized lower GI bleeding, not refractory shock.

questions.right: The red-flag words are 'hypotensive despite receiving blood' : the patient has failed resuscitation, and a diffusely tender abdomen suggests an intra-abdominal catastrophe rather than a simple colonic bleed. This recall's key is laparotomy, following the surgical teaching (Sabiston) that persistent hemodynamic instability in GI bleeding despite resuscitation is an indication for operation, as endorsed by the compiler and the confirmed examiner.
questions.kc: Lower GI bleeding ladder: All: resuscitate (large-bore IV, blood, reverse anticoagulants); exclude upper source Stable: colonoscopy after bowel prep Unstable but responding: CT angiography, then embolization Unresponsive to resuscitation: surgery (laparotomy) Recurrent obscure bleed: tagged RBC scan, capsule endoscopy
questions.ep: 'Despite receiving blood' is the phrase that flips angiography to laparotomy.

questions.stem: A patient presents with lower Gi bleeding with fresh blood per rectum and was given resuscitation with fluids and blood, but the patient became unstable . (See report) ( Blood pressure 80/60 mm Hg ) What is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.A: FFP is part of resuscitation only when there is coagulopathy (for example anticoagulant use or massive transfusion); it does not stop a bleeding lesion and no coagulopathy is stated.
why.B: Angiography with embolization is the usual step for an unstable patient who responds partly to resuscitation; this card's key treats failure to respond to resuscitation as the trigger for surgery instead (the examiner's own answer was angiography and was counted as his mistake).
why.D: Emergency colonoscopy needs a hemodynamically stable patient and usually bowel preparation; it is unsafe and slow in a patient at 80/60 despite resuscitation.

questions.right: This recall's key is laparotomy because the patient became unstable (BP 80/60) despite resuscitation with fluids and blood; the compiler's rule (Sabiston) is that persistent hypotension despite resuscitation in lower GI bleeding means operative control. Most confirmed examinees chose laparotomy. Note that current algorithms place CT angiography or catheter angiography with embolization before surgery in unstable patients, reserving surgery for failure of these.
questions.kc: Acute lower GI bleeding: stability decides. Stable: colonoscopy (after bowel prep); if not tolerating prep or high suspicion of active bleeding: CT angiography Unstable: resuscitate, then CT angiography and catheter angiography/embolization Unstable despite resuscitation (exam rule) or failed embolization: laparotomy Source unknown after workup: tagged RBC scan, small bowel evaluation
questions.ep: Unstable but responding to fluids: angiography; still unstable after fluids and blood: the exam key goes to laparotomy.

questions.stem: 12 yo present with fresh bleed per rectum. Colonoscopy done and showed Blood oozing from ileocecal valve ?

why.A: Angiodysplasia is a cause of painless bleeding in the elderly, typically in the right colon, and would be seen in the colon itself.
why.C: Crohn disease presents with chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss and growth failure, and colonoscopy would show ulcerated, inflamed ileum rather than blood coming from above.

questions.right: In a 12 year old with fresh rectal bleeding , blood oozing from the ileocecal valve means the colon is clean and the source lies proximally in the small bowel. The commonest cause of painless small bowel bleeding in children is Meckel diverticulum, whose ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates the adjacent ileum. It is confirmed with a technetium 99m pertechnetate scan.
questions.kc: Painless rectal bleeding: age points to the cause. Child or young adult, small bowel source: Meckel diverticulum → Tc 99m pertechnetate scan Elderly: diverticulosis or angiodysplasia Colonoscopy normal plus negative upper source → small bowel (Meckel scan in young, capsule endoscopy in adults) Meckel rule of 2: 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, often symptomatic before age 2
questions.ep: Blood coming through the ileocecal valve means look upstream: in a child that is Meckel.

questions.stem: A patient bleeding with stool, with a mass that projects and reduce spontaneously . What grade of hemorrhoid?

why.A: Grade 1 hemorrhoids bleed but do not prolapse at all.
why.C: Grade 3 hemorrhoids prolapse and need to be pushed back manually.
why.D: Grade 4 hemorrhoids are permanently prolapsed and cannot be reduced.

questions.right: Internal hemorrhoids that prolapse and reduce spontaneously are grade 2. The key is what happens to the prolapse: no prolapse is grade 1, spontaneous reduction is grade 2, manual reduction is grade 3, irreducible is grade 4.
questions.kc: Internal hemorrhoid grades and treatment: Grade 1: bleeding, no prolapse: fiber, fluids, topical Grade 2: prolapse, reduces spontaneously: rubber band ligation (or sclerotherapy) Grade 3: prolapse, manual reduction: band ligation, surgery if failed Grade 4: irreducible: hemorrhoidectomy Over 45 with bleeding: colonoscopy to exclude cancer
questions.ep: "Reduces by itself" = 2; "pushes it back" = 3.

questions.stem: 24 years old with recurrent on and off PR bleeding after defecation. She has manually reduction of hemorrhoids after defecation ( grade 3 ) was diagnosed. On examination: 3 hemorrhoids 2,7,10 O'clock Hb was low . What is the Definitive treatment ?

why.A: Observation is not appropriate for recurrent bleeding causing anemia; it is reserved for asymptomatic hemorrhoids found incidentally.
why.B: Band ligation is the usual office treatment for grade 1 to 2 (and some small grade 3) hemorrhoids; it is less durable for large, three column grade 3 disease and is not the definitive option asked for here.
why.D: Conservative measures (fiber, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths) are the first step for every grade, but they do not correct prolapse or stop recurrent bleeding with anemia.

questions.right: This is a young patient with "recurrent" bleeding from grade 3 hemorrhoids (prolapse needing manual reduction) involving all three primary positions and already causing anemia ("Hb was low"). The lead-in asks for the "definitive" treatment, and for symptomatic grade 3 disease with complications such as anemia, excisional hemorrhoidectomy gives the lowest recurrence and is the definitive option.
questions.kc: Internal hemorrhoid grades and treatment. Grade 1 (bleed, no prolapse): conservative, then banding or sclerotherapy Grade 2 (prolapse, reduces spontaneously): banding Grade 3 (needs manual reduction): banding, or hemorrhoidectomy if large, recurrent or failed Grade 4 (irreducible): hemorrhoidectomy Age 45 to 50 or older or red flags: colonoscopy before treating
questions.ep: Watch the lead-in: "initial" for grade 3 can be banding, but "definitive" means hemorrhoidectomy.

questions.stem: Pt complaining of bleeding during and after defecation for 10d. There is also itching and discomfort ?

why.A: Anal fissure: bleeding with SHARP, tearing pain during and lasting after defecation (often with constipation); pain is the key clue, and it is absent here.
why.C: Fistula in ano: persistent perianal discharge (pus/mucus) from an external opening, usually after a perianal abscess; not bleeding with stools.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: Bleeding during and after defecation with itching and discomfort (not severe pain) is the picture of haemorrhoids: bright red bleeding plus perianal pruritus and mucus discharge from prolapsing cushions. The recaller is sure pain was not described, which removes the defining feature of a fissure.
questions.kc: Bright red rectal bleeding: decide by pain and swelling. Painless bleeding, pruritus, prolapse: internal haemorrhoids Bleeding with severe sharp pain on defecation: fissure Acute painful purplish perianal lump: thrombosed external haemorrhoid Chronic discharge after an abscess: fistula Painful fluctuant swelling with fever: perianal abscess
questions.ep: Itching alone does not make it a fissure; the word that flips to fissure is PAIN on defecation.

questions.stem: A man presents with painless rectal bleeding during defecation. On examination, hemorrhoidal tissue is noted to prolapse during straining but reduces spontaneously . He was treated with injection sclerotherapy , after which his symptoms completely resolved. Which of the following is the most likely type of hemorrhoids?

why.A: External: below the dentate line with somatic innervation, so they are painful; injection sclerotherapy is not used for them.
why.B: Thrombosed: an acutely painful, tense, purplish lump; managed by excision if early or conservatively, not sclerotherapy.
why.C: Prolapsed: describes the behaviour (a grade), not the type; these are internal haemorrhoids that happen to prolapse.

questions.right: Painless bleeding , tissue that prolapses on straining and reduces spontaneously (grade II) and a cure with injection sclerotherapy all point to internal haemorrhoids. They lie above the dentate line, where the mucosa has visceral innervation, so bleeding and sclerotherapy injection are painless.
questions.kc: Internal haemorrhoid grading and treatment. Grade I: bleed, no prolapse: diet/fibre, sclerotherapy Grade II: prolapse, reduce spontaneously: banding or sclerotherapy Grade III: need manual reduction: banding, surgery if failed Grade IV: irreducible: haemorrhoidectomy External: below dentate line, painful
questions.ep: 'Prolapsed' is a grade, not a type: internal haemorrhoids can prolapse, external ones are below the dentate line.

questions.stem: A 46 YO Patient With Hemorrhoids Present With Fresh Blood However , Patient Had ANEMIA & Hb Of ~10-11 , What's Next Step In Management?

why.A: Conservative care (fibre, fluids, topical agents) is first line for low-grade hemorrhoids in a young patient without red flags; here anaemia must be investigated first.
why.B: Hemorrhoidectomy is for grade III-IV or failed office treatment, but only after malignancy has been excluded.
why.C: Band ligation suits grade I-III internal hemorrhoids once colonoscopy has excluded another bleeding source.

questions.right: Hemorrhoids cause bright red bleeding but rarely anaemia ; anaemia (Hb about 10-11) is a red flag that demands exclusion of colorectal cancer even when hemorrhoids are clearly present. In addition, at age 46 the patient is within the colorectal screening age (start age lowered to 45). So colonoscopy comes before any hemorrhoid treatment.
questions.kc: Rectal bleeding with hemorrhoids: scope first if any of these. Age ≥45 Anaemia or iron deficiency Change in bowel habit, weight loss Family history of colorectal cancer Then treat by grade: conservative, banding, hemorrhoidectomy (grade IV)
questions.ep: Hemorrhoids do not explain anaemia until a colonoscopy says so.

questions.stem: 30-year-old presented with intermittent perianal pain associated with purulent discharge. Examination confirmed a low-lying perianal fistula with an external opening posteriorly close to the anal verge . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

why.A: MRI pelvis maps complex fistulas: recurrent, high, multiple tracts, or Crohn's disease. A simple low fistula does not need it.
why.B: Fistulography is an old, less accurate test, largely replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound. It has no role in a simple low fistula.
why.D: Lateral internal sphincterotomy treats a chronic anal fissure (sharp pain on defecation, posterior midline, sentinel tag) that fails medical therapy. It is not a fistula operation.

questions.right: A "low-lying" fistula with the external opening "close to the anal verge" is a simple fistula involving little or no sphincter. It is treated by fistulotomy (laying open the tract), which has a high cure rate and a low risk of incontinence when little sphincter is divided. Imaging is not needed for a simple, clinically clear fistula.
questions.kc: Perianal fistula management. Simple low fistula: fistulotomy High or complex fistula (much sphincter involved): seton, MRI to map Known Crohn's with complex fistula: MRI, antibiotics, then infliximab if refractory Recurrent fistulas, Crohn's not known: colonoscopy Goodsall rule: posterior external opening tracks to the posterior midline
questions.ep: Low and simple = lay it open; high or complex = seton and MRI.

questions.stem: Fistula at 7 o'clock Where will it open most likely?

why.A: A 7 o'clock opening lies behind the transverse anal line, so its track curves to the posterior, not the anterior, midline; anterior external openings run straight to the nearest crypt rather than to the anterior midline.
why.C: A left lateral internal opening is not expected; posterior tracks curve to the midline rather than staying lateral.
why.D: "Left medial" is not a recognized site for a fistula internal opening and does not follow Goodsall's rule.

questions.right: By Goodsall's rule (patient in lithotomy, 12 o'clock anterior), an external opening behind the transverse anal line follows a curved track to an internal opening in the posterior midline (6 o'clock). 7 o'clock is in the posterior half, so its internal opening is most likely in the posterior midline.
questions.kc: Goodsall's rule: draw a transverse line across the anus. Opening in front of the line (anterior half): straight radial track to the nearest crypt Opening behind the line (posterior half): curved track to the posterior midline Exception: anterior opening more than about 3 cm from the verge may curve to the posterior midline Simple low fistula: fistulotomy Complex or multiple fistulas: MRI to map the tracts
questions.ep: Positions 4 to 8 o'clock (lithotomy) are posterior and go to 6 o'clock; 10 to 2 o'clock are anterior and go straight in.

questions.stem: A 44 year old presented with 1 year of perianal discharge . NO CHANGE IN BOWEL HABITS (did not mention any family Hx of crohns). On examination, personal fistulas were found on 7 and 3 o'clock (2 openings). What is the most appropriate next step?

why.B: A fistulogram is an older, less accurate test that poorly shows secondary tracts and sphincter involvement; MRI has replaced it.
why.C: Endoanal ultrasound is a reasonable alternative in expert hands, but MRI is better for complex, multiple or high tracts and is the standard answer.
why.D: Colonoscopy is chosen when Crohn's disease is suspected (diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain, change in bowel habits); some teaching sends multiple fistulas to colonoscopy first, but this stem deliberately removes those clues.

questions.right: Two external openings (7 and 3 o'clock) with a year of discharge make this a complex fistula. Before any surgery the tracts, internal openings and relation to the sphincters must be mapped, and pelvic MRI is the gold standard for this. The stem stresses no change in bowel habits and no Crohn's history, which argues against starting with an IBD workup.
questions.kc: Perianal fistula workup by complexity. Simple low fistula: examination, then fistulotomy Complex (multiple, recurrent, high): MRI pelvis to map tracts Bowel symptoms or suspected Crohn's: colonoscopy Known Crohn's fistula: MRI, drain sepsis (seton), antibiotics, then anti TNF therapy
questions.ep: Add diarrhea, weight loss or a family history of Crohn's to the stem and the answer can shift to colonoscopy.

questions.stem: 28-year-old patient presented to the clinic complaining of perianal discharge. He reported history of on-off abdominal pain . He reported family history of Crohn's disease. On examination, three fistula openings at 3, 7 and 9 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?

why.B: MRI pelvis maps the fistula tracts and abscesses; it is the next step when Crohn's is already known, and is still needed here before surgery, but it does not establish the underlying diagnosis.
why.C: Fistulogram is an old contrast study with poor accuracy that has been replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound.
why.D: This option was not recalled; other choices a student may meet here are fistulotomy (only for a simple low fistula, and avoided in suspected Crohn's because of poor healing and incontinence risk) or infliximab (only after Crohn's is confirmed).

questions.right: "Three fistula openings" make this a complex (multiple) fistula, and the background of "on-off abdominal pain" with a "family history of Crohn's" points to undiagnosed Crohn's disease. In a complex fistula without a known Crohn's diagnosis, the next step is colonoscopy with biopsies to confirm Crohn's, because the underlying disease changes the whole management (medical therapy and biologics rather than aggressive fistula surgery).
questions.kc: Complex perianal fistula: first look for Crohn's. Simple low fistula: fistulotomy Complex fistula + Crohn's NOT known: colonoscopy to confirm Crohn's Complex fistula + Crohn's known: MRI pelvis to assess the tracts Then antibiotics; refractory: infliximab Crohn's clues: intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, family history
questions.ep: Multiple fistulas with Crohn's clues: colonoscopy; the same fistulas with no bowel clues: MRI.

questions.stem: Male (30s to 40s) presented with perianal discharge for months. He denied history of bowel changes . On examination he had 3 perianal sinuses at 3,5 and 7. Proctoscopic exam was normal . Next step?

why.B: Endoanal ultrasound is a reasonable alternative but is operator dependent and less accurate than MRI for complex, high or branching tracts.
why.C: Fistulogram has poor accuracy and has been replaced by MRI.
why.D: Colonoscopy is chosen when the history suggests Crohn's (abdominal pain, diarrhea, family history of Crohn's); with no bowel changes and a normal proctoscopy it does not define the fistula.

questions.right: "Three perianal sinuses" means a complex fistula, and the surgeon needs a map of the tracts, branches and any hidden abscess before operating. Here there is no pointer to Crohn's: he "denied history of bowel changes" and "proctoscopic exam was normal" . Pelvic/perineal MRI is the most accurate test for fistula anatomy, which is why it is the key here.
questions.kc: Complex fistula workup depends on whether Crohn's is suspected. No Crohn's clues: MRI pelvis/perineum to map the tracts Crohn's clues but not diagnosed: colonoscopy Known Crohn's: MRI pelvis Endoanal US: alternative to MRI, operator dependent Fistulogram: obsolete
questions.ep: Read the bowel history: "no bowel changes, normal proctoscopy" turns the answer from colonoscopy to MRI.

questions.stem: A patient has a perianal fistula with an external opening at the 7 o'clock position. What is the most common site for the internal opening ?

why.A: Left lateral is not a classic internal opening site; under Goodsall's rule only anterior openings run straight (radially) to the nearest crypt, and 7 o'clock is posterior.
why.B: Midline anterior is wrong because the opening is posterior; the anterior midline is not the classic target of any Goodsall pattern, since anterior openings run radially to the nearest crypt.
why.D: A straight lateral (radial) tract applies to external openings anterior to the transverse line, not to a posterior opening at 7 o'clock.

questions.right: Goodsall's rule: draw a transverse line across the anus (3 to 9 o'clock in lithotomy). An external opening posterior to this line, such as "7 o'clock" , follows a curved tract to an internal opening in the posterior midline (6 o'clock). This is why midline posterior is correct here.
questions.kc: Goodsall's rule (lithotomy position, 12 o'clock = anterior): External opening posterior to the 3 to 9 line: curved tract to the posterior midline (6 o'clock) External opening anterior to the line: straight radial tract to the nearest crypt Exception: anterior openings far (more than about 3 cm) from the anal verge may still curve to the posterior midline Most fistulas arise from infected anal glands (cryptoglandular)
questions.ep: "Posterior curves to the midline, anterior goes straight"; 7 o'clock sits in the posterior half.

questions.stem: A 44 year old female presented with 1 year of perianal discharge . No change in bowel habits . On examination, perianal fistulas were found on 7 and 3 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?

why.B: Colonoscopy is the answer when Crohn's disease is suspected: diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anaemia, rectal bleeding or extraintestinal features. Another examinee favoured it because complex or multiple fistulas can be the first sign of Crohn's.

questions.right: This recall's key is pelvic MRI : two perianal fistulas (at 3 and 7 o'clock) after a year of discharge make this a complex fistula, and MRI is the imaging standard to map the tracts, their relation to the sphincters and any hidden abscess before surgery. The compiler stresses that there are no bowel symptoms (no change in bowel habit, anaemia, bleeding or extraintestinal signs), and major texts give no recommendation to screen for Crohn's with colonoscopy in that setting.
questions.kc: Perianal fistula workup. Simple low fistula: clinical exam, fistulotomy Complex (multiple, recurrent, high, crossing sphincter): MRI pelvis (or endoanal US) and examination under anaesthesia Bowel symptoms, anaemia, extraintestinal features: colonoscopy for Crohn's Crohn's fistula: antibiotics, seton, anti-TNF (infliximab)
questions.ep: Multiple fistulas without bowel symptoms: map with MRI; scope only if Crohn's features exist.

questions.stem: Perianal pain and pruritus fluctuating mass and there was high WBCs and fever , they did NOT mention sizes. Appropriate next?

why.A: IV antibiotics alone cannot sterilise a walled-off pus collection; they are an adjunct (for cellulitis, sepsis, diabetes or immunosuppression), never a replacement for drainage.
why.C: Fistulotomy treats an established chronic fistula tract; it is not done for an acute abscess, and a fistula may or may not develop after drainage. D. This option was not recalled; other choices students meet are sitz baths or analgesia alone (inadequate for an abscess) and needle aspiration (used for small breast abscesses, not perianal ones).

questions.right: A "fluctuant mass" with "perianal pain" , "fever" and "high WBCs" is a perianal abscess. Fluctuation means pus has collected, and pus needs drainage: incision and drainage is the treatment, with antibiotics only as an adjunct in selected patients. The size does not change this.
questions.kc: Abscess = drain it. Perianal abscess: painful, tender, fluctuant swelling + fever + leukocytosis: incision and drainage Antibiotics: adjunct only (cellulitis, sepsis, diabetes, immunosuppression) Chronic discharge after a burst abscess = fistula: fistulotomy if simple and low Anal hematoma: painful swelling with normal vitals and WBC
questions.ep: Fluctuation is the trigger: fluctuant pus goes to drainage, antibiotics alone are the classic wrong option.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old diabetic patient complains of a painful perianal swelling with fever for the last 3 days (see report) (Temperature 38.0°C) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Anal fissure gives sharp pain during and after defecation with fresh bleeding; there is no swelling or fever (except a sentinel tag in chronic fissure).
why.B: Uncomplicated (internal) hemorrhoids cause painless bright red bleeding and prolapse; they are not febrile, tender swellings.
why.D: Thrombosed piles cause an acutely painful, tender bluish perianal lump, but they do not cause fever; a fever of 38.0°C here points to infection.

questions.right: A painful perianal swelling with fever (38.0°C) over 3 days in a diabetic patient is a perianal abscess. Fever and systemic signs separate an infected collection from the non- infective anal conditions, and diabetes is a risk factor for perianal sepsis. Treatment is prompt incision and drainage.
questions.kc: Painful perianal lump: fever decides. Painful swelling + fever/leukocytosis: perianal abscess: incision and drainage Painful bluish lump, afebrile: thrombosed external hemorrhoid (perianal hematoma) Pain on defecation + bleeding, no lump: fissure Painless bleeding: internal hemorrhoids Recurrent discharge after drained abscess: fistula in ano
questions.ep: Take away the fever and the same painful lump becomes thrombosed piles.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old man with no previous medical history, presented with 3-weeks history of bloody diarrhoea . He reported frequent urges to defecate , associated with mild lower abdominal cramps. He had experienced similar attacks in the past, but milder associated with bloating and loose stool, which was mucus with few blood drops . Abdominal examination was soft with mild tenderness at left lower quadrant but no guarding. (Vitals: BP 110/70 mmHg; HR 76 /min; Temperature 36.6 °C; O2 sat 95 %) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Diverticulitis: an older patient with acute LLQ pain, fever and leukocytosis; not recurrent bloody diarrhoea in a teenager.
why.B: Ischaemic colitis: an elderly patient with vascular risk factors, sudden pain then bloody diarrhoea, thumbprinting at watershed areas; not a relapsing course at 17.
why.C: Crohn's disease: usually non-bloody diarrhoea, RLQ pain, weight loss, perianal disease, mouth ulcers; rectal urgency with blood favours UC.

questions.right: A 17-year-old with 3 weeks of bloody diarrhoea , urgency (rectal involvement), previous milder attacks with mucus and blood, and LLQ tenderness has a relapsing colitis starting in the rectum: ulcerative colitis. Normal vitals and a soft abdomen fit a mild to moderate flare.
questions.kc: UC vs Crohn's. UC: rectum upward, continuous, bloody diarrhoea, urgency/tenesmus, LLQ Crohn's: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural, RLQ pain, fistulas, perianal disease, weight loss Ischaemic colitis: elderly, acute, watershed (splenic flexure) Diverticulitis: older, LLQ pain, fever
questions.ep: Blood plus urgency/tenesmus in a young patient = UC; non-bloody diarrhoea plus RLQ pain and weight loss = Crohn's.

questions.stem: Which of following is associated with the highest risk of malignant transformation ?

why.B: Tubular adenoma is the most common adenoma but has the lowest malignant risk of the three adenoma types.
why.C: Hyperplastic polyps are non-neoplastic and carry negligible risk (small distal ones); they rank lowest.
why.D: Tubulovillous adenoma has intermediate risk, between tubular and pure villous adenoma.

questions.right: Among colorectal polyps, the villous adenoma carries the highest risk of malignant transformation. Risk rises with villous architecture, size above 1 cm and high-grade dysplasia, so a pure villous adenoma ranks above mixed and tubular forms.
questions.kc: Polyp cancer risk: villous > tubulovillous > tubular > hyperplastic. Risk rises with villous component, size above 1 cm, high-grade dysplasia Hyperplastic: non-neoplastic Sessile serrated lesions: premalignant (serrated pathway)
questions.ep: "Villous = villain": the more villous, the higher the cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has progressive constipation. DRE reveals a hard bleeding mass. Proctoscopy shows a large annular ulcerating rectal mass approximately 10 cm from the anal verge. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis is normal .

why.B: Abdominoperineal resection is for very low tumors involving the sphincter complex; a tumor at 10 cm can usually be removed with sphincter preservation, and surgery comes after full work up.
why.C: Anterior resection is the likely eventual operation for a tumor at 10 cm (after pelvic MRI and neoadjuvant therapy if locally advanced), but not before colonoscopy excludes synchronous lesions.
why.D: Diverting colostomy is for complete or near complete obstruction or perforation; this patient has progressive constipation, not acute obstruction.

questions.right: A 67-year-old with a rectal mass 10 cm from the anal verge found on proctoscopy, with a normal staging CT , needs the whole colon examined before any operation. Full colonoscopy rules out synchronous tumors or polyps elsewhere in the colon (and provides a biopsy), which could change the extent of resection. He is not described as obstructed, so colonoscopy is safe.
questions.kc: Colorectal cancer found on limited endoscopy: complete colonoscopy, then stage, then treat by stage. Colonoscopy: synchronous lesions and tissue diagnosis CT chest, abdomen and pelvis: distant staging Rectal cancer: pelvic MRI for local (T and N) staging Early rectal cancer: surgery (anterior resection or APR) Locally advanced: neoadjuvant chemoradiation, surgery, then chemotherapy Acute obstruction: surgery first, colonoscopy contraindicated
questions.ep: Bowel obstruction flips the order: relieve the obstruction surgically first and do colonoscopy later.

questions.stem: Year-old man undergoes colonoscopy, which reveals a 1.5 cm polyp in the colon. Histopathology: 1.3 Tubular Adenoma COMPLETELY Resected . When should the next colonoscopy screening be performed?

why.A: A 3 to 6 month repeat is for incomplete or piecemeal resection of a large polyp, to check the site for residual tissue. The stem says COMPLETELY resected.
why.C: Ten years is the interval after a normal colonoscopy in an average risk person, or after small hyperplastic polyps. An advanced adenoma needs closer follow up.
why.D: No surveillance is wrong because adenomas, especially those ≥10 mm, carry a risk of metachronous neoplasia.

questions.right: A tubular adenoma of 10 mm or larger is an advanced adenoma by size. When it is "COMPLETELY" resected the surveillance colonoscopy is repeated in 3 years. The word completely is the key: it rules out the short interval used for incomplete or piecemeal removal.
questions.kc: Post-polypectomy surveillance interval. Normal colonoscopy, average risk: 10 years 1 to 2 small (<10 mm) tubular adenomas: 7 to 10 years Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous component or high grade dysplasia: 3 years Piecemeal resection of a large polyp: 6 months Malignancy risk: villous > tubulovillous > tubular > hyperplastic
questions.ep: Size ≥1 cm makes it advanced: 3 years, unless removal was incomplete.

questions.stem: Young patient (30s or 40s) with a right inguinal hernia that bulges but reduces manually, he reduced it every time it bulges for many years, and last time this morning . He presented with vomiting and abdominal pain , On examination: mild abdominal tenderness, NO tenderness at the inguinal (hernia site) bilaterally, and NO bulge felt at the inguinal (hernia site) bilaterally. What is the most appropriate step:

why.B: Urgent hernia repair is for an obstructed or strangulated hernia that is felt in the groin (tender, irreducible); here nothing is palpable, so the diagnosis must be confirmed first, and laparotomy rather than groin repair may be needed.
why.C: Repair in two days (semi elective) ignores new obstructive symptoms after self reduction; a possibly ischemic loop cannot wait.
why.D: Reassurance is unsafe: vomiting and abdominal pain after forced reduction may mean obstruction or a reduced strangulated segment.

questions.right: A long standing reducible right inguinal hernia that he reduced himself this morning , followed by vomiting and abdominal pain with no bulge and no tenderness at the hernia site, raises reduction en masse or reduction of a compromised loop: the hernia is gone from the groin but bowel may still be trapped or ischemic inside the abdomen. Examination cannot confirm this, so CT abdomen and pelvis is the most appropriate step to look for obstruction, a trapped sac or ischemic bowel before deciding on surgery.
questions.kc: Hernia states guide urgency; symptoms after self reduction with an empty groin = image for reduction en masse. Reducible: elective repair (open mesh first line; laparoscopic for bilateral or recurrent) Irreducible, non tender: early repair Obstructed or strangulated (tender, irreducible, systemic signs): emergency surgery Obstruction with an occult cause: examine the groin, then image Reduction en masse: sac and contents pushed back together, still constricted
questions.ep: No bulge and no groin tenderness plus obstructive symptoms after reduction: think reduction en masse and image, do not just reassure.

questions.stem: Patient with irreducible hernia and negative cough impulse what is the most appropriate step?

why.A: Reassurance is never right for a hernia that cannot be reduced; it only fits a non-hernia swelling such as divarication of recti (midline bulge, intact fascia).
why.B: Ultrasound helps when the diagnosis is uncertain (for example an occult groin hernia or a lump of unclear nature); here the hernia is clinically established and delaying surgery for imaging risks strangulation.

questions.right: An "irreducible" hernia with a "negative cough impulse" means the contents are stuck in the sac and the neck is tight enough that pressure no longer transmits, raising concern for incarceration with obstruction or strangulation. A hernia cannot be cured conservatively, and an irreducible one is at risk of compromise, so the most appropriate step is surgical exploration and repair.
questions.kc: Hernia states and what they mean. Reducible: soft, positive cough impulse, elective repair Irreducible (incarcerated): cannot be pushed back, needs surgery Obstructed: irreducible plus vomiting and distension, urgent surgery Strangulated: tense, very tender, red skin, systemic signs, emergency surgery Loss of cough impulse suggests a tight neck or that the lump is not a hernia
questions.ep: A negative cough impulse in a known hernia is a warning sign of incarceration, not a reason to reassure.

questions.stem: A patient presents following hernia repair . What is the best advice to prevent the recurrence of the hernia?

why.A: Laxatives for 6 months: avoiding constipation and straining helps in the early postoperative period, but months of laxatives is not standard advice; correct only if the stem stresses chronic constipation.
why.C: Compression bandage for 3 months: does not protect the repair; compression is used for lymphoedema or to support a seroma, not to prevent recurrence.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: Recurrence after hernia repair is driven by raised intra-abdominal pressure and strain on the healing repair while the tissue/mesh incorporates. Among the options, avoiding heavy lifting during the healing period addresses this directly and is the classic exam advice to prevent recurrence.
questions.kc: Hernia recurrence risk factors and prevention. Raised intra-abdominal pressure: heavy lifting, chronic cough, straining (constipation, BPH) Patient factors: smoking, obesity, poor nutrition Technical: tension repair, wound infection Advice: avoid heavy lifting during healing, treat cough/constipation/prostatism, stop smoking, lose weight
questions.ep: If the question asks what to fix BEFORE repair, think of the cause of raised pressure (cough, constipation, BPH).

questions.stem: A Patient Post Hernia Repair , What Is Advice To Prevent Recurrence Of Hernia?

opts.C: Avoid Lifting Heavy Objects For 6 Months

why.A: Compression bandages are used for lymphoedema or venous disease; neither a bandage nor a hernia belt (truss) prevents recurrence after repair.
why.B: Long-term laxatives are not routine; they are used short term only if constipation causes straining, and 6 months of laxatives is unnecessary.

questions.right: After hernia repair, the classic exam advice to prevent recurrence is to avoid straining and heavy lifting that raise intra-abdominal pressure while the repair heals, commonly quoted as about 6 months. Of the options, this is the only one that targets the mechanism of recurrence.
questions.kc: Recurrence prevention after hernia repair targets raised intra-abdominal pressure. Avoid heavy lifting and straining during healing Treat chronic cough, constipation, prostatism Stop smoking, lose weight Mesh repair lowers recurrence compared with suture repair
questions.ep: Pick the option that lowers intra-abdominal pressure, not a device.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old female with long-standing incisional hernia presents to ER with abdominal pain and fecalith discharge . Her hernia is strangulated with ulcers and necrosis . All vitals are normal. Management?

why.A: Dressings are local wound care and do nothing for dead bowel; they suit a superficial wound infection only.
why.B: Laparoscopy is used for elective repair of uncomplicated incisional hernias; a contaminated, necrotic, fistulating hernia requires open exploration and resection.
why.C: MRI wastes time and adds nothing; the diagnosis is clinical and management is urgent surgery.

questions.right: This is a strangulated incisional hernia with skin ulceration and necrosis and fecal discharge (bowel necrosis or perforation with an enterocutaneous fistula). Strangulation is a surgical emergency regardless of age or normal vitals: she needs an open laparotomy to resect non-viable bowel, debride necrotic tissue and close the defect (mesh avoided in a contaminated field).
questions.kc: Hernia states and treatment. Reducible: elective repair Irreducible (not tender): early elective repair Obstructed: urgent surgery Strangulated (tender, skin changes, necrosis): emergency open surgery with resection of non-viable bowel Contamination: avoid permanent synthetic mesh
questions.ep: Normal vitals do not cancel strangulation; necrosis means emergency laparotomy.

questions.stem: Elderly women with previous laparotomy for sigmoidectomy after complicated diverticulitis, with incisional hernia symptomatic painful

why.A: Reassurance is only for small asymptomatic hernias in patients unfit for surgery; this hernia is painful and symptomatic.
why.B: Open repair without mesh (suture repair) has high recurrence rates and is reserved for very small defects or a contaminated field where mesh is avoided.
why.C: Laparoscopic repair for an incisional hernia is always done with mesh; 'laparoscopic repair' alone is incomplete compared with the option that specifies mesh reinforcement.

questions.right: A symptomatic, painful incisional hernia after a midline laparotomy should be repaired, and incisional hernias of any meaningful size are repaired with mesh because suture-only repair has unacceptably high recurrence. In an elderly patient (higher wound-complication risk) with a clean field and a moderate defect, laparoscopic repair with mesh reinforcement gives fewer wound infections and faster recovery, as the compiler's cited guidance describes.
questions.kc: Incisional hernia repair choice. Symptomatic: repair; mesh for almost all Laparoscopic mesh: higher wound-risk patients (obese, smokers, comorbid), defects under about 10 cm Open (with mesh/component separation): large defects, loss of domain, contamination, low- risk patients Suture alone: only tiny defects or contamination
questions.ep: Incisional hernia = mesh; choose the option that says mesh.

questions.stem: Newborn had right inguinal hernia (reducible) , and right high ride testis, and left inguinal hernia . Most appropriate next step:

why.A: Waiting until 6 years is never appropriate for an inguinal hernia; delay exposes the infant to incarceration and testicular or bowel ischemia. Waiting applies to hydrocele (until about 1 to 2 years) or umbilical hernia (until about 4 to 5 years), not inguinal hernia.
why.C: Observation is for a communicating hydrocele in infancy (often resolves by 1 to 2 years) or an umbilical hernia (often closes by about 4 to 5 years), not for an inguinal hernia.

questions.right: Any inguinal hernia in a newborn or infant is an indication for surgery, because it will not close spontaneously and the risk of incarceration is highest in early infancy. The treatment of pediatric inguinal hernia is herniotomy (high ligation of the patent processus vaginalis), done soon after diagnosis; here it is bilateral, and the high-riding right testis can be addressed (orchidopexy) at the same time.
questions.kc: Pediatric groin rule: Inguinal hernia (reducible, cough or crying impulse): herniotomy, soon after diagnosis, no mesh Incarcerated: attempt reduction, then repair within days; failed reduction: emergency surgery Hydrocele (transilluminates): observe until about 1 to 2 years Umbilical hernia: observe until about 4 to 5 years unless large or complicated Undescended testis: orchidopexy by about 6 to 18 months
questions.ep: "Wait" belongs to hydrocele and umbilical hernia; any inguinal hernia in a child gets herniotomy.

questions.stem: you can examine newborn right reducible inguinal hernia , high raising testies. Left inguinal hernia with no swelling

why.A: Observation is right for a hydrocele (transilluminates, often resolves by 1-2 years) or an umbilical hernia, not an inguinal hernia, which risks incarceration.
why.C: Mesh repair is for adults; children have no posterior wall weakness and need only sac ligation, and mesh would impede growth.
why.D: Waiting is the approach for umbilical hernia (surgery if not closed by around 4-5 years); delaying an inguinal hernia repair risks incarceration and testicular ischaemia.

questions.right: Despite the confusing wording, the core is a newborn with a right reducible inguinal hernia . Infant inguinal hernias are due to a patent processus vaginalis, never close spontaneously, and carry a high risk of incarceration in the first months, so they are repaired promptly by herniotomy (high ligation and excision of the sac, no mesh). The left side with no swelling needs no surgery.
questions.kc: Pediatric groin and umbilical swellings. Inguinal hernia: herniotomy soon after diagnosis Incarcerated: attempt reduction, repair within 24-48 h Hydrocele: observe until 1-2 years Umbilical hernia: observe; surgery if persists at 4-5 years or >2 cm after 2-3 years Undescended or retractile testis: separate issue, orchidopexy around 6-12 months if undescended
questions.ep: Child + inguinal hernia = herniotomy, never mesh, never wait.

questions.stem: The newborn comes to the follow up clinic. you notice that there is a single testis in the scrotum, and the other is the inguinal canal but can be pushed down to the scrotum manually . What is the diagnosis?

why.A: An undescended testis cannot be manipulated into the scrotum (or springs straight back up on release); a palpable one needs orchidopexy, a non palpable one laparoscopy.
why.C: Torsion presents with acute severe pain, swelling and a tender high riding testis, not an incidental painless finding at a routine clinic visit.

questions.right: The decisive clue is that the testis lying in the inguinal canal can be pushed down to the scrotum manually . A testis that can be brought fully into the scrotum is classified as retractile: it is normally descended but pulled up by an active cremasteric reflex. It needs reassurance and periodic follow up, not surgery.
questions.kc: Testis outside the scrotum: can you bring it down and does it stay? Brought into the scrotum and stays: retractile → observe yearly Brought down but springs back: gliding testis, managed as undescended Palpable but cannot reach the scrotum: undescended → orchidopexy (ideally 6 to 18 months) Non palpable: diagnostic laparoscopy Painful, high riding, absent reflex: torsion → surgery
questions.ep: A retractile testis can ascend later and become undescended, so it still needs follow up.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old baby was admitted with an inability to tolerate food and non- bilious vomiting over the past 2-days. On examination, he appears to be dehydrated. There is an olive shaped mass palpable in the epigastric region measuring 2 × 2 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

why.B: Balloon dilatation does not durably relieve a thick muscular hypertrophy and is not standard; it is used for some adult peptic pyloric strictures or anastomotic strictures.
why.C: Gastrojejunostomy is a bypass for adult gastric outlet obstruction (for example unresectable distal gastric cancer); it is far too morbid for an infant with a simple muscle hypertrophy.

questions.right: Non-bilious vomiting plus a palpable "olive shaped mass" in the epigastrium is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Definitive treatment is surgical: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, which splits the hypertrophied pyloric muscle down to the mucosa. The "dehydrated" clue means fluids and electrolytes are corrected first, but among the listed options pyloromyotomy is the management.
questions.kc: Pyloric stenosis: correct fluids/electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy. Typical age 2 to 8 weeks, firstborn male, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hungry after feeds Exam: olive in epigastrium/RUQ, visible peristalsis Labs: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis Imaging: ultrasound (thickened, elongated pylorus) Immediate step: IV fluid and electrolyte correction Definitive: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
questions.ep: If the lead-in says "immediate" or "first" step in a dehydrated infant, the answer flips to fluid and electrolyte correction, not surgery.

questions.stem: A woman in her 40s present with abdominal pain for 24 hours and nausea Physical examination shows positive murhpy sign US: multiple gall bladder stones, thickened wall and pericholecystic fluid Febrile ptn Vitally stable Labs High ALP ALT 60 (slight elevation) WBC 18000 What is the most appropriate management

opts.B: laproscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission

why.A: Interval (delayed, about 6 weeks) cholecystectomy is for patients presenting late (beyond about 72 hours to a week), with a dense inflammatory mass, or too unwell for surgery; this patient is early and stable.
why.C: IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics are the initial supportive step, but they are not the definitive management the question asks for; on their own they risk recurrence and complications.

questions.right: Pain for 24 hours with fever, positive Murphy sign , WBC 18000 and an ultrasound showing stones, a thick wall and pericholecystic fluid is acute calculous cholecystitis. The patient is vitally stable and presents well within 72 hours, so the best management is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission, after starting fluids, analgesia and antibiotics. Early surgery shortens stay and avoids recurrent attacks while waiting.
questions.kc: Acute cholecystitis: supportive care first, then early laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Clinical: RUQ pain >4 to 6 hours, fever, Murphy sign, leukocytosis First imaging: ultrasound (stones, thick wall, pericholecystic fluid) Initial: NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics Definitive: laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within 72 hours High surgical risk or acalculous: percutaneous cholecystostomy Jaundice, fever, dilated CBD: cholangitis → ERCP first
questions.ep: Mildly raised ALP and ALT are common in cholecystitis; marked jaundice or a dilated CBD would add a search for a duct stone before surgery.

questions.stem: Patient came to the ER with severe abdominal pain and tenderness unstable imaging ? showed gallstone and gallbladder thickness 9x7 mm . The most appropriate step

why.B: Open cholecystectomy has no advantage as a first choice; it is used when laparoscopy is not feasible or as a conversion for difficult anatomy or bleeding.
why.C: Interval cholecystectomy suits a stable patient presenting late or with a settled inflammatory mass, not a sick, unstable patient who needs source control now.
why.D: Observation is never enough for symptomatic cholecystitis with instability; untreated it can progress to gangrene, perforation and sepsis.

questions.right: Severe pain and tenderness with gallstones and a thickened gallbladder wall indicate acute cholecystitis, and a patient described as unstable raises concern for a complicated (gangrenous or perforated) gallbladder. That calls for emergency source control rather than delay, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the standard approach, converting to open only if needed. Resuscitation and IV antibiotics run alongside.
questions.kc: Timing of cholecystectomy in acute cholecystitis. Stable, early (<72 hours): early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission Late presentation or inflammatory mass: antibiotics then interval cholecystectomy Complicated (gangrene, perforation, emphysematous): emergency cholecystectomy Too sick or high risk for surgery: percutaneous cholecystostomy Asymptomatic stones: no surgery
questions.ep: If percutaneous cholecystostomy were offered for a patient too unstable for anesthesia, it would compete with emergency surgery.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows a diffusely calcified gallbladder without stones. What is the most appropriate management?

why.B: Percutaneous biopsy of a suspected gallbladder malignancy risks seeding the tract and bile leak, and does not treat the condition; the gallbladder is removed instead.
why.C: Cholecystostomy tube is a temporising drainage for acute (often acalculous) cholecystitis in critically ill or unfit patients, not for a chronically calcified gallbladder.
why.D: Observation is inappropriate in a symptomatic patient with a porcelain gallbladder because of its cancer association.

questions.right: A diffusely calcified gallbladder (porcelain gallbladder) is associated with gallbladder carcinoma, and this patient is also symptomatic with 2 months of RUQ pain. The appropriate management is cholecystectomy, which treats symptoms, removes the malignancy risk and gives tissue for histology.
questions.kc: Gallbladder surgical indications: Porcelain gallbladder: cholecystectomy (malignancy association) Symptomatic gallstones and acute cholecystitis (early, within about 72 hours): laparoscopic cholecystectomy Polyp 10 mm or more: cholecystectomy Acalculous cholecystitis in the critically ill: cholecystostomy tube Asymptomatic gallstones: usually observe
questions.ep: Critically ill ICU patient + distended GB without stones = cholecystostomy tube; calcified GB wall = cholecystectomy.

questions.stem: 64 year old male came with right upper quadrant pain for 2 months. US:- Calcified wall gall bladder without stones X:- ray : Calcified wall gall bladder without stones What is the most appropriate management:

why.A: Observation may be discussed for an incidental, asymptomatic porcelain gallbladder in a poor surgical candidate, but this patient has symptoms.
why.C: Percutaneous biopsy of a suspected gallbladder cancer risks tumour seeding and bile leak, and a calcified wall is not a mass to biopsy; the gallbladder is removed and examined instead.
why.D: A cholecystostomy tube is temporary drainage for acute cholecystitis in a patient too sick for surgery; it does not treat a porcelain gallbladder.

questions.right: A calcified gallbladder wall on ultrasound and X-ray is a porcelain gallbladder , which is linked to gallbladder carcinoma. This patient is also symptomatic (RUQ pain for 2 months) and 64, so cholecystectomy is indicated, both to treat symptoms and to remove the cancer risk; the examiner answered laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
questions.kc: Indications for cholecystectomy beyond gallstone symptoms. Porcelain gallbladder (cancer risk) Gallbladder polyp 1 cm or more, or growing Symptomatic gallstones or after biliary colic, cholecystitis, gallstone pancreatitis Acute cholecystitis too sick for surgery: cholecystostomy tube Mass or thick irregular wall: stage with CT, then radical resection
questions.ep: Calcified wall = porcelain gallbladder = cholecystectomy, even with no stones.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the clinic with right upper quadrant (RUQ) abdominal pain that started about 1 hour after eating a fatty meal. The pain was sharp, colicky, and has now subsided. She has had similar episodes in the past , usually after meals. On examination, she is now stable, afebrile, with no tenderness. (See report) Abdominal Ultrasound: a 2 cm polyp inside the gallbladder What is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.A: Order CT scan to further characterize the lesion
opts.C: Observe and repeat ultrasound in 6 months

why.A: CT adds little to characterizing a gallbladder polyp already measured on ultrasound; it is used for staging if malignancy is strongly suspected (for example invasion of the liver), which is not described.
why.C: Ultrasound surveillance is for small asymptomatic polyps (under 10 mm without risk factors); a 2 cm symptomatic polyp should not be watched.
why.D: Antibiotics and conservative care are for acute cholecystitis (fever, persistent pain, Murphy sign, thick wall); she is afebrile and non-tender.

questions.right: Two indications for cholecystectomy coexist: the polyp is 2 cm (well above the 10 mm threshold, carrying real malignant risk) and the patient is symptomatic with recurrent postprandial RUQ colic after fatty meals. Either alone justifies removal, so laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the next step. She is currently stable and pain-free, so this is a planned procedure.
questions.kc: Gallbladder polyp: size and symptoms decide. 10 mm or more: cholecystectomy 6 to 9 mm with a risk factor (age over 50, PSC, Indian ethnicity, sessile): cholecystectomy Growth of 2 mm or more on follow-up: cholecystectomy Symptoms attributable to the gallbladder: cholecystectomy Small, asymptomatic, no risk factors: ultrasound surveillance
questions.ep: A 5 mm asymptomatic polyp flips the answer to surveillance ultrasound.

questions.stem: man presents to the emergency department with right upper quadrant (RUQ) abdominal pain, fever , and jaundice. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated liver enzymes and serum bilirubin . What is the most appropriate Diagnostic imaging investigation?

why.B: Abdominal ultrasound is the first line, cheap bedside test showing gallstones and duct dilation, and is the answer when the lead-in is 'initial' or 'first'; it often misses distal CBD stones, which is why it was not keyed for 'most appropriate diagnostic'.
why.C: CT is less sensitive than ultrasound or MRCP for gallstones and CBD stones; it is chosen for suspected malignancy, pancreatitis complications or an unclear acute abdomen.

questions.right: RUQ pain, fever and jaundice are Charcot triad, and raised bilirubin with liver enzymes indicate biliary obstruction (ascending cholangitis, usually from a CBD stone). This recall's key is MRCP because the lead-in asks for the most appropriate diagnostic imaging: MRCP is the most accurate non invasive test to show the CBD, the level and the cause of obstruction (stones, stricture) before ERCP. Note that ultrasound is the usual first line test in this picture.
questions.kc: Charcot triad = cholangitis: US first, MRCP to define the duct, ERCP to diagnose and treat. Initial imaging: abdominal ultrasound (stones, dilated ducts) Best non invasive look at the CBD: MRCP Diagnostic and therapeutic: ERCP (biliary decompression) Reynolds pentad (plus hypotension, confusion): urgent decompression Labs: leukocytosis, high bilirubin, ALP and GGT
questions.ep: 'Initial' imaging in Charcot triad = ultrasound; MRCP wins only if the lead-in stresses the most accurate or diagnostic test.

questions.stem: 60-year-old man presents with jaundice, pruritus, and weight loss . Abdominal ultrasound: Dilated intrahepatic bile duct with no gallstones What is the next investigation?

why.A: HIDA scan tests cystic duct patency for acute cholecystitis (or bile leak); it adds nothing in a jaundiced patient with a suspected tumour.
why.B: ERCP is now mainly therapeutic (stenting, stone extraction, brushings), so it is not the first diagnostic test here; it is right for drainage of an obstructed duct or for CBD stones with cholangitis.
why.C: This option was not recalled; if it had been CT abdomen (pancreas protocol) or MRCP, that would usually be preferred over EUS.

questions.right: Painless obstructive jaundice with pruritus and weight loss in a 60-year-old, with dilated ducts and no gallstones , points to a malignant obstruction (pancreatic head or periampullary tumour). After ultrasound, the usual next step is cross-sectional imaging (pancreas- protocol CT or MRCP), but as the compiler notes, neither CT nor MRI was offered. Among the options, EUS is the best next investigation: it images the pancreatic head and distal bile duct in detail and allows fine-needle biopsy for tissue diagnosis.
questions.kc: Painless jaundice + weight loss = malignancy until proven otherwise. Step 1: abdominal ultrasound (dilated ducts? stones?) Step 2: pancreas-protocol CT (diagnosis and staging) or MRCP EUS ± FNA: small lesion not seen on CT, or tissue needed ERCP: therapeutic (stent, stones, brushings) HIDA: acute cholecystitis
questions.ep: If CT or MRCP appears in the options, it beats EUS as the next investigation.

questions.stem: elderly, epigastric pain for 3m, wt loss , jaundice and dark urine. There was dilatation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct . Labs: cholestatic picture (They did not mention if the gallbladder is palpable or shrunk)

why.A: Klatskin tumor (hilar cholangiocarcinoma) blocks the hepatic duct confluence, so only the intrahepatic ducts dilate and the gallbladder is collapsed; here the extrahepatic ducts are dilated too.
why.B: Gallbladder cancer usually presents with RUQ pain or mass on a background of gallstones, and when it causes jaundice it does so by invading the hilum/common hepatic duct, leaving the distal CBD undilated.

questions.right: An elderly patient with weight loss and progressive obstructive jaundice ( "jaundice and dark urine" , cholestatic labs) has a malignant biliary obstruction. The level is set by the imaging: "dilatation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts" means the block is at the lower end of the CBD, which fits ampullary (periampullary) cancer. The compiler's rule applies here: do not think Klatskin unless the gallbladder is collapsed and only intrahepatic ducts are dilated.
questions.kc: Level of biliary obstruction = which ducts are dilated. Intrahepatic only + collapsed gallbladder: Klatskin (hilar) tumor Intra + extrahepatic + distended gallbladder: distal obstruction (ampullary, pancreatic head, distal cholangiocarcinoma) Courvoisier: palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice = malignancy, not stones Ampullary cancer may cause intermittent jaundice and occult GI bleeding
questions.ep: Dilated CBD rules out a hilar lesion; Klatskin needs a collapsed gallbladder and a normal CBD.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman underwent an uneventful laparoscopic cholecystectomy . 2 weeks later , she presents to the Emergency Department with vague abdominal pain (see lab results and report). (Vitals: BP 117/59 mmHg; RR 19 /min; HR 83 /min; Temp 37.4 °C; SpO2 95 %. Labs: Hb 103 g/L [130-170 male, 120-160 female]; WBC 7.8 x 10^9/L [4.5-10.5]; Total bilirubin 3.7 umol/L [3.5-16.5]) CT scan: Large collection in the sub-hepatic area . Which of the following is most appropriate next step?

why.A: Open operative drainage is reserved for failed minimally invasive treatment, major bile duct injury or an unstable patient with peritonitis.
why.B: CT guided drainage is the usual first step to empty a large collection after cholecystectomy, and several sources prefer it here; it is not this recall's key, which targets the leak itself.
why.C: Laparoscopic re-exploration is more invasive than image guided or endoscopic treatment in a stable patient; it is used for multiple collections or failed drainage.

questions.right: This recall's key is ERCP with biliary stent placement because a large subhepatic collection two weeks after an uneventful laparoscopic cholecystectomy is most often a biloma from a cystic duct stump leak. ERCP with a stent (or sphincterotomy) lowers the pressure in the bile duct so the leak can seal. Normal WBC, temperature and bilirubin show a stable, uninfected patient without obstruction.
questions.kc: Bile leak after cholecystectomy: drain the collection, then treat the leak. Collection (biloma or abscess): percutaneous image guided drainage Confirmed leak (bile in drain, HIDA leak): ERCP with sphincterotomy or stent Major duct injury or transection: hepaticojejunostomy by a biliary surgeon Unstable or generalized peritonitis: surgery
questions.ep: Other versions of this recall in the deck carry percutaneous drainage as the key; read the options, because without ERCP the drainage option is the answer.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman underwent an uneventful laparoscopic cholecystectomy . 2 weeks later , she presents to the Emergency Department with vague abdominal pain (see lab results and report). (Vitals: BP 117/59 mmHg; RR 19 /min; HR 83 /min; Temp 37.4 °C; SpO2 95 %. Labs: Hb 103 g/L [130-170 male, 120-160 female]; WBC 7.8 x 10^9/L [4.5-10.5]; Total bilirubin 3.7 umol/L [3.5-16.5]) CT scan: Large collection in the sub-hepatic area . Which of the following is most appropriate next step?

why.A: Open operative drainage is for an unstable patient, generalized peritonitis or failure of percutaneous drainage.
why.C: Laparoscopic drainage is a reoperation; it is kept for multiple or inaccessible collections or failed percutaneous drainage. D. Option not recalled; the examiner was certain it was neither ERCP with stent nor CT guided drainage.

questions.right: A large subhepatic collection two weeks after laparoscopic cholecystectomy is a biloma or abscess. The patient is stable (normal vitals, WBC 7.8), so the least invasive effective treatment is percutaneous image guided drainage , which empties the collection and confirms whether it is bile. In this examiner's version there was no ERCP option, so drainage is the clear key.
questions.kc: Intra-abdominal collection after surgery: size and stability decide. Small (under 4 x 4 cm): antibiotics Large (4 x 4 cm or more), stable: percutaneous drainage Multiple collections: laparoscopy Unstable: laparotomy Bile in the drain: add ERCP with stent to seal the leak
questions.ep: If ERCP with stent appears among the options, a different version of this recall was keyed to it; drainage of the collection is still the logical first step.

questions.stem: A Female patient presents 2 weeks after cholecystectomy with vague abdominal pain. Imaging shows a 10–15 cm subhepatic fluid collection consistent with a biloma . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.A: Observation: only for small, asymptomatic collections; a 10 to 15 cm biloma with pain needs drainage.
why.B: Surgical drainage: reserved for failure of percutaneous drainage, generalized biliary peritonitis or major duct injury; too invasive as first step.
why.D: MRCP: helps map a suspected major bile duct injury, but it does not treat the collection; the collection is drained first.

questions.right: A 10 to 15 cm subhepatic biloma 2 weeks after cholecystectomy is a large collection that will not resolve on its own and risks infection. The treatment is image-guided percutaneous drainage , which is minimally invasive and both diagnostic and therapeutic. If the drain keeps putting out bile (an ongoing leak, e.g. from the cystic duct stump), ERCP with sphincterotomy/stent is added.
questions.kc: Bile leak after cholecystectomy. Collection (biloma/abscess): percutaneous image- guided drainage Persistent leak (cystic stump, duct of Luschka): ERCP with sphincterotomy and/or stent Major duct transection: MRCP/cholangiography then surgical repair (hepaticojejunostomy) Biliary peritonitis or failed drainage: surgery
questions.ep: Large collection: drain it first; ongoing bile leak through the drain: ERCP stent.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman underwent an uneventful laparoscopic cholecystectomy . Two weeks later, she presented to the Emergency Department with vague abdominal pain. (See report) CT scan: Large collection in the subhepatic area . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

why.A: Open operative drainage is for unstable patients, peritonitis, or failure of percutaneous drainage; it is unnecessarily invasive here.
why.B: CT-guided drainage is itself a percutaneous technique (image guidance by CT or ultrasound); the key uses the broader term "percutaneous drainage", so the general option is the one keyed.
why.D: Laparoscopic drainage is reserved for multiple or inaccessible collections or failed percutaneous drainage, not a single large accessible collection.

questions.right: Two weeks after cholecystectomy, a large subhepatic collection in a patient with only vague pain (stable) is most likely a biloma (bile leak from the cystic duct stump or a duct of Luschka) or an abscess. A large collection in a stable patient is drained percutaneously under image guidance. ERCP with sphincterotomy or stent is added if the leak persists.
questions.kc: Post-op intra-abdominal collection: size, number and stability decide. Small (under about 4 × 4 cm): antibiotics Large single collection, stable: percutaneous image-guided drainage Multiple collections: laparoscopy Unstable or peritonitis: laparotomy Post-cholecystectomy biloma with persistent leak: add ERCP with stent
questions.ep: Another version of this recall is keyed to ERCP with biliary stent; that answer fits when the question asks how to treat the bile leak itself rather than the collection.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with fever. Physical examination confirmed tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay: Positive for Entamoeba histolytica . CT scan: Large (10 ×15 cm), septated abscess in the right lobe of the liver with poorly defined margin. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

why.A: Cephalosporins cover the bacteria of a pyogenic liver abscess, not Entamoeba histolytica.
why.C: Percutaneous catheter drainage is the main treatment of a large pyogenic abscess; in an amoebic abscess it is reserved for failure of metronidazole or impending rupture.
why.D: Aspiration is not the first step for an amoebic abscess; it is used for no clinical response to metronidazole after a few days, diagnostic doubt, or a large left lobe abscess near the pericardium.

questions.right: Fever, RUQ pain and ELISA positive for Entamoeba histolytica confirm an amoebic liver abscess. Amoebic abscesses respond to drug therapy, so the initial management is metronidazole even when the abscess is large and septated. Aspiration or drainage is added only if medical therapy fails, the diagnosis is uncertain or rupture threatens; the lead-in word "initial" was emphasised.
questions.kc: Liver abscess: identify the organism, then pick the first step. Amoebic (positive serology, travel, dysentery): metronidazole first, then a luminal agent Pyogenic (biliary source, bacteremia): antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage Hydatid (Echinococcus, daughter cysts): albendazole, then surgery or PAIR for large or complicated cysts Amoebic abscess drainage: failure of therapy, diagnostic doubt, risk of rupture
questions.ep: Size and septations do not change the first step for an amoebic abscess; they do for pyogenic and hydatid lesions.

questions.stem: A 25-Year-Old Man Recently Returned From India And Presents With Right Upper Quadrant Abdominal Pain, Fever, And Fatigue. Laboratory Tests Reveal Elevated Liver Enzymes, And An Abdominal Ultrasound Shows A Solitary Liver Mass . He Has No History Of Alcohol Use, Hepatitis, Or Malignancy. What Is The Most Likely Diagnosis?

why.A: Pyogenic abscess is typically in older patients with biliary disease (stones, cholangitis), diabetes or recent abdominal sepsis, and is often multiple; the travel history points to amebic.
why.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma arises in cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B/C, with weight loss and a raised AFP; this man has no liver disease, and fever with travel suggests infection.
why.D: Hydatid cyst follows contact with dogs and sheep and is often asymptomatic or causes a dull ache; it shows a cyst with daughter cysts or calcification and does not usually cause fever unless infected or ruptured.

questions.right: A young man "recently returned from India" with "RUQ pain, fever" , raised liver enzymes and a "solitary liver mass" on ultrasound, without alcohol, hepatitis or malignancy, is the classic amebic liver abscess.
