Entamoeba histolytica is endemic in South Asia, typically affects young men, and produces a single abscess, usually in the right lobe. Diagnosis is by serology, and treatment is metronidazole followed by a luminal agent.
questions.kc: Liver mass + fever: the setting decides the organism. Amebic: young man, travel to endemic area (India, Mexico), solitary right lobe abscess, treat with metronidazole Pyogenic: older, biliary source or diabetes, often multiple, drainage + antibiotics Hydatid: dogs/sheep, daughter cysts, albendazole and surgery or drainage HCC: cirrhosis/HBV, weight loss, high AFP
questions.ep: Travel to India + fever + single liver lesion = amebic; most amebic abscesses resolve with metronidazole without drainage.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis evaluated for focal lesion at US abdomen. He is asymptomatic. Currently on diuretics with well-controlled ascites (Labs: Hb 110 g/L [130-170 male]; Platelets 123 x10^9/L [150-400]; INR 1.5 [0.8- 1.2]; Total bilirubin 16 umol/L [3.5-16.5]; AST 98 IU/L [12-40]; ALT 65 IU/L [5-40]; ALP 120 IU/L [39-117]; Albumin 30 g/L [34-56]). CT scan of liver: Demonstrated a 6 cm lesion with arterial enhancement at Rt lobe, portal vein and hepatic veins were patent. Which of the following is the best treatment option?

why.A: Sorafenib is systemic therapy for advanced HCC with vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. The veins are patent and there is no spread here.
why.B: Transplant fits HCC within Milan criteria (single lesion ≤5 cm or up to 3 lesions each ≤3 cm). A single 6 cm tumor is outside them.
why.C: Resection is for a single mass under 6 cm in a well compensated liver without significant portal hypertension. Here the tumor is 6 cm and the patient has ascites and thrombocytopenia.

questions.right: An arterially enhancing lesion in a hepatitis B cirrhotic liver is HCC. This one is a single "6 cm" tumor with patent portal and hepatic veins (no vascular invasion), but the liver is not well compensated: ascites needing diuretics, albumin 30, INR 1.5, low platelets (Child-Pugh B with portal hypertension). A single mass of 6 cm or more in this setting is treated with TACE, which is the keyed answer.
questions.kc: HCC treatment by size, number and liver function. Single mass under 6 cm, good liver function: surgical resection Within Milan criteria with decompensated cirrhosis: liver transplant Single mass ≥6 cm or multiple masses, no vascular invasion: TACE Vascular invasion or metastases: systemic therapy (sorafenib) If TACE is not offered for a 6 cm lesion, choose resection
questions.ep: The highlighted word is ascites: it signals the liver cannot tolerate resection.

questions.stem: Patient diagnosed with acute pancreatitis 2 weeks ago, now present to ER Complain of persistent mild abdominal pain and tenderness, showed cyst measure 4 cm . How you will manage?

why.A: Observation is the usual choice for a collection under 6 cm, less than 6 weeks old, without infection or complications, since most resolve spontaneously; the source keyed drainage here because the pain and tenderness persisted.
why.B: Internal (endoscopic) drainage is for a mature walled pseudocyst that is large (over 6 cm), persistent beyond 6 weeks, growing or clearly symptomatic; at 2 weeks the wall is not mature.
why.D: Surgical removal is not done for pseudocysts; surgery (cystogastrostomy) is reserved for failed endoscopic drainage or suspected cystic neoplasm.

questions.right: This recall's key is external (percutaneous) drainage; the examiner is sure the cyst was 4 cm, 2 weeks after acute pancreatitis, with persistent mild pain and tenderness. The source treats a persistently symptomatic collection as needing drainage, and percutaneous drainage is the less invasive option that does not need the mature wall that internal drainage requires. Learn the size, age and infection rules below, because they decide this question type.
questions.kc: Pancreatic fluid collection: size, age and infection decide. Pseudocyst forms after about 4 weeks; earlier it is an acute peripancreatic fluid collection Under 6 cm, under 6 weeks, asymptomatic or mild: observation Over 6 cm, over 6 weeks, growing or symptomatic: endoscopic internal drainage Infected collection or abscess (fever, leukocytosis, gas on CT): percutaneous drainage regardless of size or time CT is the best imaging
questions.ep: Percutaneous (external) drainage is the answer when the stem adds fever, leukocytosis or gas; without infection, small and early means observe.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man was treated conservatively for acute pancreatitis 2 months ago . He now presents with a 4-week history of persistent epigastric fullness and early satiety . He has no vomiting or gastrointestinal bleeding. On examination, he is hemodynamically stable with mild epigastric fullness and no signs of peritonitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?

why.A: Endoscopy looks at the gastric lumen and would only show extrinsic compression; it is used later for endoscopic (EUS-guided) drainage, not to diagnose the collection. It would be right for dyspepsia with red flags or upper GI bleeding, which are absent here.
why.C: Ultrasound can detect a pseudocyst and is useful for follow-up, but it is operator dependent, limited by bowel gas and cannot define the anatomy needed for planning. It is the first test for suspected gallstone pancreatitis or biliary colic.
why.D: A plain film cannot show a fluid collection; it is for suspected perforation (free air) or obstruction (dilated loops), and this patient has no vomiting or peritonism.

questions.right: Acute pancreatitis "2 months ago" followed by "persistent epigastric fullness and early satiety" is the classic picture of a pancreatic pseudocyst (or walled-off collection) compressing the stomach. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is the investigation of choice: it confirms the collection, measures its size and wall, shows its relation to the stomach and detects complications (necrosis, infection, pseudoaneurysm) that decide drainage. The compiler adds that even if the lead-in said "next", the answer would still be CT, not ultrasound.
questions.kc: Pseudocyst = peripancreatic fluid collection with a fibrous wall, ≥4 weeks after acute pancreatitis. Clues: early satiety, epigastric fullness or mass, persistent raised amylase Diagnosis: contrast CT abdomen Asymptomatic: observe, many resolve Symptomatic or complicated: drainage, usually endoscopic (cystgastrostomy) Complications: infection, rupture, bleeding (pseudoaneurysm), gastric outlet obstruction
questions.ep: Weeks after pancreatitis with early satiety: think pseudocyst and order CT, not endoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient with severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the groins and scrotum , his pain is severe that he cannot stay still and keep rolling , he has hematuria and urine analysis has blood and epithelial cells he has nausea & vomiting High WBC. What is the diagnosis?

why.B: Appendicitis causes periumbilical pain migrating to the RLQ; the patient lies still because movement worsens peritoneal pain, and frank hematuria is not a feature.
why.C: A strangulated inguinal hernia presents with a tender, irreducible groin lump with obstruction (vomiting, distension), not hematuria or restless writhing.
why.D: Cholecystitis gives persistent RUQ pain with fever and a positive Murphy sign, not groin and scrotal radiation with hematuria.

questions.right: Severe colicky pain radiating from the loin or lower abdomen to the groin and scrotum , a patient who "cannot stay still and keeps rolling", and hematuria are the classic picture of ureteric colic from a stone. Nausea and vomiting are common, and a mildly raised WBC does not exclude it.
questions.kc: Renal colic: Restless, writhing patient (peritonitis patients lie still) Loin to groin/scrotum (or labia) radiation, hematuria Imaging of choice: non-contrast CT KUB (ultrasound in pregnancy and children) Stone with fever or infection and obstruction: urgent decompression (stent or nephrostomy) Small stone (under about 5 to 10 mm): analgesia and medical expulsive therapy
questions.ep: Rolling around in pain = colic (stone); lying motionless = peritonitis.

questions.stem: Patient Had Severe Loin Pain That Radiates To The Scrotum , He Is Rolling On The ground From The Severity of The Pain , NO FEVER What's Diagnosis?

why.B: Pyelonephritis gives flank pain with fever, rigors, costovertebral angle tenderness and pyuria; the patient lies still rather than writhing. A stone with fever means an infected obstructed kidney needing urgent decompression.

questions.right: Severe colicky loin pain radiating to the scrotum (loin to groin) with a restless patient rolling on the ground is classic ureteric colic from a stone moving down the ureter. The decisive negative is no fever , which argues against infection.
questions.kc: Renal colic. Clues: sudden loin-to-groin colicky pain, restless patient, haematuria Imaging: non-contrast CT KUB (ultrasound in pregnancy and children) Analgesia: NSAIDs first line Stone + fever or infection: urgent decompression (stent or nephrostomy) plus antibiotics
questions.ep: Writhing patient = colic; patient lying still = peritonitis or infection.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old male presents to the ER with complaints of pain in the right loin region. He also experiences nausea, vomiting, and dysuria. He is unable to sit still due to the severity of the pain and keeps moving but cannot find a comfortable position. What is the likely diagnosis?

why.A: Appendicitis starts periumbilically and shifts to the RIF with anorexia and low fever; the patient lies still because movement worsens peritoneal pain.
why.C: Lower UTI (cystitis) gives dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort, not severe loin pain with writhing.
why.D: Pyelonephritis causes loin pain and dysuria, but with fever, rigors and costovertebral tenderness; the pain is constant rather than writhing colic, and no fever is described.

questions.right: Severe right loin pain with nausea, vomiting and dysuria in a patient who is "unable to sit still" and keeps moving is classic renal/ureteric colic. Restlessness is the key discriminator: patients with peritoneal irritation lie still. A stone at the vesicoureteric junction explains the dysuria. Confirm with non-contrast CT KUB.
questions.kc: Renal colic: loin to groin colicky pain in a restless patient. Associated: nausea, vomiting, hematuria, dysuria with distal stones Imaging: non-contrast CT KUB (ultrasound in pregnancy and children) Small uncomplicated stone (under about 10 mm): NSAID analgesia, fluids, trial of passage; alpha-blocker helps distal stones over 5 mm Infected obstructed kidney (fever + stone): urgent decompression (stent or nephrostomy)
questions.ep: Add fever and rigors to the same loin pain and the answer shifts to pyelonephritis (or an infected obstructed kidney).

questions.stem: A ... years old patient came for painless hematuria for 3 days Which of the following is the INITIAL investigation:

opts.B: KUB (no mention of the modality just "KUB")
opts.C: Cystoscopy+ CT Urography (both in the same answer)

why.B: A plain KUB film only shows radio-opaque stones and has no role as a first test for hematuria; it is used in follow-up of known radio-opaque stones, usually in a patient with colicky pain, not painless bleeding.
why.C: Cystoscopy plus CT urography is the definitive evaluation of confirmed painless hematuria in an adult (to exclude urothelial cancer of bladder and upper tract), so it is the right answer for 'best/most appropriate next step after urinalysis', not the initial test.

questions.right: The lead-in asks for the INITIAL investigation of 'painless hematuria for 3 days'. Urinalysis with microscopy comes first: it confirms true hematuria (RBCs, not myoglobin, pigments or food dyes), and shows clues that steer the rest of the work-up such as dysmorphic RBCs, casts or proteinuria (glomerular source) versus infection. Only once hematuria is confirmed and non- glomerular does the urological work-up (imaging plus cystoscopy) follow.
questions.kc: Hematuria: confirm it first, then localize it. Step 1: urinalysis with microscopy (true RBCs? casts? protein? infection?) Glomerular features (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria): renal work-up, not cystoscopy Painless gross hematuria in an adult: think bladder cancer until proven otherwise Upper tract: CT urography; lower tract: cystoscopy (both needed in high-risk adults) KUB: radio-opaque stones only
questions.ep: Same scenario but 'best / definitive next step' after a confirmed urinalysis: cystoscopy with CT urography.

questions.stem: A man in his 67 presents with hematuria . On digital rectal examination, there is mild tenderness. Complete blood count shows anemia with hemoglobin levels of 100 g/L (normal range 130-170 g/L). Urine culture shows no growth . Urinalysis reveals red blood cells without casts . What is the most appropriate NEXT step?

why.B: The culture already showed no growth, so infection is excluded; repeating it only delays the cancer workup.
why.C: Prostate biopsy is guided by a raised PSA or a hard nodular prostate on DRE, and is done transrectally or transperineally; mild tenderness does not justify it and it does not evaluate the bladder.
why.D: Unexplained non glomerular hematuria in an older man always needs evaluation; observation is only for proven transient causes.

questions.right: A 67 year old man with hematuria , a sterile urine culture and RBCs without casts (so not glomerular) has a urothelial cancer until proven otherwise; anemia adds concern. Full hematuria workup is imaging of the upper tract (CT urography) plus cystoscopy for the bladder; with no CT among the options, cystoscopy is the next step.
questions.kc: Hematuria in an older adult: exclude infection and glomerular causes, then image and scope. Casts, dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria: glomerular, refer to nephrology Positive culture: treat UTI, then repeat urinalysis Sterile, non glomerular: CT urography (upper tract) plus cystoscopy (bladder) Smoking and older age: highest risk for bladder cancer
questions.ep: Mild prostate tenderness with sterile urine tempts toward prostatitis or prostate biopsy, but hematuria in an older man still needs cystoscopy (plus CT urography for the upper tract).

questions.stem: 50 old male age came to the clinic concerned about seeing blood in his urine . While obtaining history the patient complained of Right Flank pain . No history of trauma or History Of Prior stones. On examination there's right flank tenderness and enlarged prostate On DRE. Urinalysis : 20 RBC What is The most appropriate investigation

why.A: Cystoscopy evaluates the bladder and urethra; it is chosen for painless hematuria in older patients (bladder cancer risk) or suspected bladder pathology, not for flank pain pointing to the kidney or ureter.
why.C: Plain X-ray (KUB) misses radiolucent stones and cannot assess a renal mass; it is used mainly to follow up known radio-opaque stones.

questions.right: Hematuria with "right flank pain" and "flank tenderness" localizes the problem to the upper urinary tract, where the main concerns are a renal or ureteric stone and a renal tumor (RCC); both are diagnosed on CT. The "enlarged prostate on DRE" is an incidental finding in a 50 year old man and does not explain flank pain, so CT KUB is the most appropriate investigation.
questions.kc: Hematuria: let the associated symptom choose the test. Flank pain plus hematuria: CT (non contrast for stone; contrast phases if a mass is suspected) Painless hematuria in an older smoker: cystoscopy plus upper tract imaging LUTS with enlarged prostate and normal urinalysis: BPH workup, alpha blocker Pregnant or child with colic: ultrasound first
questions.ep: Do not let the incidental enlarged prostate pull you to cystoscopy; flank pain sends you to CT.

questions.stem: ~50 old male age came to the clinic concerned about seeing blood in his urine . While obtaining history the patient complained of right flank pain . No history of trauma or history of prior stones. On examination there's right flank tenderness and enlarged prostate On DRE. Urinalysis : 20 RBC What is The most appropriate investigation

why.A: Cystoscopy: evaluates the bladder (urothelial cancer) and is part of the workup of painless visible haematuria in an older patient or a smoker; it does not assess flank pain or the kidney/ureter.
why.C: X-ray (KUB): misses radiolucent stones and small ureteric stones; used for follow-up of known radio-opaque stones, not for diagnosis.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: Haematuria with right flank pain and flank tenderness points to an upper-tract cause, most commonly a ureteric/renal stone, even without a prior stone history. Non-contrast CT KUB is the most accurate first-line imaging for stones and also shows other renal causes of haematuria. The enlarged prostate is an incidental finding for age and does not explain flank pain.
questions.kc: Haematuria workup is driven by the company it keeps. Flank pain/colic: non- contrast CT KUB Painless haematuria, older age or smoker: CT urography plus cystoscopy Pregnancy or child with colic: ultrasound BPH symptoms alone: no imaging needed first
questions.ep: Painful haematuria = stone, image with CT KUB; painless haematuria in an older man = cancer until proven otherwise, needs cystoscopy.

questions.stem: An elderly man with a known history of BPH presents to OPD with difficult urination, frequency, urgency, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He has been treated with an alpha-blocker for the past 2 years , with persistent symptoms . What is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.A: Adjust the dose of the alpha-blocker

why.A: Adjusting the alpha-blocker dose adds little after 2 years of persistent symptoms; failed medical therapy is an indication for surgery (adding a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for a large prostate is the other medical option, and it is not offered).
why.B: Suprapubic catheterization is for acute retention when urethral catheterization fails or is contraindicated (e.g. urethral trauma or stricture), not for chronic symptoms.
why.C: Clean intermittent catheterization is for patients with a hypocontractile (neurogenic) bladder or those unfit for surgery, not first choice after failed medical therapy.

questions.right: This man has BPH with persistent bothersome symptoms despite 2 years of alpha-blocker therapy , i.e. failed medical treatment. Failure of medical therapy is an indication for surgical management, and TURP is the standard procedure.
questions.kc: BPH ladder: Mild symptoms: watchful waiting, lifestyle measures Bothersome LUTS: alpha-blocker (fast relief) Large prostate: add 5-alpha reductase inhibitor (shrinks gland over months) Failed medical therapy or complications (recurrent retention, stones, recurrent UTI, hematuria, renal impairment): TURP Acute retention: urethral Foley catheter first
questions.ep: Acute retention: catheter first; failed medical therapy: TURP.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is suffering from urinary hesitancy (difficulty initiating urination). He has had diabetes for 10 years, his Body Mass Index (BMI) is 41 and ultrasound showed Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) . What is the contributing risk factor?

why.B: Obesity (BMI 41) is associated with larger prostates and more urinary symptoms as part of the metabolic syndrome, but it is a secondary association; the established principal risk factor is age.
why.C: Diabetes is also linked to BPH and LUTS (and can cause bladder dysfunction itself), but like obesity it is a weaker, modifiable association, not the main risk factor.
why.D: BPH needs normal androgen levels (DHT), not excess; hyperandrogenemia is not a recognized cause, and men castrated before puberty do not develop BPH.

questions.right: Ageing is the single most important risk factor for BPH: prostate enlargement and lower urinary tract symptoms such as "hesitancy" rise steadily with age, and this man is "60" . BPH also requires intact testicular androgens (DHT), but it is age acting on the androgen- dependent gland that drives the hyperplasia. The examiner answered Age, which matches the textbook rule.
questions.kc: BPH risk factors: age first, then androgen status and metabolic factors. Age: main, non-modifiable risk factor Androgens: DHT must be present (basis of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors) Obesity, diabetes, metabolic syndrome: associated, modifiable Diagnosis: clinical (symptoms + DRE), ultrasound for size and post-void residual; initial treatment: alpha blocker; definitive: TURP
questions.ep: When age appears among "risk factor" options for BPH, age wins over obesity and diabetes.

questions.stem: patient with BPH who is on alpha blocker for 2 years with no improvement came back with urinary incontinence and other symptoms. The best next step ?

why.A: Changing or adjusting the alpha blocker suits a patient with partial response and no complications; after 2 years of failure with new incontinence, more of the same drug will not relieve the obstruction.

questions.right: BPH is treated first with an alpha blocker, and surgery is indicated when medical therapy fails or complications appear. This patient has had no improvement after 2 years and now has urinary incontinence (likely overflow from chronic retention) with other symptoms, so the definitive treatment, transurethral resection of the prostate, is the best next step.
questions.kc: BPH treatment ladder. Mild symptoms: watchful waiting and lifestyle measures Moderate symptoms: alpha blocker (rapid relief) Large prostate: add a 5 alpha reductase inhibitor (shrinks gland over months) Surgery (TURP) for failed medical therapy or complications: refractory retention, overflow incontinence, recurrent UTI, bladder stones, hematuria, renal impairment Acute retention: Foley catheter and urine culture first
questions.ep: Overflow incontinence in BPH signals chronic retention, which is an indication for surgery, not another tablet.

questions.stem: 60-year-old diabetic male with a BMI of 41 and BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia) complains of urine retention. What is the risk factor of this condition?

why.B: Obesity (BMI 41) is associated with larger prostate volume and LUTS as part of the metabolic syndrome, but it is a weaker, modifiable association compared with age.
why.C: Diabetes is linked to LUTS and can cause retention through autonomic (neurogenic) bladder dysfunction, but it is not the main risk factor for BPH itself.
why.D: Prostate growth needs androgens (DHT), which is why castrated men do not develop BPH, but excess androgen is not a recognized risk factor; it is a distractor built on that fact.

questions.right: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, and the urinary retention it causes, is above all a disease of aging: its prevalence rises steeply with each decade after 40 to 50. Among the factors in this "60-year-old", age is the strongest and best established risk factor.
questions.kc: BPH essentials. Main risk factors: increasing age and intact testicular androgens Presentation: LUTS, retention, sometimes hematuria Acute retention: Foley catheter plus urine culture Initial treatment: alpha blocker; add 5 alpha reductase inhibitor for large glands Definitive: TURP
questions.ep: Androgens are necessary for BPH but are not its risk factor; age is.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Department, complaining of back pain and increasing difficulty with passing urine (Labs: Prostate-specific antigen 84 [0-4]; Alkaline phosphatase 410 IU/L [39-117]; Albumin 41 g/L [34-56]; Gamma glutamyltransferase 19 IU/L [6-37]). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Prostatitis can raise PSA, but it presents with fever, perineal pain and dysuria, and does not cause a raised bone ALP with back pain.
why.C: Bladder cancer classically presents with painless hematuria in a smoker; it does not cause a PSA of 84.
why.D: BPH causes the voiding symptoms and may raise PSA modestly, but not to 84 and not with back pain and bone ALP elevation.

questions.right: An elderly man with urinary obstructive symptoms plus back pain and a markedly raised PSA (84, normal 0 to 4) has prostate cancer with likely spinal bone metastasis. The raised ALP (410) with normal GGT and albumin shows a bone, not liver, source of the ALP, supporting osteoblastic metastases.
questions.kc: Elderly man + LUTS + back pain = metastatic prostate cancer. PSA markedly raised; ALP high with normal GGT = bone source Commonest metastatic site: bone (spine), osteoblastic (sclerotic) Diagnosis: DRE, MRI prostate, then biopsy Staging: bone scan (or PSMA PET), CT BPH: LUTS with normal or mildly raised PSA
questions.ep: High ALP with high GGT points to the liver; high ALP with normal GGT points to bone.

questions.stem: 4... years old Patient was concerned about prostate CA. His father was diagnosed with prostate CA at age of 78 and his friend told him about a test to screen for prostate CA . He was good, no symptoms . DRE: soft, smooth and small prostate, palpable medial sulcus . What is the best management?

why.B: Annual DRE alone is not a recommended screening strategy; it has poor sensitivity and he does not yet qualify for screening.
why.C: Repeating or ordering PSA is a screening step for men of screening age or at high risk (for example a father or brother diagnosed young); he is neither, and nothing in the stem calls for a delayed PSA.
why.D: Transurethral ultrasound (the prostate is actually imaged transrectally, TRUS) is used to guide biopsy or assess an abnormal prostate (raised PSA, nodular DRE); it is not a screening test.

questions.right: This man is in his "40s" , has "no symptoms" , and a normal DRE ( "soft, smooth and small prostate, palpable medial sulcus" ). His father was diagnosed at "age of 78" ; family history raises risk meaningfully when a first-degree relative is diagnosed at a young age (before about 65), so he is effectively average risk. Average-risk screening is not offered in the 40s, so reassurance with counselling about when to discuss screening later is the best management.
questions.kc: Prostate cancer screening is a shared decision based on age and risk, not offered to average-risk men in their 40s. Average risk: discuss PSA screening from around age 50 (or 55 to 69 by USPSTF) High risk (Black men, first-degree relative diagnosed young, BRCA): discuss earlier, from about 40 to 45 Father diagnosed in old age: little extra risk Screening tool = PSA; TRUS/MRI and biopsy only after an abnormal result Normal DRE: smooth, rubbery, median sulcus palpable
questions.ep: The age of the relative at diagnosis decides it: father at 78 = average risk; father at 55 = start discussing early.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old medically free was fine and suddenly had left sided lower abdominal pain. Examination confirms a slightly elevated, tender left testis with redness and edema of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Epididymo-orchitis is more gradual, often with fever or urinary symptoms, a testis in normal position and relief on elevation (Prehn sign); Doppler shows increased flow. Sudden onset with a high riding testis points to torsion.
why.C: Incarcerated inguinal hernia is an irreducible tender lump extending up into the groin, usually in an infant, with possible obstruction; the testis itself is not elevated.
why.D: Torsion of a testicular appendage gives tenderness localized to the upper pole, a blue dot sign and a normally (vertically) positioned testis; it is managed conservatively.

questions.right: A 12-year-old with sudden pain and a slightly elevated (high riding), tender testis has testicular torsion: the twisted cord shortens and pulls the testis up. Adolescents often report the pain in the lower abdomen rather than the scrotum, and scrotal redness and edema follow as the testis becomes ischemic. This is a surgical emergency explored without waiting for imaging.
questions.kc: Acute scrotum in a child: high riding tender testis = torsion until proven otherwise. Torsion: sudden severe pain, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex; explore without imaging Appendage torsion: upper pole tenderness, blue dot, vertical testis; NSAID Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, increased flow on Doppler; antibiotics Idiopathic scrotal edema: bilateral, painless redness spreading to groins Incarcerated hernia: irreducible lump extending to the groin, infants
questions.ep: Lower abdominal pain in a boy: always examine the scrotum; torsion often presents as 'abdominal' pain.

questions.stem: 14 years old boy came with sudden severe left abdominal and groin pain on examination you find out transillumination test negative , severe tender on touch, slight elevated testicle . What is diagnosis?

why.B: Direct inguinal hernia occurs in older men through Hesselbach triangle, is usually a painless reducible bulge and rarely strangulates; it is rare in a 14-year-old.
why.C: Indirect inguinal hernia is a groin swelling extending to the scrotum that increases with straining; if incarcerated it is a tender irreducible groin lump, but the testis is not elevated.
why.D: Hydrocele is a painless, fluctuant swelling that transilluminates; this one is tender and transillumination is negative.

questions.right: A 14-year-old with sudden severe abdominal and groin pain, a very tender, slightly elevated testis and a negative transillumination test has testicular torsion. The elevated testis reflects the twisted, shortened cord, and adolescents commonly refer the pain to the groin or lower abdomen. Negative transillumination rules out a fluid collection, and the severe tenderness rules out the painless conditions.
questions.kc: Sudden severe pain + elevated tender testis = torsion; transillumination positive = hydrocele. Torsion: high riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex, emergency exploration Hydrocele: painless, transilluminates, can get above it Inguinal hernia: cannot get above it, cough impulse, extends from groin Indirect: lateral to inferior epigastric vessels; direct: medial (Hesselbach triangle)
questions.ep: A non transilluminating scrotal mass is NOT automatically a hernia; with sudden severe pain and an elevated testis it is torsion.

questions.stem: A pedia patient with sudden severe pain, high-riding testis , absent cremasteric reflex . What Is initial step, and ultrasound is not provided in the facility ?

opts.B: Manual detorsion and follow up after patient relief

why.B: Manual detorsion (open book rotation) is only a temporising measure when surgery is not immediately available; it can fail or be incomplete and never replaces urgent exploration and fixation of both testes.

questions.right: Sudden severe pain , a high riding testis and an absent cremasteric reflex make testicular torsion a clinical diagnosis. Imaging is not needed when torsion is clinically likely, so the missing ultrasound changes nothing: the child needs urgent surgical exploration with detorsion and orchidopexy, because testicular salvage falls sharply after about 6 hours.
questions.kc: Acute scrotum: torsion is a surgical emergency diagnosed clinically. Torsion: sudden severe pain, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex → urgent exploration Doppler only if the diagnosis is uncertain, and it must not delay surgery Torsion of appendage: upper pole pain, blue dot sign → NSAIDs Epididymo orchitis: gradual onset, increased flow on Doppler → antibiotics
questions.ep: No ultrasound is a distractor: suspected torsion goes straight to theatre.

questions.stem: A 13 (Or 14) YO Child With Acute Testicular Pain 3hours Ago . Tactical Are Slightly Elevated (Didn’t Tell vertical vs Horizontal) Diagnosis?

why.B: Torsion of the testicular appendix keeps the testis in a normal vertical, non-elevated position with tenderness localized to the upper pole and sometimes a blue dot sign; it is managed conservatively.
why.C: Epididymo-orchitis has a more gradual onset with fever, urinary symptoms or sexual exposure and pain relieved by elevation (Prehn sign); the testis is not high riding and Doppler shows increased flow.
why.D: A hernia presents as a groin/scrotal swelling extending up into the inguinal canal (reducible or, if incarcerated, irreducible); an isolated elevated tender testis does not suggest it.

questions.right: An adolescent (13 to 14 years, the peak age) with acute testicular pain of only 3 hours and a testis that is "slightly elevated" (high riding) is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. The twisted spermatic cord shortens and pulls the testis upward, often lying horizontally. It is a surgical emergency: explore without delaying for imaging.
questions.kc: Acute scrotum: position of the testis decides. Torsion: sudden severe pain, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex: urgent exploration Appendix testis torsion: upper pole tenderness, vertical normal testis, blue dot: NSAID, rest Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, fever, dysuria, increased Doppler flow: antibiotics Doppler only if the diagnosis is uncertain
questions.ep: Vertical, non-elevated testis with superior pole tenderness flips the answer to torsion of the appendix testis.

questions.stem: Diabetic patient, came with a pain that is out proportion , Bulle , Crepitus , pain extends further than the erythema , weak pulse What to do next?

why.A: IV antibiotics are needed, but "LOCAL" debridement is inadequate for infection spreading along fascial planes beyond the visible skin change. Local debridement plus antibiotics fits a localized abscess or infected ulcer.
why.B: Conservative wound care fits a clean, non-infected chronic wound. In necrotizing fasciitis delay to surgery is the main driver of death.
why.D: An X-ray may show soft tissue gas, but imaging must not delay surgery once the clinical picture is clear. Imaging fits an unclear case such as suspected osteomyelitis under a diabetic ulcer.

questions.right: A diabetic with "pain out of proportion", bullae, crepitus and pain extending "further than the erythema" has necrotizing soft tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis). This is a surgical emergency: wide, aggressive debridement down to healthy fascia, repeated every 24 to 48 hours, with broad spectrum IV antibiotics. The compiler highlights that the key distractor is the word LOCAL in option A.
questions.kc: Necrotizing fasciitis = early, wide, repeated surgical debridement + IV antibiotics. Clues: pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, dishwater discharge, skin anesthesia, systemic toxicity Tenderness beyond the erythema margin Risk: diabetes, immunosuppression, IV drug use Perineal or genital site: Fournier gangrene, same treatment Cellulitis: red, warm, tender, no crepitus: antibiotics alone
questions.ep: Crepitus or pain beyond the redness means go to theatre, not to radiology.

questions.stem: A guy with severe perineal pain and swelling, discoloration that is expanding with crepitus , what is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Cellulitis gives localized redness, warmth and pain with fever, but without crepitus, skin necrosis or rapid dusky spread.
why.B: Testicular torsion causes sudden testicular pain with a high-riding, horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex, without perineal crepitus or skin discoloration.

questions.right: Severe perineal pain and swelling with expanding discoloration and crepitus (gas in tissues) is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia, i.e. Fournier gangrene. Pain out of proportion, rapid spread and crepitus are the warning signs; it is a surgical emergency needing urgent debridement and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
questions.kc: Fournier gangrene: Risk factors: diabetes, immunosuppression, alcohol, obesity, perineal infection or trauma Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, dusky or necrotic skin, crepitus Polymicrobial (aerobes plus anaerobes) Management: urgent radical surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics + resuscitation Do not delay surgery for imaging
questions.ep: Crepitus in a soft tissue infection = gas-forming necrotizing infection, never simple cellulitis.

questions.stem: Case of left leg redness and tenderness after minor trauma, fever spiking. He finish full Course of antibiotic but still there is pain and tenderness What is the cause

why.B: A resistant organism (such as MRSA) is possible, but a spiking fever with persistent localized pain after a full course points first to an undrained collection; switching antibiotics without draining it fails.
why.C: The stem states the full course was completed, which excludes non compliance.

questions.right: Redness and tenderness after minor trauma is cellulitis. Persistent pain, tenderness and a spiking fever despite a full course of antibiotics mean a collection has formed: pus inside an abscess cavity is poorly reached by antibiotics. The cause is an abscess , which needs incision and drainage (ultrasound can confirm it).
questions.kc: Infection not settling on antibiotics: look for a collection. Spiking (swinging) fever = undrained pus until proven otherwise Skin and soft tissue: ultrasound, then incision and drainage Post operative abdomen: US or CT, then percutaneous drainage Pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapid spread: necrotizing fasciitis, urgent debridement
questions.ep: "Ubi pus, ibi evacua": antibiotics alone do not cure an abscess.

questions.stem: A male patient gets pustules after shaving . What is the diagnosis?

why.A: Furuncle (boil): a single deep, painful, tender nodule around one follicle that points and drains; it is more than a crop of tiny pustules.
why.B: Carbuncle: several adjacent infected follicles forming a large indurated plaque with multiple discharging openings, classically on the nape of the neck in a diabetic.
why.D: Option not recalled.

questions.right: Pustules appearing after shaving are small, superficial infections or inflammation of individual hair follicles: folliculitis. Shaving abrades the skin and opens the follicles to Staph aureus, giving 1 to 2 mm perifollicular red papules and pustules in the beard area (sycosis barbae when deep and persistent). There is no deep tender nodule or multi-headed plaque, so this is the most superficial level of follicular infection.
questions.kc: Follicular infection ladder by depth and size: Folliculitis: superficial, small papule/pustule centred on a hair Furuncle: deep single follicle, tender nodule with a core Carbuncle: several follicles joined, multiple openings, nape of neck, diabetics Pseudofolliculitis barbae: ingrown curly beard hairs after close shaving (inflammatory, not primarily infective)
questions.ep: Tiny pustules after shaving = folliculitis; one big tender nodule = furuncle; multi- headed plaque = carbuncle.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with multiple painful nodules in both axillae . The lesions have been recurrent for the past year and are associated with a foul odor. On examination, there are multiple bilateral axillary nodules with purulent discharge and multiple sinus openings . What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Acne conglobata causes interconnecting nodules and sinuses mainly on the back, chest and face, not confined to the axillae.
why.B: A furuncle is an acute infection of a single hair follicle; recurrent furuncles do not form chronic interconnected sinus tracts in both axillae.
why.C: An infected sebaceous (epidermoid) cyst is a solitary lesion with a punctum, not bilateral recurrent nodules with multiple sinuses.

questions.right: Recurrent painful nodules in both axillae with purulent discharge , foul odour and multiple sinus openings in a young woman is hidradenitis suppurativa, a chronic inflammatory disease of follicles in apocrine bearing intertriginous skin (axillae, groin, gluteal cleft). Bilateral distribution, recurrence and sinus tracts are its signature.
questions.kc: Hidradenitis suppurativa: nodules + abscesses + sinus tracts + scarring in apocrine areas. Sites: axilla, groin, inframammary, perianal, gluteal cleft Risk: obesity, smoking, female sex Mild: topical clindamycin, weight loss, stop smoking Moderate: oral tetracyclines Severe: adalimumab; wide excision of affected skin Carbuncle: several follicles, single site, often neck
questions.ep: Bilateral + recurrent + sinus tracts in skin folds = HS; a single acute lesion = furuncle or abscess.

questions.stem: 45 years old male or female, has a mass 5 cm in right upper limb, ( MRI shows a mass from triceps ) what to do next?

why.A: Incisional biopsy is the fallback when core biopsy is nondiagnostic; it contaminates more tissue planes and must be placed along the line of the future resection.
why.B: Excisional biopsy is for small superficial lesions (<5 cm) likely to be benign; "shelling out" an unsuspected sarcoma leaves residual tumour and contaminated margins and worsens the definitive operation.
why.D: PET is not a first step; staging (CT chest for lung metastases) follows a tissue diagnosis.

questions.right: A 5 cm mass arising from the triceps (deep to the fascia) is a suspected soft tissue sarcoma: masses >5 cm, deep, enlarging or painful are treated as sarcoma until proven otherwise. After MRI has defined the lesion, the next step is image-guided core needle biopsy, which gives enough tissue for histological type and grade with minimal contamination. Biopsy should be done (or planned) at the sarcoma center so the tract can be excised with the definitive resection.
questions.kc: Suspected limb soft tissue sarcoma: Red flags: >5 cm, deep to fascia, growing, painful Imaging: MRI of the limb Tissue: image-guided core needle biopsy Staging: CT chest (lungs are the main metastatic site) Treatment: wide local excision ± radiotherapy Biopsy tract placed so it can be excised with the tumour
questions.ep: Small superficial lump = excise; big or deep lump = core biopsy first.

questions.stem: A 2 (or 3) year-old child is brought to the Emergency Department after her older sibling pulled her by the hand while playing. The child holds her right arm slightly flexed and pronated against her body and refuses to use it and there's click. There is no swelling, ecchymosis, or focal tenderness . What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Supracondylar fracture follows a fall on an outstretched hand and gives swelling, tenderness and often deformity around the elbow; none are present here.
why.C: Clavicle fracture follows a fall on the shoulder or outstretched hand and causes point tenderness and often a bump over the clavicle, not a pulling injury with a non tender limb.
why.D: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) is an overuse tendinopathy of adults, with tenderness over the medial epicondyle.

questions.right: A toddler (2 to 3 years) pulled by the hand , now holding the arm slightly flexed and pronated and refusing to use it, with no swelling, bruising or focal tenderness , is the classic radial head subluxation. Axial traction pulls the radial head through the annular ligament; a click may be felt. Treatment is reduction by supination with flexion or by hyperpronation, with no imaging needed.
questions.kc: Pulled arm in a child aged 1 to 4: nursemaid's elbow. Mechanism: traction on the extended, pronated arm Arm held slightly flexed and pronated, child refuses to use it No swelling, bruising or point tenderness Diagnosis is clinical; no X-ray needed with a typical history Reduction: supination plus flexion, or hyperpronation
questions.ep: Any swelling, bruising or bony tenderness, or a fall instead of a pull, means X-ray for a fracture before any manipulation. 51 topics, 85 questions

questions.stem: A 50 years old male, reported an elevated blood pressure 150/90 on multiple occasions , he known of hyperlipidemia on atrovstatin, Vital signs: BP: 143 /85 BMI: 31 What is the most appropriate action:

opts.C: I forgot ( smth related to measuring bp and following it )

why.B: Lifestyle modification and weight loss alone fits stage 1 hypertension in a low-risk patient with no other risk factors or target organ damage; his dyslipidemia raises his risk. Lifestyle advice is still given together with the drug.
why.C: Simply rechecking and following BP is not needed because elevated readings are already documented on multiple occasions.
why.D: Option not recalled.

questions.right: BP has been raised "on multiple occasions" (150/90), so hypertension is established, and he already carries additional cardiovascular risk: "hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin" and obesity ("BMI 31"). This recall's key is to start antihypertensive medication because confirmed hypertension in a patient with raised overall cardiovascular risk warrants drug therapy alongside lifestyle advice rather than lifestyle alone. By ACC/AHA thresholds, readings of 150/90 are already stage 2, where drugs plus lifestyle are recommended.
questions.kc: Starting drugs in hypertension depends on BP level and overall risk. Confirm on repeated readings (or ambulatory/home monitoring) Low-risk stage 1: lifestyle first, then drugs if not controlled Stage 1 with high CV risk, diabetes, CKD or organ damage: drugs + lifestyle Stage 2: drugs + lifestyle Lifestyle advice applies to everyone
questions.ep: The extra risk factor (dyslipidemia on a statin) is what moves the answer from lifestyle alone to medication.

questions.stem: 27 years old female with already diagnosed HTN with no medication or supplements are being taken by the patient. she had multiple episodes of Pulmonary edema and flushing in the past. she is obese and have high HTN, and on physical exam she has right sided flank bruit , other examinations are stated to be normal what the most appropriate study to confirm diagnosis? (Patient is only obese)

opts.D: Radiological Plain radiographs of the abdomen

why.B: Renal ultrasound (Doppler) is a reasonable screening test, but it is operator dependent and limited by body habitus, so in an obese patient it is less reliable than CT.
why.C: Intravenous pyelogram outlines the collecting system and was an old, insensitive screen for renovascular disease; it is obsolete.
why.D: A plain abdominal X ray cannot show the renal arteries; it only shows calcification or radiopaque stones.

questions.right: A young woman with hypertension, recurrent flash pulmonary edema and a flank bruit points to renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis, fibromuscular dysplasia at this age). The compiler explains the options were plain CT and plain US, and in an obese patient CT images the renal arteries and kidneys more reliably than ultrasound, so CT of the kidney is the key; in practice this means CT angiography.
questions.kc: Suspected renal artery stenosis: noninvasive angiography (CTA or MRA) confirms; catheter angiography is the gold standard. Clues: young woman (FMD) or older atherosclerotic patient, resistant HTN, abdominal or flank bruit, flash pulmonary edema, rise in creatinine after ACE inhibitor Doppler US: screening, limited by obesity and operator CTA: avoid if poor renal function (contrast); MRA alternative FMD: string of beads, treat with angioplasty
questions.ep: Obese patient: choose CT over US; poor renal function: MRA instead of CTA.

questions.stem: A 40 -year-old male, 5-pack -year smoker presents to the Emergency Room with a sudden onset of retrosternal chest pain radiating to the neck. His blood pressure is 150/92 . ECG: ST-segment depression in II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most considerable risk factor?

why.A: Smoking is a strong modifiable risk factor, but here the exposure is light (5 pack-years); it would be the answer in a heavy smoker with normal BP.
why.B: Male sex is a non-modifiable risk factor and the stem gives no feature that makes it dominant over a raised BP.
why.C: Age is a risk factor in men from about 45 years; at 40 his age adds little and is non- modifiable.

questions.right: The lead-in asks for the most considerable (most significant, modifiable) risk factor for this acute coronary syndrome ("ST depression in II, III, aVF"). His BP is 150/92 , which is in the stage 2 hypertension range and is a major, independent driver of atherosclerosis and myocardial oxygen demand. Compared with only a 5 pack-year smoking history and a relatively young age, hypertension carries the greatest weight in this vignette, which is why the confirmed key is hypertension.
questions.kc: Coronary risk factors: weigh the one the stem quantifies most heavily. Modifiable: hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, obesity, inactivity Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history of premature CAD Exam stems put the key factor as a number (BP value, pack- years, HbA1c) Light smoking (few pack-years) usually signals it is not the intended answer
questions.ep: If the stem stressed heavy smoking (e.g. 30+ pack-years) with normal BP, smoking would flip to the answer.

questions.stem: Elderly pt chest pain and SOB. Examination systolic murmur radiated to the axilla . ECG PICTURE Showing: ST elevation In Lead 1 & AVL +/- V5 & V6 . +ve trop 2. Unstable hypotensive . What is Cause of hypotension: A. Why wrong: Option not recalled by the source (possibly cardiogenic shock).

why.B: PE causes hypotension with right heart strain (tachycardia, hypoxia, raised JVP, S1Q3T3 or RV strain pattern), not a lateral STEMI with an axillary radiating murmur.
why.C: Drug induced hypotension (e.g. nitrates or beta blockers) is possible in MI, but the stem gives no drug and offers a structural clue, the new murmur, that explains the shock.

questions.right: The ECG shows a lateral STEMI (ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6) and the patient has a new systolic murmur radiating to the axilla with hypotension . A new apical murmur to the axilla after MI is acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture, which causes sudden volume overload and cardiogenic shock. Exam rule: if MR is among the options choose it; if it is not offered, choose cardiogenic shock.
questions.kc: New murmur after MI with hypotension = mechanical complication. Apical pansystolic to axilla: acute MR (papillary muscle) Harsh pansystolic at left sternal border with step up in O2: VSD rupture No murmur, raised JVP, muffled sounds, PEA: free wall rupture/tamponade Lateral STEMI: I, aVL, V5, V6, usually circumflex
questions.ep: Systolic murmur to the axilla in an MI patient with shock: answer MR, not just cardiogenic shock, if MR is offered.

questions.stem: 61-year-old man comes to the clinic with a 2-day history of dyspnoeaon exertion . He has a long standing hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination is unremarkable except for rare crackles at the bases of the lungs. Which of the following

why.B: CRP is a nonspecific inflammatory marker; it would help in suspected infection or inflammation, not ventricular dysfunction.
why.C: CK reflects muscle (including myocardial) injury; it does not assess ventricular function.
why.D: Troponin T marks myocardial injury such as acute coronary syndrome; it would be right with chest pain or ischemic ECG changes.

questions.right: A hypertensive smoker with new "dyspnoea on exertion" and "crackles at the bases" raises suspicion of heart failure from left ventricular dysfunction. BNP is released from stretched ventricular myocardium and is the most helpful blood test for detecting or excluding heart failure; a normal level makes it unlikely.
questions.kc: Cardiac biomarkers: BNP / NT-proBNP: ventricular stretch, heart failure (high negative predictive value) Troponin: myocardial injury, ACS CK: muscle injury, less specific CRP: inflammation Raised BNP then confirm with echocardiography
questions.ep: Dyspnea + basal crackles in a hypertensive = think heart failure, test BNP then echo.

questions.stem: Elderly women known DM HTN has a history of IHD years before. Came complaining of increasing shortness of breath, increased when she lay down . No chest pain , no other complains. Vitals normal. (The question came with 2 clear pictures: first picture ECG, second picture not remembered) What is the cause of this patient complaint?

why.A: Acute coronary syndrome would usually bring chest pain or ECG/troponin changes; none was described, and the question asks what explains the orthopneic dyspnea.
why.C: Pulmonary embolism gives sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with risk factors (immobility, surgery); dyspnea does not worsen on lying flat.
why.D: Decompensated heart failure is the underlying syndrome, but the immediate cause of breathlessness on lying down is the fluid in the lungs; with normal vitals the examiners keyed pulmonary edema.

questions.right: An elderly diabetic hypertensive woman with prior IHD now has progressive dyspnea worse lying flat (orthopnea) with no chest pain and normal vitals. Orthopnea reflects pulmonary venous congestion from left ventricular failure, so the direct cause of her complaint is pulmonary edema . The question asks for the cause of the symptom, and two 100 scorers chose B over the competing A and D.
questions.kc: Dyspnea patterns point to the cause. Orthopnea / PND, basal crackles, S3: pulmonary edema from LV failure Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, risk factor: PE Chest pain with ST or troponin change: ACS Prior MI is the commonest cause of LV systolic failure
questions.ep: 'Cause of the complaint' asks for the mechanism of the symptom (fluid in alveoli), not the label of the underlying disease.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with heart failure. The Doctors put him on sacubatril/valsartan, Spirono , Metoprolol and discharge, on follow up he's fully normal, asymptomatic , but the lab showed HYPERKALEMIA (it was mild elevation (5.8) ). What to do A. Why wrong: Option not recalled by the source.

why.B: Stopping sacubitril/valsartan removes the cornerstone mortality drug for a mild, asymptomatic rise; the ARNI is reduced or stopped only for severe hyperkalemia, worsening renal function or symptomatic hypotension after the MRA has been adjusted.
why.D: Increasing furosemide would lower potassium but he is euvolemic and asymptomatic; loop diuretics are titrated to congestion, not used to treat drug induced hyperkalemia, and would risk volume depletion and AKI.

questions.right: This patient is on guideline therapy for HFrEF (ARNI, beta blocker and the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone) and is asymptomatic with only mild hyperkalemia (5.8) . Spironolactone is the drug most responsible for potassium retention and is the one titrated first when K rises: a mild rise (above about 5.5 but below 6) is handled by halving the spironolactone dose and rechecking K, while K of 6 or more means stopping it. This keeps the mortality benefit of the ARNI and beta blocker.
questions.kc: Hyperkalemia on HFrEF therapy: adjust the aldosterone antagonist first. K above 5.5 (mild): halve spironolactone dose, recheck K and creatinine K 6 or more: stop spironolactone Persistent problem: review ARNI/ACEi dose, stop K supplements and NSAIDs Step ladder: ACEi/ARB/ARNI, then beta blocker, then MRA
questions.ep: Asymptomatic mild hyperkalemia on triple HF therapy: cut the spironolactone, keep the ARNI.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) presents with palpitations and is found to have atrial fibrillation . Which of the following is the most appropriate medication?

why.B: Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node and is used to terminate or diagnose SVT; it does not convert or control AF.
why.C: Diltiazem, a non dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is negatively inotropic and contraindicated in HFrEF.
why.D: Propranolol is a non selective beta blocker without proven mortality benefit in heart failure; if a guideline beta blocker such as bisoprolol or carvedilol were offered it would be preferred.

questions.right: In a patient with HFrEF and atrial fibrillation, rate control must avoid negative inotropes that worsen heart failure. Digoxin controls ventricular rate without depressing contractility. As the compiler notes, the only beta blocker offered is propranolol , which is not one of the mortality benefit HF beta blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), so digoxin is the key.
questions.kc: AF rate control: beta blocker or CCB normally; in HFrEF use an HF beta blocker or digoxin, never non dihydropyridine CCBs. Target resting HR under about 110 (lenient) or under 80 (strict, symptomatic) Unstable AF: synchronised DC cardioversion Acute decompensated HF with fast AF: digoxin or amiodarone HF beta blockers: bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate Anticoagulate per CHA2DS2-VASc
questions.ep: If bisoprolol, carvedilol or metoprolol is among the options, it beats digoxin for HFrEF with AF.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is admitted with palpitations of 4-hour duration. He had similar attack a month ago but did not seek medical advice. His initial electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate. He subsequently converted to sinus rhythm. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate to maintain sinus rhythm ?

why.A: Digoxin only slows AV nodal conduction (rate control); it does not keep the atria in sinus rhythm. Best for rate control in AF with heart failure or a sedentary patient.
why.B: Bisoprolol is a first-line rate control drug; it slows the ventricular response but is not the rhythm control answer here.
why.C: Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for rate control (avoid in HFrEF); it does not maintain sinus rhythm.

questions.right: The lead-in asks for a drug to maintain sinus rhythm after AF has already converted, which is rhythm control, not rate control. He has recurrent paroxysmal AF ("similar attack a month ago") and the ventricular rate was already controlled, so the goal now is preventing recurrence. Amiodarone is the only antiarrhythmic (rhythm control) agent among the options.
questions.kc: AF drug choice: rate control vs rhythm control. Rate control (target HR <100): beta blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin (if heart failure) Rhythm control / maintain sinus rhythm: antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone Unstable AF: electrical cardioversion Stroke prevention: CHA2DS2-VA ≥2 means anticoagulate
questions.ep: "Maintain sinus rhythm" or "prevent recurrence" = rhythm control drug; "control the rate" = beta blocker or CCB.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is diagnosed with persistent atrial fibrillation . His past medical history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes . He has no contraindications to any anti- thrombotic treatments. What antithrombotic treatment should be considered first line for this patient?

why.A: Dual antiplatelet therapy is less effective than anticoagulation for stroke prevention in AF with comparable bleeding risk.
why.B: Clopidogrel alone is not adequate stroke prevention in AF.
why.D: Aspirin alone is no longer recommended for AF stroke prevention; it would only be reasonable if the patient refuses all anticoagulation.

questions.right: "Persistent atrial fibrillation" with "hypertension" (1 point) and "type 2 diabetes" (1 point) gives a CHA2DS2-VASc of 2 in a man, and with "no contraindications" he needs oral anticoagulation. Among the options, warfarin is the only anticoagulant and so is first line here.
questions.kc: AF stroke prevention by CHA2DS2-VASc: C: heart failure 1; H: hypertension 1; A2: age ≥75 = 2 D: diabetes 1; S2: prior stroke/TIA = 2 V: vascular disease 1; A: age 65-74 = 1; Sc: female 1 Men ≥2 (women ≥3): anticoagulate DOACs preferred over warfarin unless mechanical valve or moderate-severe mitral stenosis
questions.ep: If a DOAC is offered it beats warfarin; if not, warfarin beats any antiplatelet.

questions.stem: 40-year-old woman comes for follow-up. She had rheumatic fever 15 years ago and smokes 10 cigarettes/day for 15 years. On examination she has regular rhythm, BP 154/56 , HR 68, and a blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the aortic area . What is the most appropriate advice for future preventive health maintenance?

why.A: Annual chest X-ray is not a screening test for lung cancer or valve disease; lung cancer screening uses low dose CT in older heavy smokers, and she does not qualify.
why.B: Colorectal cancer screening starts at 45 to 50 years for average risk adults and is usually by colonoscopy; at 40 with no risk factors it is not indicated.
why.D: Dental antibiotic prophylaxis is limited to prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and transplant valvulopathy; native rheumatic valve disease alone does not qualify.

questions.right: Previous rheumatic fever , a blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the aortic area and a wide pulse pressure (154/56) indicate chronic aortic regurgitation from rheumatic valve disease. A newly detected murmur needs transthoracic echocardiography to confirm the lesion and measure its severity, LV size and ejection fraction, which decide follow up intervals and timing of valve surgery. That is the most useful step for her future cardiac health.
questions.kc: Murmur after rheumatic fever: New murmur: transthoracic echo first Early diastolic decrescendo + wide pulse pressure: AR Rheumatic carditis: secondary penicillin prophylaxis by duration rules IE prophylaxis only for prosthetic valve, prior IE, certain congenital disease
questions.ep: Rheumatic valve disease alone does not need dental IE prophylaxis; the new murmur needs an echo.

questions.stem: 40 years old female came to follow up clinic, she was in good health 2 years ago when examined. Past medical history of Rheumatic fever 15 years ago. She smokes 10 cigarettes for 15 years. On current examination she has good heart rhythm and blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area . BP 154/56 HR 68 What is the most appropriate advice for future preventive health maintenance?

opts.D: Prophylaxis Abx before the dental procedure

why.A: Annual chest X-ray is not a screening tool for smokers and does not assess a valve lesion; lung cancer screening uses low-dose CT in eligible heavy smokers.
why.B: Flexible sigmoidoscopy is colorectal screening and is not relevant to a new heart murmur; she is also below the usual screening age.
why.D: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work is reserved for high-risk groups such as prosthetic valves or previous endocarditis, not native rheumatic valve disease.

questions.right: A "blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur at the aortic area" with a wide pulse pressure ("BP 154/56") after "rheumatic fever" is aortic regurgitation, a new finding compared with her normal exam 2 years ago. A new valvular lesion needs echocardiography to confirm it, grade severity and assess left ventricular size and function, which decides follow-up and the timing of surgery.
questions.kc: Aortic regurgitation: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur, left sternal edge/aortic area Wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse Causes: rheumatic, bicuspid valve, aortic root dilatation, endocarditis Investigation: echocardiography Surgery: symptoms, or LV dilatation/dysfunction
questions.ep: Any new murmur in a patient with rheumatic history = echo now.

questions.stem: Patient kc of HF and had stent a few years ago presents with Dyspnea and had pale cold extremities and was hypotensive , started on IV fluids, then given norepinephrine at 0.2 mcg/kg/min. Patient is not responding and remains hypotensive. Most appropriate next step?

why.A: Increasing norepinephrine raises afterload and squeezes a failing ventricle further without improving contractility; the cold extremities signal low output, not low vascular tone.
why.B: Dopamine is associated with more arrhythmias and worse outcomes than norepinephrine in cardiogenic shock; no longer favoured.
why.D: More fluids in a failing heart that did not respond to the first bolus worsen pulmonary congestion; fluid helps only hypovolemic or fluid responsive patients.

questions.right: Known heart failure with prior stent, cold pale extremities and hypotension is cardiogenic shock : the problem is low cardiac output (pump failure). After norepinephrine restores perfusion pressure, persistent shock calls for an inotrope ; dobutamine increases contractility and output, and it is added to (not replacing) norepinephrine because it may lower BP on its own.
questions.kc: Shock: warm vs cold guides the drug. Cardiogenic (cold, wet): norepinephrine for BP + dobutamine for output Septic (warm early): fluids, then norepinephrine, then vasopressin Hypovolemic: fluids / blood Refractory cardiogenic: mechanical support (IABP, Impella) and revascularisation if ischemic
questions.ep: Cold extremities with HF = inotrope problem; warm vasodilated shock = vasopressor problem.

questions.stem: Icu pts who was given 6L of fluid and still hypotensive (BP low, calculated 63) he's 70 kg his urine was 20ml/hr and cvp is 10cm (next step)

why.A: Furosemide in a hypotensive, under-perfused patient worsens hypotension and renal perfusion; oliguria here is from shock, not fluid overload.
why.C: Another 2 L of NS is wrong after 6 L with CVP 10; further fluid adds overload (pulmonary edema) without improving perfusion. A fluid bolus is right only when the patient is still fluid- responsive.

questions.right: The patient has received 6 L of fluid and is still hypotensive (MAP about 63) with oliguria (20 ml/hr in 70 kg) and a CVP of 10 , meaning he is adequately filled. This is fluid- refractory shock, so the next step is a vasopressor, and norepinephrine is the first-line agent.
questions.kc: Shock ladder. Step 1: crystalloid resuscitation (30 ml/kg in sepsis) Still hypotensive after adequate fluid: norepinephrine, target MAP ≥65 Add vasopressin, then consider epinephrine or hydrocortisone if refractory Oliguria in shock: treat perfusion, not with diuretics
questions.ep: Large fluid volume already given plus normal-to-high CVP = stop fluids, start norepinephrine.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man, who was medically free, was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with massive pulmonary embolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

why.A: Warfarin is long-term oral anticoagulation, started after initial treatment; it takes days to work and does nothing for a massive clot now.
why.C: LMWH is first line for hemodynamically stable PE; in massive PE it does not remove the clot fast enough. Heparin follows successful thrombolysis.
why.D: Dabigatran is an oral option for stable PE after initial parenteral anticoagulation, not for unstable PE.

questions.right: Massive pulmonary embolism means PE with severely impaired circulation (shock or sustained hypotension). In this setting the most appropriate initial treatment is systemic thrombolysis to dissolve the clot and relieve right ventricular failure. A young, medically free man has no obvious contraindication to lysis.
questions.kc: PE treatment depends on circulation. Unstable (massive): thrombolysis Unstable + lysis contraindicated or failed: embolectomy Stable: LMWH or heparin, then oral anticoagulant Anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE despite it: IVC filter
questions.ep: Stable PE (normal BP) flips the answer to LMWH; only massive/unstable PE gets thrombolysis.

questions.stem: 65 YO Smoker MALE , Most Important Screen

why.B: Colorectal cancer screening applies to all adults from mid-life regardless of smoking; it is important, but the question singles out smoking and male sex, which point to AAA.

questions.right: A "65 YO Smoker MALE" fits the guideline group for one-time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm (men aged 65-75 who have ever smoked). Smoking and male sex are the strongest risk factors for AAA, and rupture is usually fatal, which makes AAA the most important screen for this specific profile.
questions.kc: AAA screening: Men 65-75 who have ever smoked: one-time abdominal ultrasound Risk factors: smoking, male, age, family history, hypertension Large or rapidly growing aneurysm: refer for repair Smaller aneurysm: ultrasound surveillance, stop smoking
questions.ep: "Male + smoker + 65" is the trigger phrase for AAA ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 60-something-year-old man with known COPD, controlled with bronchodilators , comes for a routine follow-up . He quit smoking 12 years ago. *symptom exacerbate during winter* His oxygen saturation ranges from 89% to 91% . What is the most appropriate management?

why.A: Long-term azithromycin is added for patients with frequent exacerbations despite optimal inhaled therapy (and is weighed against hearing loss, QT prolongation and resistance); this patient is controlled and only worse in winter.
why.C: Long-term oxygen requires resting PaO2 ≤55 mmHg (SpO2 ≤88%) on 2 readings, or PaO2 56 to 59 mmHg with cor pulmonale, edema or polycythemia; SpO2 89 to 91% without these does not qualify.
why.D: This is a recall note that influenza vaccine was not among the options; if it had been listed, annual influenza vaccine would be an equally standard preventive measure.

questions.right: A stable COPD patient at "routine follow-up", controlled on bronchodilators, with SpO2 "89% to 91%" and exacerbations in winter needs preventive care. Vaccination (pneumococcal and annual influenza) is recommended for all COPD patients and reduces lower respiratory infections and exacerbations; with influenza not offered, pneumococcal vaccine is the answer. As the compiler notes, SpO2 89 to 91% does not meet criteria for home oxygen.
questions.kc: Stable COPD extras: Vaccines for all: influenza yearly, pneumococcal, COVID-19 (and pertussis per guidelines) Survival benefit: smoking cessation, long-term oxygen when indicated LTOT: PaO2 ≤55 mmHg or SpO2 ≤88%, or 56 to 59 mmHg with cor pulmonale, edema, hematocrit >55% Frequent exacerbations despite therapy: azithromycin or roflumilast Pulmonary rehabilitation for symptomatic patients
questions.ep: SpO2 ≤88% at rest flips the answer to home oxygen; 89 to 91% does not.

questions.stem: A 65- yo male kc of SEVERE COPD presents with exertional dyspnea, drowsiness and cyanosis for the last 2 days. On examination he is alert but somnolent with bilateral wheezing. Vitals: No fever, Bp 100/60, Rr 10 , O2 sat 84%, Hypercapnic and hypoximic on ABG, PH 7.25 exactly. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step

why.B: High flow oxygen at 15 L/min via non rebreather in a CO2 retainer worsens hypercapnia and narcosis; COPD oxygen is titrated to a target saturation of about 88 to 92% via controlled delivery.
why.C: NIV (BiPAP) is right for an alert, cooperative COPD patient with pH 7.25 to 7.35 and raised PCO2 despite medical therapy; it fails here because he is somnolent with a slowing respiratory rate.

questions.right: This is an acute exacerbation of severe COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure and pH 7.25 , which on its own would suggest NIV. The decisive clues are the drowsiness/somnolence and a respiratory rate of only 10 : the patient is tiring and his airway protection and cooperation are failing, which are contraindications to NIV. A patient who cannot protect the airway or is exhausted needs intubation and mechanical ventilation.
questions.kc: COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic acidosis: NIV vs intubation. Alert, cooperative, pH below 7.35 with high PCO2: NIV Drowsy, low GCS, exhaustion, falling RR, poor gag, copious secretions, vomiting, haemodynamic instability: intubate NIV failing after 1 to 2 hours: intubate Oxygen target in COPD: 88 to 92%
questions.ep: A slow respiratory rate plus drowsiness in hypercapnic COPD is not improvement, it is exhaustion: intubate, do not BiPAP.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever and a productive cough of yellowish sputum. Medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is a smoker . His chest examination reveals decreased breath sounds throughout and crackles at the right lung base. Other systemic examination is unremarkable (see report). Chest radiograph: Right lower lobe infiltrates. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

opts.A: Admit him, start ceftriaxone and azithromycin

why.B: IV amoxicillin alone misses atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila); inpatient CAP needs a beta lactam plus macrolide.
why.C: Azithromycin monotherapy is only for healthy outpatients without comorbidities and with low local macrolide resistance; diabetes excludes it.
why.D: Cefuroxime without azithromycin lacks atypical cover. In the original recall this option read 'cefuroxime and azithromycin' and was the key, so read the wording carefully.

questions.right: This is community acquired pneumonia (fever, purulent sputum, crackles, right lower lobe infiltrate ) in a diabetic smoker . A comorbidity rules out macrolide monotherapy and requires beta lactam plus macrolide (or a respiratory fluoroquinolone). In this modified recall the outpatient option lacks azithromycin, so ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the only option giving typical plus atypical cover, which is why the source keys A.
questions.kc: CAP regimen follows setting and comorbidity. Healthy outpatient: amoxicillin, doxycycline or a macrolide Outpatient with comorbidity (DM, CKD, heart, lung, liver, alcohol): beta lactam + macrolide, or respiratory FQ Inpatient non ICU: ceftriaxone + azithromycin, or respiratory FQ CURB65 0 to 1: home; 2: consider admission; 3 or more: admit / ICU
questions.ep: Same stem, different option D: with 'cefuroxime AND azithromycin' answer outpatient; without azithromycin, answer A.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old patient presents with cough, fever, and lung consolidation . Laboratory results show neutrophilia . No other medical comorbidities . What is the most likely causative organism?

why.B: Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia is classically post-influenza, in IV drug users or with cavitating/necrotising lesions; not the default in a healthy adult.
why.C: E. coli and other Gram-negatives cause pneumonia mainly in hospital-acquired, aspiration or debilitated patients, not in healthy community patients.
why.D: Listeria causes meningitis and sepsis in neonates, the elderly, pregnancy and immunosuppression; it is not a cause of community-acquired pneumonia in a healthy adult.

questions.right: Cough, fever and lung consolidation with neutrophilia in a previously healthy adult ("no other medical comorbidities") is typical community-acquired pneumonia, and Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of CAP.
questions.kc: Pneumonia organism by setting. Healthy community adult: S. pneumoniae Atypical (dry cough, bilateral infiltrates): Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, viruses Post-influenza, cavitation: S. aureus Alcoholic, currant-jelly sputum: Klebsiella Hospital-acquired: Pseudomonas, Gram-negatives HIV with CD4 <200: Pneumocystis
questions.ep: No special risk factor given = most common organism = S. pneumoniae.

questions.stem: A prisoner presents with fever, productive foul-smelling green sputum , weight loss, and shortness of breath. He appears cachectic. Chest X-ray shows a mass with thick wall and irregular borders and an air–fluid level in the left lower lobe. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.B: Chemotherapy requires a tissue diagnosis of malignancy; a cavitating carcinoma (often squamous) is in the differential, but foul purulent sputum indicates an abscess.
why.C: Surgical resection is reserved for abscesses that fail prolonged antibiotics and drainage, massive hemoptysis, or proven resectable cancer.
why.D: Bronchoscopy with BAL is right when obstruction by a tumor or foreign body is suspected, the abscess does not respond to antibiotics, or TB needs sampling; it is not the first step for a typical abscess.

questions.right: Foul smelling green sputum , fever and a thick walled cavity with an air fluid level in the lower lobe is a lung abscess, typically from aspiration of mixed anaerobic and aerobic oral flora (risks: alcohol, poor dentition, reduced consciousness, institutional settings). Treatment is prolonged antibiotics with anaerobic cover, with sputum or fluid sampling (aspiration) for culture and drainage if it does not resolve. The foul odour and air fluid level point to infection rather than tumor or TB.
questions.kc: Cavitating lung lesion, sort by clue: Foul sputum, air fluid level, dependent lobe: lung abscess, antibiotics with anaerobic cover Upper lobe cavity, night sweats, weeks of symptoms: TB, AFB stain and culture Older smoker, hemoptysis, thick irregular wall without foul sputum: cavitating carcinoma No response to antibiotics: bronchoscopy
questions.ep: An air fluid level with foul sputum is an abscess: treat with antibiotics first, not surgery or chemotherapy.

questions.stem: 30 years old man teacher medically free present to ER with fever, cough for 3 day . No night sweating. CXR show right lobe consolidation and 25 mm pleural effusion decubitus . What is initial management:

why.B: Anti TB drugs need a TB picture (weeks of fever, night sweats, weight loss, upper lobe cavitation, lymphocytic exudate with high ADA); this is a 3 day acute illness with no night sweats.
why.C: IV antibiotics are needed for the pneumonia, but with a sizable effusion the key initial step the question tests is sampling the fluid; antibiotics alone would be right for pneumonia with a small (under 10 mm) effusion.
why.D: IV fluids are supportive only; there is no sign of shock or dehydration in the stem.

questions.right: This is community acquired pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion of 25 mm on the decubitus film . An effusion more than about 10 mm thick on lateral decubitus is large enough to sample, and the lead in asks for the initial step on this effusion: diagnostic thoracocentesis to check pH, glucose, LDH, Gram stain and culture, which decides whether it is complicated and needs a chest drain. Antibiotics are given as well, but the question targets the effusion work up.
questions.kc: Parapneumonic effusion: tap anything that layers more than 10 mm on decubitus film. Diagnostic tap: pH, glucose, LDH, protein, Gram stain, culture Drain if pus, positive Gram stain/culture, pH below 7.2, low glucose or loculation TB effusion: lymphocytic exudate, ADA most sensitive
questions.ep: Pneumonia plus a sampleable effusion: the initial step is diagnostic thoracocentesis, not just antibiotics.

questions.stem: 60 yo man presented with a complaint of shortness of breath and cough for 2 weeks, he has a strong history of smoking , this is not the first time he present, history is positive for weight loss , on exam he had dulness on the right side, CT showed right sided effusion. Thoracentesis showed Exudative effusion (pH 7.3, slightly below normal, protein high, glucose low 1.5) what is the most appropriate next step?

why.A: Surgical decortication removes a thick pleural peel in organised empyema or fibrothorax with trapped lung in a fit patient; it is not palliation for malignant effusion. Other options a student might consider: repeated therapeutic taps (only for slow reaccumulation or very short prognosis), chest tube drainage (empyema: pH below 7.2 or pus), and CT / pleural biopsy for tissue diagnosis.

questions.right: A heavy smoker with weight loss , a recurrent right effusion and an exudate with low glucose and mildly low pH has a malignant pleural effusion until proven otherwise. A recurrent symptomatic malignant effusion is palliated by definitive drainage: an indwelling tunnelled pleural catheter or pleurodesis.
