Pleurodesis was not among the options, so the tunnelled catheter is the answer.
questions.kc: Recurrent symptomatic malignant effusion: IPC or pleurodesis. Light criteria: fluid/serum protein above 0.5 or LDH above 0.6 = exudate Malignancy clues: smoker, weight loss, recurrence, bloody fluid Trapped lung or failed pleurodesis: indwelling tunnelled catheter Empyema (pus, pH below 7.2, low glucose): chest tube drainage Organised empyema with trapped lung: decortication
questions.ep: 'Not the first time' plus weight loss in a smoker = malignant and recurrent: think IPC / pleurodesis, not decortication.

questions.stem: A man in his 60s with known adenocarcinoma presented with mild dyspnea and clubbing. Vitals: BP 117/?, RR 18, HR 118, Temp 36°C, O2 95%. Imaging showed right spiculated apical nodules with abnormal uptake. Negative hormone receptors test. Management?

why.A: Observation is not appropriate for a confirmed malignancy with PET uptake; it is reserved for small indeterminate nodules being followed.
why.B: Chemotherapy is used as adjuvant after resection, for neoadjuvant downstaging or for advanced (stage IV) disease, not as the definitive treatment of resectable disease.
why.C: Radiotherapy (including stereotactic) is the choice for early stage disease when the patient is medically unfit for or refuses surgery.

questions.right: The recall is read as a primary lung adenocarcinoma : a spiculated apical lesion with abnormal uptake (PET avid), only mild dyspnea and O2 95%, with no metastases described. For localised, resectable non small cell lung cancer in a patient fit for surgery, resection (lobectomy) offers the best chance of cure, which is why the key is surgery.
questions.kc: NSCLC: stage decides; early stage and fit = surgery. Stage I to II (and selected IIIA): lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node sampling Unfit for surgery: stereotactic body radiotherapy Stage III unresectable: concurrent chemoradiotherapy Stage IV: systemic therapy guided by molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, PD-L1) Apical (Pancoast) tumour: neoadjuvant chemoradiation then surgery Clubbing is common in adenocarcinoma and does not imply metastasis
questions.ep: Metastases or malignant pleural effusion flip the answer to systemic therapy, not surgery.

questions.stem: 38yrs male SOB, confusion presented to icu had urti 5 days ago and detriorated Vitals normal only oxygen 75 ABG all normal

why.A: COPD needs years of smoking and chronic symptoms in an older patient; a 38 year old with an acute post viral illness does not fit.
why.C: Myasthenic crisis after an infection causes weakness, ptosis, bulbar signs and hypoventilation with rising CO2; there is no weakness described and confusion is not a feature.
why.D: Drug overdose (e.g. opioids, sedatives) causes hypoventilation with low respiratory rate, miosis or reduced consciousness and hypercapnia; the stem gives no drug history and a URTI preceding the decline.

questions.right: This recall's key is pulmonary edema: a previously healthy 38 year old who deteriorated after a URTI 5 days ago with breathlessness, confusion and oxygen saturation 75% could have cardiogenic edema from viral myocarditis or non cardiogenic edema (ARDS) after a viral illness, and severe hypoxemia explains the confusion. Note that pulmonary edema this severe would not give a normal ABG, so the recalled 'ABG all normal' does not fit this key.
questions.kc: Acute hypoxemia after a viral illness in a young adult: Viral myocarditis: heart failure picture, pulmonary edema ARDS/viral pneumonia: bilateral infiltrates, non cardiogenic edema Myasthenic crisis or GBS: weakness with hypercapnic failure Overdose: hypoventilation, hypercapnia, drug history
questions.ep: Low SpO2 with a normal ABG is a saturation gap: think methemoglobinemia or CO before pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A patient went to smoking cessation clinic, the doctor decides to prescribe a medication, which one has higher success rate ?

why.A: Clonidine has some effect on withdrawal but is a second line agent limited by sedation and hypotension; its success rate is lower than varenicline.
why.B: Escitalopram (SSRI) has no proven benefit for smoking cessation.
why.C: Bupropion is an effective first line agent, but its quit rates are lower than varenicline; it is also contraindicated in epilepsy and eating disorders because it lowers the seizure threshold.

questions.right: The question asks which drug has the higher success rate , not which is used first. Varenicline, a partial agonist at the nicotine receptor, gives the highest abstinence rates of the single agents and outperforms both bupropion and single form nicotine replacement in trials.
questions.kc: Smoking cessation drugs: varenicline has the highest single agent success rate. Options: NRT, bupropion, varenicline (all first line in current guidelines) Many exam keys list NRT as the initial therapy and varenicline as second line Bupropion: avoid in seizures, bulimia, anorexia Combination NRT (patch + short acting) approaches varenicline efficacy Second line: clonidine, nortriptyline
questions.ep: "Highest success rate" = varenicline; "initial therapy" in some keys = NRT; "patient with epilepsy" = avoid bupropion.

questions.stem: A Patient Presents With Dull Chest Pain That Is Not Related To Activity . The Pain Is More Prominent After Spicy Meals Or Emotional Stress And Increases With Lying Flat . Hb: 110 (Lower Than Normal) How To Establish The Diagnosis?

why.A: Barium swallow is the first test for dysphagia (especially suspected achalasia or ring/web), or when endoscopy is not possible; it cannot biopsy or assess mucosa well.
why.C: Esophageal manometry diagnoses motility disorders (achalasia, diffuse spasm) and is done before anti-reflux surgery; it is not used to diagnose GERD with anemia.
why.D: 24-hour pH monitoring is for refractory symptoms with a NORMAL endoscopy, to prove reflux is the cause; it comes after endoscopy.

questions.right: Chest pain worse after spicy meals and lying flat , not related to exertion, is reflux (GERD). The decisive clue is Hb 110 : anemia is an alarm feature, so the diagnosis must be established with upper endoscopy, which shows esophagitis, ulcers, Barrett's or a tumour and allows biopsy. Empirical PPI is only for typical reflux without alarm features.
questions.kc: Reflux work-up: Typical GERD, no alarm features: empirical PPI trial Alarm features (anemia, weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding, older age): endoscopy first Refractory GERD with normal endoscopy: pH (impedance) monitoring Before fundoplication: manometry Dysphagia to solids and liquids: think achalasia, barium then manometry
questions.ep: Low Hb in a reflux stem converts 'trial PPI' into 'scope now'.

questions.stem: Vomiting blood 2 hours, melena 2 days . Indigestion and abdominal epigastric tenderness , pallor, DRE show melena only. BO 95/60 (sure). Most definitive investigation?

why.B: Colposcopy examines the cervix and has no role in GI bleeding; if the intended option was colonoscopy, that is for lower GI bleeding (hematochezia), not hematemesis with melena.
why.C: CT angiography is used when bleeding is brisk and endoscopy cannot find or control the source (or for lower GI bleeding), leading to embolization; it is not the first definitive test for an upper GI bleed.
why.D: Chest X-ray can show free air if perforation is suspected or aspiration, but it cannot identify a bleeding source.

questions.right: "Vomiting blood" with "melena 2 days", epigastric tenderness, indigestion and pallor is an upper GI bleed, most likely a peptic ulcer. The lead-in asks for the "most definitive investigation": upper endoscopy identifies the source, stratifies rebleeding risk and allows therapy (injection, clipping, thermal) in the same session, ideally within 24 hours after resuscitation. The BP of 95/60 calls for resuscitation first, but it does not change the definitive test.
questions.kc: Upper GI bleeding: Hematemesis or melena (or coffee-ground vomitus): upper source Step 1: ABC, two large-bore IV lines, crossmatch, PPI infusion Transfuse if Hb below 7 (8 with cardiac disease) Endoscopy within 24 hours (diagnostic and therapeutic) Liver disease signs: add octreotide and ceftriaxone, endoscopy within 12 hours Endoscopy fails: CT angiography and embolization, then surgery
questions.ep: "Initial" step in an unstable bleed = resuscitation; "definitive" investigation = upper endoscopy.

questions.stem: Chronic Liver Disease presented to ER with hematemesis fails to control with octreotide and ligation . Most appropriate next step?

why.A: Surgical shunts or devascularization are now rarely used; they have high mortality in decompensated cirrhosis and are a last resort when TIPS is unavailable or not possible.
why.C: A second endoscopic attempt can be considered for early rebleeding after initial control, but when bleeding cannot be controlled despite drugs plus banding, repeating the same therapy delays effective rescue.
why.D: Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tube) controls massive bleeding temporarily, but it is only a bridge (for up to about 24 hours) to TIPS because bleeding recurs on deflation and complications are high.

questions.right: In variceal bleeding, "fails to control with octreotide and ligation" means failure of combined vasoactive and endoscopic therapy. The definitive rescue treatment is TIPS, which lowers portal pressure by shunting portal blood into the hepatic vein and stops bleeding in most refractory cases. The compiler states the answer is correct, although the card is not confirmed from the other section.
questions.kc: Acute variceal bleed ladder: Resuscitate, restrictive transfusion (Hb target about 7 to 8) Vasoactive drug (octreotide or terlipressin) + IV ceftriaxone Endoscopy within 12 hours: band ligation Failure: balloon tamponade or esophageal stent as a bridge Definitive rescue: TIPS After control: nonselective beta-blocker + repeat banding
questions.ep: Uncontrolled torrential bleed in an unstable patient = balloon as a bridge; definitive rescue = TIPS.

questions.stem: 35 male has metallic valve on warfarin anticoagulant, drowsy complaining of bloody stool. Examination: cold periphery, hypotension and pallor. (Vitals: BP 90/65 mmHg; Hb 6 (low); WBC 12 (high); platelets 550 (high); PT 40 (prolonged); APTT 60 (prolonged); INR 7 ) what is the most appropriate INITIAL therapy in the FLUID terms ?

why.A: Ringer lactate is a crystalloid for volume replacement; it dilutes the remaining clotting factors and does nothing for an INR of 7. It is the first fluid in a bleeder with normal coagulation.
why.C: Normal saline is the initial resuscitation fluid in GI bleeding when coagulation is normal (e.g. NSAID ulcer with Hb above 7); here the problem is warfarin coagulopathy, and saline worsens dilution.
why.D: Packed RBC are needed (Hb 6, shock) and are given alongside reversal, but they do not correct the INR, so bleeding continues; this would be the answer in hemorrhagic shock without anticoagulation.

questions.right: The decisive clues are metallic valve on warfarin , INR 7 with prolonged PT and APTT, and a major bleed with shock (bloody stool, drowsy, cold periphery, BP 90/65, Hb 6). This is warfarin associated life threatening bleeding, so the priority is to reverse the coagulopathy: the bleeding will not stop while the INR is 7. Prothrombin complex concentrate (the 'purified protein factor' option) replaces factors II, VII, IX and X within minutes in a small volume and is given with IV vitamin K. As the compiler notes, BP 90/65 is acceptable under permissive hypotension, so reversal comes before large volume crystalloid.
questions.kc: Warfarin + bleeding = reverse first (PCC or FFP) plus IV vitamin K, then transfuse as needed. Bleeding on warfarin: admit, IV vitamin K plus PCC (preferred, fast, small volume) or FFP No bleeding, INR above 10: hold warfarin, oral vitamin K No bleeding, INR 4 to 10: hold warfarin, consider low dose oral vitamin K GI bleed without coagulopathy: crystalloid first, transfuse if Hb below 7 (8 with cardiac disease) PT measures extrinsic (VII), APTT intrinsic; warfarin lowers II, VII, IX, X
questions.ep: Shock plus GI bleed normally means crystalloid or blood, but once the stem says warfarin with a high INR, the answer flips to reversal with PCC.

questions.stem: 35 male has metallic valve on warfarin anticoagulant, drowsy complaining of bloody stool . Examination: cold periphery, hypotension (WRITTEN In Question) and pallor. Vitals signs: BP 90/65 mmHg; Hb 6 (low); WBC 12 (high); Thrombocytosis 550 (high); PT 40 (prolonged); APTT 60 (prolonged); INR 7 . what is the Most Appropriate?

why.A: Ringer lactate supports volume but does nothing for the INR of 7, and large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and worsen bleeding.
why.C: Normal saline is the same problem as RL: volume without reversal; it is the answer for bleeding with a normal INR.
why.D: Packed RBCs are needed with Hb 6 and shock, but replacing blood while the patient remains anticoagulated will not stop the bleeding; some examinees choose RBC for an "initial" version.

questions.right: A patient with a mechanical valve on warfarin has active GI bleeding with shock and INR 7 ; the bleeding is driven by the coagulopathy, so urgent reversal is the priority. The recommended reversal for warfarin-related major bleeding is IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (preferred over FFP because it is faster and low-volume). The compiler endorses PCC for both "initial" and "most appropriate" wording.
questions.kc: Warfarin and high INR. Major bleeding (any INR): hold warfarin, IV vitamin K plus PCC (or FFP if PCC unavailable) No bleeding, INR >10: hold warfarin, oral vitamin K No bleeding, INR 4 to 10: hold warfarin, recheck, consider low-dose oral vitamin K Mechanical valve: reverse for life-threatening bleed, then restart anticoagulation once safe
questions.ep: Bleeding plus high INR: the drug that fixes the coagulopathy (PCC) beats fluids and blood alone.

questions.stem: patient with HTN and A.fib on warfarin, complaining of nose bleed. Recently he started taking herbal supplements . INR 4.4 What is the management?

opts.B: Stop herpal and reacheck INR in 48 hours

why.A: Aspirin does not provide adequate stroke prevention in AF and adds bleeding risk; stopping anticoagulation is wrong for a minor bleed with a correctable cause.
why.C: Switching to a DOAC is a reasonable long term choice for non valvular AF with unstable INRs, but it is not the immediate step for a high INR caused by a removable interaction with minor bleeding.

questions.right: The INR of 4.4 is above the AF target of 2 to 3, and the cause is the newly started herbal supplement interacting with warfarin. The bleeding is minor (epistaxis) with no sign of instability, so management is to remove the cause, hold or reduce warfarin and recheck the INR within 1 to 2 days; vitamin K with FFP or PCC is reserved for major bleeding. Warfarin should not be abandoned because he still needs AF stroke prevention.
questions.kc: High INR on warfarin: Major bleeding: stop warfarin, IV vitamin K plus PCC or FFP, admit Minor bleeding: hold warfarin, consider oral or IV vitamin K, recheck INR, find the cause No bleeding, mildly high INR: omit or reduce dose and recheck Always look for interacting drugs, herbs, diet changes AF/DVT target INR 2 to 3
questions.ep: High INR after a new herbal product: stop the herb and recheck, do not drop anticoagulation for AF.

questions.stem: A national health authority is planning to implement a cancer prevention and screening program. The decision will be based on the overall impact and public health burden Which of the following cancers would be the most appropriate target for such a national screening program?

why.A: Pancreatic cancer has no effective, affordable screening test for the general population; screening is only considered in very high-risk inherited groups.
why.C: Lung cancer screening (low-dose CT) is targeted to heavy current or former smokers, not a whole-population programme.
why.D: Esophageal cancer has no general-population screening; endoscopic surveillance is limited to high-risk groups such as Barrett's esophagus.

questions.right: A population screening programme needs a common cancer with a high burden, a detectable precursor or early stage, and an acceptable, effective test. Colorectal cancer fits all: it is among the commonest cancers, adenomas can be found and removed, and FOBT or FIT and colonoscopy reduce mortality in average-risk adults.
questions.kc: Population screening needs burden + detectable early phase + acceptable test + effective treatment. Average-risk national programmes: colorectal, breast, cervical CRC: start at 45 (choose 50 if 45 not offered); colonoscopy every 10 years or annual FOBT/FIT Lung: low-dose CT only for high-risk smokers
questions.ep: "National" screening = average-risk population; lung CT is targeted, not national.

questions.stem: 45 years old comes for colorectal cancer screening, everything is normal + NEGATIVE family History , and ask about when to do screening? A. Why wrong: Option A was not recalled. If it read "now (at 45) and every 10 years", it would match current guidelines and beat C; otherwise C stays the best listed choice.

why.B: Every 5 years is the interval for flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography, not for a normal colonoscopy in an average risk person.
why.D: Starting at 60 is too late for an average risk adult and would miss years of screening in which many cancers and advanced adenomas are found. The 10 year interval is right, but the start age is not.

questions.right: This is an average risk adult: age 45, normal examination and "NEGATIVE family history". Screening colonoscopy, if normal, is repeated every 10 years. The compiler explains that "now and every 10 years" was not among the choices, so the examiner applied the older starting age of 50 with the 10 year colonoscopy interval, which is the only listed option combining an accepted start age with the correct colonoscopy interval.
questions.kc: Average risk colorectal cancer screening. Start at 45 (if 45 is not offered, choose 50); continue to 75 Colonoscopy: every 10 years Flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography: every 5 years FIT: every year; stool DNA test: every 3 years Positive stool test: colonoscopy First degree relative with CRC before 60: start at 40 (or 10 years before the relative's age), colonoscopy every 5 years
questions.ep: If an option says now (at 45) and every 10 years, it beats at 50 and every 10 years.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the clinic requesting screening for colorectal cancer because he is concerned about his risk. His relative was diagnosed with colorectal cancer at the age of 50 . When should colorectal cancer screening be initiated in this patient?

opts.A: Screen at 50 and repeat after 5 years.
opts.B: Screen at 50 and repeat after 10 years.
opts.C: Start screening now and repeat after 10 years

why.A: Waiting until 50 ignores his family history; starting at 45 (or 50 in older keys) is the rule for average risk adults only.
why.B: Starting at 50 with 10 yearly colonoscopy is the old average risk schedule, which does not apply to someone with an affected relative.

questions.right: A relative diagnosed with colorectal cancer at 50 makes this man higher than average risk, and screening for such patients starts at age 40 (or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, which here is also 40). He is 40 now, so screening should start now; the source keys the option that starts screening immediately.
questions.kc: Colorectal cancer screening start. Average risk: 45 (choose 50 if 45 is absent), colonoscopy every 10 years One first degree relative diagnosed at 60 or older: start at 40, average risk intervals First degree relative under 60, or two first degree relatives: start at 40 or 10 years before the youngest case, colonoscopy every 5 years Positive FOBT or FIT: colonoscopy
questions.ep: The age of the relative at diagnosis sets both the start age and the interval.

questions.stem: 40 Y.O male with a family history of "A" Relative Diagnosed With colon cancer At Age Of 50 in a relative when to screen

why.B: Starting at 50 ignores the family history; 50 was the old average risk start (now 45), and even a second degree relative would not make 'every 5 years from 50' correct.
why.C: Start at 50 with 10 yearly colonoscopy is the old average risk schedule; a relative with CRC brings the start forward to 40.
why.D: Age 60 is not a start age in any colorectal schedule.

questions.right: A family history of colon cancer in a relative diagnosed at age 50 places him above average risk, so screening starts at 40 years (or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, which is also 40). He is 40, so screening starts now . The degree of relative is not stated and there is no 'now and every 5 years' option, so 'now and every 10 years' is the only option with the correct start age (keyed by ACG reasoning in the source).
questions.kc: Colorectal screening start depends on risk. Average risk: start at 45 (choose 50 if 45 absent); colonoscopy every 10 years One first degree relative diagnosed at 60 or older: start at 40, average risk intervals (colonoscopy every 10 years) First degree relative diagnosed under 60 (or 2 first degree relatives): start at 40 or 10 years before the youngest diagnosis, whichever is earlier; colonoscopy every 5 years Second degree relative only: treated as average risk FAP / Lynch: start in adolescence / early 20s
questions.ep: Pick the option with the right START age first (40 or 10 years before the relative); the interval is secondary when no 'every 5' option exists.

questions.stem: 65 years old woman presents to the ER with complaint of change in bowel habits bloody sometimes, weight loss , pale skin. what is the initial step in management?

why.A: Fecal occult blood testing is a screening tool for asymptomatic average-risk people; with visible bleeding and alarm features it adds nothing and only delays colonoscopy.

questions.right: A "65 years old" with "change in bowel habits", rectal "bloody" stool, "weight loss" and pallor has red-flag symptoms of colorectal cancer. Symptomatic patients go straight to colonoscopy, which visualizes the whole colon and allows biopsy for tissue diagnosis.
questions.kc: Suspected colorectal cancer: Alarm features: age over 50, bleeding, weight loss, anemia, change in bowel habit Symptomatic: colonoscopy with biopsy Asymptomatic: screening (FIT/FOBT, colonoscopy) Positive FOBT: always colonoscopy Staging after diagnosis: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, CEA
questions.ep: FOBT is for screening the well; symptoms of cancer mean colonoscopy.

questions.stem: X -year-old patient presents with bloody diarrhea and a positive family history, as his mother and brother have the same condition. The guaiac test is positive. What is the likely diagnosis?

why.A: Ulcerative colitis also presents with bloody diarrhea in young adults and has a family tendency, but it is polygenic, not a clear dominant pattern of mother and sibling affected; choose UC when urgency, tenesmus, mucus and recurrent flares are emphasised without such a family history.
why.B: Diverticulosis is a disease of older adults and presents with painless large-volume bleeding, not inherited bloody diarrhea in a young patient.
why.D: Peutz-Jeghers is also autosomal dominant, but its hallmark is mucocutaneous pigmentation of the lips and mouth with hamartomatous small bowel polyps causing intussusception; no pigmentation is described here.

questions.right: Bloody diarrhea (guaiac positive) with the same condition in both mother and brother points to an autosomal dominant inherited disorder. Familial adenomatous polyposis is autosomal dominant, presents in the teens or twenties with rectal bleeding and diarrhea from hundreds of colonic adenomas, and fits this vertical plus sibling pattern best. The compiler notes that age does not separate FAP from UC; the strong family pattern does.
questions.kc: Familial adenomatous polyposis: Autosomal dominant (APC gene); onset typically mid teens to 20s Hundreds to thousands of adenomas, colon "carpeted" with polyps Near 100% colorectal cancer risk if untreated At-risk relatives: screening colonoscopy from early adolescence even if asymptomatic Treatment: prophylactic (procto)colectomy
questions.ep: Add perioral pigmentation and the answer becomes Peutz-Jeghers; remove the family history and add urgency/tenesmus and it becomes UC.

questions.stem: Long case .. A patient in his early twenties presents with intermittent diarrhea, sometimes , and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy with biopsy reveals skip lesions , areas of inflammation alternating with normal mucosa, and strictures . What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Ulcerative colitis is continuous mucosal inflammation starting from the rectum without skip areas, and strictures are uncommon; it would be right with bloody diarrhea and continuous proctocolitis.
why.C: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional disorder with a normal colonoscopy and biopsy.
why.D: Celiac disease affects the small bowel (villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy) with positive tTG-IgA, not colonic skip lesions.

questions.right: A young adult with chronic diarrhea and abdominal pain whose colonoscopy shows "skip lesions" (inflamed segments alternating with normal mucosa) and "strictures" has Crohn's disease. Crohn's inflammation is patchy and transmural, which produces skip lesions, strictures, fistulas and abscesses.
questions.kc: Crohn's vs ulcerative colitis: Crohn's: mouth to anus (terminal ileum common), skip lesions, transmural, granulomas Crohn's: strictures, fistulas, perianal disease, cobblestoning UC: rectum upward, continuous, mucosal, crypt abscesses UC: bloody diarrhea, PSC association Smoking worsens Crohn's; associated with lower UC risk
questions.ep: Skip lesions, strictures, fistulas, granulomas = Crohn's; continuous from the rectum = UC.

questions.stem: patient known case of ulcerative colitis For 7 Years presents with abdominal pain and ..., labs show: high billirubin. MRCP: multifocal strictures of the intrahepatic and extra hepatic bile ducts . Whats the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Acute (ascending) cholangitis presents with fever, RUQ pain and jaundice (Charcot triad) from an obstructing stone or stricture, not multifocal strictures throughout the biliary tree; it can complicate PSC.
why.B: Acalculous cholecystitis is gallbladder inflammation in critically ill patients (ICU, burns, sepsis, TPN) and does not cause bile duct strictures.
why.C: Primary biliary cholangitis affects middle-aged women, destroys small intrahepatic ducts that are invisible on MRCP, and is diagnosed by anti-mitochondrial antibody; the large ducts are normal.

questions.right: A patient with "ulcerative colitis for 7 years", cholestatic jaundice and MRCP showing "multifocal strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts" has primary sclerosing cholangitis. PSC is strongly associated with UC (most PSC patients have IBD), and MRCP showing multifocal strictures with intervening dilatation (beading) is the diagnostic test.
questions.kc: PSC vs PBC: PSC: men, UC association, intra and extrahepatic ducts, p-ANCA, MRCP beading PBC: women, small intrahepatic ducts, AMA, normal MRCP, treat with ursodeoxycholic acid PSC risks: cholangiocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, gallbladder cancer UC + PSC: yearly colonoscopic surveillance from diagnosis Definitive treatment for PSC: liver transplant
questions.ep: Big ducts beaded on MRCP = PSC; normal ducts with positive AMA = PBC.

questions.stem: Middle age man, presented with i think abdominal pain for few months almost 3 , 1 year ago he visited Thaliand and malesia There was negative culture

why.B: Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei) classically affects middle aged men but needs extra intestinal clues: migratory arthralgia, fever, lymphadenopathy, cardiac or CNS involvement (oculomasticatory myorhythmia); PAS positive macrophages on duodenal biopsy confirm it. None are given here.

questions.right: A man with months of GI symptoms beginning after residence/travel in Thailand and Malaysia (tropical regions) with negative cultures fits tropical sprue: a post infectious malabsorption syndrome of the tropics causing chronic diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, weight loss and later folate and B12 deficiency. It is treated with folic acid plus tetracycline. Whipple disease is rare and should be chosen only when a specific extra intestinal clue is given.
questions.kc: Chronic malabsorption, choose by clue: Tropical residence/travel, negative stool cultures: tropical sprue (folate + tetracycline) Arthralgia, CNS or cardiac signs, PAS positive macrophages: Whipple Gluten trigger, anti tTG positive: celiac Persistent travel diarrhea with positive stool microscopy: giardiasis
questions.ep: Do not pick Whipple without joints, heart or CNS clues; travel to the tropics points to tropical sprue.

questions.stem: A 40-50 -year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus On Aspirin presents to the clinic before travelling abroad. She asks about prophylaxis against travelers' diarrhea . Laboratory investigations show: Serum creatinine: ~100s (Maybe 120) . Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis?

why.A: Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis is reserved for selected high risk travelers (e.g. severe immunosuppression); risks include tendon rupture, QT prolongation and C. difficile, and they need dose adjustment in renal impairment.
why.C: Probiotics have inconsistent evidence for preventing travelers' diarrhea and are not a recommended prophylaxis.
why.D: Bismuth subsalicylate does reduce travelers' diarrhea and would be the usual non antibiotic option, but it contains salicylate: avoid with aspirin (salicylate toxicity, bleeding) and with renal impairment.

questions.right: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for travelers' diarrhea is not recommended for most travelers, because the illness is usually self limited and prophylaxis carries side effects, resistance and C. difficile risk. This woman with diabetes and mildly raised creatinine is not in the high risk group that might justify it, and she takes aspirin , which makes bismuth subsalicylate unsuitable. The advice is food and water precautions with early self treatment if diarrhea develops.
questions.kc: Travelers' diarrhea prophylaxis: Most travelers: no antibiotic prophylaxis, food and water hygiene Bismuth subsalicylate: option, but avoid with aspirin, anticoagulants, renal impairment, children Antibiotic prophylaxis: only selected high risk travelers Treatment if it occurs: fluids, loperamide, azithromycin for severe or dysenteric
questions.ep: Aspirin plus bismuth subsalicylate equals salicylate excess: remove bismuth, then the answer is no antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 27 year old male k/c ALL admitted for chemotherapy ; after 19 days he complains of crampy RLQ pain for the past 2 hours with diarrhea. He had blood with the last bowel motion Physical exam revealed grade 1 oral mucositis and RLQ tenderness with rebound. Labs: vitally stable, pancytopenia ( wbc 0.9 ) What is the most appropriate investigation?

why.A: Upper GI endoscopy examines the esophagus, stomach and duodenum, which do not explain RLQ peritonism, and instrumentation is risky in severe neutropenia.
why.B: Colonoscopy is relatively contraindicated in neutropenic enterocolitis because of the high risk of perforation of the thin, inflamed bowel wall.
why.D: Ultrasound can show bowel wall thickening but is operator dependent and less sensitive for complications; CT is the preferred test.

questions.right: A patient with ALL about 19 days into chemotherapy , profoundly neutropenic (WBC 0.9) , with mucositis, RLQ pain, diarrhea, blood and rebound tenderness has neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) until proven otherwise. CT of the abdomen (CAT scan is the same test) is the investigation of choice: it shows bowel wall thickening of the cecum and detects perforation, pneumatosis or abscess, as the compiler agrees.
questions.kc: Neutropenic fever + RLQ pain + diarrhea after chemo = typhlitis; diagnose with CT. Typically 10 to 14 days or more after cytotoxic chemotherapy, at the neutrophil nadir CT: cecal wall thickening, pneumatosis, perforation Avoid endoscopy, barium enema, rectal exams Treat: bowel rest, IV fluids, broad spectrum antibiotics covering anaerobes, G-CSF if needed Surgery for perforation, uncontrolled bleeding or deterioration
questions.ep: A child with suspected appendicitis gets US first; a neutropenic adult with RLQ pain gets CT.

questions.stem: male 30s came with red urine and Jundice , on exam (nothing significant) note: No other symptoms or signs as simple as that. (Labs: Hb low (90); platelets normal i think 450; heptoglobin low ; LDH high ; High indirect bilirubin ) Which on of the following helps to diagnose?

why.B: Reticulocyte count confirms that the anemia is regenerative (marrow responding, as in hemolysis or bleeding) but does not identify the cause; it is the answer when the question asks for the next or initial test in an unexplained anemia. C. Option C was not recalled by the examinee, so it cannot be assessed (the recaller notes a blood film was not among the options).
why.D: Cold agglutinin titre is a second-line test done after the Coombs test is positive for complement (C3) to confirm cold agglutinin disease; it is not the first diagnostic test.

questions.right: The labs prove hemolysis: low Hb, "haptoglobin low, LDH high, high indirect bilirubin", with red urine (hemoglobinuria) and jaundice. The lead-in asks which test "helps to diagnose" the cause: the direct Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test is the key test that separates immune (autoimmune hemolytic anemia) from nonimmune hemolysis, and its pattern (IgG vs C3) guides further workup. The compiler stresses that this stem did not say "next"; a different recall of the same scenario asking for the next step was keyed to reticulocyte count.
questions.kc: Hemolysis workup: Confirm hemolysis: high LDH, low haptoglobin, high indirect bilirubin, high reticulocytes Blood film: spherocytes, schistocytes, bite cells Direct Coombs: immune vs nonimmune Warm AIHA: IgG, DAT IgG positive Cold AIHA: IgM, DAT C3 positive, then cold agglutinin titre Coombs negative with hemoglobinuria: think PNH (flow cytometry) or G6PD
questions.ep: "Next" step in anemia = reticulocytes; test that "diagnoses" the cause of hemolysis = Coombs.

questions.stem: 39 y.o with mycoplasma pneumonia started on antibiotics and supportive therapy. On day 3 She started complaining of yellowish discoloration of the eyes and mild abdominal pain. (Labs: Platelet LOW; Reticulocyte 4 (high) ; ALT normal, AST 70-80?; Haptoglobin 0.4 )

why.A: Observation lets the drug keep causing hemolysis; drug-induced hemolysis must be addressed by removing the cause.
why.C: Corticosteroids are first line for warm autoimmune hemolysis; they are not the first step in drug-induced hemolysis and are ineffective in cold agglutinin disease.
why.D: Rituximab is given intravenously, not orally, and is used for symptomatic primary cold agglutinin disease or refractory warm AIHA; Mycoplasma-related cold agglutinin hemolysis is usually self-limited.

questions.right: Three days after starting antibiotics she develops jaundice with hemolysis ( high reticulocytes, low haptoglobin , raised AST with normal ALT) and low platelets. Mycoplasma cold agglutinin hemolysis usually appears in the second or third week of illness, so a new hemolysis right after a drug is started points to drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia . The first and most important step is to stop the offending antibiotic ; the compiler strongly endorses this.
questions.kc: Hemolysis after a new drug: stop the drug first. Hemolysis markers: high retics, low haptoglobin, raised LDH and indirect bilirubin, AST more than ALT Drug-induced: onset soon after drug, stop the drug Mycoplasma cold agglutinins: IgM, onset weeks into illness, avoid cold, rituximab if severe Warm AIHA: IgG, steroids first
questions.ep: Timing is the clue: days after a new drug means drug-induced; weeks into Mycoplasma means cold agglutinins.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old female known case of sickle cell disease presented hypoxic, tachypneic, febrile with new right side infiltration on chest x-ray. What will you give beside antibiotic?

why.A: Allopurinol treats hyperuricemia and gout; it has no role in acute chest syndrome.
why.B: Hydroxyurea raises HbF and reduces the frequency of future crises and chest syndrome; it is preventive, not acute treatment.
why.D: Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant for rheumatological disease and has no role in sickle cell crises.

questions.right: Fever, tachypnea, hypoxia and a new infiltrate in a patient with sickle cell disease is acute chest syndrome . Being hypoxic marks it as severe, and severe acute chest syndrome is an indication for exchange transfusion alongside antibiotics, oxygen and analgesia. Exchange lowers the HbS fraction without raising viscosity.
questions.kc: Sickle cell transfusion: simple vs exchange. Simple: severe symptomatic anemia, sequestration, aplastic crisis, mild acute chest syndrome Exchange: severe or progressive acute chest syndrome, acute stroke, multiorgan failure Hydroxyurea: long-term prevention of crises and chest syndrome
questions.ep: If asked how to REDUCE future episodes, the answer flips to hydroxyurea.

questions.stem: sickle symptoms and askes what NOT present in electrophoresis to confirm the diagnosis?

why.B: HbS is present and predominant in sickle cell disease; it is the defining band.
why.C: HbC is also absent in HbSS, but its absence only tells you this is not HbSC disease; it does not confirm sickle cell anemia. The absence of HbA is what separates disease from trait.
why.D: HbF is present and often raised in sickle cell disease as a compensatory response.

questions.right: In homozygous sickle cell anemia (HbSS) the patient has no normal beta chains, so HbA is absent on electrophoresis. The pattern is predominant HbS with raised HbF and normal HbA2. The absence of HbA is what distinguishes sickle cell disease from sickle cell trait.
questions.kc: Hb electrophoresis patterns. Sickle cell anemia (SS): HbA absent, HbS predominant, HbF raised Sickle cell trait (AS): HbA more than HbS HbSC disease: HbS + HbC, no HbA Beta thal major: HbA absent or very low, HbF very high Beta thal minor: HbA2 raised
questions.ep: Trait has BOTH HbA and HbS; disease has NO HbA. The lead-in asks what is NOT present.

questions.stem: Female patient came with painless neck mass . She has history of wight loss and fever for 3 months. Her labs showed (Labs: high creatinine ; low albumin; high K ; High uric acid ; High Magnesium; low calcium ) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?

why.B: TB lymphadenitis causes a painless neck mass with fever and weight loss, but it does not release cell contents to cause hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia and hypocalcemia with AKI.
why.C: Sarcoidosis causes hilar or cervical lymphadenopathy but typically HYPERcalcemia (granuloma 1-alpha hydroxylase), the opposite of this low calcium.
why.D: Option not recalled; if lymphoma itself were offered it would be the underlying cause to consider.

questions.right: A painless neck mass with fever and weight loss for 3 months suggests a rapidly growing lymphoma, and the labs show the tumor lysis pattern: high K, high uric acid, low calcium with raised creatinine (AKI). The compiler notes lymphoma was not an option, so the best answer is spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome from the underlying high-turnover tumor.
questions.kc: Tumor lysis syndrome labs. High: potassium, phosphate, uric acid, creatinine Low: calcium (binds phosphate) Spontaneous TLS can occur before chemo in bulky, fast tumors (Burkitt, high-grade lymphoma, leukemia) Hypercalcemia instead points to sarcoid, TB granuloma or malignancy-related PTHrP
questions.ep: Low calcium with high K and urate = TLS; high calcium with a neck mass = think sarcoid or PTHrP.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man known to have Hodgkin 's lymphoma, undergoing chemotherapy, developed tumor lysis syndrome . Which of the following is the most likely expected disturbance?

why.A: Hypokalemia is wrong: lysed cells release their potassium, raising serum K.
why.B: Both are reversed: TLS raises potassium and lowers calcium.
why.D: Hyperkalemia is right, but calcium falls (bound by released phosphate); hypercalcemia suggests PTHrP or bone metastases instead.

questions.right: Chemotherapy for a high-turnover tumor (Hodgkin lymphoma) lyses cells and releases intracellular potassium (hyperkalemia) and phosphate ; phosphate binds calcium and precipitates, giving hypocalcemia . So the expected pair is hyperkalemia with hypocalcemia.
questions.kc: TLS = "the high ones come out of the cell". Hyperkalemia: arrhythmia risk Hyperphosphatemia: calcium phosphate deposits, AKI Hypocalcemia: tetany, seizures Hyperuricemia: urate nephropathy Prevention: hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase
questions.ep: Calcium is the only one that goes DOWN in TLS.

questions.stem: A patient with Burkitt Lymphoma (DLBCL In Another Recall) is receiving B-CHOP chemotherapy. Laboratory results show hyperkalemia (6) and hypocalcemia. ( Unable to urinate ) What is the most appropriate management (in addition to hydration) ? Uric Acid Not Mentioned.

why.B: Thiazides are used to reduce urinary calcium in hypercalciuric stone disease; they do not help TLS and can worsen hyperuricemia.
why.C: Allopurinol blocks NEW uric acid formation, so it is for prevention in moderate-risk patients; it does not remove existing urate or treat hyperkalemia, and uric acid was not even reported here.
why.D: Prednisolone has no role in treating TLS; steroids are part of some chemotherapy regimens and can themselves trigger lysis.

questions.right: This is established tumor lysis syndrome after chemotherapy, with hyperkalemia (6), hypocalcemia and reduced urine output . The lead-in asks for management (not prevention) in addition to hydration; once the patient is volume replete, a loop diuretic (Lasix) promotes urine flow and potassium excretion. The compiler notes rasburicase is not offered and stresses management versus prevention.
questions.kc: TLS: prevention vs management. Prevention: hydration plus allopurinol (moderate risk) or rasburicase (high risk) Management: aggressive hydration, rasburicase, loop diuretic once euvolemic Treat hyperkalemia per standard protocol Refractory oliguria/hyperkalemia: dialysis Different recall (high phosphate only): phosphate binder
questions.ep: "Management" with oliguria and high K = loop diuretic after hydration; "prevention" = allopurinol or rasburicase.

questions.stem: A patient received high irradiation (20 Gray , normal 11 Gray). He complained of abdominal pain, malaise, nausea, vomiting , and loss of appetite. What is the cause?

why.A: Stroke would present with focal neurological deficits, not abdominal pain and vomiting after irradiation.
why.B: Radiation-induced malignancy is a late effect appearing years later, not an acute symptom complex.
why.D: Anaphylaxis is an IgE-mediated reaction to an allergen with urticaria, wheeze and hypotension; radiation does not cause it.

questions.right: This is acute radiation syndrome after a very high whole-body dose ("20 Gray"). Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise and anorexia are the prodromal and gastrointestinal features of injury to rapidly dividing cells. The hematopoietic system is the most radiosensitive tissue and is ablated at doses far below this, so among the listed options bone marrow destruction is the only radiation-related mechanism and is the source's key. The GI mucosal injury that produces these exact symptoms is not offered as an option.
questions.kc: Acute radiation syndrome: damage follows cell turnover. Most radiosensitive: bone marrow, GI mucosa, gonads, lymphocytes Hematopoietic syndrome: pancytopenia, infection, bleeding GI syndrome at higher doses: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea Very high doses: neurovascular syndrome Late effects: malignancy, cataract, fibrosis
questions.ep: Malignancy is a LATE radiation effect; acute symptoms after exposure point to destruction of rapidly dividing tissue.

questions.stem: A patient presented with vomiting and diarrhea approximately 4-5 times per day for several days. His creatinine one week earlier was approximately 65 umol/L. Current labs showed: (Labs: Elevated urea; Creatinine ~160 umol/L ; Urine osmolality ~250 mOsm/kg ; Urine sodium ~60 mmol/L ; Specific gravity: value not recalled accurately) What is the most likely cause of the acute kidney injury?

why.A: Prerenal azotemia is right when urine Na is below 20, FENa below 1%, urine osmolality above 500 and BUN:creatinine ratio above 20; here urine Na is high and urine is dilute.
why.C: Postrenal obstruction needs a reason for obstruction (prostate, stones, anuria, hydronephrosis on ultrasound); nothing in the stem suggests it.
why.D: Acute on chronic disease needs a raised baseline; creatinine was a normal 65 one week ago.

questions.right: Vomiting and diarrhea started a prerenal insult, but the labs show the tubules are no longer working: urine sodium about 60 (above 40) and urine osmolality about 250 (dilute, below about 350) with low specific gravity. Intact tubules in prerenal AKI would avidly retain sodium and concentrate urine, so these indices indicate the prolonged hypoperfusion has progressed to acute tubular necrosis. Creatinine more than doubling in a week from a normal baseline also fits an acute intrinsic injury.
questions.kc: AKI urine indices: Prerenal: urine Na below 20, FENa below 1%, urine osm above 500, high SG, BUN:Cr above 20 ATN: urine Na above 40, FENa above 2%, urine osm below 350, low/fixed SG, muddy brown casts Prolonged prerenal state can convert to ATN
questions.ep: Prerenal history does not mean prerenal AKI: let the urine Na and osmolality decide.

questions.stem: 35-year-old man comes to the Emergency Room after falling while running a marathon . He has dark urine that is dip-stick positive for large blood, but no RBCs on microscopic analysis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

why.A: Forced diuresis with diuretics is not first line; loop diuretics can worsen volume depletion. They are considered only for fluid overload after adequate volume repletion.
why.C: There is no infection; antibiotics would be right for a urinary tract infection with pyuria and bacteriuria.
why.D: Blood pressure is not the issue; lowering it in a volume-depleted patient can reduce renal perfusion and worsen AKI.

questions.right: A "marathon" runner after a fall with dark urine that is dipstick positive for "large blood" but has "no RBCs" on microscopy has myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis. Myoglobin is toxic to the renal tubules, so the priority is aggressive IV isotonic hydration to maintain a high urine output and prevent acute kidney injury.
questions.kc: Rhabdomyolysis: dipstick heme positive + no RBCs = myoglobin (or hemoglobin). Confirm with markedly raised CK Mainstay: early aggressive IV isotonic fluids Watch potassium (hyperkalemia), calcium, phosphate Complication: acute kidney injury Dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis or AKI
questions.ep: Dipstick blood positive but microscopy negative for RBCs means pigment, not hematuria.

questions.stem: Patient with hypertension for 10 years and recently diagnosed with DLP and DM 5m ago, his BP is 170/110 and A1c is 7, he has Creatinine level of >200. What is the cause of the renal failure?

why.A: Diabetic nephropathy needs years of diabetes and typically shows albuminuria and often retinopathy; 5 months of well controlled DM does not explain established renal failure. Other alternatives: renovascular disease (asymmetric kidneys, flash edema) and primary glomerular disease (active sediment, heavy proteinuria).

questions.right: The decisive timeline is hypertension for 10 years but diabetes only 5 months with a near target A1c of 7. Diabetic nephropathy takes years of hyperglycemia and announces itself with albuminuria first, so renal failure with creatinine above 200 is best explained by long standing, poorly controlled hypertension (BP 170/110) causing hypertensive nephrosclerosis .
questions.kc: Cause of CKD follows the longest standing exposure. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis: long HTN, bland sediment, mild proteinuria, small kidneys Diabetic nephropathy: years of DM, microalbuminuria first, retinopathy usually present Screen diabetics annually with urine albumin/creatinine ratio Both: ACEi/ARB for renoprotection
questions.ep: Read the durations: the disease present for 10 years, not the one diagnosed 5 months ago, owns the kidney damage.

questions.stem: A 50 YO Male Presented With Progressive Fatigue And Bilateral Flank Pain. His Father Required Dialysis At Age Of 60. He Has Lower Limb Pitting Edema But No Fluid Overload (LITERALLY WRITTEN LIKE THIS). Ultrasound: Bilaterally Enlarged Kidneys With Multiple Cysts Distributed Throughout Renal Cortex (+/- Medulla?). eGFR: 6 Months Ago 36; Now 18 . What's Most Appropriate NEXT Step?

why.A: Renal biopsy is unnecessary; ultrasound with family history already establishes ADPKD.
why.B: IV steroids treat inflammatory glomerulonephritis; ADPKD is a genetic cystic disease that does not respond to steroids.
why.C: Dialysis is started for urgent indications (acidosis, refractory hyperkalemia, fluid overload, uremic symptoms) or end-stage disease; he has none, and the stem stresses no fluid overload.

questions.right: Bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts and a father on dialysis is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. His eGFR has fallen from 36 to 18 in 6 months (now CKD stage 4, rapidly progressing) and he has no fluid overload or other urgent dialysis indication. The most appropriate next step is to start planning renal replacement therapy, and pre- emptive referral for kidney transplant evaluation is the preferred route at this eGFR.
questions.kc: Advanced CKD: plan ahead of dialysis need. Progressive CKD 4: refer for transplant evaluation and RRT planning Pre-emptive transplant gives the best outcomes Urgent dialysis (AEIOU): acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload, uremia ADPKD diagnosis: ultrasound + family history, no biopsy
questions.ep: "No fluid overload" is placed to remove the dialysis option; without an AEIOU indication, prepare for transplant.

questions.stem: 60-year-old patient with CKD , hypertension, diabetes , currently on metformin, ACE inhibitor, and statin, with an atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk of 18%. What is the next recommended therapy?

why.B: Sulfonylureas lower glucose but have no cardiorenal benefit and cause hypoglycemia, which is more likely as renal function falls.
why.C: Fibrates treat severe hypertriglyceridemia; they do not reduce cardiovascular events on top of statins and need dose caution in CKD.
why.D: Ezetimibe is added when LDL remains above target on maximally tolerated statin; no LDL value is given to justify it, and it does nothing for the kidney.

questions.right: This diabetic has CKD and high cardiovascular risk and is already on metformin, an ACE inhibitor and a statin. Current diabetes and KDIGO guidance add an SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin in type 2 diabetes with CKD, independent of HbA1c, because it slows CKD progression and reduces heart failure and cardiovascular events. It is the only option with proven cardiorenal benefit here.
questions.kc: T2DM with CKD: metformin (if eGFR allows) + ACEi/ARB + statin + SGLT2 inhibitor. SGLT2i: slows CKD, lowers HF admissions and CV events GLP1 RA: preferred if established ASCVD or weight is the issue, or SGLT2i not tolerated Ezetimibe: LDL not at goal on max statin Fibrate: very high triglycerides (pancreatitis risk) Sulfonylurea: cheap glucose lowering, no organ protection, hypoglycemia
questions.ep: Diabetes plus CKD or heart failure in the stem: think SGLT2 inhibitor before any other added drug.

questions.stem: A patient presents with periorbital eye swelling, hematuria , and hypertension. He had a sore throat 3 weeks ago . ASO titre: positive What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic picture (heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia) in adults, linked to PLA2R antibodies, malignancy or drugs, not a post-infectious nephritic syndrome.
why.B: IgA nephropathy gives hematuria within 1 to 2 days of a URTI (synpharyngitic), often recurrent, with normal ASO and complement.

questions.right: Nephritic syndrome ( hematuria, periorbital edema, hypertension ) appearing 3 weeks after a sore throat with a positive ASO titre is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The latent period of 1 to 3 weeks and evidence of recent group A strep infection are the decisive clues.
questions.kc: Timing after sore throat separates the two: days = IgA nephropathy; 1 to 3 weeks = PSGN. PSGN: cola urine, edema, HTN, low C3, raised ASO or anti DNase B Impetigo related PSGN: latency 3 to 6 weeks PSGN treatment: supportive (salt and fluid restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives), penicillin for residual infection Prognosis good in children; C3 normalises within 6 to 8 weeks IgA: normal complement, recurrent episodes
questions.ep: Hematuria 1 to 2 days after the sore throat flips the answer to IgA nephropathy.

questions.stem: A female patient with a brain tumor (possibly glioblastoma) and a history of seizures/intellectual disability presented with hyponatremia and other electrolyte abnormalities, including hypokalemia and borderline-low chloride. What is the most likely cause?

why.B: Cerebral salt wasting also occurs with intracranial disease (classically subarachnoid hemorrhage or neurosurgery), but the patient is hypovolemic (dehydration, hypotension) and treated with saline; no volume depletion is described here.
why.C: Psychogenic polydipsia causes hyponatremia with maximally dilute urine (osmolality below about 100) and is seen in psychiatric patients; the brain tumour gives a more direct cause.
why.D: Other causes (adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, diuretics) must be excluded when diagnosing SIADH, but none is suggested by this stem.

questions.right: A "brain tumor (possibly glioblastoma)" with seizures presenting with hyponatremia is most likely SIADH: intracranial tumours cause excess ADH release through hypothalamic irritation or ectopic secretion. SIADH gives euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium. Low chloride follows the dilution, and the hypokalemia does not argue against it.
questions.kc: Hyponatremia with brain disease: SIADH: euvolemic, urine osm >100, urine Na >40, low uric acid; treat with fluid restriction CSW: hypovolemic, high urine Na, treat with saline (± fludrocortisone) Psychogenic polydipsia: urine osm <100 Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before calling SIADH Correct no faster than about 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours (osmotic demyelination)
questions.ep: Same brain lesion: euvolemic = SIADH (restrict fluid); dehydrated = cerebral salt wasting (give saline).

questions.stem: An Elderly???? Patient 2 Days Post Hip Surgery Developed Confusion And Drowsiness . During Surgery , He Was Given Hypotonic Fluids D5W. (Labs: Serum Na 121 ; Serum Osm ~250; Urine Osm 600; Urine Sodium 46) What's The Management

why.B: Normal saline is for hypovolemic hyponatremia; in SIADH (urine osm 600) the salt is excreted and water retained, so Na can fall further. Furosemide with restriction suits hypervolemic states.
why.C: Hypertonic 3% saline is right for severe or clearly symptomatic acute hyponatremia, but correction must be controlled; 'RAPID correction' causes osmotic demyelination. The other 120 scorer chose this.
why.D: Option not recalled; cannot be assessed.

questions.right: The labs show hypotonic hyponatremia (Na 121, serum osm about 250) with concentrated urine (urine osm 600) and high urine sodium (46): an SIADH pattern, provoked post operatively and worsened by hypotonic D5W. The compiler keys fluid restriction with monitoring , treating this as non severe hyponatremia appearing 2 days post op, the routine treatment of euvolemic SIADH; his rule is that symptoms developing within 2 days of surgery go to hypertonic saline, after 2 days to fluid restriction. Option C is also undermined by 'RAPID correction', which risks osmotic demyelination.
questions.kc: Hyponatremia: confirm low serum osm, judge symptoms and volume, then treat. Severe or moderately severe symptoms (seizure, coma, vomiting, confusion, marked drowsiness), especially if acute under 48 h: 3% saline as controlled boluses SIADH (euvolemic, urine osm high, urine Na above 30): fluid restriction Hypovolemic: 0.9% saline Hypervolemic: fluid restriction ± loop diuretic Limit correction (roughly ≤10 mmol/L in 24 h) to avoid osmotic demyelination
questions.ep: 'Confusion and drowsiness' pushes many toward 3% saline; the word 'RAPID' is what makes C wrong in every school.

questions.stem: An Elderly???? Patient X Days Post Hip Surgery Developed Confusion And Drowsiness . During Surgery , He Was Given Hypotonic Fluids D5W (Labs: Serum Na 121; Serum Osm ~250; Urine Osm 600; Urine Sodium 46) What's The Management

why.B: Normal saline with furosemide is used for SIADH that fails fluid restriction or with volume overload; normal saline alone can worsen SIADH because the kidney retains the water and excretes the salt.
why.C: Hypertonic 3% saline is the treatment for hyponatremia with moderately severe or severe symptoms, but correction must be controlled, never "RAPID"; overly fast correction risks osmotic demyelination. The examiner (120 in Medicine) and another examinee chose this option.
why.D: Option not recalled.

questions.right: This recall's key (the compiler's) is fluid restriction and monitoring: low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine ("Urine Osm 600") and urine sodium 46 after hypotonic D5W post-operatively is SIADH-type hyponatremia, whose standard treatment is fluid restriction. The compiler treats it as chronic (unknown number of days) and mild, where slow correction is safer, and states he would choose hypertonic saline if onset were within 2 days.
questions.kc: Hyponatremia management depends on symptoms and timing, not sodium alone. Severe symptoms (seizures, coma, vomiting): 3% saline bolus Moderate symptoms (confusion, drowsiness): cautious 3% saline Mild/asymptomatic chronic SIADH: fluid restriction Acute (under 48 h) tolerates faster correction than chronic Limit correction to about 8-10 mmol/L in 24 h
questions.ep: Confusion and drowsiness are moderately severe symptoms; the word "RAPID" in option C is the trap regardless of which side you take.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female with a history of vomiting for 3 months And she has been experiencing dehydration, dry mucous membranes , and agitation for the past 2 weeks. She admitted to using methamphetamine. Vital signs: BP: 140/? mmHg. No labs. What best explains her symptoms?

why.A: Chronic kidney disease would need evidence of established renal impairment; in a 25 year old with no labs, a chronic disease is not the best explanation for vomiting related dehydration.
why.B: Liver toxicity (methamphetamine can cause hepatotoxicity) would show jaundice, RUQ pain or raised enzymes; nothing in the stem suggests it.
why.D: Acute pancreatitis is an acute illness with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back; it would not explain three months of vomiting.

questions.right: Three months of vomiting with dehydration, dry mucous membranes and agitation points to fluid and electrolyte loss: vomiting causes hypokalemia, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis and sodium disturbance, which can produce agitation and confusion. Methamphetamine adds to agitation, poor intake and dehydration. Electrolyte disturbance is the single explanation that ties the vomiting to the current symptoms.
questions.kc: Prolonged vomiting: think electrolytes. Hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis Hypo or hypernatremia from losses and water intake Symptoms: weakness, agitation, confusion, arrhythmia Stimulants (methamphetamine): agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, poor intake
questions.ep: When the stem gives chronic vomiting plus dehydration and no labs, the best explanation is the electrolyte disturbance, not a distant organ disease.

questions.stem: A male patient presents with features of Cushing's syndrome. Laboratory tests show both ACTH (15) and cortisol (8) are elevated . TSH Normal. What is the most likely type of Cushing's syndrome?

why.B: An adrenal adenoma secretes cortisol autonomously and suppresses pituitary ACTH, so ACTH is low, not high; low ACTH leads to adrenal CT.
why.C: Exogenous steroids suppress ACTH, and measured cortisol is low unless the drug is hydrocortisone itself; ACTH would not be elevated.
why.D: Ectopic ACTH (e.g. small cell lung cancer) is ACTH dependent too, but usually gives markedly high ACTH, hypokalemia, weight loss and pigmentation; with only mildly raised ACTH the pituitary is the most likely source.

questions.right: Both ACTH and cortisol are elevated , so this is ACTH dependent Cushing syndrome. The most common ACTH dependent cause by far is a pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease), which typically produces a modest rise in ACTH as in this stem. Ectopic ACTH is the alternative but usually gives very high ACTH with a rapid, severe course.
questions.kc: Cushing: measure ACTH to split dependent from independent. Low ACTH: adrenal adenoma/carcinoma or exogenous steroids, do adrenal CT High ACTH, mild rise: pituitary adenoma (most common), do pituitary MRI High ACTH, very high, hypokalemia: consider ectopic High dose dexamethasone suppresses pituitary, not ectopic; IPSS if unclear
questions.ep: High ACTH plus high cortisol: think pituitary first; low ACTH: think adrenal or exogenous.

questions.stem: A female patient presents with features of Cushing 's syndrome for 4 months (she had purple striae and weight gain). Laboratory tests show bp140/xx (Labs: K 2.9, significantly low; High cortisol 8am 840, 4pm 500; ACTH 15 (high) ; TSH 4 (normal)) What is the most likely diagnosis ?

why.B: Adrenal adenoma is ACTH-independent: cortisol suppresses ACTH, so ACTH would be low, not high.
why.C: Exogenous steroid use suppresses the axis; ACTH and often measured endogenous cortisol are low, and there is a drug history.
why.D: Ectopic ACTH (e.g. small cell lung cancer, carcinoid) gives very high ACTH, rapid onset, prominent hypokalemia, weight loss and often few classic cushingoid features; more common in men and smokers.
why.E: Iatrogenic Cushing is the same as exogenous steroids: low ACTH, which contradicts this patient's high ACTH.

questions.right: Cushingoid features (purple striae, weight gain) with high cortisol that stays high in the afternoon (8am 840, 4pm still 500 instead of falling to low levels) confirm Cushing syndrome. A high ACTH makes it ACTH-dependent, which means pituitary or ectopic; in a woman with classic gradual cushingoid features and only modestly raised ACTH, a pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) is the most common and most likely cause.
questions.kc: Cushing: ACTH sorts the cause. Low ACTH: adrenal adenoma/carcinoma or exogenous steroids High ACTH: pituitary (most common) or ectopic High-dose dexamethasone suppresses: pituitary, then MRI pituitary Not suppressed: ectopic, then CT chest
questions.ep: Severe hypokalemia is a classic hint toward ectopic ACTH, but with classic striae and only modestly high ACTH in a woman, pituitary remains the key answer.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman, not known to have any medical illness, complains of increased sleepiness, fatigue, and constipation for the last few months. She is on a very healthy diet, is not a smoker, and does not drink alcohol. Examination reveals an overweight patient, not in distress, with no lymphadenopathy or masses (see lab results). (Labs: TSH 16 ; T4 low; TPO Ab 64 ; TG Ab high) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism (low TSH, high T4) driven by TSH receptor antibodies, with goitre and eye signs.
why.B: Subacute thyroiditis presents with a painful tender thyroid, fever and high ESR after a viral illness, usually with an initial thyrotoxic phase.
why.C: Sick euthyroid syndrome occurs during acute severe illness (e.g. ICU); low T3 with normal or low TSH, not a TSH of 16 in a well outpatient.

questions.right: Sleepiness, fatigue, constipation and weight gain are hypothyroid symptoms, confirmed by TSH 16 with low T4 (primary hypothyroidism). Positive anti TPO and anti thyroglobulin antibodies in a young woman establish autoimmune Hashimoto's thyroiditis , the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in iodine sufficient regions.
questions.kc: Thyroid function patterns. High TSH, low T4, positive TPO / Tg antibodies: Hashimoto Low TSH, high T4, diffuse uptake, TSH receptor antibodies: Graves Painful thyroid, high ESR, low uptake: subacute thyroiditis Acute illness, low T3, normal or low TSH: sick euthyroid Treat Hashimoto hypothyroidism with levothyroxine
questions.ep: Painless + hypothyroid + antibodies = Hashimoto; painful neck = subacute.

questions.stem: lady with SLE was put on 60mg steroid dose and instead of tapering she took it daily for 6 weeks , she was later found dead in her bathtub . What is the likely cause of death?

why.A: Steroids raise peptic ulcer risk and can mask peritonitis, but a perforated duodenal ulcer usually causes hours of severe abdominal pain before death rather than sudden collapse.
why.C: Acute cerebral (CNS lupus) vasculitis is a feature of active SLE; high dose steroids treat it rather than cause it, so it is unlikely while on 60 mg daily.
why.D: Mesenteric ischemia with perforation causes pain out of proportion and an evolving acute abdomen, not a sudden unexplained death; it is not a typical steroid complication.

questions.right: High dose prednisolone ( 60 mg daily for 6 weeks without tapering) causes sodium and water retention and a rise in blood pressure, and SLE patients often already have renal disease adding to hypertension. Sustained steroid induced hypertension predisposes to a hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, which can cause sudden collapse and death, as in a patient found dead in the bathtub . This recall's key is the hypertensive bleed as the most likely sudden fatal event.
questions.kc: Complications of prolonged high dose glucocorticoids: Hypertension, fluid retention, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia Peptic ulcer (masked peritonitis), infection Osteoporosis, avascular necrosis, myopathy Psychosis, cataract, adrenal suppression (crisis if stopped abruptly)
questions.ep: Sudden death on prolonged high dose steroids in this recall is explained by steroid induced hypertension and intracerebral bleeding.

questions.stem: Male, hypertensive, presents after an episode of left upper limb weakness that lasted for 5 minutes then completley resolved On examination there was No carotid bruit or cardicac murmurs and a Normal ECG What is the most appropriate next step

why.A: CT angiography of the neck images the carotids well but uses contrast and radiation; it is used to confirm or plan surgery after duplex, not as the first test.
why.B: MRI brain (diffusion weighted) is part of the full TIA work up to look for infarction, but it does not assess the carotid stenosis that changes immediate management here.

questions.right: A 5 minute episode of left upper limb weakness that completely resolved is a TIA in the anterior (carotid) circulation. With no murmur and a normal ECG , a cardioembolic source is less likely and the key question is carotid stenosis, which would need endarterectomy. Carotid duplex (Doppler) ultrasound is the first, noninvasive test for this.
questions.kc: TIA with resolved symptoms: urgent work up for the cause. Brain imaging: MRI with diffusion preferred, CT if MRI unavailable Neurovascular: carotid duplex first, then CTA or MRA Cardiac: ECG, prolonged rhythm monitoring, echocardiography Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70 to 99%: endarterectomy Start antiplatelet and statin; anticoagulate if AF
questions.ep: If the ECG showed AF, the answer would shift to anticoagulation rather than carotid imaging.

questions.stem: Old male presented with left side body weakness resolve completely after 20 minutes brain Ct normal carotid ultrasound: 55% Carotid stenosis Bilaterally What is the most appropriate next step?

why.B: Apixaban is an anticoagulant for cardioembolic TIA, for example with atrial fibrillation; no such source is given.
why.C: Warfarin is also for cardioembolic sources (AF, mechanical valve); it is not used for atherosclerotic carotid disease.
why.D: Carotid endarterectomy is clearly indicated for symptomatic severe stenosis (about 70- 99%); moderate stenosis is considered only in selected patients and antiplatelet therapy comes first regardless.

questions.right: Left-sided weakness that "resolve[d] completely after 20 minutes" with a normal CT is a TIA. The next step is antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) to prevent stroke, with risk-factor control. The carotid stenosis of "55%" is moderate; intervention is not the first step.
questions.kc: TIA management: Image brain to exclude hemorrhage Start antiplatelet (aspirin) + statin, control BP Carotid duplex for anterior circulation symptoms Symptomatic 70-99% stenosis: endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks AF or cardioembolic source: anticoagulation
questions.ep: Anticoagulate for the heart (AF), antiplatelet for the arteries.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient develops sudden ipsilateral facial weakness and sensorineural hearing loss . Which artery is most likely affected?

why.B: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome; facial weakness and hearing loss are not features.
why.C: MCA stroke causes contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia or neglect; the facial weakness is contralateral and hearing is not lost.
why.D: ACA stroke causes contralateral leg more than arm weakness with abulia and urinary incontinence, not facial palsy with deafness.

questions.right: Ipsilateral facial weakness plus sensorineural hearing loss localizes to the lateral caudal pons and inner ear. The AICA supplies the lateral pons (facial nucleus) and gives off the labyrinthine artery to the cochlea, so AICA occlusion (lateral pontine syndrome) uniquely combines facial palsy with deafness. Other features can include vertigo, ipsilateral ataxia and contralateral pain and temperature loss.
questions.kc: Brainstem stroke clue words: Facial palsy + hearing loss (lateral pons): AICA Dysphagia, hoarseness, Horner, crossed sensory loss (lateral medulla): PICA Contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia: MCA Contralateral leg weakness: ACA
questions.ep: Hearing loss is the AICA clue, because the labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA.

questions.stem: Hypertensive pt long case but it tells you that through imaging that the patient has a hemorrhagic stroke , he can move his pupils but they are pin point , and he can not speak or move his body, where is the lesion ? BP was 190/xx

why.B: Medullary lesions give bulbar signs (dysphagia, dysarthria), respiratory and cardiovascular instability, and lateral medullary features (crossed sensory loss, Horner); pinpoint pupils are not the hallmark.
why.C: Basal ganglia (putaminal) hemorrhage, the most common hypertensive site, gives contralateral hemiparesis and gaze deviation toward the lesion, not bilateral pinpoint pupils.

questions.right: A hypertensive hemorrhage producing pinpoint pupils with inability to speak or move the body (quadriplegia, often with coma or a locked-in picture) localises to the pons . Pontine hemorrhage disrupts descending sympathetic fibres, giving tiny but reactive pupils, and damages the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts bilaterally.
questions.kc: Hypertensive hemorrhage sites. Putamen (most common): contralateral hemiparesis, eyes deviate to lesion Thalamus: contralateral sensory loss, eyes look down and in Pons: pinpoint pupils, quadriplegia, coma or locked-in Cerebellum: ataxia, vomiting, occipital headache; may need urgent decompression
questions.ep: Pinpoint pupils: think pons (or opioids); in a hypertensive bleed it is the pons.

questions.stem: Female 20 came with Right upper limb weakness and numbness since 1 week + left facial severe pain especially when she brushes her teeth . Most appropriate

why.A: Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves (e.g. GBS, neuropathy); MS is a central demyelinating disease, so NCS is normal.
why.B: LP (oligoclonal bands) supports an MS diagnosis but is done after MRI when imaging is not conclusive; it is not the most appropriate first test.
why.C: CT with iodinated contrast is much less sensitive for white matter plaques; CT is the first test in acute stroke to exclude bleeding, not for suspected demyelination.

questions.right: A 20 year old woman with trigeminal neuralgia (severe facial pain triggered by brushing teeth) plus a separate right arm weakness and numbness points to a central lesion: either a single crossed brainstem (pontine) lesion or more than one site. Trigeminal neuralgia in a young patient, especially with other deficits, should raise multiple sclerosis. MRI brain with gadolinium is the most sensitive test, showing demyelinating plaques and, with contrast, active enhancing lesions.
questions.kc: Young patient with trigeminal neuralgia or multifocal deficits: suspect MS. Best test: MRI brain (and spine) with gadolinium Plaques: periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord CSF oligoclonal bands: supportive NCS: peripheral disease only
questions.ep: Trigeminal neuralgia under 40 or with another deficit is MS until proven otherwise: order MRI with gadolinium.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department 1 hour after a first- time generalized tonic-clonic seizure . He has no previous history of seizures, neurological problems, recent illness, medication use, or illicit drug use. His vital signs and neurological examination are normal , and laboratory studies are normal. What is the most appropriate initial step in management?

why.A: An ECG is part of any first seizure assessment to look for cardiac syncope mimics (e.g. long QT), but the step the question targets after normal labs is excluding a structural brain lesion.
why.B: EEG classifies the seizure and estimates recurrence risk, but it is done after imaging, usually as an outpatient.
why.D: LP is indicated when there is fever, meningism, altered sensorium or immunosuppression suggesting CNS infection; none are present here, and imaging should precede LP.

questions.right: A first time generalized tonic clonic seizure in a young adult with no provoking factors and normal vitals, neuro exam and labs needs neuroimaging to exclude a structural cause (tumor, bleed, vascular malformation). Head CT is the initial imaging in the emergency department; MRI and EEG follow as outpatient work up. Once metabolic causes are excluded by labs, imaging is the next step.
questions.kc: First unprovoked seizure in an adult: Glucose, electrolytes, toxicology: exclude provoked causes Neuroimaging: CT in ED, MRI as the definitive study EEG: after imaging, to classify and predict recurrence LP only if infection suspected
questions.ep: First seizure with normal labs and exam: image the brain before EEG.

questions.stem: Lady in the 70s has type 2 DM on metformin 1 g BID had problem in naming and calling things lately. For example she says animal instead of cat when she sees a cat. She has no memory impairment or personality changes . There are similar condition in her family . Her family are worried about her. What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Vascular dementia presents with stepwise decline, executive dysfunction and focal signs in a patient with vascular risk factors; diabetes alone does not explain an isolated semantic naming problem.
why.B: Alzheimer disease starts with recent memory loss; language problems come with memory decline, so preserved memory argues against it.
why.D: B12 deficiency (relevant with long term metformin) causes memory and attention problems, neuropathy and anemia, not a selective loss of word meaning; it is a reversible cause to check, not the best fit here.

questions.right: Her problem is naming : she loses word meaning and uses a general category ( says animal instead of cat ), with no memory impairment or personality change and a family history . This is the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia, which belongs to the frontotemporal dementia spectrum and is associated with anterior temporal lobe atrophy. FTD often runs in families, and the language variant can present before behavior changes.
questions.kc: Dementia types by first deficit: Recent memory loss first: Alzheimer Behavior/personality change or language (naming, word meaning) with spared memory: frontotemporal Stepwise, executive, vascular risks: vascular Fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism: Lewy body Semantic variant: temporal lobe atrophy on imaging
questions.ep: Memory spared but word meaning lost (cat becomes animal): think frontotemporal, not Alzheimer.

questions.stem: Old woman, struggling with remember names , and calling the specific names with general ones ( like animal instead of cat ), no personality changes , what do you except to see in imaging?

why.A: Caudate atrophy (boxcar ventricles) is Huntington disease: chorea, psychiatric change and dementia in a younger patient with family history.
why.B: Hippocampal (medial temporal) atrophy is Alzheimer disease, which starts with episodic memory loss for recent events rather than loss of word meaning.
why.D: Scattered vascular (white matter) injury is vascular dementia: stepwise decline, focal deficits, vascular risk factors and early executive dysfunction.

questions.right: Difficulty with names and replacing specific words with general category words ("animal" instead of "cat") is loss of word meaning, the hallmark of semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (semantic dementia), a frontotemporal dementia subtype. With "no personality changes", the language variant rather than the behavioral variant fits, and imaging shows anterior temporal lobe atrophy , usually left-predominant.
questions.kc: Dementia and its imaging. Alzheimer: hippocampal/medial temporal atrophy FTD behavioral: frontal atrophy, disinhibition, apathy Semantic variant PPA: anterior temporal atrophy, word meaning loss Huntington: caudate atrophy Vascular: multiple infarcts, white matter lesions NPH: ventriculomegaly
questions.ep: Recent-event memory loss = hippocampus (Alzheimer); losing word meaning = anterior temporal lobe.

questions.stem: 43 MALE came to ER with 3 days history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and brisk reflexes in both legs, with urinary retention, inability to walk, and a sensory level of T10 . [Pain Not Mentioned] What is the diagnosis?

why.A: Transverse myelitis gives the same subacute, painless sensory-level myelopathy, often after infection; it is diagnosed only after MRI excludes compression and shows cord inflammation.
why.B: GBS is a peripheral neuropathy with areflexia, no sensory level and usually no early sphincter loss; brisk reflexes rule it out.
