why.C: Cauda equina affects lower motor neurons: reduced reflexes, saddle anesthesia, and no thoracic sensory level.

questions.right: Bilateral leg weakness with brisk reflexes , urinary retention and a sensory level at T10 is an acute myelopathy (spinal cord lesion). The source keys cord compression : any acute myelopathy with a sensory level is treated as compression until urgent MRI of the spine proves otherwise, because it needs emergency decompression or steroids and radiotherapy. The compiler holds firmly to this answer.
questions.kc: Acute paraparesis: localise first. Upper motor neuron + sensory level + bladder: spinal cord (compression vs transverse myelitis) Areflexia + ascending weakness, no level: GBS Lower motor neuron + saddle anesthesia + low back pain: cauda equina Every acute myelopathy: urgent whole-spine MRI Back pain and cancer history favour compression
questions.ep: Brisk reflexes exclude GBS and cauda equina; the real fork is compression vs transverse myelitis.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old lady known case of asthma and alcohol consumption presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. days after the accident , she starts to have tremors, sweating, and hallucination and orthostatic changes (bp:160/xx HR 110) What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

why.B: Chlordiazepoxide is a correct benzodiazepine for withdrawal, but on its own it omits thiamine, which every patient with heavy alcohol use needs to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy; the combined option is more complete.
why.C: IV fluids are supportive and needed, but they do not treat withdrawal; giving dextrose fluids before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

questions.right: An alcohol user who develops tremor, sweating, hallucinations and autonomic hyperactivity (BP 160, HR 110) days after admission (the MVA stopped her drinking) has severe alcohol withdrawal, approaching delirium tremens. Initial treatment is a benzodiazepine to control withdrawal plus thiamine (given before glucose) to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, so the combined option is most appropriate.
questions.kc: Alcohol withdrawal timeline and treatment. 6 to 24 h: tremor, anxiety, sweating 12 to 48 h: hallucinosis, withdrawal seizures 48 to 96 h: delirium tremens (confusion, autonomic instability) Treatment: benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide / diazepam; lorazepam if liver disease or elderly) Always thiamine before glucose
questions.ep: In any alcohol patient, the option that includes thiamine beats the same drug without it.

questions.stem: 30 YO Man present to clinic with repeated episodes of joint pain for 3 months , now complaining of right knee pain, no fever tenderness or systemic manifestations and no recent history of illness (that's how they said it specifically). Wbc normal. Uric acid: 400 (High Normal) (Normal <480). Urea 7 (9 In Other Recall) (High). What's the cause

why.B: Pseudogout (CPPD) affects the elderly, often the knee, and is linked to hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis and hypomagnesemia; a healthy 30 year old man is atypical.
why.C: Reactive arthritis follows a GI or genitourinary infection by 1 to 4 weeks, often with urethritis or conjunctivitis; the stem specifically says no recent illness.
why.D: Septic arthritis is an acute hot joint with fever and raised WBC (synovial WBC usually above 50,000); here there is no fever, normal WBC and a recurrent pattern.

questions.right: A 30 year old man with repeated episodes of joint pain over 3 months and now an acute knee attack, with no fever , normal WBC and no preceding illness, fits recurrent gout. A uric acid in the high normal range does not exclude gout, because serum urate can fall during an acute attack. Young male sex and episodic attacks are the decisive clues; joint aspiration with negatively birefringent needle crystals would confirm it.
questions.kc: Acute monoarthritis: pick by host and history. Young or middle aged man, recurrent episodes, diuretics, alcohol: gout Elderly, knee, chondrocalcinosis: pseudogout Preceding GI/GU infection, eye or urethral signs: reactive arthritis Fever, leukocytosis, single hot joint: septic (exclude first) Serum urate may be normal during a gout flare
questions.ep: Normal uric acid does not rule out gout during an attack; recurrence in a young man does.

questions.stem: Patient with back pain, worsening at morning and improving within an hour after movement , positive schober test . What examination should be done next?

why.B: CNS weakness is not a typical AS association; neurological assessment is for cauda equina or spinal fracture with new symptoms.
why.C: The cardiac association of AS is AORTIC regurgitation (aortitis), not mitral, and it is examined when symptomatic rather than as the routine next step.
why.D: The lung association is apical pulmonary fibrosis (and restricted chest expansion), not pulmonary hypertension.

questions.right: Inflammatory back pain ( morning stiffness improving with movement ) plus a positive Schober test (reduced lumbar flexion) indicates ankylosing spondylitis. Its most common extra-articular feature is acute anterior uveitis, which can threaten vision, so the eye should be examined next.
questions.kc: Ankylosing spondylitis extra-articular "A"s. Anterior uveitis (most common) Aortic regurgitation, aortitis, conduction block Apical lung fibrosis Achilles enthesitis Diagnosis: sacroiliitis on X-ray/MRI, HLA-B27 Treatment: NSAIDs first, then TNF inhibitors
questions.ep: If a distractor says mitral or pulmonary hypertension for AS, it is a twist on the real aortic and apical fibrosis associations.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old Saudi man is evaluated because of a 3-month history of fever and back pain that radiates to his legs. His examination reveals bony tenderness over the entire back. Blood culture shows gram-negative coccobacilli . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Tuberculosis (Pott disease) can cause chronic fever and spinal pain, but Mycobacterium is an acid-fast bacillus and is not grown as Gram-negative coccobacilli on routine blood culture.
why.C: Leishmaniasis (visceral) gives fever, massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia; it is a protozoan diagnosed on marrow or splenic aspirate, not blood culture bacteria.
why.D: Schistosomiasis is a fluke infection causing hematuria (S. haematobium) or hepatosplenic disease; diagnosis is by ova in urine or stool.

questions.right: A Saudi man with 3 months of fever , back pain radiating to the legs, diffuse spinal bony tenderness and Gram-negative coccobacilli on blood culture has brucellosis with spinal (musculoskeletal) involvement. Brucella is the classic Gram-negative coccobacillus acquired from raw milk or livestock, and spondylitis is its commonest focal complication.
questions.kc: Brucellosis essentials. Organism: Gram-negative coccobacillus, zoonosis (raw milk, livestock) Picture: undulant fever, sweats, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly Spine/sacroiliitis is the commonest focal complication Treatment: doxycycline plus rifampicin or streptomycin
questions.ep: "Gram-negative coccobacilli" plus Saudi plus chronic fever and back pain = brucellosis, not TB.

questions.stem: An epidemiologist is examining the causes of malaria recurrence amongst prior malaria patients. Which of the following plasmodia is responsible for recurrence?

why.A: P. falciparum has no hypnozoites; recurrence is from treatment failure (recrudescence) or reinfection, and it is the cause of severe malaria rather than relapse.
why.B: P. ovale also forms hypnozoites and can relapse, but it is far less common; vivax is the expected answer when one species is asked.
why.C: P. malariae has no hypnozoites; it can cause very late recrudescence from persistent low-level blood infection and is linked to nephrotic syndrome.

questions.right: Recurrence (relapse) after apparent cure is caused by dormant liver forms called hypnozoites, which reactivate weeks to months later. P. vivax is the classic and most common cause of relapsing malaria, which is why primaquine (or tafenoquine) is added to clear liver stages.
questions.kc: Malaria species: Vivax and ovale: hypnozoites, relapse, need primaquine (check G6PD) Falciparum: severe and cerebral malaria, no relapse Malariae: quartan fever, late recrudescence, nephrotic syndrome Knowlesi: rapid daily cycle, Southeast Asia
questions.ep: Relapse = hypnozoites = vivax/ovale; recrudescence = surviving blood stages.

questions.stem: 50 -year-old man presents to the clinic for a routine follow-up visit. He has a history of hypertension that is well controlled on antihypertensive therapy. He had a hemorrhagic stroke 2 years ago but has fully recovered with no residual neurological deficits. He received the seasonal influenza vaccine 6 months ago . Which of the following vaccines should be administered at this visit according to best-practice recommendations?

why.B: Hepatitis A vaccine is for risk groups (travel to endemic areas, chronic liver disease, men who have sex with men, drug use); he has no indication.
why.C: Herpes zoster vaccine is the same vaccine as the shingles vaccine (option A); the source keyed the 'shingles' wording, so two options with the same meaning suggest one was misrecalled.
why.D: Influenza vaccine is given once each season; he received it 6 months ago and there is no booster for the same season.

questions.right: The decisive clue is his age of 50 : the recombinant zoster (shingles) vaccine is recommended for all adults aged 50 and over, given as two doses. The previous hemorrhagic stroke and controlled hypertension are not contraindications. His influenza vaccine was 6 months ago , so it is not yet due.
questions.kc: Adult vaccines by age and risk: Age 50 or more: recombinant zoster vaccine, 2 doses Pneumococcal: older adults (US guidance lowered the age to 50 in 2024) and risk groups All adults: yearly influenza, Td/Tdap booster every 10 years Hepatitis A/B: risk based
questions.ep: A healthy adult at 50 years for a routine visit: the age clue points to shingles vaccine.

questions.stem: A 35 healthy woman, her mother was diagnosed by breast cancer at 43 and her father by colon cancer at 54, which screening should she do?

why.B: Mammogram at 40 and colonoscopy at 50 is the average-risk schedule; with a first- degree relative diagnosed with breast cancer at 43 and colon cancer at 54, both should start earlier.
why.C: Option not recalled. Alternatives a student might weigh: average-risk screening (too late here) or genetic counselling/BRCA testing, which needs a stronger pattern such as multiple relatives, ovarian or male breast cancer.
why.D: Option not recalled. If it offered colonoscopy now, that would be too early: a first-degree relative with colon cancer at 54 moves her start to age 40.

questions.right: Her mother had breast cancer at 43 (first-degree relative, premenopausal), which puts her at increased risk: screening starts about 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis (here 33) but not before 30, so at 35 she should already have annual mammography. Her father's colon cancer at 54 does mean earlier colonoscopy (at 40, or 10 years before the relative's age), but she is 35, so the screening due now is the mammogram.
questions.kc: Family history shifts screening earlier. Average-risk breast: mammography from age 40 First-degree relative with breast cancer: start 10 years before her age at diagnosis, not before 30, annually Average-risk colorectal: start at 45 (50 if 45 not offered) First-degree relative with CRC <60: colonoscopy at 40 or 10 years before, every 5 years
questions.ep: Do the arithmetic from the relative's age: 43 minus 10 = 33, so a 35-year-old is already due.

questions.stem: After a new outbreak of covid in the city of Wuhan. Which entity is responsible for sounding the international alarm ?

why.A: The local government detects and reports the outbreak upward but has no international authority.
why.B: The national government must notify WHO under the IHR, but it does not declare international emergencies.
why.D: Egypt has no role in a Wuhan outbreak; distractor.

questions.right: Under the International Health Regulations , countries must notify WHO of events that may be of international concern, and only the WHO Director General can declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern , which is the international alarm. For COVID 19 that declaration was made by WHO in January 2020.
questions.kc: Global outbreak responsibility. WHO: coordinates, declares PHEIC (and announced the pandemic in March 2020) National authority (e.g. Ministry of Health): surveillance and notification to WHO Local authority: detection, investigation, local control
questions.ep: 'International alarm' = WHO; 'report to WHO' = the national government.

questions.stem: A doctor sends the cancer screening results to an elderly patient via his personal email , what is the problem with this?

opts.A: Email may be accessed by unauthorized individuals
opts.B: Patient may not understand the terms used in the email
opts.C: Patient may have forgotten his password

why.B: Patient may not understand the terms: a valid communication concern for any written result, but it is not the main ethical or legal problem with using personal email.
why.C: Patient may have forgotten his password: an access inconvenience, not a breach of duty; it is not why the practice is wrong.
why.D: Option not recalled.

questions.right: Sending screening results to a personal email is a breach of patient confidentiality: personal email is not a secure channel and the message can be read by unauthorised people (family members with access, hacking, wrong recipient). Health information must be shared through secure, approved channels or in person, which is the core problem the question tests.
questions.kc: Confidentiality rules: Share health data only through secure, institution-approved channels Abnormal or significant results (e.g. cancer screening) are best discussed in person Disclose to third parties only with consent or a legal/public safety requirement
questions.ep: When a channel is insecure, the answer is confidentiality (unauthorised access), not convenience.

questions.stem: Patient DM HTN on medications lisinopril and metoprolol admitted to the hospital to undergo a surgical procedure. After the operation he was transferred to the surgical ward but he was given IV morphine for pain control (stem: medication weren’t documented ). Which of the following is the critical mistake in the scenario?

why.A: A pharmacy error means a wrong drug or dose was dispensed; nothing was dispensed wrongly here, the drugs were simply never listed.
why.B: A manufacturing defect concerns the product itself; no faulty medication is described.
why.D: Poor post op assessment is vague; the specific failure the stem points to ('medications were not documented') is reconciliation at transfer.

questions.right: The patient's home medications ( lisinopril and metoprolol ) were not documented at the transition from operation to the surgical ward, so his chronic regimen was not continued or reviewed. Comparing and documenting all medications at every transition of care is medication reconciliation ; skipping it is the critical system error (stopping a beta blocker abruptly risks rebound tachycardia and ischemia).
questions.kc: Medication reconciliation: compile, compare, communicate at every transition (admission, transfer, discharge). Aim: prevent omissions, duplications, dosing errors, interactions Beta blocker abrupt withdrawal: rebound tachycardia, ischemia Error categories: prescribing, dispensing (pharmacy), administration, monitoring
questions.ep: 'Medications were not documented' after a transfer is the giveaway word for reconciliation.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient admitted to the hospital follows different social media diets and asks for advice. What's the most appropriate advice?

opts.B: Follow diets shared on social media
opts.D: Refer to a verified diet resources

why.A: Telling him to avoid all social media is paternalistic and unrealistic; some online information is reliable, and the aim is to teach him how to judge it.
why.B: Following unverified social media diets risks unsafe advice, e.g. extreme carbohydrate restriction causing hypoglycemia on insulin or sulfonylurea.
why.C: Self experimentation with diets in a hospitalised diabetic is unsafe and unmonitored.

questions.right: The patient is actively seeking diet information. Respecting his interest while protecting him means directing him to verified, evidence based sources (dietitian, diabetes association, reputable health authority material) rather than banning or endorsing social media. This supports shared decision making and health literacy.
questions.kc: Health information counselling: acknowledge, educate, redirect to credible sources. Refer to a dietitian / diabetes educator Recommend reputable organisations and official guidance Avoid dismissing the patient's interest
questions.ep: Communication questions: the middle path (guide to trusted sources) beats both 'forbid' and 'go ahead'. 55 topics, 84 questions

questions.stem: A 4 day old baby presented to your clinic with slightly yellow body discoloration. He is feeding well . What is the cause of his jaundice?

why.A: Hemolytic disease (Rh/ABO isoimmunization) causes jaundice within the first 24 hours with anemia and a rapid rise; not mild jaundice on day 4 in a thriving baby.
why.C: G6PD deficiency can cause significant neonatal jaundice (often from day 2 to 3, more in boys and with a family history), sometimes without any trigger; suspect it when jaundice is early, severe or rising, not mild in a thriving baby.
why.D: Thalassemia (beta) does not present in the newborn period because HbF predominates; it shows at around 6 months with anemia.

questions.right: A 4-day-old with only "slightly yellow" skin who is feeding well has benign, non-pathological jaundice. This recall's key is breast milk jaundice because it is the only benign, non-hemolytic option listed; strictly, mild jaundice on day 4 in a thriving baby is physiological or breastfeeding-associated jaundice, while true breast milk jaundice appears after the first week. The other options are hemolytic causes that give early, rapidly rising jaundice, often with pallor or an unwell baby.
questions.kc: Neonatal jaundice by timing. First 24 h: always pathological (hemolysis, sepsis) Day 2 to 7: physiological; breastfeeding (poor intake) jaundice After day 7, persisting weeks in a thriving breastfed baby: breast milk jaundice Beyond 2 to 3 weeks: check conjugated bilirubin (biliary atresia)
questions.ep: Jaundice in the first 24 hours, or rapidly rising and severe, flips the answer to a hemolytic cause.

questions.stem: A newborn boy is admitted for severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and is started on intensive phototherapy. Despite treatment, his bilirubin levels fail to decrease and are currently measured at 309 µmol/L (approximately 18.1 mg/dL). What is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.A: Phenobarbital induces hepatic glucuronyl transferase but acts over days; it is used in Crigler-Najjar type II, not as rescue for failed phototherapy.
why.C: Hydration supports phototherapy in a dehydrated baby but does not replace exchange when phototherapy has failed.
why.D: Option not recalled; IVIG is a possible distractor and is used in isoimmune hemolysis to reduce the need for exchange, but it is an adjunct, not the step when phototherapy has failed.

questions.right: The newborn has severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and the bilirubin fails to decrease despite intensive phototherapy . When intensive phototherapy fails, or bilirubin reaches the exchange threshold for age and risk factors, exchange transfusion is the next step to rapidly remove bilirubin (and antibodies if hemolytic) and prevent kernicterus.
questions.kc: Neonatal unconjugated jaundice ladder. Plot bilirubin on age-specific (hours) chart with risk factors Above phototherapy line: phototherapy Rising despite intensive phototherapy or at exchange line: exchange transfusion Any signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: immediate exchange Isoimmune hemolysis: consider IVIG
questions.ep: Exchange depends on the age-specific threshold and response, not on one absolute number; failure of intensive phototherapy is the trigger here.

questions.stem: Baby with kernicterus and neurological sequelae. Expected physical examination finding?

why.A: Spasticity reflects upper motor neuron damage (periventricular leukomalacia in prematurity, cortical injury); not the basal ganglia lesion of kernicterus.
why.B: Ataxia comes from cerebellar damage, not bilirubin injury to the basal ganglia.
why.C: Hypotonia is seen early in acute bilirubin encephalopathy and in many neonatal conditions, but it is not the classic chronic sequela; it often evolves into another CP type.

questions.right: In kernicterus , unconjugated bilirubin deposits in the basal ganglia (especially the globus pallidus). Basal ganglia injury produces dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy, so the expected neurological sequela is involuntary choreoathetoid movements and dystonia.
questions.kc: Cerebral palsy type follows the lesion site. Basal ganglia (kernicterus, HIE): dyskinetic/athetoid Periventricular white matter (prematurity): spastic diplegia Cerebellum: ataxic Chronic kernicterus tetrad: athetosis, upward gaze palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dental enamel dysplasia
questions.ep: Prematurity points to spastic diplegia; kernicterus points to dyskinetic CP.

questions.stem: Term neonate delivered by cesarean , has retractions and flaring. Was given oxygen. X-ray shows hyperaeration and interstitial infiltrates (written like this, No X-Ray) What's the next step in the management?

why.A: Antibiotics (after blood culture) are right when sepsis or pneumonia is suspected: maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, GBS, unstable baby or worsening course; none are given here.
why.C: Echocardiogram is right when cyanotic congenital heart disease or persistent pulmonary hypertension is suspected, e.g. hypoxia not improving with oxygen or a murmur; this baby responds to oxygen. D. Option not recalled.

questions.right: A term neonate born by caesarean section with tachypnoea, retractions and flaring that responds to oxygen, and a chest X-ray with hyperaeration and streaky interstitial (perihilar) markings, is transient tachypnoea of the newborn. It results from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid (no labour, no vaginal squeeze) and resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so management is supportive: oxygen as needed and monitoring.
questions.kc: Neonatal respiratory distress by clue: Term + CS, hyperinflation, fluid in fissure/streaky markings: TTN, supportive Preterm, ground glass + air bronchograms, low volumes: RDS, surfactant/CPAP Meconium-stained, post-term, patchy infiltrates: meconium aspiration Risk factors for infection, unstable: pneumonia/sepsis, antibiotics
questions.ep: TTN has HYPERinflated lungs; RDS has LOW lung volumes with ground glass.

questions.stem: A 39 weeks pregnant female, on examination amniotic fluid was noted to have a dark green color . What's the most appropriate action to be done [[[ DURING ]]] delivery?

opts.C: Oropharyngeal suction before delivering the rest of body

why.A: NICU transfer is an after-delivery decision (e.g. a distressed infant of a diabetic mother); it is not an action during delivery.
why.B: Immediate endotracheal intubation was once used for a non-vigorous infant after birth; it is not a routine intrapartum action and current guidance no longer advises routine intubation for suction.
why.D: IV antibiotics are for maternal chorioamnionitis or GBS prophylaxis; meconium staining alone is not an indication.

questions.right: This recall's key is C because the question asks what to do during delivery with thick, dark green meconium-stained fluid, and older teaching was to suction the mouth and pharynx at the perineum once the head delivers, before the shoulders and body, to reduce meconium aspiration. The compiler stresses this is different from the after-birth NICU recall.
questions.kc: Meconium-stained liquor. Older teaching: intrapartum oropharyngeal suction at the perineum Current neonatal resuscitation: no routine intrapartum suction, no routine tracheal suction Have a resuscitation-skilled team at delivery Vigorous baby: routine care with mother; non- vigorous: standard resuscitation steps
questions.ep: Note the lead-in "DURING delivery" versus "after delivery"; the exam key here is the older suction-at-perineum answer.

questions.stem: Term baby with meconium aspiration syndrome intubated and ventilated due to hypoxia and hypercapnia . Which of the following can assess complications?

why.A: Bronchoscopy is not used to assess MAS complications; routine airway suctioning for meconium is no longer recommended and bronchoscopy adds risk in an unstable ventilated neonate.
why.B: Pulmonary function tests cannot be performed meaningfully in a ventilated neonate and do not detect PPHN.
why.D: Lung ultrasound can show consolidation or pneumothorax at the bedside, but it does not assess pulmonary hypertension, the main complication that changes management.

questions.right: In meconium aspiration syndrome needing ventilation for hypoxia and hypercapnia, the key complication is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) with right-to-left shunting through the ductus and foramen ovale. Echocardiography confirms PPHN (estimates pulmonary pressure, shows shunt direction and right ventricular function) and excludes structural heart disease, guiding therapy such as inhaled nitric oxide.
questions.kc: MAS complications: PPHN (echo), air leak (CXR or transillumination), chemical pneumonitis, infection. PPHN clue: pre-ductal saturation higher than post-ductal Confirm: echocardiography Treat: optimize ventilation and oxygen, inhaled nitric oxide, ECMO if refractory
questions.ep: Hypoxic ventilated term baby after meconium: think PPHN and order an echo.

questions.stem: A infant baby has bronchopulmonary dysplaisa . Team has difficulty weaning off mechanical ventilation. Most appropriate management?

opts.D: Increase tidal volume and inspirtory pressure

why.A: Abrupt cessation of ventilation in a ventilator-dependent infant risks respiratory collapse; weaning is gradual.
why.B: Long-term steroids carry serious risks in preterm infants (adverse neurodevelopment, growth failure, infection), so prolonged courses are avoided.
why.D: Raising tidal volume and inspiratory pressure causes further volutrauma and barotrauma, the very mechanism that produces BPD.

questions.right: An infant with "bronchopulmonary dysplasia" who cannot be weaned from mechanical ventilation is the setting in which a short course of low-dose systemic corticosteroid (dexamethasone) is used to facilitate extubation. Short, low-dose courses improve lung mechanics while limiting the neurodevelopmental harms seen with prolonged or high-dose steroids.
questions.kc: BPD (chronic lung disease of prematurity): Oxygen need at 36 weeks corrected age Prevention: gentle ventilation, early CPAP, caffeine, surfactant Difficult extubation: short low-dose dexamethasone course Supportive: nutrition, diuretics in selected cases, oxygen Avoid prolonged or high-dose steroids
questions.ep: "Short" versus "long" term is the whole question; steroids help, but only briefly.

questions.stem: newborn delivered to a diabetic mother presents with respiratory distress and desaturation (No Numbers, Just Desat) shortly after birth. Physical examination is unremarkable except for signs of respiratory distress and macrosomia . What is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.B: NICU admission, glucose monitoring, and observation

why.A: Intubation is for respiratory failure (apnea, poor effort, failure of non-invasive support); nothing here shows that degree of compromise.
why.C: Immediate surfactant is for confirmed or highly likely RDS in a preterm baby needing ventilation; it is not the first step before assessment.
why.D: Empirical antibiotics are for sepsis risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture, GBS); the stem gives none and the cause here is metabolic and maturational.

questions.right: An infant of a diabetic mother is at risk of hypoglycemia , respiratory distress (delayed surfactant maturation, transient tachypnea), polycythemia and hypocalcemia. With respiratory distress and desaturation but an otherwise unremarkable examination , the most appropriate next step is NICU admission with oxygen and support as needed, close glucose monitoring , and observation, since hypoglycemia itself can worsen the distress.
questions.kc: Infant of a diabetic mother. Macrosomia, birth trauma, shoulder dystocia Hypoglycemia (fetal hyperinsulinism): monitor glucose early Respiratory distress: delayed surfactant, TTN Polycythemia, jaundice, hypocalcemia, cardiomyopathy
questions.ep: In any infant of a diabetic mother who is unwell, check glucose; hypoglycemia is the common, treatable culprit.

questions.stem: A Baby delayed separation of umbilical cords and bleeding from the site. Labs of coagulation prolonged PT PTT . platelets count normal . There is delay in clot time.

why.A: Haemophilia A (factor VIII): only PTT is prolonged with a normal PT; it usually presents later with haemarthrosis, or with circumcision bleeding.
why.B: Von Willebrand disease: mucosal bleeding with prolonged bleeding time and normal or mildly prolonged PTT; PT is normal.
why.D: Thrombocytopenia is excluded by the normal platelet count and would not prolong PT or PTT.

questions.right: Bleeding from the umbilical stump in a baby with both PT and PTT prolonged and a normal platelet count points to a deficiency of several clotting factors across both pathways. Vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX and X, so its deficiency (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, especially if vitamin K was not given at birth) prolongs both PT and PTT.
questions.kc: Neonatal bleeding by coagulation pattern: PT and PTT prolonged, platelets normal: vitamin K deficiency (or common pathway factor X/V/II deficiency, liver disease) PTT alone: haemophilia A or B Normal PT, PTT and platelets with umbilical stump bleeding: factor XIII deficiency Delayed cord separation without bleeding: leukocyte adhesion deficiency Low platelets: alloimmune or maternal ITP, sepsis/DIC
questions.ep: Both PT and PTT long with normal platelets in a newborn = vitamin K deficiency; normal tests with stump bleeding = factor XIII.

questions.stem: Child bleeds after umbilical stump. His mother has SLE . THE child has normal PTt and pt with PLT 18000 what is the TREATMENT?

why.B: Steroids are a second-line option in immune neonatal thrombocytopenia and act too slowly for an actively bleeding baby.
why.C: FFP replaces clotting factors; it is for coagulopathy with prolonged PT/PTT, whereas here both are normal.
why.D: Vitamin K with PCC treats hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, which prolongs PT and PTT with normal platelets; the opposite of this picture.

questions.right: Bleeding from the umbilical stump with normal PT and PTT but platelets 18,000 is isolated neonatal thrombocytopenia. A mother with SLE can pass IgG antiplatelet antibodies across the placenta, causing immune-mediated destruction of the baby's platelets. In an actively bleeding neonate the treatment is platelet transfusion plus IVIG , which blocks antibody-mediated clearance and raises the count.
questions.kc: Neonatal bleeding: read platelets and PT/PTT first. Low platelets, normal PT/PTT, maternal ITP/SLE: immune thrombocytopenia, give platelets + IVIG if bleeding Prolonged PT and PTT, normal platelets, no vitamin K at birth: hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, give vitamin K Low platelets + prolonged PT/PTT in a sick baby: DIC, treat cause, replace products
questions.ep: Umbilical bleeding alone makes students reach for vitamin K; normal PT/PTT with very low platelets points to immune thrombocytopenia instead.

questions.stem: A newborn presents with microcephaly , a distended abdomen, and marked hepatosplenomegaly . Natal history is significant for maternal diabetes. Laboratory investigations show pancytopenia (Labs: low WBC; low hemoglobin; low platelets; elevated AST and ALT). What is the most appropriate next step in management?

why.A: Chromosomal analysis suits dysmorphic features or multiple anomalies (for example trisomy 13 or 18); it does not explain hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia.
why.C: Abdominal US would confirm organomegaly already found on exam but does not identify the cause.
why.D: CT of the abdomen adds radiation without diagnostic value here; head imaging (cranial US or CT for calcifications) may follow, but the etiological test is TORCH screening.

questions.right: A newborn with microcephaly , hepatosplenomegaly , pancytopenia (especially low platelets) and raised transaminases has the picture of a congenital infection, classically CMV. The most appropriate next step is TORCH screening (with CMV PCR of urine or saliva in the first 3 weeks). Maternal diabetes is a distractor: it causes macrosomia, hypoglycemia and cardiac or sacral anomalies, not this picture.
questions.kc: Microcephaly + hepatosplenomegaly + thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia + raised LFTs in a newborn = congenital infection (TORCH). CMV: commonest; periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, petechiae or blueberry muffin rash Toxoplasmosis: diffuse intracranial calcifications, hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis Rubella: cataract, PDA, deafness Syphilis: snuffles, rash on palms and soles, periostitis CMV diagnosis must be within first 3 weeks to prove congenital infection
questions.ep: Maternal diabetes in the stem is bait; the triad of microcephaly, organomegaly and cytopenias always points to TORCH.

questions.stem: A Baby with nausea and vomiting, labs showed metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia , hyponatremia and hypoglycemia . Congenital Adrenal hyperplasia because of 21-hydroxylase is suspected. (diagnosis written in the recall) What is the most appropriate initial management?

opts.A: IV hydrocortisone and isotonic normal saline

why.B: Oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone are the long-term maintenance therapy once the infant is stable; a vomiting, hypoglycemic infant in crisis needs IV treatment.
why.C: Sodium bicarbonate and insulin treat the acidosis and hyperkalemia symptomatically; insulin is dangerous in a hypoglycemic infant, and both resolve with fluids and hydrocortisone.
why.D: Option not recalled; if it was dextrose alone, it corrects the glucose but misses the steroid and sodium deficit.

questions.right: Vomiting with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis and hypoglycemia in suspected 21-hydroxylase CAH is a salt-wasting adrenal crisis. The initial management is resuscitation with isotonic normal saline plus IV (stress-dose) hydrocortisone, with a dextrose bolus/infusion for the hypoglycemia; hydrocortisone at high dose also provides mineralocorticoid effect.
questions.kc: Salt-wasting CAH crisis (usually 2nd to 3rd week of life). Labs: low Na, high K, acidosis, low glucose, high 17-OH progesterone Acute: normal saline bolus, IV hydrocortisone, dextrose for hypoglycemia Maintenance: oral hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone (+ salt in infancy) Autosomal recessive; girls ambiguous genitalia, boys present with crisis
questions.ep: A stable infant in clinic needing long-term treatment flips the answer to oral hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone.

questions.stem: Patient with maple syrup disease (stated in the question that the pt has this disease) and ask about dietary restrictions ?

opts.C: Give good calorie diet but restrict leucine

why.A: Phenylalanine restriction is the treatment of phenylketonuria (musty or mousy odour, fair skin, intellectual disability), not MSUD.
why.B: Sodium phenylacetate and sodium benzoate are nitrogen scavengers used for hyperammonemia in urea cycle disorders, not a dietary restriction for MSUD.

questions.right: Maple syrup urine disease is a defect of the branched chain alpha ketoacid dehydrogenase, so the branched chain amino acids ( leucine , isoleucine, valine) accumulate; leucine is the most neurotoxic. Treatment is a lifelong diet restricted in branched chain amino acids, especially leucine, with enough calories to prevent catabolism (which releases these amino acids from muscle).
questions.kc: MSUD = branched chain amino acids; restrict leucine, give high calories. Neonate: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, burnt sugar or maple syrup urine odour Diagnosis: raised plasma leucine, isoleucine, valine, alloisoleucine Acute crisis: stop protein, high calorie IV glucose (plus insulin), dialysis if severe Some forms respond to thiamine PKU: restrict phenylalanine; urea cycle defects: low protein + scavengers
questions.ep: Musty odour = PKU (restrict phenylalanine); sweet maple syrup odour = MSUD (restrict leucine).

questions.stem: A hypotonic newborn had tongue fasciculations . EMG showed denervation . The parents were concerned about the child's condition. What is the appropriate counseling?

opts.B: Muscle biopsy is needed to determine management
opts.C: There is a new therapy that is more effective if started early
opts.D: With good nutrition, life expectancy can increase.

why.A: Reassurance is wrong: untreated SMA type 1 is progressive with respiratory failure, usually fatal within the first 2 years.
why.B: Muscle biopsy is not needed: the diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for SMN1 deletion, and EMG already shows a neurogenic (not myopathic) process; biopsy is for suspected myopathies.
why.D: Good nutrition is part of supportive care but does not change the natural course; survival depends on respiratory support and disease-modifying therapy.

questions.right: A hypotonic newborn with tongue fasciculations and denervation on EMG has spinal muscular atrophy (SMN1 deletion, anterior horn cell loss). Disease-modifying therapies now exist (nusinersen, onasemnogene abeparvovec gene therapy, risdiplam), and their benefit is greatest when started early, ideally before motor neurons are lost, so this is the appropriate counselling. The compiler notes there was no 'symptomatic treatment' option among the choices.
questions.kc: Spinal muscular atrophy: Floppy infant, alert face, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations, bell-shaped chest EMG: denervation; confirm with SMN1 genetic test Treatment: nusinersen, gene therapy, risdiplam; earlier = better Supportive: respiratory, nutrition, physiotherapy
questions.ep: Floppy baby + tongue fasciculations = SMA; counsel that early disease-modifying therapy gives the best outcome.

questions.stem: A 5 month old child came with hypotonia and decreased proximal muscle power , present reflexes but weak, no fasciculation . Normal feeding and swallowing. Good eye contact and responds to sounds. EMG showed myopathy CK normal What is the Diagnosis?

why.A: Cerebral palsy is a central (brain) disorder: developmental delay, abnormal tone that becomes spastic, brisk reflexes, often poor social or cognitive development, and a normal EMG.
why.B: Congenital muscular dystrophy causes active muscle necrosis, so CK is typically markedly raised; the normal CK here argues against it.
why.D: SMA (anterior horn cell disease) gives absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and a neurogenic, not myopathic, EMG.

questions.right: The clues localize to muscle: hypotonia with proximal weakness , reflexes present , no fasciculations , normal cognition ( good eye contact , responds to sound), myopathic EMG and normal CK . A myopathic EMG with normal CK is typical of congenital myopathy (structural myopathies such as central core or nemaline), where there is little muscle fibre breakdown.
questions.kc: Floppy infant: localize the lesion. Central (CP, syndromes): normal power for tone, brisk reflexes, delay in cognition Anterior horn (SMA): areflexia, fasciculations, neurogenic EMG, alert baby Muscular dystrophy: myopathic EMG, high CK Congenital myopathy: myopathic EMG, normal or mildly raised CK, biopsy diagnostic NMJ (infant botulism): ptosis, poor feeding, constipation
questions.ep: Same picture with a markedly high CK flips the answer to congenital muscular dystrophy.

questions.stem: A mother brings her 6-month-old baby to the well-baby clinic. What is the most consistent gross motor development expected at this age?

why.B: Mature palmar grasp is a fine motor skill, not gross motor (and the more mature pincer grasp appears around 9 months).
why.C: Pulls to stand is a 9-month gross motor milestone; expecting it at 6 months is too early.
why.D: Rolls from prone to supine is a 4-month milestone, so it is earlier than this age (supine to prone is the 6-month rolling milestone).

questions.right: Sitting without support is the gross motor milestone taught for 6 months . Of the options, it is the only gross motor skill that matches this age: pulling to stand is a 9-month skill, rolling prone to supine is already achieved at 4 months, and mature palmar grasp is fine motor.
questions.kc: Gross motor ladder: 4 months: head control, rolls prone to supine 6 months: sits (with/without support), rolls supine to prone 9 months: crawls, pulls to stand 12 months: cruises / walks independently
questions.ep: Read the rolling direction: prone to supine is 4 months, supine to prone is 6 months.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy who was delivered at term vaginally without complications is brought for assessment and is found to have normal development. Which of the following gross motor milestones is present at this age?

why.A: Walking holding onto furniture (cruising) is a gross motor skill of about 10-12 months.
why.B: Mature pincer grasp is a fine motor skill of about 10-12 months, so it fails twice: wrong domain and wrong age.
why.D: Rolling prone to supine is achieved around 4 months; it is still present at 6 months but is not the age-defining skill, which is why the earlier milestone is the distractor.

questions.right: The lead-in asks which "gross motor" skill is present in a normally developing "6-month-old". Sitting without support (initially briefly, often in tripod posture) is the classic 6- month gross motor milestone in the offered options; the compiler strongly endorses it, noting rolling supine to prone was not an option.
questions.kc: Gross motor milestones: 4 months: rolls prone to supine, head steady 5-6 months: rolls supine to prone 6 months: sits (tripod / briefly without support) 9 months: sits well, pulls to stand, crawls 12 months: cruises, first steps
questions.ep: If "rolls supine to prone" is offered for a 6-month-old, some keys choose it over sitting; read the options.

questions.stem: child who can identify colors and articulate words , age in years:

why.A: At 2 years the child jumps on 2 feet and uses 2-word phrases; naming colors is not expected yet.
why.B: At 3 years the child can point to a color when asked and speaks 3-word sentences with about 75% intelligibility; naming colors comes later at 4.
why.D: At 5 years expect balancing on one foot for 10 seconds, using future tense and counting; nothing in the stem requires 5-year skills.

questions.right: Being able to identify (name) colors is a 4-year milestone, and clear articulation of words (speech mostly intelligible to strangers) also fits 4 years. Using the milestone method, the child is at least the age of the oldest milestone achieved, which is 4 years.
questions.kc: Color and speech milestones. 3 years: points to a color, 3-word sentences, 75% intelligible 4 years: names colors (4 colors), tells a story, hops on 1 foot, speech intelligible to strangers 4 to 5 years: draws a square, counts 5 years: balance 10 s on one foot, future tense
questions.ep: Pointing to a color = 3 years; naming/identifying colors = 4 years.

questions.stem: A child has started to develop a sense of individuality. She recognizes strangers and becomes frightened when What is the most likely age (in months)?

why.A: At 6 months infants begin to recognize strangers, but fearful stranger anxiety is not yet established.
why.B: At 7 months stranger wariness may be starting, but the classic fearful reaction is placed later in the first year.
why.C: Option not recalled.

questions.right: Fear of strangers (stranger anxiety) is a sign that the infant now distinguishes familiar people from unfamiliar ones and has developed a sense of self versus others. It emerges in the second half of the first year and is well established and peaking around 9-10 months, so 10 months is the best fit among the options (12 months was not offered).
questions.kc: Social milestones: 2 months: social smile 6 months: recognizes strangers 9-10 months: stranger anxiety, waves bye-bye, plays peek-a-boo About 12-18 months: separation anxiety peaks
questions.ep: "Recognizes" strangers is earlier (about 6 months); "frightened" by strangers is later (about 9-10 months).

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant seen in the clinic. Rubbing side of the mouth with tip of the little finger is one of the primitive reflexes (see image). Which of the following is the name of this reflex?

why.B: Stepping: holding the baby upright with the soles touching a surface produces alternating walking movements; it involves the feet, not the mouth.
why.C: Parachute: a protective reflex where the infant extends the arms when tipped forward; it appears later in infancy (around 8 to 9 months) and persists for life, so it is not present at 2 weeks.
why.D: Lateral neck (tonic neck) reflex: turning the head produces the fencing posture of the limbs; it is elicited by head rotation, not by touching the mouth.

questions.right: Stroking the side of the mouth makes the infant turn the head and mouth toward the stimulus: this is the rooting reflex. It is present from birth, helps the baby find the nipple, and disappears by about 4 months.
questions.kc: Primitive reflexes by stimulus: Rooting: stroke cheek/mouth corner, head turns toward it (gone ~4 months) Sucking: object in mouth Moro: head drop, arms extend then flex (gone ~6 months) Asymmetric tonic neck: head turn, fencing posture Stepping: soles on surface Parachute: appears late in infancy, never disappears
questions.ep: Mouth stimulus = rooting (or sucking); parachute is the reflex that appears late and stays.

questions.stem: 6 months old infant brought to vaccination clinic He had huge swelling at injection site when previous DTaP given Now he have URTI with temperature 37.9 What to do regarding the Dtap vaccine ?

why.B: Delaying 2 months leaves the infant unprotected against pertussis with no benefit; there is no reason to postpone.
why.C: Deferral is only for moderate to severe acute illness; a mild URTI with low-grade fever is not a reason to wait.
why.D: Omitting pertussis (DT) is reserved for encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis- containing dose; a local swelling does not justify it.

questions.right: A large local swelling after a previous DTaP and a mild URTI with temperature 37.9 are both not contraindications. Extensive local reactions are benign and do not recur in a dangerous way, and minor illness with or without low-grade fever should not delay vaccination, so the DTaP is given now on schedule.
questions.kc: DTaP: true contraindications are few. Contraindications: anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component; encephalopathy within 7 days of a prior dose Precaution (defer): progressive or unstable neurological disorder; moderate/severe acute illness Not contraindications: local swelling, mild fever, mild URTI, febrile seizure history, family history of seizures
questions.ep: Encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose is what flips the answer to dropping the pertussis component.

questions.stem: Pediatric have a severe persistent asthma that was vaccinated by influenza and after it develop urticaria, syncope what to do?

opts.D: Give influenza vaccine with steroids and antihistamine

why.A: Stopping all vaccines is wrong; the contraindication applies only to the vaccine (or component) that caused the reaction, and other vaccines are still needed.
why.C: Live attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine is contraindicated in children with severe asthma or recent wheeze, and does not remove the anaphylaxis risk to influenza vaccine components.
why.D: Premedication with steroids and antihistamines does not prevent anaphylaxis and is not a way to give a vaccine that caused a serious reaction.

questions.right: Urticaria with syncope right after the influenza vaccine is a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) . A serious allergic reaction to a previous dose of a vaccine is an absolute contraindication to further doses of that same vaccine , so influenza vaccine is not given again, while the rest of the schedule continues. The child's "severe persistent asthma" also rules out the live intranasal alternative.
questions.kc: Anaphylaxis to a dose = absolute contraindication to that vaccine only. Absolute: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or to a vaccine component Precaution: moderate or severe acute illness Not contraindications: mild illness, antibiotics, penicillin allergy, local reaction or mild fever Intranasal (live) flu vaccine: avoid in severe asthma, recent wheeze, immunosuppression
questions.ep: A mild local reaction or low fever after a vaccine is NOT a contraindication; only a serious allergic reaction stops that vaccine.

questions.stem: 9 months came for vaccine what is contraindicated this visit?

why.B: Penicillin allergy is not a contraindication to vaccination; only allergy to a vaccine component matters.
why.C: Current antibiotic therapy is not a contraindication; vaccinate on schedule.
why.D: Recent exposure to an infectious disease is not a contraindication; vaccinate on schedule.

questions.right: The question asks what would defer vaccination at this visit . A moderate or severe acute illness (with or without fever) is a recognised precaution: the vaccine is postponed until the child recovers, so that a reaction is not confused with the illness. All the other options are classic misconceptions that should not delay vaccination.
questions.kc: Vaccine contraindications vs misconceptions. Absolute: anaphylaxis to a prior dose or a vaccine component Precaution (defer): moderate or severe acute illness Vaccinate anyway: mild illness with or without fever, convalescence Vaccinate anyway: antibiotics, recent exposure, penicillin or other non-vaccine allergy
questions.ep: Mild illness (e.g. a cold, low-grade fever) is NOT a reason to defer; only moderate or severe illness is.

questions.stem: Pedia immunduffincy recurnt infection and atopy what to not give

why.A: DTaP is an inactivated toxoid and acellular vaccine; it is safe in immunodeficiency, though the response may be weaker.
why.C: Hib is an inactivated conjugate (polysaccharide) vaccine and is safe; immunodeficient children actually need protection against encapsulated organisms.
why.D: H. influenzae type b vaccine is the same inactivated conjugate vaccine as Hib; it is safe and recommended.

questions.right: A child with an immunodeficiency , recurrent infections and atopy (eczema) suggests a primary immunodeficiency such as Wiskott Aldrich syndrome. Live attenuated vaccines can cause disseminated vaccine strain disease in these children, and among the options only varicella is a live vaccine, so it is the one not to give.
questions.kc: Immunocompromised child = no live vaccines. Live vaccines: MMR, varicella, BCG, oral polio (OPV), rotavirus, yellow fever, intranasal influenza Inactivated: DTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV, hepatitis B, hepatitis A, injectable influenza Wiskott Aldrich: eczema + recurrent infections + thrombocytopenia (small platelets), X linked HIV: varicella and MMR may be given if CD4 is not severely low
questions.ep: Same rule applies to household contacts? No: siblings can receive MMR and varicella; only OPV is avoided in contacts.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant present to Emergency Room with cough, sneezing . circumoral cyanosis occasional with frothy secretion from mouth for the 3 days. On examination, she looks well with moderate tachypnea and intercostal retraction. Chest reveals scatted rhonchi and crackles all over but good air entry. (Vitals: BP 80/50 mmHg; HR 138/min; RR 48/min; Temp 36.6; SpO2 91 %) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Heart failure in infants presents with feeding difficulty, sweating with feeds, poor weight gain, hepatomegaly, gallop or murmur; the URTI prodrome and diffuse rhonchi fit infection better.
why.C: Asthma is not diagnosed in a 2-month-old; recurrent wheeze responding to bronchodilators, atopy and older age are needed.
why.D: GERD causes regurgitation, irritability with feeds and possibly aspiration, but not a coryzal prodrome with diffuse crackles and wheeze.

questions.right: A 2-month-old , afebrile, with URTI symptoms ( cough, sneezing ) for 3 days, then lower respiratory signs ( tachypnea, intercostal retraction, scattered rhonchi and crackles ) and SpO2 91% is classic bronchiolitis, most often RSV. The frothy secretions and episodic circumoral cyanosis reflect secretions and apnea/hypoxia episodes common in young infants with bronchiolitis.
questions.kc: Bronchiolitis: under 2 years (peak under 6 months), RSV, winter. URTI prodrome, then cough, tachypnea, retractions, crackles and/or wheeze Clinical diagnosis; no routine CXR or labs Supportive: oxygen if SpO2 below about 90 to 92%, nasal suction, feeding support/IV fluids Not recommended routinely: salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics Risk of apnea in young infants and preterms
questions.ep: Recurrent episodes in an older child with atopy point to asthma, not bronchiolitis.

questions.stem: 3 month old child presents with increasing dyspnea for 3 days, then 2 days of sneezing . His older brother recently had an upper respiratory tract infection. What's the most likely organism?

why.A: Adenovirus causes bronchiolitis less often and usually adds fever, pharyngitis and conjunctivitis (pharyngoconjunctival fever); nothing here points to it.
why.B: Influenza gives abrupt high fever, myalgia and systemic toxicity, often in seasonal outbreaks; it is a less common cause of infant bronchiolitis.
why.C: Parainfluenza is the main cause of croup: barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor in a 6 month to 3 year old, none of which are described.

questions.right: A 3 month old with progressive dyspnea plus coryza ( sneezing ) after exposure to a sibling with a URTI is the classic setting of bronchiolitis, and RSV is by far its commonest cause in infants under 1 year. There is no barking cough or stridor (croup) and no high fever with myalgia (influenza), so RSV wins by exclusion, as the compiler notes. Older children and adults carry RSV as a simple cold and pass it to young infants at home.
questions.kc: Infant (under 1 year) + coryza then increasing respiratory distress = bronchiolitis = RSV. Bronchiolitis: URTI prodrome then wheeze, crackles, tachypnea, hyperinflation on CXR RSV: commonest cause; peak in winter; sick contact usually an older sibling Croup: parainfluenza, barking cough, stridor Pharyngoconjunctival fever: adenovirus Management of bronchiolitis is supportive (oxygen, hydration, suction)
questions.ep: If the stem adds barking cough and stridor, switch to parainfluenza (croup); infant + cold + breathing difficulty without those = RSV.

questions.stem: A school-aged child with asthma came to the ER with acute asthma exacerbation, SpO2 95% , peak flow meter at best 60, can complete full sentences , took two puffs of salbutamol at home, mild wheeze on auscultation. Which is the most appropriate management?

opts.D: Give salbutamol by spacer then reassess

why.A: Oral steroids are reasonable add-ons in a moderate attack, but hospitalization is not indicated in a child who is talking in sentences with SpO2 95% before even assessing the response to SABA.
why.B: Salmeterol (LABA) is a controller for chronic step-up therapy and has no role in treating an acute attack.
why.C: Ipratropium is added for severe or life-threatening attacks, or when there is a poor response to repeated SABA; it is not the first move in a mild-moderate attack.

questions.right: The child has a mild to moderate exacerbation: SpO2 95% (above 92%), "can complete full sentences" and only "mild wheeze" . The first step for this severity is a short-acting beta-2 agonist delivered by MDI with spacer (as effective as a nebulizer), repeated as needed, and then reassessing response before deciding on discharge or escalation.
questions.kc: Acute asthma in children: grade severity first, then treat. Mild/moderate: SpO2 >92%, talks in sentences: SABA via spacer, reassess Severe: SpO2 <92%, too breathless to talk, PEF 33 to 50%: add ipratropium and systemic steroid Life-threatening: silent chest, cyanosis, PEF <33%, exhaustion Poor response: IV magnesium, admission
questions.ep: SpO2 <92% or inability to talk upgrades the attack to severe, and then ipratropium and steroids become correct.

questions.stem: (A case about an asthmatic child that is not following doctor’s orders in using the inhaler ) In an asthmatic child with frequent exacerbations, what is the best preventive method?

why.A: Diet control has no established role in preventing asthma exacerbations; it would matter only for obesity-related or food-allergy contexts.
why.C: Environmental control is right when the stem gives no specific problem or points to triggers (smoke, pets, dust mites); here the stated problem is inhaler misuse.
why.D: Option not recalled; another distractor could be stepping up medication, which is wrong until technique and adherence are fixed.

questions.right: The stem stresses that the child is "not following doctor's orders in using the inhaler" . Poor inhaler technique and adherence are the commonest reasons for frequent exacerbations, so the most useful preventive step is teaching correct inhaler use (with a spacer) before any other change. The compiler agrees with B, noting that neither inhaler type nor environmental triggers were mentioned.
questions.kc: Before stepping up asthma therapy, check technique, adherence and triggers. Stem says inhaler misuse: teach technique Stem is bland, no clue: environmental control Technique and adherence fine but uncontrolled: step up
questions.ep: Do not mix it up with the bland 6-year-old recall where the answer is environmental control; the clue here is the misused inhaler.

questions.stem: 6 years old known case of bronchial asthma and recurrent acute asthma exacerbation. Which of the following is most helpful teaching points for prevention of his exacerbation ?

opts.D: Patient Skills using peak flow rate

why.A: "Advance asthma tips" is vague and not a specific preventive measure.
why.C: Spacer skills would be the answer if the stem described poor inhaler technique or non- adherence; nothing of the sort is given here.
why.D: Peak flow monitoring is a self-assessment tool for action plans; it monitors rather than prevents exacerbations and is effort-dependent, so less reliable in young children.

questions.right: This is a bland question with no clue about inhaler technique or a specific trigger: a 6-year-old with recurrent exacerbations and the lead-in asks for the most helpful teaching point for prevention . Avoiding triggers (allergens, smoke, dust mites, viral exposure) is the core preventive education for childhood asthma, and the compiler marks B confirmed by a 100/120 examinee.
questions.kc: Asthma prevention teaching depends on the stem's clue. No clue given: environmental (trigger) control Inhaler misuse described: teach technique / spacer Uncontrolled despite good technique: step up therapy
questions.ep: If the stem mentions the child is not using the inhaler correctly, the answer flips to inhaler technique.

questions.stem: A mother is worried about her son who has asthma . What is the most appropriate counseling ?

opts.A: He will develop chronic lung disorder
opts.B: Childhood asthma will disappear by adolescence
opts.C: He will have asthma for the rest of his life
opts.D: No correlation between childhood and adulthood asthma

why.A: Progression to chronic lung disease is not the usual course of childhood asthma; this is unnecessarily alarming and inaccurate.
why.C: Lifelong asthma is not the rule; most children improve or remit, though persistent or atopic asthma may continue.
why.D: There IS a relationship: some childhood asthma persists or relapses in adulthood, particularly with severe disease or atopy.

questions.right: The reassurance a worried parent should get is that many children with asthma grow out of it , with symptoms often remitting by adolescence, especially in milder, episodic disease. The recall's option B expresses this favourable natural history.
questions.kc: Childhood asthma prognosis. Many outgrow it, often by adolescence Persistence more likely with severe disease, atopy/eczema, parental asthma, smoking exposure Remitted asthma can relapse in adulthood
questions.ep: Counselling questions favour the evidence-based reassuring answer, not the extreme "always" or "never" options.

questions.stem: Child came to ER before 12 hours with fever and SOB, yesterday he had sore throat and dysphasia, on exam he looks toxic immobile in a chair opens his mouth with drooling of saliva , tachycardic, tachypneic, Fever 40 What's the next step?

why.A: Intubation in the ER (the recall stresses ER, not OR) is avoided: agitating the child or attempting a difficult airway outside a controlled setting with ENT backup can precipitate complete obstruction. It is right only for a child in arrest or complete obstruction with no time to move.
why.C: Ward admission is unsafe: the child needs continuous airway monitoring and readiness for intubation or surgical airway, which a ward cannot provide.
why.D: Nebulized steroids (or epinephrine) treat croup, which has a barking cough, low-grade fever and a non-toxic child; they do not protect the airway in epiglottitis.

questions.right: A toxic child with fever 40, sore throat and dysphagia who sits immobile with mouth open and drooling has acute epiglottitis. The airway can close suddenly, so the priority is a controlled, expert-secured airway: urgent transfer to the PICU (with anaesthesia and ENT) for intubation, keeping the child calm and upright, before any sepsis workup or invasive procedure.
questions.kc: Epiglottitis: airway first, in a controlled setting. Clues: toxic, high fever, drooling, tripod or immobile with open mouth, rapid onset over hours Do not lie flat, examine the throat or take bloods before the airway is secure Secure airway (ICU or OR with ENT/anaesthesia), then cultures and IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin) Croup: barking cough, stridor, not toxic: steroids ± nebulized epinephrine
questions.ep: Drooling and toxic look = epiglottitis; never instrument the airway in an uncontrolled ER setting.

questions.stem: child with URTI for 3 days and now coming with stridor and drooling saliva (only these 2 symptoms), next step?

why.A: A chest X ray does not assess the upper airway and delays airway control; a lateral neck film (thumb sign) is also no longer recommended when obstruction is suspected.
why.B: An upper GI study is for swallowing or esophageal problems; it is irrelevant and dangerous in a child with impending airway obstruction.
why.D: CT of the upper airway requires lying the child flat and leaving a safe area, which can precipitate complete obstruction; airway first, imaging later.

questions.right: A child who after a URTI develops stridor with drooling has an upper airway obstruction (epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis or a supraglottic process) that can close suddenly. The priority is to secure the airway in a controlled setting: direct laryngoscopy in the operating room, with anaesthesia and ENT ready for intubation or tracheostomy. Do not upset the child or send them away for imaging.
questions.kc: Stridor + drooling = airway emergency; secure the airway in the OR. Epiglottitis: toxic, high fever, drooling, tripod sitting, muffled voice, no barking cough Keep child calm, on parent's lap; no throat exam, no IV, no imaging first Laryngoscopy and intubation in OR by the most experienced anaesthetist, ENT on standby Then IV ceftriaxone (H. influenzae type b, strep, staph) Croup: barking cough, stridor, no drooling, treat with dexamethasone and nebulised epinephrine
questions.ep: Barking cough with stridor but no drooling = croup, managed medically, not in the OR.

questions.stem: 4 months old infant is brought to the clinic due to cyanosis during crying and poor weight gain . and growth is below the 3rd centile admitted as case of Tracheomalacia . What is the next best step in management?

why.A: Inhaled corticosteroids treat airway inflammation (asthma); tracheomalacia is a structural collapse of the tracheal wall and does not respond to steroids.
why.B: Home oxygen may support hypoxemia but does not address the dynamic airway collapse causing cyanotic spells and growth failure.
why.D: Beta 2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle and can actually worsen malacia by reducing airway wall tone; they are not indicated.

questions.right: Most tracheomalacia is mild and improves as the trachea stiffens with growth, but this infant has features of severe disease: cyanosis during crying (airway collapse episodes) and failure to thrive below the 3rd centile . Severe or life threatening tracheomalacia needs surgical evaluation (bronchoscopy and procedures such as aortopexy or tracheostomy), so referral for surgical consultation is the next step.
questions.kc: Tracheomalacia: mild = conservative; severe = surgery. Presents with expiratory stridor or barking cough, worse with crying, feeding and infections Diagnosis: dynamic (flexible) bronchoscopy Mild: observation, most resolve by 1 to 2 years Severe (cyanotic or apneic spells, failure to thrive, recurrent pneumonia): aortopexy, tracheopexy, stenting or tracheostomy Often associated with tracheoesophageal fistula or vascular rings
questions.ep: Without cyanotic spells or growth failure, the answer would be reassurance and observation.

questions.stem: A 7 months old baby with recurrent admissions due to pneumonia and on examination he has bilateral monophasic expiratory wheezing . What is the definitive diagnostic method?

why.A: Chest X-ray is the first screening study for pneumonia or hyperinflation, but it cannot show dynamic airway collapse or define the lesion, so it is not definitive.
why.B: Spirometry needs a cooperative patient (usually age ≥5-6 years) and is the diagnostic test for asthma; it cannot be done in a 7-month-old.
why.C: Echocardiography is right when a cardiac cause of wheeze or recurrent chest infection is suspected (left-to-right shunt, heart failure); it does not visualize the airway lumen.

questions.right: An infant with recurrent admissions for pneumonia and a bilateral monophasic expiratory wheeze points to a fixed central airway problem (tracheomalacia or bronchomalacia, airway compression, retained foreign body) rather than asthma, whose wheeze is polyphonic and variable. A monophasic wheeze arises from one large narrowed airway. Flexible bronchoscopy directly visualizes the trachea and bronchi, shows dynamic collapse or obstruction, and allows lavage for recurrent infection, so it is the definitive test.
questions.kc: Recurrent pneumonia + fixed (monophasic) wheeze in an infant = look inside the airway: bronchoscopy. Polyphonic, variable wheeze responsive to bronchodilator: asthma or viral wheeze, clinical diagnosis Monophasic, fixed wheeze: central airway lesion (malacia, compression, foreign body) Tracheomalacia: bronchoscopy; laryngomalacia (inspiratory stridor): laryngoscopy Spirometry only from school age
questions.ep: Monophasic wheeze = one large airway narrowed; do not treat it as asthma and look for a structural cause.

questions.stem: 5 years-old diagnosed with pneumonia 4 days back and treated with oral antibiotics. Presented today with increased work of breathing and shortness of breath. Oxygen saturation on room air is 85% . On examination there is bilateral crepitation (HR: 160/m; RR: 60; ABG: PCO2: 70; Ph: 7.2; PO2: 60) What is the diagnosis?
questions.kc: How to decide: describe what the data prove, then the most specific valid label. Low PaO2 + normal/low CO2: hypoxemic (type 1) failure High CO2 + low pH: hypercapnic (type 2) acute failure ARDS: bilateral infiltrates, acute onset, non-cardiac, defined with oxygen/ventilatory support Septic shock: sepsis + circulatory dysfunction Most specific label the data support wins; check whether ARDS is among the options
questions.ep: Decide by the option list: if ARDS is offered and the stem gives bilateral infiltrates or oxygen support data, it is the more specific label; without it, the gas only proves respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A pediatric patient in the PICU on mechanical ventilation due to sepsis-related respiratory failure. What can we do regarding mechanical ventilation to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury ?

opts.A: Zero positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to prevent barotrauma
opts.B: Increase tidal volume with carbon dioxide reserve
opts.D: Low tidal volume to maintain permissive hypercapnia

why.A: Zero PEEP allows alveoli to collapse and reopen with each breath (atelectrauma), worsening injury; adequate PEEP is part of protective ventilation.
why.B: Larger tidal volumes overdistend the lung and cause volutrauma, the main mechanism of ventilator-induced injury.
why.C: Hyperventilation to wash out CO2 needs high volumes or rates, increasing lung stress, and the resulting hypocapnia reduces cerebral blood flow; it is only a brief rescue for raised intracranial pressure.

questions.right: Ventilator-induced lung injury comes mainly from overdistension (volutrauma) and repeated alveolar collapse. Lung-protective ventilation uses low tidal volumes and accepts a raised CO2 ("permissive hypercapnia") as long as pH is tolerable, which is exactly what this option describes for a septic child with respiratory failure in the PICU.
questions.kc: Lung-protective ventilation: small breaths, enough PEEP, tolerate CO2. Low tidal volume (per ideal body weight) Limit plateau/inspiratory pressure Adequate PEEP to keep alveoli open Permissive hypercapnia if pH acceptable Avoid both overdistension and collapse
questions.ep: Do not chase a normal PaCO2 on the ventilator; high CO2 is accepted to protect the lung.

questions.stem: 7 Years old complains of chronic clear thin nasal discharge and nasal itching , o/e there is periorbital dark swollen and pale turbinates mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: A nasal foreign body gives unilateral, foul smelling, purulent or blood stained discharge, usually in a younger child, not bilateral clear discharge with itching.
why.C: Nasal TB is rare and presents with crusting, ulceration or a granulomatous mass, often with systemic symptoms; it does not cause itching with pale turbinates.

questions.right: A 7 year old with chronic clear thin rhinorrhea and nasal itching , with dark swelling under the eyes ( allergic shiners ) and pale, boggy turbinates , has allergic rhinitis. These atopic signs are bilateral and chronic, which excludes a local cause.
questions.kc: Itchy nose + clear discharge + pale boggy turbinates + allergic shiners = allergic rhinitis. Other signs: allergic salute (transverse nasal crease), Dennie Morgan lines, sneezing bouts Associated with asthma and eczema (atopy) Treatment: allergen avoidance, intranasal corticosteroid (most effective), oral non sedating antihistamine Unilateral foul discharge in a child = foreign body
questions.ep: Unilateral, foul smelling discharge flips the answer to foreign body.

questions.stem: Child complaining of nasal purulent discharge, eye pain, periorbital swelling and severe headache. On examination there is frontal bone tenderness and restricted extraocular movements . What is the most appropriate?

opts.D: Refer to ear, nose, and throat (ENT)

why.A: Oral amoxicillin treats uncomplicated sinusitis or preseptal cellulitis; orbital involvement needs admission and IV antibiotics.
why.C: Reassurance is dangerous: complications include subperiosteal abscess, vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis and brain abscess.
why.D: ENT referral is needed, but the CT that defines the extent and the need for drainage is the decisive immediate step; the referral comes alongside it, not instead.

questions.right: Purulent nasal discharge with frontal bone tenderness means sinusitis, and the addition of eye pain, periorbital swelling, restricted extraocular movements and severe headache means it has spread into the orbit (orbital cellulitis), with possible intracranial extension. An urgent contrast enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses is the most appropriate step to define abscess and intracranial spread, alongside IV antibiotics and ENT/ophthalmology input.
questions.kc: Sinusitis + restricted eye movement, proptosis, pain on eye movement or reduced vision = orbital cellulitis: urgent contrast CT + IV antibiotics. Preseptal: lid swelling only, normal eye movements and vision, oral antibiotics Orbital: from ethmoid (commonest) or frontal sinusitis Frontal tenderness + severe headache: consider frontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess (Pott puffy tumour) or intracranial spread Surgery if abscess or no improvement in 24 to 48 h
questions.ep: Normal eye movements and vision with lid swelling only = preseptal cellulitis, treated with oral antibiotics, no CT.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with swelling, redness, and tenderness around the right eye. Cannot open eye due to swelling, the child has normal eye movements and vision . There is no proptosis or pain with eye movement . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Orbital cellulitis requires involvement behind the septum: proptosis, painful or restricted eye movement and reduced vision, all explicitly absent here.
why.C: Conjunctivitis causes a red eye with discharge and minimal lid swelling, not a tender, swollen lid that closes the eye.
why.D: An allergic reaction gives itchy, non tender, often bilateral lid edema without redness and tenderness of infection.

questions.right: Unilateral eyelid swelling, redness and tenderness so marked the eye cannot open, but with normal eye movements and vision , no proptosis and no pain on eye movement , is periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis. The infection is anterior to the orbital septum, so the globe and its muscles are spared.
questions.kc: The orbital septum divides preseptal from orbital cellulitis. Preseptal: lid swelling, erythema, normal eye movement, vision, no proptosis; oral antibiotics (amoxicillin clavulanate) Orbital: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, pain on movement, reduced vision, chemosis; admit, IV antibiotics, CT Causes: preseptal from local skin trauma or bites; orbital from sinusitis Hib vaccination reduced bacteremic cases
questions.ep: Any proptosis, restricted or painful eye movement or reduced vision flips the answer to orbital cellulitis.

questions.stem: A mother brings her 2-month -old infant because she is concerned that the baby may have a squint. What is the most appropriate assessment?

why.B: Cover test is the definitive test for manifest strabismus but needs fixation and cooperation; it is used in older infants and children rather than as the first assessment of a 2-month- old.
why.C: Referral to ophthalmology is right for an abnormal red reflex, a constant squint, or a squint persisting beyond about 4 months; referring before examining is premature (this was the examiner's own answer, counted as his presumed mistake).
why.D: Reassurance without examination is unsafe; intermittent misalignment is common before 4 months, but the eyes must be examined first to exclude leukocoria.

questions.right: The mother is only concerned that her 2-month-old may have a squint; the baby has not been shown to have one. The appropriate assessment is examination with the red reflex test, which is done at every well-baby visit, checks symmetry of the reflexes (an asymmetric reflex suggests misalignment) and excludes leukocoria from retinoblastoma or cataract, which can present as a squint. The compiler answers red reflex for both recall versions, especially this 'just concern' version.
questions.kc: Approach to a possible squint in an infant: Examine first: red reflex (symmetry, leukocoria) and corneal light reflex (Hirschberg) Intermittent squint < 4 months: common, follow up Constant squint, or any squint after about 4 months: refer Abnormal or white red reflex: urgent ophthalmology referral Cover test: older, cooperative child
questions.ep: Never refer or reassure a 'maybe squint' before examining: red reflex is the first assessment at 2 months.

questions.stem: 5y/o child came in pre school clinic just to check for pre school, you found the right ? eye misaligned what to do NEXT / initial?

opts.A: Refer to pediatric optha next day
opts.D: Gather Detailed History That Point Out history that point out for possible perinatal

why.A: Referral to pediatric ophthalmology is the definitive management of persistent strabismus in a child over 4 months, but it usually follows confirmation of the deviation; there is no emergency to justify 'next day'.
why.B: Glasses are prescribed by the ophthalmologist after cycloplegic refraction (e.g. accommodative esotropia); 'urgent glasses' without assessment is never correct.
why.C: The Hirschberg (corneal light reflex) test is the screening test for strabismus and is what many would do first to confirm the 'misaligned' eye; not the key in this source.
why.D: trauma ✓ correct

questions.right: This recall's key is D: the examinee (100 in Pediatrics) chose to begin with a detailed history , looking for a cause of the deviation such as birth or perinatal trauma (a cranial nerve palsy), onset, and family history, before acting. History is the logical opening step of any assessment at a screening visit. The compiler kept this as probably confirmed but hinted he disagreed.
questions.kc: Strabismus in a child: confirm, then refer. Hirschberg: symmetric centred reflex is normal; reflex displaced temporally = esotropia, nasally = exotropia Cover test: confirms manifest deviation Any strabismus beyond about 4 months: refer to pediatric ophthalmology (amblyopia risk) Acquired sudden strabismus: consider cranial nerve palsy or intracranial lesion Leukocoria with strabismus: urgent referral (retinoblastoma)
questions.ep: Most exams key the corneal light reflex for 'screen / confirm', and referral for 'management'; this recall's examiner chose history.

questions.stem: 5y/o child came in pre school clinic just to check for pre school, you found the right ? eye misaligned what to do NEXT / initial?

opts.A: Refer to pediatric optha next day
opts.D: detailed history that point out for possible perinatal trauma

why.A: Referral to pediatric ophthalmology is needed for persistent strabismus after 4 months, but in this key it comes after the initial assessment.
why.B: Glasses are prescribed after a refraction by ophthalmology (e.g. accommodative esotropia); "urgent glasses" without assessment is never the first step.
