why.C: The Hirschberg corneal light reflex test is the standard screening test to detect or confirm strabismus; in this recall the examiner chose it and it was counted as a mistake, because history taking was keyed as the initial step.

questions.right: This recall's key is D, following the compiler's reasoning that the lead-in asks for the NEXT / initial step in a well 5-year-old found to have a misaligned eye: the evaluation starts with a detailed history (onset, birth and perinatal history including trauma, family history, visual symptoms) before further testing or referral. The compiler records this answer as probably confirmed by other examinees.
questions.kc: Strabismus in a child. Intermittent deviation up to 4 months can be normal Screening: Hirschberg (corneal light reflex), cover test Any persistent strabismus: refer to pediatric ophthalmology (amblyopia risk) New strabismus in an older child: think nerve palsy, mass, trauma
questions.ep: Two versions of this recall exist; both are keyed to history taking, while a "screening method" question is keyed to Hirschberg.

questions.stem: toddler pt came with SOB, and Palpitations upon exercise, history Reveals URTI 3 days ago , examination reveals gallop rhythm , vitals were provided, high HR, what clue you into diagnosis?

why.A: History of URTI is non-specific: it precedes croup, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, asthma attacks and myocarditis alike.
why.B: Tachypnoea occurs in any respiratory or cardiac illness, fever or anxiety; it does not localise the problem to the heart.
why.C: Tachycardia is non-specific (fever, dehydration, pain, anxiety, anaemia); persistent tachycardia out of proportion to fever raises suspicion but is less specific than a gallop.

questions.right: A toddler with dyspnoea and palpitations on exertion a few days after a viral URTI suggests viral myocarditis with heart failure. Among the findings, the gallop rhythm (S3) is the specific clue to the heart: it reflects a failing, volume-overloaded ventricle and points the diagnosis to a cardiac cause (myocarditis/cardiomyopathy).
questions.kc: Viral myocarditis in children: Follows a viral illness (enterovirus/coxsackie B, adenovirus) Heart failure signs: gallop, tachycardia out of proportion, hepatomegaly, poor perfusion ECG: low voltage, ST/T changes, arrhythmia; troponin raised Echo: reduced function Supportive heart failure care; IVIG is sometimes used
questions.ep: When the question asks which finding points to the diagnosis, pick the most specific sign (gallop = heart), not the common ones.

questions.stem: 8 yo boy, in his last visit to OPD he was found to have High blood pressure and after subsequent readings blood pressure was normal . BP 13x/90, BMI 27 he has family history of HTN. What is the best way to prevent HTN in this kid?

why.B: A sedentary lifestyle is itself a risk factor for obesity and hypertension; the preventive advice is the opposite, increased physical activity.
why.C: Correct BP measurement (proper cuff size, repeated readings) is needed to diagnose or exclude hypertension, but it does not prevent the disease; here repeat readings were already normal.

questions.right: The compiler stresses this is about prevention : the child had one high reading that normalised on repeat, so he does not have hypertension yet. His modifiable risk factor is excess weight ( BMI 27 at 8 years is in the obese range) on top of a family history of HTN , so weight loss through diet and activity is the best way to prevent future hypertension.
questions.kc: Pediatric HTN prevention = treat modifiable risk factors, mainly obesity. Elevated reading must be confirmed on repeated visits with the correct cuff size before labelling HTN Obese child + family history = high risk of primary HTN First step for elevated BP or stage 1 HTN: lifestyle (weight reduction, DASH style diet, less salt, regular exercise) Drugs only if lifestyle fails or target organ damage or stage 2
questions.ep: Read the lead in: if asked how to confirm the diagnosis, proper repeated measurement wins; if asked how to prevent, weight loss wins.

questions.stem: Intussusception case with red currant jelly stool . Where is the pathologic location?

why.A: Ileoileal intussusception is less common; it tends to be transient or caused by a lead point (e.g. Meckel's diverticulum, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, polyp).
why.B: Jejunoileal intussusception is rare and not the classic paediatric pattern.
why.D: Jejunojejunal intussusception is uncommon, mostly seen with a lead point or transient in adults, not the typical currant jelly case.

questions.right: Classic childhood intussusception with red currant jelly stool is most often ileocolic : the terminal ileum telescopes into the caecum and colon at the ileocaecal valve, usually around hypertrophied Peyer's patches. This produces the sausage-shaped mass and the target sign on ultrasound.
questions.kc: Intussusception: ileocolic, 6 months to 3 years. Clues: colicky crying with legs drawn up, vomiting, sausage mass, currant jelly stool Diagnosis: ultrasound (target or doughnut sign) Treatment: resuscitate, then air or saline enema reduction Surgery: peritonitis, perforation, or failed enema
questions.ep: Typical idiopathic paediatric intussusception = ileocolic; small bowel types suggest a lead point.

questions.stem: Child presenting with vomiting crying and red currant jelly stool , what is the origin of this pathology?

why.A: Ileoileal intussusception is uncommon and is typically seen with a pathological lead point or after surgery, not as the classic idiopathic childhood type.
why.B: Ileojejunal is not a recognized common pattern; telescoping normally runs in the direction of peristalsis (proximal into distal).
why.C: Jejunojejunal intussusception is rare in children and is more associated with lead points such as polyps (e.g. Peutz-Jeghers) or feeding tubes.

questions.right: "Vomiting, crying and red currant jelly stool" in a child is intussusception. The most common site in children is where the terminal ileum telescopes into the cecum and colon (ileocolic/ileocecal), usually from a lead point of hypertrophied Peyer patches after a viral illness. So the origin is ileocecal.
questions.kc: Intussusception: most common cause of bowel obstruction from about 6 months to 3 years. Site: ileocolic (ileocecal), the vast majority Triad: colicky pain, vomiting, red currant jelly stool Sausage-shaped mass; empty right lower quadrant Diagnosis: ultrasound (target sign) Treatment: air or contrast enema reduction; surgery if peritonitis or perforation
questions.ep: Red currant jelly stool = late sign of bowel ischemia; its absence does not exclude intussusception.

questions.stem: 5-day old Greenish vomit , mildly tender abdomen irritable child. What is the most diagnostic test

why.A: Endoscopy has no role in diagnosing malrotation in a neonate; it cannot show the bowel's position or rotation.
why.C: Lower GI contrast study (enema) can show an abnormally placed caecum but is less reliable; it is the test for distal obstruction such as Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus.
why.D: Abdominal X-ray is the usual initial film (may show a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with little distal gas, or be completely normal), but a normal film never excludes volvulus, so it is not the most diagnostic.

questions.right: A 5-day-old with green (bilious) vomiting has malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise, a surgical emergency. The lead-in asks for the most diagnostic test: an upper GI contrast study shows the abnormal duodenojejunal flexure position or a corkscrew or beak sign.
questions.kc: Neonate with bilious vomiting = malrotation/volvulus until proven otherwise. Most diagnostic: upper GI contrast study Initial: abdominal X-ray (may be normal) Unstable or peritonitis: straight to laparotomy (Ladd procedure) Non-bilious projectile vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks: pyloric stenosis, ultrasound
questions.ep: "Initial" test = X-ray; "most diagnostic" for bilious vomiting = upper GI contrast.

questions.stem: Pyloric Stenosis , INITIAL :

why.B: IV normal saline is the correct resuscitation fluid and is often the keyed answer when NPO is not offered, but it follows stopping oral feeds when "initial" is asked.

questions.right: The lead-in asks for the "INITIAL" step. In infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis the infant keeps vomiting with every feed, so feeding is stopped (NPO) first; then IV fluids correct the dehydration and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis before pyloromyotomy. The compiler stresses that you cannot resuscitate while the mother is still feeding the baby.
questions.kc: Pyloric stenosis: Male infant about 2-8 weeks, non-bilious projectile vomiting Hungry after vomiting, palpable olive, visible peristalsis Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis Diagnosis: ultrasound NPO, IV fluids (normal saline, add potassium once passing urine), then pyloromyotomy Surgery only after electrolytes are corrected
questions.ep: Pyloromyotomy is never the emergency step; correct the alkalosis first.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with recurrent abdominal pain for 2 weeks , decreased appetite, and a tender mass in the RLQ . Vitals: BP 90/60, HR 100, Temp 37.5°C. WBC is 19.52. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

why.A: Ultrasound is first line for suspected uncomplicated appendicitis in children and spares radiation, but it is less definitive for an established mass or abscess.
why.B: Erect abdominal X-ray is nonspecific (may show an appendicolith or free air) and cannot confirm an abscess or phlegmon.
why.D: Barium enema is obsolete for appendicitis and risky if there is perforation or abscess; it is used for other conditions such as intussusception.

questions.right: Two weeks of RLQ pain with a tender RLQ mass , low-grade fever and WBC 19.5 points to complicated appendicitis (appendicular abscess or phlegmon). The lead-in asks which test will confirm the diagnosis: CT best defines a mass, abscess or perforation and is used for complicated appendicitis regardless of age.
questions.kc: Appendicitis imaging depends on patient and complication. Uncomplicated, child or pregnant: ultrasound Non-pregnant adult: CT (best sensitivity) RLQ mass after days to weeks (abscess or phlegmon): CT at any age Abscess: drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
questions.ep: Child with simple RLQ pain = US; child with RLQ MASS after weeks = CT.

questions.stem: A child was riding a bicycle, and then he sustained a handlebar injury , he presented to the ER with abdominal pain and tenderness , And Nausea & Vomiting , they mentioned that the abdominal pain is in the upper abdomen , What's Most Likely Injured Abdominal Organ

why.A: The spleen is the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma overall, especially with left upper quadrant blows or left lower rib fractures and signs of bleeding; the handlebar mechanism specifically points to the pancreas.
why.B: Liver injury follows right upper quadrant or right lower rib trauma and presents with hemorrhage; it is not the signature handlebar injury.
why.D: Bladder injury follows lower abdominal or pelvic trauma (pelvic fracture, full bladder) and presents with hematuria or inability to void, not upper abdominal pain.

questions.right: A handlebar injury in a child delivers a focused blow to the epigastrium that crushes the pancreas (and duodenum) against the vertebral column. Upper abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting fits pancreatic injury, which is the classic answer for handlebar trauma; the compiler notes this was confirmed by a full-score examinee in Pediatrics.
questions.kc: Mechanism to organ: Handlebar injury: pancreas (and duodenal hematoma) Lap seat belt sign: bowel (duodenum), Chance fracture, bladder Left lower rib fractures: spleen Right lower rib fractures: liver Pelvic fracture: bladder, posterior urethra Pancreatic injury imaging: CT with contrast; amylase may be normal early
questions.ep: If the question asks the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma without a handlebar mechanism, choose spleen.

questions.stem: 3 years child brought by parents telling you that he has been spotting blood per rectum . Doctor tell them that it is common and preventable problem. What is the likely diagnosis?

why.A: Juvenile polyp is the classic cause of PAINLESS rectal bleeding in children aged 2 to 5, but it is less common than fissure and not preventable.
why.C: Hemorrhoids are extremely rare in young children; think of portal hypertension if seen.
why.D: Placeholder option, not a diagnosis.

questions.right: In a 3 year old with spotting of blood per rectum , the commonest cause is an anal fissure , usually from passing hard stool in constipation. The lead in clues 'common' and 'preventable' fit exactly: fissures are frequent in toddlers and are prevented by treating constipation (fluids, fibre, stool softeners).
questions.kc: Rectal bleeding in children by clue. Hard stool, pain on defecation, streaks of blood: anal fissure (most common) Painless bright red bleeding, age 2 to 5: juvenile polyp Painless massive bleeding, under 2 years: Meckel diverticulum Red currant jelly stool with colicky pain: intussusception Bloody diarrhea with fever: infectious colitis
questions.ep: 'Common and preventable' = fissure (prevent constipation); 'painless and recurrent' would push you to polyp.

questions.stem: 9 year old child presents with 2 months history of epigastric pain that wakes him up at night , mother mentioned a hx of PUD, what is the confirmatory test?

why.A: CBC may show iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss, but it is nonspecific and cannot confirm an ulcer.
why.B: Abdominal ultrasound looks for biliary, pancreatic or solid organ disease and cannot see mucosal ulcers; it is useful when gallstones or another structural cause is suspected.
why.D: Stool antigen is a good noninvasive test for H. pylori infection and to confirm eradication, but a positive result does not prove an ulcer, and in children guidelines favour diagnosing H. pylori at endoscopy rather than by a noninvasive test alone.

questions.right: Epigastric pain for 2 months that "wakes him up at night" with a family history of PUD points to peptic ulcer disease, usually H. pylori related in children. The lead-in asks for the "confirmatory test": upper GI endoscopy is the gold standard because it visualizes the ulcer directly, and biopsy allows histology and H. pylori testing (rapid urease, culture and sensitivity).
questions.kc: Confirming PUD = upper GI endoscopy with biopsy. Night pain relieved by food: duodenal ulcer Pain worse after meals: gastric ulcer H. pylori noninvasive tests: urea breath test, stool antigen (screening and post-eradication check) Children: H. pylori is diagnosed by endoscopic biopsy, not by noninvasive tests alone Barium study only if endoscopy unavailable
questions.ep: "Confirmatory" or "gold standard" for an ulcer is endoscopy; a stool antigen only confirms the bug.

questions.stem: A 14 year old patient with ulcerative colitis failed to respond to many medical therapies. The patient has fulminant disease complicated by toxic megacolon . Which of the following is the most appropriate URGENT treatment?

why.B: Methotrexate is a slow-acting steroid-sparing agent (more for Crohn's maintenance); it has no role in an acute toxic megacolon.
why.C: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are part of the supportive bundle (with IV steroids, bowel rest, fluids) in early toxic megacolon, but they do not treat a colon that has failed medical therapy.
why.D: TPN/bowel rest is supportive nutrition only; it does not prevent perforation.

questions.right: The child has fulminant UC complicated by toxic megacolon and has "failed to respond to many medical therapies" . Toxic megacolon carries a high risk of perforation, and once medical rescue has failed the definitive, urgent treatment is (subtotal) colectomy with end ileostomy.
questions.kc: Toxic megacolon: colon dilated (>6 cm on X-ray) plus systemic toxicity. Initial: NPO, IV fluids, IV steroids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, stop opioids/anticholinergics No improvement in 24 to 72 h, or failed medical therapy: colectomy Perforation, hemorrhage, worsening dilatation: emergency colectomy Dilatation >10 cm: high perforation risk
questions.ep: A first presentation of toxic megacolon gets medical rescue first; failed medical therapy, as here, means surgery.

questions.stem: A four-year-old child presented to the pediatric ER with a four-day history of dark urine and jaundice preceded by diarrhea , nausea, and vomiting. She’s attending a daycare school where multiple episodes with kids have been reported. ALT was 600. AST was 500 high. What is the most indicated management?

why.A: Liver transplant is reserved for fulminant hepatic failure (encephalopathy, severe coagulopathy); transaminases of a few hundred with a stable child do not justify it.
why.C: Acyclovir treats HSV/VZV infections, including rare HSV hepatitis in neonates or immunocompromised hosts; it has no activity against hepatitis A.
why.D: Ribavirin was used for hepatitis C (with interferon) and some other viral infections (e.g. RSV, hepatitis E in chronic cases); not hepatitis A.

questions.right: A 4-year-old in daycare with an outbreak , a GI prodrome ( diarrhea, nausea, vomiting ) then jaundice and dark urine , with ALT 600 and AST 500, is acute hepatitis A (fecal-oral spread). Hepatitis A is self-limiting in children and has no specific antiviral, so management is supportive: rest, hydration and monitoring for liver failure (INR, encephalopathy).
questions.kc: Hepatitis A: picornavirus, fecal-oral, daycare/food outbreaks. Children often mild or anicteric; adults more jaundice Diagnosis: anti-HAV IgM Treatment: supportive Contacts: hepatitis A vaccine (or immunoglobulin in selected groups) within 2 weeks Never chronic
questions.ep: Rising INR or encephalopathy turns supportive care into referral for transplant evaluation.

questions.stem: 10 year old girl with rash, fatigue, joint pain. She has direct hyperbilirubinemia , elevated ALT (written like this without numbers) and IgG with positive autoantibodies . What is the treatment?

why.A: Exchange transfusion is for severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (risk of kernicterus); this is a conjugated, hepatitic picture in an older child.
why.C: Phototherapy only works on unconjugated bilirubin in neonates; it has no role in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia or hepatitis.
why.D: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections such as cholangitis or liver abscess, which would present with fever and sepsis, not autoantibodies and high IgG.

questions.right: A 10-year-old girl with fatigue, arthralgia, rash, raised ALT and jaundice plus high IgG and positive autoantibodies (ANA/anti-smooth muscle or anti-LKM1) has autoimmune hepatitis. Treatment is immunosuppression: corticosteroids (prednisolone) to induce remission, with azathioprine added as a steroid-sparing maintenance agent.
questions.kc: Autoimmune hepatitis: Typically female, with other autoimmune features (arthralgia, rash) Raised ALT/AST, high IgG Type 1: ANA, anti-smooth muscle; type 2 (children): anti-LKM1 Liver biopsy: interface hepatitis Treatment: steroids + azathioprine; transplant if liver failure
questions.ep: Hepatitis + high IgG + autoantibodies in a girl = autoimmune hepatitis: steroids plus azathioprine.

questions.stem: developed large neck swelling on the left side. On exam it is large 10 cm in size, US FNA showed clear lymphatic fluid . What is the appropriate management?

why.B: Observation may be reasonable for a small asymptomatic lesion, but a 10 cm mass threatens the airway and is unlikely to regress spontaneously.
why.C: Chemotherapy treats malignancy such as lymphoma; a lymphatic malformation is a benign developmental lesion.
why.D: Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation and would harm developing tissues in a child.

questions.right: A large (10 cm) lateral neck swelling whose aspirate is clear lymphatic fluid is a cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation). It does not respond to chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and a lesion this size risks airway compression, infection and haemorrhage, so it needs active treatment; among the options, surgical excision is the appropriate management.
questions.kc: Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation): benign, transilluminant, posterior triangle, clear lymph on aspiration. Small, asymptomatic: observe Large or symptomatic: surgical excision or sclerotherapy (macrocystic lesions) Associations: Turner syndrome, trisomies (prenatal) Complications: airway compression, infection, bleeding into the cyst
questions.ep: Clear lymph on FNA = lymphatic malformation, never chemo or radiotherapy.

questions.stem: 15 months old boy with empty right hemiscrotum. On examination confirmed right empty hemiscrotum and groin but the left side is normal. What to do?

why.A: Observation is only acceptable until about 6 months of age; waiting to 3 years raises the risk of infertility and malignancy and delays orchiopexy, which should be done by about 18 months.
why.B: The left testis is normal; orchiopexy is done on the undescended (right) side, and the side to be fixed has not even been located yet.
why.C: Exploratory laparotomy is too invasive for localisation; laparoscopy finds an intra- abdominal testis with far less morbidity.

questions.right: A 15 month old with an empty right hemiscrotum that is also empty in the groin on exam has a non-palpable undescended testis. Spontaneous descent will not happen after about 6 months, and the testis may be intra-abdominal or absent, so diagnostic laparoscopy is the investigation and treatment approach of choice: it localises the testis and allows orchiopexy in the same session.
questions.kc: Undescended testis: palpable vs non-palpable decides the approach. Wait for spontaneous descent until about 6 months (corrected age) Palpable: inguinal orchiopexy, ideally 6 to 18 months Non-palpable unilateral: diagnostic laparoscopy, then orchiopexy (one or two stage) or removal of a nubbin Bilateral non-palpable: rule out disorders of sex development (karyotype, hormones) first Imaging (US) does not change management in non-palpable testis
questions.ep: Bilateral non-palpable testes in a phenotypic boy: think congenital adrenal hyperplasia and do karyotype first, not laparoscopy.

questions.stem: A preschool child presents for his routine preschool-entry examination (see lab results). (Labs: Hb 90 [112-165]; RDW 20 [11.5-16%]; Platelets 490 x10^9/L [150- 400]; MCV 68 fL [80-95]; MCH 26 pg [28-33]; MCHC 241 g/L [260-340]; Reticulocyte 1.1% [0.2-1.2]; WBC 7.5 x10^9/L [4.5-10.5]; RBC 5 x10^12/L [4.6- 4.8]) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Aplastic anaemia: pancytopenia (low WBC and platelets) with normocytic or macrocytic cells; here WBC is normal and platelets are high.
why.B: Thalassaemia minor: microcytosis with a normal RDW and a high RBC count (Mentzer index under 13), often with mild or no anaemia; the high RDW and thrombocytosis here favour iron deficiency.
why.D: Hereditary spherocytosis: haemolysis with raised reticulocytes, high MCHC, jaundice and splenomegaly; here MCHC is low and reticulocytes normal.

questions.right: A preschool child with Hb 90 and MCV 68 has a microcytic hypochromic anaemia. The high RDW (20%) shows variable cell sizes, platelets 490 is a reactive thrombocytosis typical of iron deficiency, and reticulocytes are not raised; the compiler notes that RBC 5 is not high. Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) is about 13.6, above 13, favouring iron deficiency.
questions.kc: Microcytic anaemia: IDA vs thalassaemia trait: IDA: high RDW, low/normal RBC, reactive thrombocytosis, Mentzer > 13, low ferritin Thal trait: normal RDW, high RBC, Mentzer < 13, normal ferritin, raised HbA2 (beta) Anaemia of chronic disease: high ferritin, chronic illness
questions.ep: High RDW + high platelets in a microcytic child = iron deficiency; normal RDW + high RBC = thalassaemia trait.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the Primary Clinic because her mother noticed she is pale. She has a history of drinking cow's milk and biscuit daily and didn't eat red meat. Labs: low hbg, low mcv, low ferritin , a slight increase in reticulocyte count around 1.8 (normal 1.2). What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Hereditary spherocytosis is a hemolytic anemia: high retics, jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes and a normal or high MCHC, with normal ferritin.
why.C: Anemia of chronic disease needs a chronic inflammatory illness and shows normal or high ferritin, not low.
why.D: This option was not recalled; the recaller only remembers it was not thalassemia. Thalassemia trait would give microcytosis with normal ferritin and raised HbA2.

questions.right: A 2-year-old drinking a lot of cow's milk with no red meat has a classic dietary cause of iron deficiency (cow's milk is iron-poor and can cause occult intestinal blood loss). Labs confirm it: low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin . Low ferritin is the specific marker of depleted iron stores; the slight reticulocyte rise does not change this and fits a mild response or early iron intake.
questions.kc: Microcytic anemia: ferritin decides. Low ferritin: iron deficiency Normal or high ferritin + chronic illness: anemia of chronic disease Normal ferritin, raised HbA2, normal RDW: beta thalassemia trait Toddler + excess cow's milk + low meat intake: iron deficiency
questions.ep: Low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency; a mildly raised reticulocyte count should not push you toward hemolysis.

questions.stem: child pale eat non-food such as soil, chalk and labs showed microcytic and ferritin low ?

why.A: Zinc deficiency can cause pica, but it presents with dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea and poor growth and does not lower ferritin.
why.B: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets (bowed legs, wide wrists, hypocalcemia), not microcytic anemia with low ferritin.
why.C: Lead poisoning also causes pica and microcytic anemia, but ferritin is usually normal (unless iron deficiency coexists) and you expect basophilic stippling, abdominal pain or neurological signs and a raised blood lead level.

questions.right: Eating non-food items such as soil and chalk is pica , a well-known feature of iron deficiency. The labs ( microcytic anemia with low ferritin ) confirm depleted iron stores, so the picture is pica associated with iron deficiency anemia, treated with oral iron.
questions.kc: Pica + microcytic anemia: check ferritin. Low ferritin: iron deficiency (most common) Normal ferritin + basophilic stippling + abdominal pain or behavior change: lead poisoning Paint chips in an old house: think lead Treatment of IDA: oral iron
questions.ep: Lead poisoning shares pica and microcytosis; low ferritin is what keeps the answer on iron deficiency.

questions.stem: In the labs: +ve Direct Coombs test +ve indirect Coombs tes. Low Hg High Retics . What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Hereditary spherocytosis is a hemolytic anemia but is Coombs negative; diagnose with osmotic fragility or EMA binding.
why.C: Fanconi anemia is a bone marrow failure syndrome with low reticulocytes, pancytopenia, and skeletal (thumb, radius) anomalies.
why.D: G6PD deficiency causes Coombs-negative oxidative hemolysis after triggers (fava beans, drugs, infection) with bite cells and Heinz bodies.

questions.right: Low Hb with high reticulocytes means hemolysis, and a positive direct Coombs test shows antibody or complement coating the red cells, which defines immune (autoimmune) hemolytic anemia . A positive indirect Coombs test adds free antibody in the serum. No other listed cause is Coombs positive.
questions.kc: Hemolysis + Coombs result. DAT positive: autoimmune (warm IgG or cold IgM) or alloimmune hemolysis DAT negative + spherocytes + family history: hereditary spherocytosis DAT negative + trigger + bite cells: G6PD deficiency Low retics + pancytopenia: marrow failure (Fanconi, aplastic)
questions.ep: Spherocytes occur in both hereditary spherocytosis and warm AIHA; the Coombs test separates them.

questions.stem: Which of the following leukemia is the most common in pediatric age group?

why.A: Acute myeloid leukaemia is the second most common childhood leukaemia; it predominates in adults.
why.B: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is rare in children and occurs mainly in middle-aged adults.
why.D: Acute non-lymphoblastic leukaemia is another name for AML, so it is less common than ALL in children.

questions.right: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the most common childhood cancer and accounts for most childhood leukaemias (around three quarters), with a peak at 2 to 5 years.
questions.kc: Leukaemia by age: Children: ALL most common (peak 2 to 5 years) Adults: AML most common acute leukaemia Older adults: CLL most common overall CML: middle age, Philadelphia chromosome Down syndrome: higher risk of both ALL and AML (AMKL)
questions.ep: Acute non-lymphoblastic = AML; do not be misled by the alternative name.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the clinic with severe gram-positive bacterial pneumonia, was referred to the hospital by the family physician. This is his third infection in 4 months . He has 2 healthy sisters aged 3 and 5 years. The family lost a boy at 10 months of age to bacterial pneumonia 6 years ago. The family doctor has sent along some blood test results that shows low all classes of serum immunoglobulin levels, few B cells , but normal numbers and functioning of T cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Transient hypogammaglobulinaemia of infancy: low IgG with normal B cell numbers, milder infections, no family pattern, and recovery by early childhood.
why.B: Common variable immunodeficiency: low immunoglobulins with normal B cell numbers that fail to become plasma cells; usually presents in adolescence or adulthood and affects both sexes.
why.C: CD40 (ligand) defect: hyper-IgM syndrome with normal or high IgM and low IgG/IgA plus opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis; here all classes are low.

questions.right: Recurrent severe bacterial infections in a boy starting after maternal antibodies wane, a brother who died of pneumonia and healthy sisters suggest X-linked inheritance. All immunoglobulin classes low with very few B cells but normal T cells is X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinaemia, a BTK defect that blocks B cell maturation in the marrow.
questions.kc: Humoral immunodeficiencies: Bruton XLA: boys, after 6 months, absent B cells, all Ig low; IVIG CVID: older onset, normal B cells, low Ig Hyper-IgM (CD40L): high IgM, low IgG/IgA, PCP Selective IgA: mild, anaphylaxis to blood products Transient hypogammaglobulinaemia: normal B cells, self-limiting
questions.ep: Low all Ig + ABSENT B cells in a boy = Bruton; low Ig with NORMAL B cells = CVID or transient.

questions.stem: child with high creatinine and blood urea nitrogen below 10 percentile height weight. glomerular filtration 28 what degree renal disease?

why.A: Stage 2: GFR 60 to 89 with evidence of kidney damage.
why.B: Stage 3: GFR 30 to 59 (3a 45 to 59, 3b 30 to 44); 28 is just below this band.
why.D: Stage 5 (kidney failure): GFR below 15 or on dialysis.

questions.right: Chronic kidney disease is staged by GFR, and a GFR of 28 mL/min/1.73 m² falls in the 15 to 29 band, which is stage 4 (severe reduction). The growth failure (below the 10th percentile) is a typical consequence of CKD in children but does not change the stage.
questions.kc: CKD stages by GFR (mL/min/1.73 m²): G1: ≥90 with kidney damage G2: 60 to 89 G3a: 45 to 59; G3b: 30 to 44 G4: 15 to 29 G5: <15 or dialysis
questions.ep: Stage 4 is 15 to 29: 28 is stage 4, not 3.

questions.stem: A 2-month -old baby presented with fever, vomiting , lethargy, and poor oral intake for 2 days. Urine dipstick shows nitrites, leukocytes. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.B: Send to hospital and start IV antibiotics

why.A: Oral antibiotics are suitable for a well child older than 3 months who is tolerating oral fluids; this infant is young, lethargic and vomiting.
why.C: Option not recalled; outpatient observation or urine culture alone would be unsafe in a febrile, lethargic 2-month-old.
why.D: Option not recalled; any option delaying IV antibiotics is wrong in this age group.

questions.right: A 2-month-old with fever and a positive dipstick ( nitrites, leukocytes ) has a febrile UTI, likely pyelonephritis, and is also lethargic with vomiting and poor oral intake . Infants under 3 months with febrile UTI, and any child who is ill-looking or cannot tolerate oral fluids, need admission and IV antibiotics after urine (and blood) culture.
questions.kc: Febrile UTI: route of antibiotics depends on age and illness. Under 3 months: admit, IV antibiotics, cultures Toxic, vomiting, dehydrated: IV antibiotics Older than 3 months and well: oral antibiotics Confirm with catheter or suprapubic urine culture
questions.ep: Even a well-looking febrile infant under 3 months with a positive urine dip goes in for IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: 5 year old girl presented with fever and painful urination (dysuria) . Most appropriate management?

why.B: Ciprofloxacin is not first line in children (concern for cartilage effects) and IV therapy is not needed in a well child.
why.C: IM or IV ceftriaxone is for young infants, toxic or vomiting children, or those unable to take oral treatment.
why.D: Sodium bicarbonate (urine alkalinization) treats symptoms at most; it does not treat the infection.

questions.right: A 5-year-old with fever and dysuria has a UTI. She is beyond infancy and nothing in the stem suggests she is toxic, vomiting or unable to take oral medication, so oral antibiotics are appropriate; oral therapy is as effective as IV in well children. Oral amoxicillin is the listed oral option and is keyed as the answer.
questions.kc: Pediatric UTI: route by age and severity. Well child, tolerating oral: oral antibiotic (cefixime, amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, TMP-SMX) Young infant, toxic, vomiting, or not tolerating oral: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime Fluoroquinolones: avoid as routine first line in children
questions.ep: Fever alone does not mandate IV antibiotics in a child; toxicity, vomiting or young infancy does. Local E. coli resistance to amoxicillin often favours a cephalosporin in practice.

questions.stem: 17-Year-Old Female With Frequent Fainting And Fall, Last Time While Talking To Her Father Felt Her Legs Are Weak And Fell Down , Lost Consciousness, Then Regained Level Of Consciousness. What Is The Type Of Seizure?

why.B: Myoclonic seizures are brief, shock-like jerks of the limbs (often on waking, as in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy) with preserved consciousness; no jerks are described.
why.C: Absence seizures are brief staring spells with blinking in children, without loss of tone or falling.
why.D: Tonic-clonic seizures have stiffening then rhythmic jerking, often tongue biting, incontinence and post-ictal confusion, none of which is described.

questions.right: The story is of frequent falls where she suddenly felt her legs are weak and fell down , with brief loss of awareness then recovery, and no stiffening or jerking described. A sudden loss of postural tone causing a drop attack is the definition of an atonic seizure.
questions.kc: Seizure type by the motor feature. Loss of tone, drop attack: atonic Stiffening only: tonic Brief jerks, aware: myoclonic Staring, blinking, seconds, no fall: absence Stiff then jerking, post-ictal state: tonic-clonic
questions.ep: Brief jerks on waking in a teenager point to myoclonic seizures (juvenile myoclonic epilepsy), not atonic.

questions.stem: A case of simple febrile seizures Stem: Regarding febrile convulsions in children, which of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: There is 2% chance to develop epilepsy
opts.B: Anti epileptic medication daily will reduce the risk
opts.C: Antipyretic during fever will reduce the risk of future epilepsy
opts.D: The child will have intellectual disability

why.B: Daily antiepileptic drugs can reduce recurrence but their side effects outweigh benefit, and they do not reduce the risk of later epilepsy; not recommended for simple febrile seizures.
why.C: Antipyretics improve comfort but do not prevent febrile seizure recurrence or future epilepsy.
why.D: Simple febrile seizures do not cause intellectual disability or long-term neurological sequelae.

questions.right: For simple febrile seizures the risk of later epilepsy is only slightly higher than the general population, quoted at around 1 to 2%. The prognosis is excellent, which is why parents are reassured and no long-term treatment is given.
questions.kc: Febrile seizure: 6 months to 5 years with fever, no CNS infection. Simple: generalized, <15 min, once in 24 h Complex: focal, >15 min, or recurrent within 24 h (higher epilepsy risk) Recurrence risk about one third, higher if first seizure is under 1 year Management: treat the cause, antipyretic for comfort, reassure Prolonged seizure: rescue benzodiazepine
questions.ep: Complex features (focal, prolonged, repeated) or abnormal development raise the epilepsy risk above the simple-seizure figure.

questions.stem: 10 years old girl come to ER she has abnormal movement when sleeping in her face and limbs she has history of seizure other wise she is normal EEG showed frontotemporal spike What's the diagnosis?

why.A: Encephalitis presents acutely with fever, altered consciousness and focal signs; this child is otherwise normal.
why.B: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: adolescents with morning myoclonic jerks on waking, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and generalized polyspike-wave on EEG.
why.C: Lennox-Gastaut: multiple seizure types, intellectual disability and slow (<2.5 Hz) spike- wave on EEG, starting in early childhood; this child is normal.

questions.right: A school-age child (10 years) with nocturnal (sleep-related) focal seizures of the face and limbs , otherwise normal development, and centrotemporal ("frontotemporal") spikes on EEG has benign rolandic epilepsy (self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes). It typically remits by adolescence.
questions.kc: Childhood epilepsy syndromes by EEG. Rolandic: centrotemporal spikes, nocturnal facial seizures, normal child Absence: 3 Hz generalized spike-wave, staring spells JME: polyspike- wave, morning jerks, teenager Infantile spasms: hypsarrhythmia Lennox-Gastaut: slow spike-wave, multiple seizure types, delay
questions.ep: Seizures in sleep + face involvement + normal child + centrotemporal spikes = rolandic.

questions.stem: A Child with a typical meningitis case with neck rigidity, etc. (Labs: serum glucose 5; CSF glucose 5 ; CSF protein slightly high; CSF lymphocytes 80% ) What is the treatment?

why.A: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis: low CSF glucose (ratio <0.4), high protein and neutrophil predominance, which are absent here.
why.C: Dexamethasone is an adjunct to antibiotics in bacterial meningitis (reduces hearing loss, e.g. H. influenzae, pneumococcus); it is not a treatment for viral meningitis.
why.D: Option not recalled (recaller states it was not anti-TB or antifungal therapy, which would fit lymphocytes with LOW CSF glucose).

questions.right: The CSF shows glucose 5 with serum glucose 5 (normal ratio), protein only slightly high and 80% lymphocytes : a viral (aseptic) picture. Among the options, IV acyclovir is the treatment because HSV meningoencephalitis must be covered empirically when the CSF looks viral, as it is the treatable and dangerous viral cause.
questions.kc: CSF pattern decides the drug. Bacterial: low glucose, high protein, neutrophils: ceftriaxone + vancomycin ± dexamethasone Viral: normal glucose, normal/mildly high protein, lymphocytes: supportive, IV acyclovir if HSV possible TB: low glucose, high protein, lymphocytes: anti-TB therapy Fungal (cryptococcus): low glucose, lymphocytes, India ink
questions.ep: Lymphocytes with LOW glucose is TB or fungal, not viral; only normal glucose with lymphocytes points to acyclovir.

questions.stem: Meningitis Case About Child Got All Signs Of Meningitis: Neck Stiffness, Photophobia, Altered Consciousness After URTI . What Would You See In Lumbar Puncture?

opts.A: Elevated Leukocytes, Predominant Neutrophils, High Protein, Low Glucose
opts.B: Elevated Leukocytes, Predominant Lymphocytes, Normal Protein, Normal Glucose ✓
opts.D: Elevated Leukocytes, Predominant Lymphocytes, High Protein, Low Glucose

why.A: Neutrophils, high protein and low glucose is bacterial meningitis; it would be right with a very toxic child, high fever, purpura or Gram stain showing organisms.
why.B: correct
why.C: A normal cell count does not fit a child with clinical meningitis; it is seen in meningism without meningitis or very early disease.
why.D: Lymphocytes with high protein and low glucose suggests tuberculous (or fungal) meningitis, which has a subacute course over weeks and often cranial nerve palsies.

questions.right: The recall stresses meningitis "after URTI", and the compiler reads it as a viral (aseptic) picture. Viral meningitis gives a raised CSF white cell count with lymphocyte predominance, normal (or mildly raised) protein and normal glucose, which matches this option.
questions.kc: CSF patterns: Bacterial: high neutrophils, high protein, low glucose Viral: lymphocytes, normal/mildly high protein, normal glucose TB/fungal: lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose Normal: very few cells, normal protein and glucose
questions.ep: Low glucose with lymphocytes is not viral; think TB or fungal.

questions.stem: 5 years old girl present to emergency for fever (38.9) for 2 day , increasing in drowsiness and confusion , she has occasionally vomiting and one seizure What most important to her?

why.A: Chest X-ray looks for pneumonia; it does not explain altered consciousness and seizure.
why.C: MRI brain supports encephalitis (e.g. temporal lobe changes in HSV) but does not identify the organism; CSF analysis is the key test.
why.D: EEG helps in encephalitis or non-convulsive seizures but is non-specific and not the most important test for CNS infection.

questions.right: A 5-year-old with fever for 2 days , increasing drowsiness and confusion , vomiting and a seizure has suspected CNS infection (meningitis or encephalitis), not a simple febrile seizure. The key diagnostic test is lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, glucose, protein, culture and viral PCR. CT was not among the options; in practice, reduced consciousness or focal signs call for imaging before the LP, and antibiotics and acyclovir should not be delayed.
questions.kc: Fever + altered consciousness + seizure = CNS infection until proven otherwise. Key test: lumbar puncture (cells, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, PCR) Image first if reduced consciousness, focal signs or papilledema Start empirical antibiotics + acyclovir without delay Simple febrile seizure: brief, generalized, child returns to normal
questions.ep: A febrile seizure with full recovery needs no LP; ongoing drowsiness and confusion is what makes LP essential.

questions.stem: Pediatric patient with contact with TB positive father , is asymptomatic with normal X ray but PPD shows 14mm induration

why.A: Doing nothing is wrong: a positive test in a young contact carries a high risk of progression to active and disseminated TB.
why.B: Window "prophylaxis" is given to young exposed contacts whose test is still negative, until a repeat test; once the test is positive the child is treated for latent infection.
why.D: An IGRA adds nothing here; infection is already shown by the positive PPD with clear exposure, and the next step is treatment.

questions.right: This child is a close household contact of an infectious adult, is "asymptomatic" with a "normal X ray", and has a PPD of "14mm". That is a positive tuberculin test with no evidence of active disease, which defines latent TB infection, so the child should receive latent TB treatment to prevent progression (young children progress to severe disease more often).
questions.kc: Child contact of active TB: Evaluate: symptoms, examination, TST or IGRA, chest X- ray Positive test + normal CXR + no symptoms = latent TB, treat Positive test + abnormal CXR or symptoms = active TB, full regimen Young child with negative test = window prophylaxis, retest later Recent contact: induration ≥5 mm is positive
questions.ep: Prophylaxis is for the exposed child with a negative test; a positive test means treat latent TB.

questions.stem: A mother expresses her concern about her 2 year old child as they are living with his grandfather, who is a (open) pulmonary TB . The child received his BCG vaccine. What will you do for him?

opts.A: Reassurance as he has already taken the BCG vaccine
opts.B: Do PPD skin test and Chest X-ray
opts.C: Do Interferon Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) and start him on INH
opts.D: Do Interferon Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) and start him on 4 TB medication

why.A: BCG does not prevent infection and only partly protects against severe forms; it is never a reason to skip evaluation and prophylaxis.
why.B: Testing without treatment is the approach for children 5 and older (test, then decide); in a child under 5, waiting delays protection during the highest-risk period.
why.D: Four-drug therapy is for active TB; this child is asymptomatic with no evidence of disease.

questions.right: A "2 year old" living with a grandfather with open (infectious) pulmonary TB is at very high risk of rapid progression to severe forms such as miliary TB or TB meningitis, and BCG does not reliably protect against infection. Children under 5 who are exposed are tested and started on isoniazid preventive therapy straight away, after active disease is excluded, without waiting; this option combines testing with starting INH. The compiler's rule: under 5, start prophylaxis; 5 and above, test and wait for results.
questions.kc: Exposed child (household contact of infectious TB): Exclude active TB: symptoms, examination, chest X-ray Under 5 years: start isoniazid preventive therapy now 5 years and above: test (TST/IGRA + CXR) and act on results Active disease: full multidrug regimen BCG does not exempt from evaluation
questions.ep: Under-5 contacts get preventive INH immediately; do not let "BCG vaccinated" tempt you into reassurance.

questions.stem: Child with a history of going to birthday party , developed fever and KOPLIK spots in the mouth and mucopapular rash in the trunk - what is the mood if transition

why.A: Contaminated surfaces (fomites) matter for viruses such as RSV, rotavirus and norovirus; measles survives poorly on surfaces and fomites are not its main route.
why.B: Contaminated food and drink (faecal oral) transmit hepatitis A, enteroviruses and enteric bacteria, not measles.
why.D: Option not recalled; cannot be assessed.

questions.right: Fever, Koplik spots (pathognomonic) and a maculopapular rash spreading over the trunk after a gathering of children is measles . Measles virus spreads by respiratory droplets and airborne nuclei from respiratory secretions, and it is one of the most contagious infections; the virus can remain in the air of a room for hours, so airborne precautions are needed.
questions.kc: Measles: 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) + Koplik spots + rash face to trunk. Transmission: airborne / respiratory secretions; highly contagious Infectious from about 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset Isolation: airborne precautions (negative pressure room, N95) Supportive care plus vitamin A Complications: pneumonia, otitis media, encephalitis, SSPE
questions.ep: Measles, varicella and TB are the classic airborne trio requiring N95 / negative pressure isolation.

questions.stem: A 6 years non-vaccinated child present with cropped vesicles on the trunk with scattered scabbed lesions . Fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.A: Measles gives a maculopapular (not vesicular) rash starting on the face and spreading down, after cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.
why.C: Smallpox lesions are all at the same stage, deep and firm, and centrifugal (face and extremities, including palms and soles); it has been eradicated.
why.D: HSV causes grouped vesicles in one localised area, typically perioral or gingival (gingivostomatitis), not a generalised truncal crop rash.

questions.right: A non vaccinated 6 year old with fever and vesicles on the trunk appearing in crops , with some lesions already scabbed , shows lesions at different stages at the same time. This centripetal, polymorphic rash is the hallmark of varicella (chickenpox).
questions.kc: Vesicles in different stages + trunk predominance = varicella. Stages: papule, vesicle, pustule, crust; itchy Contagious until all lesions are crusted Varicella: centripetal, asynchronous; smallpox: centrifugal, synchronous Complications: secondary bacterial skin infection (most common), pneumonia, cerebellar ataxia, encephalitis Avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome)
questions.ep: "All lesions at the same stage" flips the answer to smallpox.

questions.stem: 3-year-old child presented with a rash on the hands and feet , now with oral ulcers and drooling. Parents report that other children at the daycare have the same presentation. What is the mode of transmission?

why.A: Vertical transmission is mother-to-baby (e.g. HIV, CMV, rubella); it cannot explain spread among daycare children.
why.C: Airborne spread by droplet nuclei is typical of measles, varicella and TB, not enteroviruses.
why.D: Droplet/respiratory secretions do contribute to HFMD spread, but the classic exam answer for enteroviral transmission is fecal-oral.

questions.right: A 3-year-old with a rash on hands and feet , oral ulcers and drooling and a daycare outbreak has hand, foot and mouth disease, caused by enteroviruses (coxsackievirus A16, enterovirus 71). Enteroviruses are classically spread by the fecal-oral route, and stool shedding continues for weeks, which explains daycare outbreaks among children in diapers.
questions.kc: HFMD: enterovirus (coxsackie A16, EV71), children under 5, oral ulcers plus palm/sole rash. Main route: fecal-oral; also contact with blister fluid and respiratory secretions Prevention: hand washing, disinfect toys and surfaces Herpangina: posterior pharyngeal ulcers only, same viruses Airborne: measles, varicella, TB Droplet: influenza, meningococcus
questions.ep: Ulcers limited to the posterior pharynx without a hand/foot rash point to herpangina, same enterovirus family.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with a pharyngitis , fever, and a diffuse, erythematous, sandpaper-like rash that began on his trunk and has now spread to his extremities. His The tongue appears bright red ( “strawberry tongue” ). What is the most likely causative organism?

why.A: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum: "slapped cheek" then a lacy reticular rash on the limbs, without pharyngitis or strawberry tongue.
why.B: Staphylococcus aureus toxin causes staphylococcal scalded skin (blistering, Nikolsky positive) or toxic shock; it is not the cause of scarlet fever after pharyngitis.
why.D: Herpes simplex causes gingivostomatitis with vesicles and ulcers, or eczema herpeticum; no sandpaper rash.

questions.right: Pharyngitis , fever, a sandpaper-like rash starting on the trunk and spreading, and a strawberry tongue in a 7-year-old is scarlet fever. It is caused by erythrogenic (pyrogenic) exotoxin-producing group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, Streptococcus pyogenes, treated with penicillin or amoxicillin.
questions.kc: Scarlet fever = GAS pharyngitis + toxin rash. Sandpaper rash, trunk to limbs, Pastia lines, circumoral pallor Strawberry tongue, later desquamation Treat: penicillin/amoxicillin (prevents rheumatic fever) Kawasaki also has strawberry tongue but fever ≥5 days, conjunctivitis, extremity changes, no pharyngitis exudate
questions.ep: Strawberry tongue plus prolonged fever, conjunctivitis and swollen hands/feet means Kawasaki, not scarlet fever.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl was attacked by a bat . Scratched and bitten . What is the most appropriate management plan?

opts.D: Clean the wound and observe for rabies symptoms

why.A: Rabies vaccines in use are inactivated (killed); there is no live rabies vaccine for humans.
why.B: Vaccine alone is for category II exposures (minor scratches/nibbling without bleeding) or for previously vaccinated people; a bat bite/scratch in an unvaccinated child needs immunoglobulin too.
why.D: Observation is acceptable only for a healthy dog or cat that can be observed for 10 days; a bat cannot be observed and rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear.

questions.right: Any bite or scratch from a bat is a category III (severe) rabies exposure. Management is thorough wound washing plus post-exposure prophylaxis with both rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin (infiltrated into and around the wound), because the immunoglobulin gives immediate passive cover until the vaccine induces antibodies.
questions.kc: Rabies PEP by WHO exposure category. Category I (touching, licks on intact skin): no PEP Category II (nibbling, minor scratch without bleeding): wound care + vaccine Category III (bite/scratch breaking skin, mucosal contact, any bat exposure): wound care + vaccine + RIG Previously vaccinated: vaccine boosters only, no RIG
questions.ep: Bats are always category III, even with a trivial or unnoticed bite.

questions.stem: A 6 y.o child came complaining of mild hip and thigh pain. On examination: he is febrile, mild moderate tenderness of hip joint, child has mild pain when walking apart from that the child is looking good US of hip: Joint effusion WBC: 11 What's the diagnosis?

why.A: Septic arthritis: an ill, toxic child who refuses to bear weight, with high fever, raised WBC (>12) and ESR/CRP; needs urgent aspiration. Here the child walks and looks well.
why.C: Osteomyelitis: focal bony (metaphyseal) tenderness, often a toxic child, and early US usually shows no joint effusion; here the finding is a hip joint effusion.
why.D: Benign childhood myositis: calf pain and tip-toe walking after influenza, with very high CK; it does not cause a hip joint effusion.

questions.right: This recall's key is toxic (transient) synovitis because the child is "looking good" , can still walk with only "mild pain when walking" , and the WBC is only 11 . An effusion on hip US is seen in both transient synovitis and septic arthritis, so the decision rests on how sick the child is: a well, weight-bearing child with a near-normal WBC meets at most one Kocher criterion (fever), which puts septic arthritis at low probability.
questions.kc: Irritable hip in a child: well and walking = transient synovitis; toxic and non-weight- bearing = septic arthritis. Kocher criteria: fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12 0 to 1 criteria: low risk; 3 to 4: high risk of septic arthritis CRP >20 adds to the risk Septic hip: urgent aspiration then washout and IV antibiotics Transient synovitis: rest, NSAIDs, review; often follows a viral illness
questions.ep: Effusion alone does not separate them; refusal to bear weight and a high WBC/ESR flip the answer to septic arthritis.

questions.stem: A 8 years old boy presented with focal pain on his left leg that is increasing in intensity Associated with local warmth and tenderness and subjective fever . He has a history of fall with penetrating wound . What is the diagnostic radiological investigation for the leg?

why.A: Plain X-ray is the first imaging to exclude fracture or foreign body, but bone changes (periosteal reaction, lytic areas) lag about 2 weeks behind infection, so it is not diagnostic early.
why.C: CT shows cortical destruction and sequestrum in chronic disease but is poor for early marrow changes and involves radiation; it is a fallback when MRI is unavailable.
why.D: Nuclear bone scan is sensitive but not specific and involves radiation; it helps when the site is unclear or multifocal disease is suspected, or when MRI is unavailable.

questions.right: Progressive focal leg pain with "local warmth and tenderness", fever and a prior "penetrating wound" is acute osteomyelitis (direct inoculation). The question asks for the "diagnostic" study: MRI is the most sensitive and specific imaging, showing marrow edema within days and defining subperiosteal or soft tissue abscess that may need drainage. As the compiler notes, X-ray is the initial study but is usually normal for the first 10 to 14 days.
questions.kc: Osteomyelitis imaging ladder: Initial: plain X-ray (often normal early) Diagnostic (best imaging): MRI Definitive: bone aspiration or biopsy and culture Blood cultures before antibiotics Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus Puncture wound through a shoe: think Pseudomonas
questions.ep: "Initial" imaging = X-ray; "diagnostic" or "best" imaging = MRI.

questions.stem: 10 yr polyarthritis and fever, small joint stiffness. Rheumatoid factor 100 (N < 58). First line:

why.A: NSAIDs relieve pain and stiffness but do not modify disease; they are first line alone only in mild oligoarticular JIA, not RF positive polyarthritis.
why.B: Systemic corticosteroids are a short bridge or used for systemic JIA with serositis or macrophage activation syndrome; intra articular steroid suits oligoarthritis. Not first line maintenance here.

questions.right: A 10 year old with polyarthritis of small joints , stiffness and a positive rheumatoid factor fits RF positive polyarticular JIA, the subtype that behaves like adult RA and is prone to erosions. For polyarticular JIA the first line disease modifying therapy is methotrexate , started early to prevent joint damage, with NSAIDs only as symptomatic adjuncts. The source confirms MTX (an examinee who chose NSAID counted it as her mistake).
questions.kc: JIA first line depends on subtype. Oligoarticular (≤4 large joints, age under 6): NSAID ± intra articular steroid Polyarticular (≥5 joints), especially RF positive: methotrexate Systemic JIA with active systemic features: steroids / IL1 or IL6 blockade RF positive polyarticular: age 9 to 12, symmetric small joints, nodules, behaves like adult RA Inadequate response to MTX: add biologic (anti TNF)
questions.ep: Many joints plus positive RF in a child means MTX, not 'start with NSAID' (the classic trap that cost a 100 scorer this mark).

questions.stem: 12 yo female patient kc of T1DM with previous DKA admissions, her mother is worried of diabetes complications. What's the most useful annual test for renal complications ?

why.A: A routine urinalysis dipstick detects only overt proteinuria and misses the early microalbuminuria stage.
why.B: Serum creatinine rises late, after significant nephron loss, so it is a poor early screening test.
why.D: HbA1c monitors glycemic control (every 3 months) and predicts risk, but it does not test for kidney damage.

questions.right: The earliest detectable sign of diabetic nephropathy is microalbuminuria (moderately increased albuminuria), so the most useful annual screening test for renal complications is a urine albumin measurement, ideally a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio . In type 1 diabetes in youth, screening starts around puberty or age 10 once diabetes has been present for several years, which fits this 12-year-old.
questions.kc: Diabetic nephropathy screening. Test: spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio yearly First sign: microalbuminuria A single abnormal ratio must be repeated to confirm persistence Confirmed albuminuria: start ACE inhibitor or ARB
questions.ep: Dipstick urinalysis looks reassuringly normal in early nephropathy; only the albumin ratio catches it.

questions.stem: A newborn is diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 10% and concurrent renal failure. The parents had previously discussed a Do-Not- Resuscitate (DNR) order with the medical team, however the order was never formally completed or signed . The patient now goes into cardiac arrest . What is the most appropriate next step?

opts.C: Initiate CPR after obtaining permission from the managing consultant
opts.D: Initiate CPR and inform the family afterward

why.A: Withholding CPR is only right when a valid, documented DNR order exists; a verbal or unsigned discussion does not count.
why.C: Seeking consultant permission delays CPR during an arrest; resuscitation must start at once and is not conditional on approval.
why.D: CPR is right, but 'inform the family afterward' makes notification the key action and implies resuscitation is provisional; with no valid DNR the correct action is a full, complete resuscitation attempt per protocol, and informing the family is routine either way.

questions.right: A DNR order only applies once it is formally completed and signed ; a discussion that was "never formally completed" has no legal effect. In the absence of a valid DNR, the default for any patient in cardiac arrest is full resuscitation, so CPR is started immediately and continued to completion per protocol.
questions.kc: No valid signed DNR = full code. DNR must be documented and signed to be acted on Discussions, intentions or unsigned forms do not count When in doubt during arrest: resuscitate Goals of care can be revisited and the order formalised after stabilisation
questions.ep: Poor prognosis (EF 10%, renal failure) tempts "do not initiate CPR", but without a signed order the answer is always to resuscitate. 14 topics, 23 questions

questions.stem: Pneumonia with X-ray picture patient had shock : Vital : hypotension Fever He started on vasopressin, antibiotics What will you find?

why.A: Systemic vascular resistance is LOW in septic shock because of vasodilation; raised resistance fits hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock, or late cold sepsis.
why.C: Raised central or vascular resistance again describes vasoconstricted states (hypovolaemic, cardiogenic), the opposite of the vasodilated septic picture.

questions.right: Pneumonia with fever and "hypotension" needing vasopressors is septic shock , a distributive shock. Widespread vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance, and the heart compensates with tachycardia and a high cardiac output (warm phase). So the expected haemodynamic finding is increased cardiac output.
questions.kc: Shock haemodynamics: read CO and SVR. Septic (warm): CO up, SVR down, PCWP low or normal Hypovolaemic: CO down, SVR up, PCWP low Cardiogenic: CO down, SVR up, PCWP high Neurogenic: hypotension without tachycardia, SVR down
questions.ep: Fever plus infection plus hypotension = high output, low resistance; raised SVR only in late (cold) sepsis.

questions.stem: A 43 years old man presented to the ER complaining of Progressive Lower limb weakness and urine incontinence and difficulty walking since 3 days , T10 sensory level . What is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Guillain-Barre syndrome causes ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia after an infection, but no sensory level and bladder involvement is late and mild; a sensory level means the cord.
why.C: Transverse myelitis gives the same picture (bilateral weakness, sensory level, bladder dysfunction developing over hours to days), often after an infection or with MS, SLE or NMO; it is diagnosed once MRI excludes compression and shows cord inflammation.
why.D: Cauda equina syndrome is a lower motor neuron lesion below L1: saddle anesthesia, sciatica, flaccid areflexic legs and retention; it cannot produce a T10 sensory level.

questions.right: Progressive lower limb weakness , urinary incontinence and a T10 sensory level localize the lesion to the spinal cord (myelopathy), not to peripheral nerves. This recall's key is cord compression, the compiler's reasoning being that compression (disc, tumor metastasis, abscess, hematoma) is by far the most common cause of an acute myelopathy in a 43-year-old man, while transverse myelitis is rare. Either way the next step is urgent MRI of the whole spine.
questions.kc: Sensory level + bladder involvement = spinal cord lesion; exclude compression with urgent MRI. Cord compression: most common cause; back pain, known cancer (lung, prostate, breast metastasize to spine) Transverse myelitis: over hours to days, post infectious or autoimmune, no compressive lesion GBS: ascending, areflexia, no sensory level Cauda equina: saddle anesthesia, LMN signs, below L1 Anterior spinal artery: sudden, spares vibration and position sense
questions.ep: Back pain or cancer history tips toward compression; a preceding infection and onset over days without pain tips toward transverse myelitis.

questions.stem: A patient presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back . Which of the following would confirm the diagnosis ?

why.A: Triglycerides: identify a CAUSE of pancreatitis (very high levels) once the diagnosis is made; they do not confirm pancreatitis.
why.C: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.
why.D: Not recalled; no option can be assessed.

questions.right: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back suggests acute pancreatitis. The diagnosis is confirmed by meeting 2 of 3 criteria; with typical pain, a serum lipase 3 or more times the upper limit of normal confirms it, and lipase is more specific and stays raised longer than amylase.
questions.kc: Acute pancreatitis diagnosis: 2 of 3 criteria. Typical epigastric pain radiating to the back Lipase or amylase 3 or more times upper limit (lipase preferred) Characteristic findings on CT/US/MRI Initial imaging: US for gallstones; CT only if diagnosis unclear or for complications after 48 to 72 h Causes to look for: gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides, calcium, drugs
questions.ep: Lipase confirms the disease; triglycerides, calcium and US look for its cause.

questions.stem: A patient received high irradiation (20 Gray, normal 11 Gray) . After 2 weeks , he started complaining of abdominal pain, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting. What is the most likely cause?

why.A: Stroke: a sudden focal neurological deficit; not a recognized consequence of acute radiation exposure presenting as GI symptoms.
why.B: Malignancy: radiation-induced cancers (leukaemia, thyroid, solid tumours) appear years later, not after 2 weeks.
why.D: Anaphylactic shock: an immediate IgE-mediated reaction within minutes of an allergen, with hypotension, urticaria and wheeze; radiation does not cause it.

questions.right: After a high whole-body radiation dose , the rapidly dividing tissues fail first: bone marrow and gut epithelium. Symptoms 2 weeks later with fatigue , nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain fit acute radiation syndrome in its manifest phase, and among the options only bone marrow destruction is a direct radiation effect in that time frame (marrow failure causes fatigue/anaemia, infection and bleeding).
questions.kc: Acute radiation syndrome: phases and organ systems. Prodrome: nausea, vomiting, fatigue within hours Latent phase: patient appears well Manifest phase: haematopoietic (pancytopenia, infection, bleeding), GI (diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain), neurovascular at the highest doses Late effects (years): malignancy, cataract, infertility
questions.ep: Weeks after radiation = marrow and gut failure; years after = cancer.

questions.stem: Seventeen-year-old female presents with decreased concentration for past 6 months; spends around 9 hours daily on social media and compares herself frequently with others. Symptoms suggestive of anxiety and depression but no prior medical treatment . What is the best course of action?

opts.B: Force her to leave social media

why.A: Antidepressants (an SSRI such as fluoxetine) are reserved for moderate to severe depression or failure of psychotherapy in adolescents, given the black-box warning on suicidality; they are not first step for untreated mild-moderate symptoms.
why.B: Forcing her off social media is coercive, damages rapport and treats a behaviour rather than the underlying disorder.
why.C: Limiting screen time is sensible supportive advice, but on its own it does not treat established anxiety and depressive symptoms; it can be part of CBT rather than the best course of action.

questions.right: A 17-year-old with 6 months of poor concentration, heavy social media use with constant self-comparison, and anxiety and depressive symptoms with no prior treatment fits mild to moderate adolescent depression/anxiety. First-line management at this age is a psychological therapy, and CBT addresses the negative self-comparison and cognitive distortions directly; medication is added only if symptoms are severe or do not respond.
questions.kc: Adolescent mild-moderate depression/anxiety: psychotherapy (CBT) first. Mild: watchful support, psychoeducation, CBT Moderate to severe or failed therapy: CBT + SSRI (fluoxetine first line) Monitor for suicidality when an SSRI is started in under 25s
questions.ep: Untreated adolescent with mild-moderate symptoms: therapy before tablets.

questions.stem: Young female with history of lack of sleep, decreased appetite, decreased concentration, loss of interest in activities, isolation . Which of the following is the most concerning ?

opts.A: Loss of interest in previously interesting activity

why.A: Loss of interest (anhedonia) is a core symptom that establishes the diagnosis of depression, but it is not itself the strongest suicide risk marker.
why.C: Change in appetite is a common somatic (neurovegetative) symptom of depression with no specific suicide risk weight.
why.D: Lack of sleep is a neurovegetative symptom of depression; it supports the diagnosis but is less concerning than isolation.

questions.right: The stem describes a depressive episode (poor sleep, appetite, concentration, anhedonia), and the lead-in asks which feature is most concerning , meaning the strongest marker of suicide risk. Isolation and social withdrawal removes protective social support and is the feature that carries the highest suicide risk among the options. The other options are diagnostic symptoms of depression rather than risk markers.
questions.kc: Depression: symptoms that diagnose vs features that raise suicide risk. Diagnose: low mood or anhedonia + sleep, appetite, concentration, energy, guilt changes Raise risk: social isolation, hopelessness, prior attempt, plan or access to means Also: male sex (completion), older age, substance use, chronic illness
questions.ep: If the lead-in asks for the diagnostic core symptom, anhedonia wins; if it asks what is most concerning, isolation wins.

questions.stem: A 20 yo male is diagnosed with schizophrenia presenting with hallucinations and AGITATION and disorganized behavior. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?

opts.A: Risperidone then Titrate to a lowest effective dose
opts.B: Olanzapine and monitor metabolic side effects

why.B: Olanzapine is an effective first line atypical, but carries the greatest weight gain and metabolic risk; the stem gives no reason to prefer it, and the key emphasises dose titration over drug choice.
why.C: Haloperidol is a typical antipsychotic with high EPS risk; reserved for acute IM rapid tranquillisation or when atypicals are unsuitable, not routine first line maintenance.
why.D: Clozapine is for treatment resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2 adequate antipsychotic trials) because of agranulocytosis risk; never first line.

questions.right: A young adult with first presentation schizophrenia (hallucinations, agitation, disorganized behaviour) and no stated metabolic risk factors is treated with a second generation antipsychotic such as risperidone, started low and titrated to the lowest effective dose to limit side effects. The source keeps A because titration to the lowest effective dose is the key principle; olanzapine is also acceptable first line, but nothing in the stem pushes toward it and its metabolic burden is higher.
questions.kc: First episode schizophrenia: start a second generation antipsychotic at low dose and titrate. Risperidone: fewer metabolic effects than olanzapine, but hyperprolactinemia and dose related EPS Olanzapine: most weight gain, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia Haloperidol: high potency typical, EPS, NMS Clozapine: after 2 failed antipsychotics; monitor neutrophils Severe acute agitation: short term IM antipsychotic ± benzodiazepine
questions.ep: If the stem lists obesity, diabetes or dyslipidemia, avoid olanzapine; clozapine only after two failed trials.

questions.stem: Pt known as a case of bibolar I came to the emergency with manic episode for 2 weeks . Impulsive buying and goal oriented behavior. The pt is on no medication . Next best step in manegment?

opts.A: lithium and watch for serum consentration
opts.C: Olanzapine for acute management of manic episode

why.A: Lithium is effective for mania and is the gold standard for maintenance, but it acts slowly (about 1-2 weeks) and needs level and renal/thyroid monitoring, so it is less suitable as the emergency step; it would be right when choosing long-term mood stabilization.
why.B: Sertraline is an antidepressant; in bipolar disorder, especially during mania, antidepressants can worsen or prolong mania and are not indicated.
why.D: Psychotherapy without medication is inadequate for acute mania; CBT is an adjunct in maintenance or for depression, not for an acute manic episode.

questions.right: A known bipolar I patient with a current "manic episode for 2 weeks" who is "on no medication" and presents to the emergency department needs rapid control of acute mania. An atypical antipsychotic such as olanzapine works quickly and is first line for acute mania, and it can also continue as maintenance.
questions.kc: Acute mania management: Stop antidepressants First line: antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, or the typical agent haloperidol) and/or lithium or valproate Severe or agitated: antipsychotic for rapid effect, short-term benzodiazepine if needed Maintenance: lithium (best evidence), valproate, some antipsychotics Valproate avoided in women of childbearing potential
questions.ep: Emergency mania wants the fastest agent (antipsychotic); lithium is the long- game drug.

questions.stem: Sexually active female , asked how to prevent STDs

why.A: Monogamy only protects if both partners are uninfected and remain faithful; it does not prevent transmission from an already infected partner, so it is not the most reliable answer.
why.B: Frequent screening detects infection after it has happened (secondary prevention); it does not prevent acquiring the STI in the first place.

questions.right: The question asks how a sexually active woman can prevent STIs, and the intervention that directly blocks transmission at every encounter is consistent and correct condom use . It works regardless of the partner's status, which is why it is the standard counselling answer for STI prevention when abstinence is not offered.
questions.kc: STI prevention ladder: abstinence > consistent condom use > mutual monogamy with a tested partner. Condoms: barrier, protect against HIV, gonorrhea, chlamydia; partial protection for HSV and HPV Hormonal contraception prevents pregnancy, not STIs Screening = early detection, not prevention Vaccination (HPV, hepatitis B) prevents specific STIs only
questions.ep: "Prevent" means primary prevention: pick the barrier method, not screening.

questions.stem: The PSA Been Used Worldwide To Detect Prostate Cancer, But Nowadays Doctor Noticed That It Has Low Specificity Which Lead To Over Treatment . What Is The Inclusion Criteria For PSA To Be Used?

opts.A: It Should Be Used For People With High Risk Or Family History
opts.B: It Should Be Used For People Who Had Symptoms
opts.C: It Should Detect The Highest Number Of People
opts.D: It Should Detect Cancer In Early Stages

why.A: Targeting high-risk men (family history, Black ancestry) is how PSA screening is offered in practice through shared decision-making, but it describes WHO is screened, not the quality required of the test.
why.B: Testing people who have symptoms is diagnosis, not screening; screening by definition is for asymptomatic people.
why.D: Detecting disease at an early, treatable stage is a core principle of screening (Wilson- Jungner criteria) and was chosen by a 120 scorer in Medicine; it is the answer if the question asks about the purpose of screening rather than the test's property.

questions.right: This recall's key is C because, as the compiler reasons, the property most valued when choosing a screening test is high sensitivity: a screening test should pick up as many affected people as possible, and positives are then sorted out by more specific confirmatory tests (for PSA, MRI and biopsy). On this view, PSA's low specificity is acceptable as long as it catches the highest number of cases.
questions.kc: Screening test essentials: Screening is for asymptomatic people Priority property: high sensitivity (few missed cases) Positives confirmed by a more specific test Condition must have a detectable early stage with effective treatment Low specificity: false positives, overdiagnosis, overtreatment (the PSA problem) PSA: shared decision-making in older men, not routine for all
questions.ep: Sensitivity matters for screening (rule out); specificity matters for confirmation (rule in).

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of heavy smoking presents for a routine health checkup. He is asymptomatic and has no known chronic medical conditions. According to preventive screening recommendations, which of the following conditions is most important to screen for in this patient?

why.A: Osteoporosis screening (DEXA) is routine for women from 65 and for men only with risk factors such as steroids or fracture; it is not the priority here.
why.B: Colon cancer screening is recommended for all average-risk adults from 45 to 75, so it also applies to him, but the question asks what is most important for this smoker; the smoking history is the clue that points to AAA.
why.D: Prostate cancer screening with PSA is not routinely recommended; it is an individual shared decision in men 55 to 69.

questions.right: A 65-year-old man with a heavy smoking history fits exactly the group for one- time AAA screening with abdominal ultrasound (men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked). It is the screening test specifically triggered by his risk profile, and finding an asymptomatic aneurysm allows surveillance or elective repair before rupture.
questions.kc: Screening by risk profile: AAA: one-time ultrasound, men 65 to 75 who ever smoked Colorectal cancer: 45 to 75, average risk Osteoporosis: women ≥65 (younger if at risk) Lung cancer: low-dose CT in heavy smokers, adults 50 to 80 PSA: shared decision, not routine
questions.ep: If 'lung cancer with low-dose CT' appeared, it would compete strongly in a heavy smoker.

questions.stem: Warfarin was not stopped by patient despite of the clear instructions, the nurse in the OR noticed that the patient did not stop the drug as instructed and informed the surgeon, so the surgeon postponed the operation :

why.A: An adverse event is harm that actually reaches the patient from medical care; here the operation was postponed and no harm occurred.
why.B: Negligence needs a breach of the duty of care by the provider causing harm; the patient did not follow instructions and the team acted correctly.
why.D: The principle of totality allows sacrificing a body part for the good of the whole person (e.g. amputation); it has nothing to do with this event.
