questions.right: A near miss is an error or unsafe situation that is caught before it reaches the patient , so no harm occurs. Here the patient continued warfarin, the OR nurse noticed and the surgeon postponed the operation, so the hazard (operating on an anticoagulated patient) was intercepted in time.
questions.kc: Patient safety terms: did the error reach the patient, and was there harm? Near miss: caught before reaching the patient No-harm event: reached the patient, no harm Adverse event: harm caused by care Sentinel event: unexpected death or serious harm
questions.ep: Stopped in time with no harm = near miss; harm done = adverse event.

questions.stem: Warfarin was not stopped by patient despite of the clear instructions, the nurse in the OR noticed that the patient did not stop the drug as instructed and informed the surgeon, so the surgeon postponed the operation :

why.A: An adverse event is harm to the patient from care, for example operating on him and causing major bleeding; here no harm occurred.
why.B: "Medical nurse" is not a patient safety classification.
why.D: The principle of totality is an ethical principle allowing a part of the body to be sacrificed for the good of the whole (e.g. amputation); it has nothing to do with error classification.

questions.right: The error (warfarin not stopped) was detected by the nurse in the OR and the surgeon "postponed the operation", so the error was intercepted before it reached the patient. An error caught before it causes harm is a near miss.
questions.kc: Patient safety terms: Near miss: error caught before reaching the patient No-harm event: error reached the patient but caused no harm Adverse event: harm caused by care Sentinel event: unexpected death or serious harm
questions.ep: Ask: did the error reach the patient and cause harm? Not reached = near miss.

questions.stem: Patient came with vaginal discharge she has done CS with episiotomy 10 days ago, the obstetrician diagnosed her with UTI and prescribed Abx, but she did not improve then she went to another obstetrician, and he found infected vaginal swab , What is the medical error done by the first obstetrician?

opts.A: Let the midwife assist him and depend on her
opts.B: Doctor failed to follow the surgical safety protocol in the OR
opts.C: No communication between the second and first obstetrician
opts.D: Genuine difference assessment or diagnosis of patient case

why.A: Delegating to and relying on a midwife would be an error of supervision, but nothing in the stem says the midwife was involved.
why.C: Lack of communication between the two doctors is a system issue arising after the event; it does not explain the first obstetrician's error in managing the patient.
why.D: A genuine difference in assessment is a legitimate difference of clinical opinion, by definition not a medical error; it fits when both doctors acted reasonably on the information available.

questions.right: The patient developed a genital tract or wound infection 10 days after an operative delivery, and the first obstetrician missed it by labelling it a UTI. Among the listed options, the only one that places the fault on the first obstetrician himself is B: an infection of the operative site implies a breach of surgical safety and aseptic practice, which is the source's key.
questions.kc: Classifying errors in patient safety questions. Error must be an act or omission by the person named in the lead-in Genuine difference of opinion: not an error Post operative fever or discharge: examine the operative site (wound, perineum) before labelling another source Communication failures: system errors, usually at handover
questions.ep: When asked what the FIRST doctor did wrong, discard options describing other people or a legitimate difference of opinion.

questions.stem: Nurse hand over to the next shift and find out that the child had peanut allergy and it's was not written or documented What kind of technical issue?

why.A: Preoperative checklist (surgical safety checklist) prevents wrong-site/wrong-patient surgery and checks allergies before an operation; this child is not in a surgical setting and the error is at shift handover.
why.C: Option not recalled (described as nonsense by the recaller).
why.D: Option not recalled (described as nonsense by the recaller).

questions.right: A food allergy that was not written or documented and only discovered during handover is a communication failure between shifts. The patient safety tool that addresses this is structured handover communication (such as SBAR), whose purpose is to decrease errors due to miscommunication.
questions.kc: Patient safety tools and what they target: Structured handover (SBAR, I-PASS): miscommunication between shifts/teams Surgical safety checklist / time-out: wrong site, wrong patient, retained items Read-back: verbal or telephone orders Allergy documentation and wristband: allergy errors
questions.ep: Information lost at shift change = handover communication failure.

questions.stem: Surgeon asked nurse to give iv epinephrine to a child, nurse said give iv epinephrine, doctor said that's right , what kind of communication?

why.A: Check-back is the TeamSTEPPS name for the receiver repeating and the sender verifying, so it describes the same loop; examination keys usually use 'closed loop' as the general term for the whole exchange.
why.C: Call-out is broadcasting critical information to the whole team at once (for example, 'airway clear, BP 80/50'), with no repeat-back and confirmation.

questions.right: The surgeon gives an order, the nurse repeats it back ('give IV epinephrine'), and the surgeon confirms ('that's right'). This three-step loop (send, repeat back, verify) is closed- loop communication , which prevents errors with high-risk drugs and verbal orders in emergencies.
questions.kc: Team communication tools: Closed loop / check-back: order, read back, confirm Call-out: announce critical information to the whole team SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (handover) Two-challenge rule: voice a safety concern twice, escalate if ignored
questions.ep: A repeat-back without the sender's confirmation is not a closed loop.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman is undergoing an operation and told the nurse she doesn’t want a blood transfusion beforehand. Now she has severe bleeding and became hypotensive . Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

opts.C: Take the consent from the patient before she loses consciousness

why.B: An ethics committee consult takes time; it cannot guide management of an acute, life- threatening bleed.
why.C: Re-confirming the wishes of a competent patient is the classic autonomy-based response, but a hypotensive, bleeding patient under anaesthesia is unlikely to give a valid informed decision; the recall key prioritises immediate transfusion.
why.D: A husband cannot consent or refuse on behalf of a competent adult woman; consent is the patient's own.

questions.right: This recall's key is A because the patient is now in a life-threatening haemorrhage with hypotension, and in an emergency doctors act to save life (and the fetus) when a valid, documented informed refusal is not in place. Her statement was only made casually to a nurse before surgery, not an informed refusal recorded by the treating doctor, so the key treats transfusion as the immediate life-saving action.
questions.kc: Consent and refusal of treatment. Competent adult: informed refusal is respected, even if life saving Emergency with no valid refusal on record and patient unable to decide: treat to save life Spouse or relative cannot consent for a competent adult Document discussions and decisions clearly
questions.ep: Valid documented informed refusal = respect it; vague prior statement plus life- threatening emergency = the key treats.

questions.stem: A patient had colorectal cancer and does not wish to do the surgery. The Patient Is Alert And Fully Aware Of His Condition And He Refuses To Be Operated On . After 3 or 4 WEEKS, The Patient Deteriorated And Developed Decreased Consciousness. His wife and son Approach You And Request You To Operate On Him. What is the most appropriate management? A. Why wrong: Option not recalled. Some versions include doing surgery if there is written consent; there was no consent in this stem, only a documented competent refusal.

opts.B: Refuse the surgery as the patient wishes
opts.C: Honer Family's Wishes And Do The Surgery

why.C: Family wishes do not override a refusal the patient made while competent; acting on them would be operating without valid consent.
why.D: An ethics committee helps when the patient's wishes are unknown or genuinely unclear; here they were clearly stated while he had capacity, so there is no dilemma to refer.

questions.right: The patient refused surgery while alert and fully aware of his condition, so his refusal was a valid, informed decision. Losing consciousness later does not cancel it: his previously expressed competent wishes still guide care, and family members cannot override them. The appropriate action is to respect his refusal and continue supportive care.
questions.kc: Competent refusal survives later loss of capacity. Competent adult may refuse any treatment, even life saving Prior competent wishes guide care after capacity is lost Family or surrogate decides only when the patient's wishes are unknown Emergency treatment without consent: only when no known prior refusal exists Ethics committee: unclear wishes or unresolved conflict
questions.ep: If the patient's wishes had never been expressed, the emergency or surrogate pathway would apply; a clear prior refusal closes that door.

questions.stem: In a scenario where a patient is on contraception, but her husband refuses it as he wants to start a family immediately, what should be the decision regarding contraception?

why.B: The husband's wish does not override the wife's; neither spouse can unilaterally impose a decision on contraception.
why.C: The patient alone deciding contradicts the expected principle for contraception within marriage in this setting; her sole consent applies to her own medical procedures (for example surgery for an incomplete abortion).
why.D: The doctor's consent is never the basis for a patient's decision; the doctor's role is to counsel and inform.

questions.right: When a married woman on contraception and her husband disagree because he wants a family , the expected answer is that contraception in a marriage is a shared decision requiring mutual consent of both spouses. The physician counsels both partners together rather than letting one side override the other, as the compiler notes this is an ethics question.
questions.kc: Contraception in marriage = mutual consent; a competent adult's own treatment = her own consent. Spouses disagree about contraception: counsel together, mutual consent Surgery on a competent adult woman: she signs her own consent, not the husband Competent patient refusing treatment: accept refusal after informing her of risks Emergency with no capacity and no surrogate: act in best interest
questions.ep: If the question is who signs consent for her own surgery, the answer flips to the patient alone.

questions.stem: An orthopedic surgeon completed a fellowship in spinal surgery and finished the program on time. He is now requesting clinical privileges to perform Complex spinal surgeries in the hospital. What should you ( Do as Certificant Provider do ) Smt like that?

opts.A: Grant privileges based on his years of experience
opts.B: Approve privileges based on completion of the Cirtificat Solely
opts.C: Do not grant privileges until he completes at least 2 years of Site clinical practice
opts.D: assess competency of his performance Before certification

why.A: Years of experience are not the same as verified competence in a specific complex procedure; privileges are procedure specific and evidence based.
why.B: A certificate shows training was completed, not that the surgeon performs the procedure safely; granting privileges on the certificate alone skips competency verification.
why.C: An arbitrary waiting period of site practice is not the criterion; a competent surgeon should not be blocked by time alone, and time alone does not prove competence.

questions.right: Clinical privileges are granted on demonstrated current competence , not on credentials alone. Completing a fellowship on time is necessary but does not prove he can safely perform complex spinal surgery in this hospital, so the credentialing body assesses his performance (case logs, references, proctored or supervised cases, a focused evaluation period) before granting the privilege. This protects patients and is the standard competency based privileging approach.
questions.kc: Privileging rule: verify credentials, then assess competence for the specific procedure before granting it. Credentialing: verify training, licence, certificates Privileging: grant specific procedures based on demonstrated competence New privileges usually start with a focused, monitored evaluation period Privileges are reviewed and renewed periodically on performance data
questions.ep: Any option that grants privileges 'solely' on a certificate or years is wrong; competence assessment is the answer.

questions.stem: A doctor has recently been coming to work drowsy and has made minor mistakes . Other physicians have also noticed that he sometimes has slurred speech , and there are rumors that he might be abusing drugs or alcohol. As a colleague, what is the most appropriate next step?

opts.A: Report to the hospital ethics committee
opts.B: Report to administration for patient safety
opts.C: Talk to him privately and wait until he solves it
opts.D: Tell the patients to go to another doctor

why.A: The ethics committee handles ethical dilemmas and policy, not the urgent operational removal of an impaired doctor from patient care; it would be right for a consultation on a dilemma, not an active safety risk.
why.C: A private talk alone, followed by waiting, leaves patients exposed while errors are already happening; it may be a reasonable first contact only when there is no ongoing risk to patients.
why.D: Telling patients to go elsewhere is unprofessional, undermines trust, and does not stop the doctor from harming other patients.

questions.right: A colleague who is "drowsy", has "slurred speech" and is already making "minor mistakes" is a possibly impaired physician, and the first duty is patient safety. The appropriate step is to report the concern through the proper channel (department head or hospital administration), who can remove him from clinical work and refer him for assessment and support. Reporting is a professional obligation, not a betrayal of the colleague.
questions.kc: Impaired colleague with risk to patients: report to the responsible authority now. Signs of impairment + errors = patient safety issue Report to supervisor / administration (line management) Do not wait, cover up or handle it alone Ethics committee = dilemmas, not urgent removal from practice The impaired doctor also deserves confidential referral for help
questions.ep: "Talk to him privately" is tempting, but once patients are at risk the answer is formal reporting.

questions.stem: Research group wants to give fish oil and screen for Alzheimers . What principle will guide the IRB ethical board in their decision?

why.B: Utilitarianism judges actions by the greatest good for the greatest number; IRBs weigh risk and benefit, but they cannot justify harming an individual for societal benefit, so it is not the guiding principle.
why.C: Ethical skepticism doubts that objective moral knowledge exists; it cannot guide a decision-making board.
why.D: "Comparativism" is not a recognised framework for research ethics review (likely a distractor).

questions.right: This recall's key is deontology: a research ethics board (IRB) judges a study by duties owed to each participant , consent, rights and protection from harm, and the welfare of the individual subject takes precedence over the benefit to science or society (as in the Declaration of Helsinki). A trial giving fish oil and screening for Alzheimer disease would be approved only if those duties are respected, regardless of expected overall gain.
questions.kc: Ethical theories in exam questions. Deontology: duty and rules, rights of the individual; respect regardless of outcome Utilitarianism/consequentialism: greatest good for the greatest number (public health, resource allocation) Virtue ethics: character of the agent Research ethics: individual participant welfare comes before society's benefit
questions.ep: If the question is about protecting a research participant, pick deontology; if it is about allocating scarce resources across a population, pick utilitarianism.

questions.stem: New drug for hypertension is being studied for it's efficacy, which of the following is the the highest evidence study?

why.A: A single RCT is the best primary study design for efficacy, but it ranks below a systematic review that pools several RCTs.
why.C: A cohort study is observational and prone to confounding; it ranks below RCTs.
why.D: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one time point and cannot establish causality; it ranks low.

questions.right: For questions about the efficacy of a treatment, the top of the evidence hierarchy is a systematic review (with meta-analysis) of randomized controlled trials , because it combines all good-quality RCTs and reduces random error and single-trial bias. A single RCT sits just below it.
questions.kc: Evidence hierarchy (therapy). Systematic review / meta-analysis of RCTs Randomized controlled trial Cohort study Case-control study Cross-sectional, case series, case report Expert opinion
questions.ep: If the options lack a systematic review, the single RCT becomes the answer.
